We therefore separated the decision into three dimensions: Truth / Verification, Urgency, and Actionability, instead of relying on one confidence score.

We also faced practical integration challenges while working with the Gonka Router, including model compatibility, response-format differences, output truncation, request timeouts, and temporary upstream 502 errors. We added strict schema validation, safer parsing, bounded timeouts, replay support, and transparent failure states without silently fabricating model results.

Another challenge was preventing AI recommendations from becoming unsafe actions. We solved this with deterministic safety gates and a mandatory Human Decision step. CrisisRoute AI records the decision and creates a tamper-evident local Proof Capsule, but never claims that a real-world action was executed.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
During a crisis, information spreads faster than it can be verified. A single message may contain a real emergency, incomplete location data, duplicated reports, or misleading information. Traditional AI chatbots can summarize these reports, but they do not provide a structured way to separate truth, urgency, and actionability before real-world action is taken.

CrisisRoute AI turns unverified crisis reports or public URLs into an evidence-backed verification workflow. It extracts claims, evaluates a Truth / Verification Score, Urgency, and Actionability, and sends the same evidence independently to two Gonka-hosted AI models for blind cross-verification.

Deterministic safety gates then check critical conditions such as medical risk, location, contact availability, resource availability, and model disagreement. High urgency does not automatically authorize dispatch — a human operator must review the case and record the final decision.

This allows crisis teams to respond quickly without confusing “urgent” with “safe to act.”

description.title: AI For Society
description.body:
CrisisRoute AI fits the AI for Society track by helping communities make safer decisions when crisis information is incomplete, unverified, or conflicting.

During emergencies such as haze, floods, fires, or medical incidents, a report may be urgent even before it can be fully verified. CrisisRoute AI separates Truth / Verification, Urgency, and Actionability, uses multiple Gonka-hosted AI models for independent cross-verification, and applies deterministic safety checks before any operational recommendation is considered.

The system deliberately keeps humans in control: AI assists, humans decide. High urgency never automatically means dispatch. This helps reduce both dangerous delays and unsafe actions caused by misinformation or missing information, creating a more accountable AI workflow for public safety and humanitarian response.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: One major challenge was saving trade expiration dates in our database using Prisma Next and Supabase, which caused serialization errors until we integrated Temporal Instant to handle date formats properly. Another challenge was making sure the AI reliably converted free-form chat messages into exact trade parameters, which we solved by setting up strict Gemini function calling with fallback extraction checks. Lastly, to prevent failed transactions and wasted gas on Base mainnet, we built pre-flight gas estimation dry runs before broadcasting any transaction.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Trading crypto options is usually too complicated for everyday users. People get confused by strike prices, expiration dates, Greeks, and complex order books, even if they just want to make a simple bet that ETH will go up or protect their portfolio from a drop. OptionsCopilot solves this with an AI chat assistant. Users can simply type what they want in plain English. The app translates their words into a real options trade with clear costs, maximum loss, and breakeven prices, allowing them to confirm and execute the trade on Base mainnet with one click.

description.title: AI × OPTIONS
description.body: OptionsCopilot directly combines artificial intelligence and options trading on Thetanuts Finance. The AI is not just a basic chatbot, it actively translates human market sentiment into real on-chain options orders on Base mainnet. By replacing complicated order books and strike selection with a simple conversational interface, our project makes Thetanuts options accessible to any everyday crypto trader.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Payroll, employee requests, statutory contributions and expense reimbursement are often handled across separate systems. This creates repetitive data entry, slow approvals, limited visibility and a dangerous gap between approving a payment and actually completing it.

Tali brings these workflows together. Employees can submit overtime, leave and receipt claims through one mobile-friendly application. Employers can review each request, understand its payroll impact, run payroll and monitor team earnings. Treasurers can manage expense limits, review exceptions and track reimbursements.

For payroll, Tali calculates employee pay together with EPF, SOCSO and EIS allocations. Approved overtime and unpaid leave are incorporated into the payable period before the final calculation. Salary and statutory payments are then executed atomically through a Sui Move contract. If any required contribution is below the mandate’s minimum, the entire transaction is rejected and no USDC moves.

For expenses, Gemini extracts structured information from receipts and timesheets, reducing manual entry. Deterministic policy checks evaluate limits, categories, dates, duplicate receipts and approved recipients. Uncertain claims are sent to a human reviewer instead of allowing AI to control funds.
Tali also supports salary streams, allowing employees to see earnings accrue over time and withdraw vested pay using their own wallet. Every confirmed payment or refusal can be independently verified through its Sui transaction.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Malaysian statutory payroll rules do not treat every payment component equally. EPF uses contribution schedules and excludes overtime from its wage basis, while SOCSO and EIS include overtime and apply wage ceilings. Unpaid leave must also reduce the wage before the statutory split is calculated. We separated each statutory calculation, encoded the correct calculation order and added extensive tests for wage bands, ceilings, overtime and leave adjustments.

Blockchain payment failures can be ambiguous. A network timeout does not necessarily mean that a transaction failed, and automatically retrying could create a duplicate payment. We solved this by deriving and storing the transaction digest before broadcasting, using atomic compare-and-set state transitions and reconciling the exact digest on demand. An uncertain payment is never automatically signed or submitted again.

Wallet connection alone was not secure enough for authentication. We implemented signed, single-use wallet challenges, one-hour HTTP-only sessions, exact-origin validation and account-switch invalidation. Receipt analyses are stored as private, short-lived drafts that can be consumed only once when creating a claim.

We also needed to make complex blockchain and payroll evidence understandable on mobile screens. Early versions contained dense calculations and long technical explanations. We redesigned the interface around clear outcomes, compact summaries and expandable evidence, allowing users to understand the result first while still giving judges access to policy checks, exchange-rate details and transaction proofs.

description.title: PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS
description.body: Tali directly addresses payroll, payouts and treasury management using USDC on Sui Testnet. Employers fund immutable payroll mandates, while separate expense mandates control reimbursements. Sui Move contracts enforce budgets, payment limits, approved recipients, expiry and statutory contribution floors. Payroll pays the employee, EPF, SOCSO and EIS atomically: either every payment succeeds together or the entire transaction is rejected. This demonstrates a real stablecoin workflow with working wallet authentication, payroll execution, expense reimbursement, salary streams and publicly verifiable transaction evidence.

description.title: AI × SUI
description.body: Tali combines AI-assisted document processing with on-chain payment execution. Gemini extracts structured information from receipt and timesheet images, reducing manual entry for employees. The extracted information is treated as untrusted input and passes through deterministic policy checks and human review where required. Once approved, a restricted backend agent can prepare payments, but Sui remains the final authority and enforces the mandate on-chain. This creates a practical AI-assisted workflow in which automation improves speed without giving the AI unrestricted control over money.

smartsplit-7c42.name: SmartSplit
smartsplit-7c42.tagline: Define the Rules. Let Sui Move the Money.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**Designing around Sui's wallet-controlled transaction model.** The frontend needs to calculate each recipient's share, split the payer's coin, construct the multi-transfer transaction, hand it off for wallet approval, and wait for on-chain indexing, all without SmartSplit ever holding custody of user funds at any step.

**Coordinating the real-world layer around the payment.** The on-chain transfer is only part of the problem. We also had to build friend and community management, payment requests, user profiles, SuiNS resolution, and a way to keep off-chain request status in sync with what's actually confirmed on-chain.

**Receipt handling.** We combined browser-based OCR with decentralized Walrus storage for receipt images, while making sure the detected amount is always shown to the user for verification or correction before they ever sign a transaction. Accuracy has to come before convenience here.

**Validation and rounding.** Equal and custom splits both needed clear validation to catch invalid or incomplete distributions before they reach the chain, along with correct rounding and dust handling, all while keeping the experience approachable for users who may have never used a crypto wallet before.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Splitting shared expenses is still mostly manual. One person pays the full bill, calculates everyone's share, tracks down wallet addresses, and chases each participant individually. The result is delayed payments, calculation errors, and no clear view of who's actually settled up.

**SmartSplit** turns this into a single coordinated, non-custodial payment workflow on Sui. Users connect their wallet, select friends or a saved community, resolve recipients by SuiNS name instead of raw addresses, attach a receipt, and choose an equal or custom split. One approved transaction then pays every recipient atomically. For cases where someone has already covered the full bill themselves, SmartSplit also supports payment requests, so the flow works whether the group is paying together upfront or reconciling after the fact.

description.title: PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS
description.body:
SmartSplit directly addresses how people send, receive, and coordinate money on Sui by turning Sui's programmable transaction model into a genuine one-to-many payment primitive: a single wallet-approved transaction pays every recipient at once, atomically. Either the entire group payment succeeds, or none of it does. That guarantee is the core of what makes this a real payments product rather than a UI wrapped around individual transfers.

The project also covers the receiving side, not just the sending side. Users can record who owes them, notify participants through the coordination layer, and let each recipient approve their own payment independently from their own wallet, closer to how real group payments actually unfold.

The current demo runs on Sui Testnet with SUI as the settlement asset, and the same workflow is built to support stablecoins as the transferred asset with no structural change, making SmartSplit applicable well beyond dinner bills: to group purchases, shared subscriptions, community pooled expenses, and everyday multi-party money movement.

winner-7eee.name: Truthline
winner-7eee.tagline: Don't trust one AI option - trust the disagreement

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Most AI fact-checkers rely on a single model's judgment and present it as the answer, even though any one model can be confidently wrong. Truthline solves this by cross-verifying every claim across three independent models running on GonkaRouter, and explicitly flagging when they disagree instead of quietly averaging that disagreement away. People can use it to check a claim they read online, paste a full article URL to have it automatically broken into individual factual claims and checked one by one, or verify claims in different languages — making it easier and safer to spot misinformation than trusting a single AI's opinion.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: The biggest hurdle was a chain of environment-configuration issues rather than logic bugs. Locally, Vercel's Python builder kept defaulting to an old Python 3.11 install even after we installed a newer version, which conflicted with a dependency requiring Python 3.12+ — fixed by clearing Vercel's build cache so it picked up the correct interpreter. We also hit a subtle bug where an environment variable name and its actual secret value got swapped in the code, causing a KeyError that looked like a missing-key problem but was actually a one-line logic mistake. On deployment, a folder named with capital letters (API instead of api) caused Vercel to silently 404 on our backend route, since routing requires an exact lowercase match. Each issue took careful log-reading (build logs vs. runtime logs vs. local terminal output) to isolate, since the same symptom (500/404 errors) had several unrelated root causes.

description.title: AI For Society
description.body:
Truthline is a multi-model fact-checking tool built specifically to run through GonkaRouter, as the track requires. Every claim — whether typed directly or pulled from a submitted URL — is sent to three independent models on GonkaRouter (Kimi, MiniMax, and DeepSeek), and their GonkaRouter Request IDs are displayed alongside each result as verifiable proof the reasoning actually ran through the network.
 
Beyond just calling the router, the project addresses a real public-value problem: single-model fact-checkers present one AI's opinion as if it were authoritative, hiding genuine uncertainty. Truthline instead cross-verifies every claim across models and explicitly flags disagreement when it happens, rather than quietly averaging it away. For longer content like news articles, it automatically breaks the piece into individual claims and scores each one separately, so users see exactly which specific statement is true or false — not one vague blended number for an entire article. It also supports multilingual claims and screens out content with nothing factual to check, directly reflecting the open-ended directions the track itself suggested (multilingual assistant, public-value AI tooling).

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**1. The network would quietly hand us the same model twice.**
DeepSeek-V4-Flash is sustainedly saturated on Gonka, and the router's default failover re-routes overflow to MiniMax. Without noticing, a share of our "DeepSeek" verifications would have been answered by MiniMax — turning two independent opinions into one opinion printed on two lines. Fix: every call sends `X-Gonka-No-Fallback: true`, so saturation returns a real 429 instead of a substitute; we compare requested vs actual model on every response; and a 429 is treated as "this leg produced no opinion" — the report degrades to *insufficient* with a "Not cross-verified" badge and confidence capped at 60, never presented as consensus. (`gonka_client.py`, `test_deepseek_429_and_minimax_ok_degrades_honestly`)

**2. Two models disagree — and averaging is a lie.**
`(90 + 10) / 2 = 50` reports a scam one model confidently caught as "medium risk". We replaced averaging with consensus bands: within 20 points they agree; 21–40 drops confidence and reports a lean; beyond 40 we refuse to average contradictory answers and say *insufficient*. Fraud risk is taken as the **maximum**, never averaged down. And an evidence gate caps confidence when no sources were found — with one deliberate exception: phishing has no web evidence by nature, so `high_risk` is read off the message's own structure. (`consensus.py`, 27 tests)

**3. The models can't browse, and can't see images.**
Gonka serves text-in/text-out models: asked to "inspect this URL" they correctly answer "I cannot access this URL", and image input isn't supported. Retrieval moved entirely to our side — `evidence.py` fetches the URL and runs a keyless web search, SSRF-guarded (private, loopback and cloud-metadata hosts blocked, redirects re-validated) — and the models reason over fenced evidence. For screenshots, local Tesseract extracts text only, the user corrects it, and only then does anything go to Gonka. We confirmed this boundary with Gonka's tech lead before building on it.

**4. Real model output is nothing like the schema.**
Reasoning models wrap JSON in ```` ```json ```` fences and `<think>` blocks, improvise labels ("TRUE", "high risk"), and sometimes score 0–1 instead of 0–100. `json_utils.py` extracts tolerantly and the verifier normalises labels and scales — but genuinely unparseable output is still rejected rather than invented (`test_unparseable_output_raises_rather_than_inventing`). One sloppy label never costs us a whole second opinion.

**5. Screenshot mode "worked" while doing nothing.**
On any machine without Tesseract, `pytesseract` raised, the exception was swallowed, and users saw "no text could be extracted" — a claim about their image when the truth was a missing engine. Two more faults hid behind it: Tesseract 5 silently drops a missing language from `eng+chi_sim` and exits 0, so Chinese failed quietly; and pytesseract doesn't strip quotes from config on Windows, so a quoted `--tessdata-dir` reached the binary with the quotes still in the path. Fix: ask Tesseract which packs exist up front, export `TESSDATA_PREFIX`, raise a distinct engine-missing error, and return an honest "OCR engine is not installed" with an editable box. Render's native Python runtime has no Tesseract at all, so the backend now ships as a Docker image. (`ocr.py`, `test_ocr.py`, `backend/Dockerfile`)

**6. Decentralised inference has a long tail.**
The same model answers in under a second or in 40, depending on which node picks up the request. Both verifications run concurrently, each bounded at 45 s with one retry, the UI shows honest stages instead of a spinner, and the frontend's OCR timeout went from 30 s to 90 s after we found a sleeping free-tier backend takes ~30 s just to wake — aborting uploads before the server had read them.

**7. One sentence that over-claimed.**
We described receipts as proof a verdict "came from the network rather than our server". Gonka's tech lead pointed out the receipt is served from GonkaRouter's database, so it's their attestation, not an independent one. We rewrote the claim everywhere it appears — UI, README, docs — to what's defensible: *independently verifiable against GonkaRouter, not something we could fabricate on our own server*, and it does not prove the claim is true.

**8. Accessibility across two scripts.**
Our risk icons were text glyphs (✓ ⚠ ✕). With a Chinese font active the browser substitutes full-width or emoji variants, so the same warning rendered at a different size in EN and ZH. We replaced them with an original inline-SVG icon set, kept the rule that no state is ever colour alone, and never merged the Truth Score with the scam-risk score — a plausible message can still be a scam.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
*A scam text lands on a parent's phone. They read Chinese. The person best placed to warn them: their adult child — reads English.* So the message gets forwarded around the family group, and nobody is sure. The tools that could settle it speak one of those languages, and answer with a confident paragraph you're meant to take on faith.

*Anxin (安心, "peace of mind")* takes a forwarded message, a link, or a screenshot and returns, in English and Simplified Chinese:

- a *Truth Score* (0–100): how strongly evidence supports the claim
- a *separate scam-risk score*:  a plausible message can still be a scam, so the two are never merged
- *three plain-language warning signs* and *what to do next*: never "call the number in the message"
- *the Gonka Request ID and public receipt* behind every model call

*How it earns trust:* two independent models (DeepSeek and MiniMax) on the Gonka network, called concurrently on identical evidence, neither shown the other's answer, pinned with X-Gonka-No-Fallback. Disagreement is shown, not averaged: within 20 points they agree, 21–40 drops confidence, beyond 40 we say insufficient. If no sources were found, confidence is capped. A precise score resting on nothing is the most misleading thing we could display.

*What it holds back:* no account, nothing stored; phone and account numbers masked before any model sees them; screenshots read by local OCR only, with the text shown for correction first; every warning is colour plus an icon plus words, in large type — for readers who are older, colour-blind, or on a bad screen.

*Live:* https://anxin-protect.com. And if what got forwarded is a meme, not a scam, it explains the joke in both languages, and says plainly that explaining isn't verifying.

Anxin is not a truth oracle. It is a transparent pause button for bilingual families.

Check our demo: [youtu.be/xfWZiAKybs8](https://youtu.be/xfWZiAKybs8)

description.title: AI For Society
description.body:
# Anxin (安心) 

## Gonka Router track

Anxin's entire reasoning and verification pipeline runs exclusively on Gonka Router. Every model call passes through a single module, `backend/app/gonka_client.py` — nothing else in the app is permitted to call a model, and no other provider exists at runtime.

Two independently pinned models, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiniMax-M2.7, are called concurrently on identical evidence, neither seeing the other's answer. Every call sets `X-Gonka-No-Fallback: true`, so a saturated router returns an honest 429 instead of silently serving the same model twice.

Disagreement is handled, not smoothed over: verdicts within 20 points are treated as agreement; a gap of 21–40 lowers confidence; beyond 40, the consensus layer refuses to average and reports the claim as unresolved rather than dressing up a single-model answer as consensus. Scam/fraud risk escalates on disagreement rather than averaging down, and confidence is capped whenever no supporting evidence was found.

Every response's Request ID, devshard, and requested-vs-actual model are captured and shown in the report, each linking to Gonka Router's public receipt — so a user, or a judge, can independently confirm results came from the live decentralized network, not a mock.

---
## AI For Society track

Anxin (安心, "peace of mind") is a bilingual English/Chinese scam and misinformation checker — the kind of "AI fact checker" the brief names as its preferred example — built for the audience misinformation actually reaches: older adults who read Chinese, and the English-reading children who try to warn them.

Users can paste text, a link, or a screenshot. Claims are extracted (via local OCR when needed, then made editable) and typed as factual, opinion, or unverifiable. Anxin's own server fetches the URL and searches the web (SSRF-guarded) so verification runs against real-time evidence, not a model's memory. Each claim gets a Truth Score (0–100) and a separate scam-risk score, with each model's reasoning shown in both English and Chinese alongside plain-language warning signs — so the explanation is legible to the people who need it most, not just to a technical reader.

User-submitted content is always fenced as untrusted data, and both models' raw verdicts are shown side by side so the reader judges any disagreement themselves, rather than Anxin silently resolving it for them.

**Submission:** live at [anxin-protect.com](https://anxin-protect.com) · documented repo with a dedicated Gonka-integration section and 165 offline tests · live fact-check demo: [youtu.be/xfWZiAKybs8](https://youtu.be/xfWZiAKybs8)

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
- **Multi-model reliability:** Running 3 AI models in parallel (DeepSeek, Kimi-K2.6, MiniMax-M2.7) surfaced real-world messiness — one model wrapped its JSON output in `<think>` reasoning tags that broke our parser, and models occasionally timed out inconsistently. We fixed the parsing bug, added retry logic, and measured real reliability (9/10 test runs achieved full 3-model consensus) before trusting the pipeline.
- **Two disconnected fact-extraction systems:** Our conversation-tracking logic and our AI-prompt signal extraction were built as two separate regex-based systems with different field names. This caused a real bug — the risk breakdown panel would show "insufficient information" even when a message clearly had salary and contact details, and facts could leak between unrelated conversations in the same session. We traced this to the root cause and unified both into a single shared extraction path.
- **OCR text doesn't look like normal sentences:** Job flyers and screenshots produce fragmented, bullet-style text very different from a typed message, which broke our narrative-focused signal extraction. We fixed this by falling back to the AI model's own extracted evidence when regex patterns come up empty, instead of only trusting rigid pattern matching.
- **Making "not enough information" feel human, not robotic:** Early versions surfaced raw debug-style text like "Model disagreement detected" directly in the chat when a message was too vague to score. We're actively refining this so the assistant asks a natural clarifying question instead of exposing internal model-consensus mechanics to the user.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
- Job scams and fake recruiter messages are widespread and often hard to spot in the moment — a vague "amazing opportunity" DM, a too-good-to-be-true salary, or a recruiter pushing you to WhatsApp/Telegram and asking for a "registration deposit."
- **JobGuard lets anyone paste a message or upload a screenshot of a job offer/recruiter DM and get an instant, evidence-based risk assessment** — not a single AI's guess, but a consensus from 3 independent models cross-checking the same message.
- If the message doesn't have enough detail to judge confidently, JobGuard asks a natural follow-up question (company name, role, pay) instead of guessing — the same way a savvy friend would probe before giving you an opinion.
- Each result comes with a category-by-category breakdown (company legitimacy, compensation realism, urgency tactics, contact method, payment requests) with real reasoning per category, not just a single opaque number.
- Built for anyone actively job hunting — students, international students unfamiliar with local hiring norms, and early-career applicants who are the most common targets of these scams.

description.title: AI For Society
description.body:
JobGuard is built around the Gonka Track's core requirement: **all AI reasoning and verification runs through Gonka Router**, using multi-model cross-verification rather than a single model's opinion.

- **Multi-model cross-verification:** every check is sent to 3 independent models via Gonka Router (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Kimi-K2.6, MiniMax-M2.7) in parallel. Results are combined into a weighted consensus, and disagreement between models is surfaced transparently rather than hidden — if models disagree, the user sees that, and confidence is adjusted accordingly.
- **Genuine public value, not a novelty demo:** job and recruitment scams are a real, common problem — especially for students and early-career job seekers who are frequent targets. JobGuard gives anyone a fast, evidence-based second opinion before they act on a suspicious offer.
- **Reasoning trace, not just a score:** each result breaks down risk by category (company legitimacy, compensation realism, urgency tactics, contact method, payment requests) with model-generated reasoning per category — matching the track's emphasis on transparent, explainable verification over a black-box number.
- **Gonka Request IDs are surfaced** in the result output, so every assessment is traceable back to the actual model calls that produced it — not a hardcoded or simulated result.

kyros-system-d556.name: Kyros System
kyros-system-d556.tagline: Protect your payment budget. Pay with certainty.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The hardest challenge was making a cross-chain flow feel simple without pretending
  that complex actions had already happened.

  We separated Base-side protection from Sui-side payouts and made every status
  explicit. Kyros never labels protection as active until a wallet confirms the final
  Thetanuts order.

  Wallet handling was another hurdle. Multiple browser wallets could be detected, and
  automatic selection created confusion. We replaced this with an explicit Sui Testnet
  wallet selector in the navigation, then display the connected wallet’s shortened
  address after connection.

  We also encountered testnet token visibility differences between wallet interfaces
  and blockchain explorers. Instead of assuming a displayed wallet balance was
  available everywhere, we built the payout flow around the connected wallet’s on-
  chain account and clear testnet-only messaging.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Kyros helps crypto-native teams protect upcoming contractor and supplier payment
  budgets from treasury volatility.

  A small Web3 agency may hold ETH or BTC, but still need to pay $10,000 in USDC over
  the next month. If the treasury asset falls before payday, the team may need to sell
  more crypto than expected, delay payments, or reduce runway.

  Kyros turns this into a clear operational flow:

  - Keep the status pending until the treasury wallet approves the final protection
    order.

  - Prepare recipient USDC payouts through Sui.

  Kyros is not designed as a trading dashboard. It makes options understandable as
  payment certainty: “Can we still pay our team if crypto drops?”

  Its target customers are small crypto-native agencies, DAO operations teams, and
  protocol teams with recurring contractor payments and volatile crypto treasuries.

description.title: PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS
description.body:
Kyros fits the Sui Payments & Stablecoins track by making stablecoin payouts easier for crypto-native teams with volatile treasuries.

Teams create a payment plan for upcoming contractor and supplier payments, then prepare recipient payouts in USDC on Sui. Our prototype includes an explicit Sui Testnet wallet-selection flow, shows the connected Sui address, and prepares a user-approved test USDC transfer. The wallet, not Kyros, controls transaction signing and keys.

Sui is the recipient-facing payment rail because it can support a simpler onboarding experience than traditional crypto payment flows. Our product direction can use zkLogin for recipients who do not want to manage seed phrases, while sponsored transactions can remove the need for recipients to hold SUI purely for gas.

Kyros combines this friction-reduced USDC payout experience with payment-budget protection planning, helping teams keep contractor payments clear, scheduled, and understandable.

description.title: BEST PRODUCT BUILT ON THE THETANUTS SDK
description.body:
Kyros uses the **Thetanuts SDK** as the Base-side market and protection layer for upcoming payment budgets.

A crypto-native team can create a $10K, $20K, or custom payment plan for contractor and supplier payouts. Kyros uses `@thetanuts-finance/thetanuts-client` to retrieve live ETH/BTC market context and active Thetanuts orders on Base, then presents protection choices in plain business language: full or partial payment-budget coverage.

Instead of presenting options as speculation, Kyros frames them as operational risk management: “Can we still pay our team if ETH falls before the due date?”

The prototype keeps the trade flow honest. Protection estimates are clearly marked as indicative, and Kyros does not claim that a trade is active until the treasury wallet reviews and confirms the final Thetanuts order, premium, and approval on Base.

This creates a product layer on top of Thetanuts infrastructure for a new customer segment: small Web3 agencies, DAO operations teams, and protocol teams with recurring USDC payment obligations and volatile ETH or BTC treasuries.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
NUTSCOPE makes crypto options easier to understand and safer to explore, especially for beginners. Instead of searching through complicated options data, users can discover live Thetanuts opportunities, understand the risks and potential payoff, and practise trades using virtual funds.

It provides a simple journey from discovering an option → analyzing it → practising with paper trading → making a real trade when ready.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of our main challenges was working with live Thetanuts data, as RPC/API availability could sometimes cause orders or market data to fail to load. We handled this by improving error handling, adding timeouts and fallbacks, and making sure the app does not replace unavailable live data with fake data.

Another challenge was making sure the options calculations were accurate, especially for break-even, maximum loss, payoff scenarios, and multi-leg strategies. We verified the formulas with test cases and reused the same calculation logic across the application.

We also faced challenges with wallet connection and real trade execution. To make trading safer, we added pre-flight checks for the wallet network, order availability, expiry, amount, and trade preview before allowing execution.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: All three GonkaRouter judge models are Chinese-lineage, GonkaRouter doesn't currently offer a non-Chinese-lineage alternative, which weakens the "independent judges" framing somewhat. We just use google translate to translate the chinese and try to understand. Other than that, one of the AI agents were supposed to perform bad, but Verity showed that they are working well instead. description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Verity tests candidate AI agents (payment/DeFi agents, in this demo) for safety and reliability, then issues a certification that's independently verifiable — not just a number your server asserts. It was built for MUBA Hacks 2026 (Sui Track — AI × Sui) and the Gonka "AI for Society" challenge.

Three pillars:

Gonka — every scenario is judged in parallel by three different models. Cross-model agreement becomes a trust signal on its own: high agreement = high confidence, low agreement = flag for review.
Sui — every test result is written as its own on-chain object the moment it completes (not batched at the end), so certification progress is visible live and can't be altered after the fact.
Multilingual testing — every scenario runs in English, Chinese, and Japanese. Score variance across languages becomes a "multilingual stability" metric — it catches agents that only fake-support non-English users via a thin translation layer.
A fourth layer, Walrus, stores the full per-model reasoning trace behind every score, so "trust us" isn't the only option — the actual judge reasoning is independently fetchable.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Technical Challenges Faced
1. Gonka Router API Integration — Implementing API authentication, request formatting, and communication with the Gonka inference gateway.
2. AI Model Reliability — Handling model failures such as HTTP 524 errors, malformed JSON, missing response content, and max_tokens termination.
3. Multi-Model Consensus — Designing a system that sends the same claim to multiple AI models and reliably handles agreement, disagreement, and failed models.
4. Truth Score Algorithm — Designing and implementing a scoring system that combines model confidence, consensus, evidence coverage, and reliability into a 0–100 score.
5. Evidence Retrieval & Ranking — Retrieving relevant evidence from external sources, filtering unusable results, and ranking the strongest evidence before sending it to the AI models.
6. Claim Extraction — Automatically extracting the core factual claim from articles and user-submitted content before verification.
7. Multi-Platform Data Integration — Handling different data structures and APIs from Reddit, X/Twitter, YouTube, Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, and web search, then normalizing them into a common format.
8. URL Content Extraction — Building platform-specific URL detection and content extraction, including dealing with Reddit's post structure and identifiers.
9. Backend–Data Service Communication — Connecting the Express backend to the separate Data service and validating responses between the two services.
10. Production Deployment Constraints — OpenCLI and browser-based integrations worked locally but some failed on Render because the required Browser Bridge/Chrome environment was unavailable.
11. Performance & Concurrency — Managing the high latency of retrieving evidence and running multiple AI models while preventing too many operations from running simultaneously.
12. Error Handling & Validation — Building safeguards throughout the pipeline to prevent invalid input, bad API responses, missing evidence, failed models, and malformed verification results from breaking the system.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
🎯 **Problem**
Information is fragmented across news websites, social media platforms and other online sources. Users need to switch between platforms, repeat searches, and compare conflicting claims to understand what is happening. This fragmentation creates several challenges:

1. Information overload: Too much content competes for attention.
2. Information gaps: Important developments may reach some people earlier than others.
3. Missed updates: Relevant information can disappear inside fast-moving feeds.
4. Misinformation: It is difficult to distinguish verified facts from rumors, opinions, or manipulated content.
5. Fear of missing out (FOMO): Users feel pressure to monitor multiple platforms continuously.
6. Time-consuming verification: Checking sources, dates, context, and competing claims requires significant effort.
7. Algorithmic filter bubbles: Platform feeds may prioritize engagement rather than relevance, accuracy, or completeness.

💡 **Solution**
InfoSauce is an AI-powered personal information radar that brings discovery, monitoring, summarization, analysis, and verification into one intelligent hub. It can gather relevant information from multiple sources, remove duplicates, highlight meaningful updates, and present the results in a clear and organized format. Instead of searching across numerous platforms, users can use InfoSauce to:

1. Discover the latest information in one place.
2. Track topics continuously and receive relevant updates.
3. Generate concise summaries of lengthy content.
4. Compare how different sources report the same event.
5. Trace important claims back to their original sources.
6. Identify conflicting information and missing context.
7. Reduce noise while avoiding important missed updates.

**🤖 Gonka Router**
InfoSauce uses Gonka Router as its AI-powered verification layer, sending extracted claims together with ranked evidence to multiple Gonka-hosted AI models for independent fact-checking. Their results are then compared through a multi-model consensus system, where disagreements are treated as uncertain, before InfoSauce calculates a Truth Score from 0–100 using model confidence, consensus, evidence coverage, and reliability. The system also returns the models' reasoning, supporting evidence, and Gonka Request IDs to provide a transparent and traceable verification process.

By combining multiple AI models, relevant external evidence, consensus-based verification, and confidence-aware scoring, InfoSauce aims to produce a more reliable and robust fact-checking result than relying on a single AI model alone.

description.title: AI For Society
description.body:
InfoSauce fits the **AI for Society** challenge by using Gonka Router's decentralized AI inference to help people identify misinformation and make more informed decisions online. Our system extracts claims from news and social media content, retrieves relevant evidence, and cross-verifies each claim using multiple Gonka-hosted AI models before generating a transparent Truth Score, reasoning, evidence, and Request IDs. By combining multi-model consensus with evidence-based verification, InfoSauce helps users distinguish trustworthy information from potentially misleading content, reducing the risk of misinformation spreading and contributing to a more informed and digitally resilient society.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
### zkLogin: "Groth16 proof verify failed" at the final on-chain step

Our zkLogin flow completes every off-chain step correctly — Google OAuth, nonce binding, server-side JWT verification, deterministic salt derivation, and the Mysten prover call all succeed — but the assembled zkLogin signature is rejected on-chain with `Groth16 proof verify failed` when it reaches a validator. We ruled out ephemeral-key staleness (it reproduced on a completely fresh login), re-checked the address-seed and `maxEpoch`assembly against the Sui docs line by line, and confirmed the prover response shape was correct — but couldn't isolate the root cause within the hackathon window.

Rather than fake it, we kept the full zkLogin implementation in the codebase and demo the **identical downstream flow** (sponsored transaction → `claim_and_link` → payout) using a standard `Ed25519Keypair` signer, which shares the exact same `Signer` abstraction. The zkLogin design and its entire off-chain half are real and working; only the final proof verification is unresolved, and we document that openly rather than leaving it hidden.

### Sui SDK v2 and the sponsored-transaction dual-signature flow

The `@mysten/sui` v2 SDK replaced `SuiClient` with `SuiGrpcClient` and changed many method shapes, so our early integration code matched no tutorial. The sharpest single bug: role resolution ("which capability objects does this address own?") silently returned nothing because the gRPC `listOwnedObjects` type filter needs a **fully-qualified datatype** (`0xPKG::relief_v3::RegistrarCap`), not the `0xPKG::relief_v3` prefix the older API accepted.

Sponsored (gasless) transactions also took real iteration: the sponsor and the user must sign the **exact same transaction bytes**, the sponsor's coin must be pinned as gas payment before the transaction is built, and both signatures are submitted together. We settled on a clean three-step split — server builds + pre-signs as sponsor → browser signs the same bytes with the user's key → server executes with both signatures — which is now the single path every end-user action flows through.

### Making multi-model AI consensus survive real model failures

Two things broke the first working version of our 3-model zone-credibility check:

- **`MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.7` is a reasoning model** that emits a `<think>…</think>` preamble before its JSON answer. Our 400-token budget was consumed entirely by that preamble, so the route failed with `No JSON found in model output`. Raising the budget to 1200 tokens fixed it.
- **`moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6` is listed by GonkaRouter's `/models` endpoint but rejected by `/chat/completions`** with `unsupported model`. Because we'd built the consensus call on `Promise.allSettled` with a persisted row per model (including failures), this upstream inconsistency degraded gracefully to a clean "2 of 3 models responded" instead of taking down the whole check. The partial-failure handling we designed for turned out to be load-bearing in practice, not just theory.

### Supabase mirror drifting out of sync after a rejected registration

Our database is a rebuildable read-mirror of chain state, kept current by an event indexer. A verifier rejecting a registration and the household re-registering is a valid flow (the contract releases the household-ID lock on rejection), but it creates a second on-chain object with the same `household_id`. Our mirror had a naive `UNIQUE(household_id)` index, so the indexer's upsert of the new row failed silently (logged, not surfaced), the new reference code was never mirrored, and lookups 404'd. We replaced it with a **partial** unique index (`WHERE status <> 2`, i.e. not-Rejected) that mirrors the contract's own semantics exactly.

### Server-side evidence extraction drowning in page chrome

For the credibility checker, a URL's page text is fetched and stripped to plain text
server-side (no headless browser). Testing against a real Wikipedia article showed the first ~2,600 characters of "extracted text" were navigation, sidebar, and table-of-contents markup — which would have consumed our 6,000-char cap before reaching any real content. We added block-level stripping of `<nav>` / `<header>` / `<footer>` / `<aside>` / `<table>` before the generic tag strip. We also tried a regex to remove specific `<div id="toc">` wrappers and deliberately removed it — regex can't balance nested tags, so it was a correctness risk pretending to be a fix.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Malaysia experiences severe, recurring monsoon flooding nearly every year. When it happens, financial aid needs to move from donors and government budgets to affected households — and today, that process is slow and opaque in ways that are well understood but not well solved:

- **Bureaucratic delay across multiple layers.** Aid moves through several administrative layers before it reaches a household, and each layer adds processing time — real households can wait weeks for funds they need immediately.
- **A gap between PPS and non-PPS victims.** People sheltering in official evacuation centres (Pusat Pemindahan Sementara) are generally easier to register and track. People who don't evacuate to a PPS — staying with relatives, in a partially damaged home, or elsewhere — often fall into a slower, less-defined process.
- **Opacity in fund flow.** Donors and the public generally cannot see, in any verifiable way, that a specific donation actually reached a specific affected household. Trust is asked for, not demonstrated.
- **Duplicate and "ghost" claims.** Without a hard, systemic guarantee that one household can only be paid once, duplicate or fraudulent claims are a structural risk, not just a hypothetical one.
- **Connectivity loss.** The disasters this system is meant to help with often damage the same telecom infrastructure people would need to access a digital wallet or app — a real design constraint, not an edge case.
- **Digital literacy and accessibility.** Elderly and digitally illiterate residents — a real and significant share of affected populations — struggle with typical crypto wallet UX (seed phrases, gas fees, unfamiliar apps).
- **No independent check that a declared disaster zone is real.** Publishing the fund flow on-chain proves money moved correctly *once a zone exists* — but a donor still has to take the relief authority's word for it that a given "disaster zone" corresponds to a real, ongoing event. A convincingly-named fake zone, or a real zone whose severity is inflated, is a scam vector transparency of *fund flow* alone doesn't close.

description.title: PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS
description.body:
- **Real workflow:** donor → transparent on-chain treasury → verified household payout — a genuine treasury + escrow + disbursement pattern (the track names "treasury", "escrow", "payroll" as target ideas).
- **Fast, intuitive UX:** zkLogin login, no wallet install, no gas — a flood-affected household claims aid with a Google account and a printed reference code.
- **Effective Sui use:** sponsored transactions and zkLogin are load-bearing — they directly remove the wallet/gas/literacy barrier that is the core problem — and Programmable Transaction Blocks bundle multi-step actions atomically.
- **Working live demo:** yes (household claim path demoed with the dev-key signer).

**Caveat:** the demo treasury holds **testnet SUI as a documented stand-in for a stablecoin**, not USDC/USDsui. The contract is written generically over `Coin<T>` /
`ReliefTreasury<T>`, so switching to a real stablecoin type is a configuration change, not a rewrite — but at demo time it is SUI. If the track requires an actual stablecoin token in
the demo, treat this as a partial fit.

description.title: AI × SUI
description.body:
Sui is the spine of the product, not an add-on:

Identity: zkLogin turns a Google login into the household's own Sui address — the login is the wallet.
Payments: a shared on-chain treasury funds fixed-tier payouts; sponsored transactions mean no user ever holds SUI.
On-chain execution: the Move contract enforces one-household-one-payout, per-zone budget caps, and "only the household's own login can set its payout address" — as code, not policy.
AI's role: GonkaRouter assists the humans who operate the system — triaging ambiguous registrations, drafting bulk registrations, and running the multi-model zone credibility check. It advises; a human always makes the funds-moving decision.

description.title: AI For Society
description.body:
We meet every mandatory requirement and most of the preferred "fact checker" criteria.

| Requirement | How MySteadyAid meets it |
|---|---|
| **Mandatory — all AI reasoning via gonkarouter.io** | Every AI call (verifier triage, bulk-registration drafting, and the zone credibility checker) runs server-side through GonkaRouter exclusively. No other inference provider anywhere. |
| Input a URL or text | The zone credibility checker takes either a source URL (fetched + extracted to plain text server-side) or pasted text. |
| Multi-model cross-verification (≥2 models encouraged) | **3 models run in parallel** on every credibility check. |
| Truth Score (0–100%) + reasoning trace | A 0–100 Evidence Credibility Score plus a per-model reasoning summary that is *required* to cite the specific evidence phrase it relied on. |
| Consensus logic for disagreement ("a major plus") | Deterministic, non-AI resolution: when models disagree, the **most cautious label wins** (any `inconsistent` outranks any `well-supported`), and the UI states plainly that the models differed. |
| Display Gonka Request IDs ("on-chain proof") | Every per-model result — successes **and** failures — is persisted and displayed with its own Gonka Request ID, on both the admin console and the public dashboard. |
| Neutrality prompt | Each model is instructed to judge only from the provided text, to treat missing evidence as `insufficient-evidence` (explicitly *not* an accusation of fraud), and to cite concrete facts. |

**On "on-chain Truth Score":** our score lives in Supabase, not on Sui. The track's concrete stated requirement — *display the Gonka Request ID to prove the result wasn't generated by a centralized server* — is met. Writing the score as a Move event is a documented, deferred enhancement (it moves no funds, and the Request-ID trail already makes every verdict auditable).

**On scope:** GonkaRouter's models have no internet access, so we don't claim autonomous fact-checking. We built an honest **evidence credibility review** — the app supplies the evidence text, the models judge whether it specifically and consistently supports the zone's claims. That is a narrower, defensible claim that plays directly to the track's "fully traceable reasoning trail" ask: a judge can read the exact text every model saw.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
# RICE — Reliable Insurance Claim Engine

*Insured, verified, paid — without the wait.*

## Inspiration

Medical insurance claims move through hospitals, insurers, third-party administrators, and payment institutions that each keep their own records of the same claim — leading to slow reconciliation, disputes over what was actually approved, and patients left waiting without a clear, shared source of truth. For someone waiting on a claim decision, that delay isn't just an inconvenience — it can be the deciding factor in whether they get life-saving treatment when they need it.

## What it does

RICE is a shared coordination layer for medical insurance claims. Every institution — hospital, TPA, insurer — works off the same claim lifecycle instead of reconciling separate records after the fact:

1. **AI verification for medical insurance claims**, via the Gonka Router — a plausibility check that produces a Truth Score, a reasoning trace, and a traceable request ID, shown transparently at every point a decision is made.
2. **Automated approval and payment for validated claims**, via smart contracts on Sui — claims that clear both the policy's coverage rules and the AI trust threshold settle automatically, with gas sponsored so no party needs to hold SUI to participate.
3. **Auditing for claim status, verification, and reasoning on Sui's blockchain network** — immutable, distributed-ledger records of the claim lifecycle that every participating institution can independently verify, without needing to trust any single party's internal database.

description.title: Challenges we ran into

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
- Mobile Compatibility: Initially we targeted full web-hosted development but hit compatibility issues with mobile devices such as Android and iOS environments. Attempting to run as web-app on Android or iOS causes it to crash. To solve this, we pivoted to building and bundling actual APK binaries using Expo Application Services (EAS Build), ensuring native execution directly on target devices rather than relying on a wrapper.

- Google OAuth Redirect: Initializing Google Sign-In to implement SUI zklogin caused URI mismatch errors the moment we moved away from localhost. we resolved this by explicitly configuring authorized origins and callbacks URIs in the Google Cloud Console for both our production web domain and backend endpoints

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Foreign workers and international students in Malaysia routinely send part of their earnings home, or receive support money from family abroad: "every month I need to send Mum 150 USDC", "this month send an extra 30 for school fees". This recurring task is harder than it should be:

- It is expensive and slow. The global average remittance cost is around 6.4% of the amount sent; banks specifically average closer to 15%. Cross-border rails are also slow to settle.

- It is easy to lose track of. Repeated transfers to several recipients, changing amounts, and one-off payments (fees, emergencies) pile up with no single view.

- It is a prime target for scams. "Urgent family emergency, send money now" social engineering preys specifically on people who send money to relatives. A person mid-transfer is exactly the wrong moment to be unprotected.

Existing apps solve the sending but not the judgement - nothing sits between "I got a worrying message" and "the money is gone".

description.title: PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS
description.body: RemitGuard AI is a cross-border family-remittance app: foreign workers and students in Malaysia use it to send and receive support money as USDC on Sui. It covers the full money-movement workflow the track asks for sending (a plain-language instruction or a manual entry becomes a reviewed transaction), receiving (incoming transfers are detected directly on-chain and shown in history, even when sent from an outside wallet), managing (recipient book, sent/received history, spending breakdown, budget planner), and automating (recurring rules with a duplicate-payment reconciliation check). It leans on the exact Sui features listed: zkLogin gives every user a self-custodial wallet from a Google sign-in with no seed phrase, every transfer is a Programmable Transaction Block built by the backend, and sponsored transactions mean the user never pays gas. The UX is a chat: you say "send Mum 150 USDC for school fees" and confirm. The whole thing runs live on web and a native Android build from one codebase. The AI scam-check layer is what makes it real-world-ready rather than just another payments demo: remittance is one of the most scammed transaction types, and RemitGuard is the only step that sits between "I got a worrying message" and "the money is gone."

description.title: AI × SUI
description.body: RemitGuard is a transaction-execution assistant. You describe a payment in natural language; two AI models parse and cross-check it; deterministic code resolves the recipient, runs the risk checks, and builds the plan; and only after you confirm does Sui execute it. Sui is integral, not an add-on, for three concrete reasons. First, no bank API lets third-party software let alone an AI agent construct and submit a payment on a user's behalf without a licensed fintech partnership; on Sui that is a PTB the backend builds directly, so the agent can genuinely act. Second, the architecture is enforced on-chain: the AI never signs anything, and the server-side confirmation token is cryptographically bound to a hash of the exact transaction bytes, so a model response alone can never move money. Third, every transfer and every fact-check verdict is independently verifiable on a public Sui explorer, so a parent or auditor doesn't have to trust our backend's word. It uses zkLogin for identity, USDC PTBs for payments, sponsored transactions for gas, and a Move package for the on-chain verification record. The AI solves a real problem, remittance friction and scam exposure. The demo is live on two platforms.

description.title: AI For Society
description.body: RemitGuard contains a full AI Fact Checker that meets the preferred spec point for point, and it is the mandatory kind of integration: every piece of AI reasoning in the product runs through Gonka Router and nothing else, via a single client. You can paste any claim, headline, tweet, or URL text into the standalone checker and get multi-model cross-verification. Two different Gonka models (DeepSeek V4 Flash and MiniMax M2.7) each read the same evidence and give an independent stance A Truth Score from 0 to 100, a full reasoning trace showing each model's rationale and the article it cited, and the Gonka Request ID for every inference call displayed in the UI as proof the reasoning ran on the network and was not fabricated by our server. Crucially, the models never answer from memory: the checker first retrieves real news through NewsAPI, and if there is no coverage the verdict is "unverifiable". It never guesses. A deterministic combiner, not another model, turns the two stances into the verdict, and disagreement is surfaced rather than averaged. Each verdict is also recorded as a hash-only event on Sui for an auditable public trail. The genuine public value is the deployment context: this checker fires at the exact moment a false "family emergency" claim would otherwise cost someone their savings.

husk-c03e.name: Husk
husk-c03e.tagline: Hi I am Husk 👋 Click to see more 👀

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**1. RFQ gas limit vs public RPC**

`requestForQuotation` estimates ~**140M gas**, but MetaMask’s default **Infura** RPC rejects anything above **25M** per tx (`exceeds maximum per-tx gas limit: 140000000 > 25000000`). Approve succeeded; RFQ failed until we switched Base RPC to **Alchemy / `mainnet.base.org`** and documented this in the README.

→ [Approve tx](https://basescan.org/tx/0xe341ebfcd2911bfdf36c7da50d53ffc628b61fa5118328a8f7be003b7aa13f49) · [RFQ tx (after fix)](https://basescan.org/tx/0x8fe7b1f864c24e3d2f9e2713a22258a0dba8a70ecb8e914b948d60d09ebab16e)

**2. Event-aligned expiry — Book vs RFQ**

OptionBook orders use standard expiries; macro coverage needs expiry at the **next Chainlink TWAP after the print**. We built a router: try Book match first, fall back to Factory RFQ with `buildSpreadRFQ` + encrypted ECDH keys in Supabase.

**3. LLM safety — numbers must not be invented**

LangGraph agent parses intent only; all strikes, premiums, and payouts come from `@thetanuts-finance/thetanuts-client` (`previewFillOrder`, `calculatePayout`). Guardrails refuse calls, leverage, and “max profit” requests. Ask Husk shows a human summary + sign CTA, not raw calldata in chat.

**4. SDK r12 settlement surface**

Thetanuts SDK 0.3 removed user-callable `payout()`; settlement is factory-driven. Our keeper **observes** `isExpired` / `isSettled` / `calculatePayout` instead of encoding a trigger that no longer exists.

**5. AgentKit vs disk / scope**

Coinbase AgentKit’s dependency tree blew local disk limits, so autonomous writes use ethers + a fail-closed `assertSafetyPolicy` (cap-gated, PUT/PUT_SPREAD only, exact USDC approve) — same safety semantics, less bundle weight.

**6. Honest liquidity at hackathon size**

We intentionally ran a **$1 USDC** RFQ on mainnet to prove end-to-end encoding. MMs did not offer — expected at sub-economic size. We treat that as a feature: the system works; liquidity is the real-world constraint.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Many individuals and organizations sign contracts without fully understanding complex legal terms, hidden obligations, financial risks, and unfavorable clauses.

Current contract review processes often face several problems:

1. Time-consuming manual review

Traditional contract analysis requires significant time and legal expertise to identify important clauses and potential risks.

2. Difficulty understanding legal language

Contract Decoder addresses these challenges by combining AI analysis with evidence verification, cross-model comparison, and transparent scoring mechanisms.

goalguard-f5b2.name: GoalGuard
goalguard-f5b2.tagline: protect the purpose, not just the asset.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
# Challenges We Ran Into

## 1. AI Responses Were Not Always Valid JSON

One specific bug occurred when some Gonka-hosted models added a `<think>...</think>` reasoning block before the requested JSON response. Even though the model’s answer was correct, our application could not parse it, which caused the entire review to fail.

We solved this by:

- Removing reasoning blocks before parsing.
- Extracting only the JSON object from the response.
- Validating every response against a strict schema.
- Giving the model one controlled retry when its output is malformed.
- Blocking the protection plan if the response still cannot be verified.

This made the three-reviewer council much more reliable without blindly trusting unpredictable AI output.

## 2. Live Options Data Can Change Quickly

Thetanuts orders can change or expire between the moment a plan is reviewed and the moment its transaction preview is generated. Using an outdated quote could show users incorrect costs or unavailable protection.

To overcome this, GoalGuard re-fetches the selected order before creating the preview. It compares the latest order with the reviewed version, checks liquidity and deadlines again, and creates a fingerprint of the quote. If anything has changed, the plan is marked as stale and the user must review fresh information.

## 3. There Was No Safe Testnet Execution Path

The Thetanuts integration for this track uses Base mainnet, so testing a complete trade could involve real funds. We did not want the demo to expose users or judges to unnecessary financial risk.

We therefore designed the hackathon version to use live market data and the real transaction-building process while stopping at an unsigned preview. The application shows exactly what would be sent on-chain, but it never requests a signature, broadcasts a transaction, or claims that the user is protected.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
# What is GoalGuard?

GoalGuard helps everyday ETH holders protect money they have set aside for important real-life goals, such as rent, tuition, travel, or emergencies, without requiring them to understand options trading.

## The Problem

Most crypto holders think about what their money is for, not about strikes, premiums, expiries, or complex trading strategies.

When ETH prices fall, money reserved for an important expense can suddenly lose value. Existing options platforms can help manage this risk, but they are often too technical for everyday users.

## How GoalGuard Helps

Users describe their goal in plain language:

> “I have $1,200 in ETH for rent next month, and I cannot afford to lose more than 5%.”

GoalGuard then:

1. Converts the goal into clear financial limits.
2. Searches live Thetanuts options for suitable downside protection.
3. Shows the cost, coverage, expiry, and possible outcomes in simple language.
4. Uses three independent Gonka reviewers to evaluate strategy, risk, and consumer clarity.
5. Generates the exact unsigned Base transaction preview for inspection.

## Why It Is Safer

GoalGuard is designed to keep the user in control:

- Financial calculations are deterministic rather than invented by AI.
- Three independent AI reviewers assess every plan.
- Any rejection, uncertainty, missing data, or stale market information stops the process.
- Users see the risks and trade-offs before any transaction.
- No private keys are sent to the server.
- The hackathon version never requests a signature, broadcasts a transaction, or moves funds.

## Why It Matters

GoalGuard makes on-chain options more understandable and approachable. Instead of asking users to become derivatives experts, it connects protection directly to the purpose behind their money.

> **In one sentence:** GoalGuard turns “I need this ETH for rent next month” into a transparent, independently reviewed downside-protection plan, making on-chain options easier to understand and safer to explore.
