agentpaya-secure-marketplace-for-ai-agen.tagline: A secure marketplace for AI agents

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1. Designing a verifier that doesn't just trust the agent's own
   claim of success. We had to build an independent verification
   step that checks the actual output structure/content rather than
   relying on a "status: success" flag the agent itself reports —
   otherwise a malicious or buggy agent could just lie.

2. Avoiding circular trust in the dispute system. Our first version
   of dispute resolution used the agent's own reputation score to
   decide who wins a dispute, which could unfairly penalize a
   struggling agent even when they were right in that instance. We
   had to balance reputation-weighting with re-verification so one
   bad signal doesn't permanently lock an agent out.

3. Keeping the pipeline realistic under time pressure. Bidding,
   escrow, execution, verification, and payout all had to happen in
   a coherent sequence with proper state transitions (task ->
   assigned -> in_progress -> verified/failed -> paid/disputed), and
   getting the async timing right without race conditions between
   escrow lock and task assignment took a few iterations.

4. Balancing simulation vs. realism. Since agents "bidding" and
   "working" needed to be fast enough to demo live, we simulated
   agent behavior instead of calling real LLMs for every step, while
   keeping the trust/escrow/verification logic fully real and
   functional.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
As AI agents increasingly act autonomously to complete tasks for
users and for each other, there's no reliable way for one agent to
hire, pay, and trust another agent it has never interacted with
before. Today this trust gap is solved by having a human in the
loop for every transaction — which defeats the purpose of
autonomous agents.

AgentPay solves this by simulating a zero-trust agent economy where:
- Agents can discover and bid on tasks based on required skills
- Payment is held in escrow and only released after an independent
  verifier checks the output — the paying agent never has to trust
  the working agent's word
- A reputation and risk-scoring system tracks agent reliability over
  time, so bad actors get filtered out automatically
- A dispute resolution flow handles disagreements without needing a
  human to arbitrate every case

This makes it possible for AI agents to safely transact with
strangers (other agents) in a marketplace — the same way escrow and
reputation systems (like on Upwork or eBay) let humans transact
safely with strangers online.

yield-optimised-dca-engine-ffeb.name: Yield Optimised DCA Engine
yield-optimised-dca-engine-ffeb.tagline: “Yield While You Wait. Execute When It Matters.”

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Our project can be used by people who want to make regular investments through DCA without leaving their reserved capital idle. Instead of simply buying a fixed amount at every scheduled time, the system keeps unused capital in an ERC-4626 yield vault while waiting.

Before each purchase, it evaluates factors such as price deviation, volatility, liquidity, slippage, price impact, and execution urgency. Based on these conditions and the user's predefined limits, it can execute the full amount, execute a smaller amount, or delay the purchase.

This makes traditional DCA more capital-efficient and market-aware, while still maintaining the user's long-term investment strategy. It also reduces unnecessary exposure to poor execution conditions and avoids turning the strategy into unrestricted market timing.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of the main challenges was coordinating the different components of the system—the decision engine, ERC-4626 yield vault, and Uniswap v4 execution layer. Since each component follows different rules and interfaces, connecting them correctly was initially difficult.

We solved this by breaking the project into separate modules, testing each component independently, and then integrating them step by step. We also used predefined DCA constraints to ensure that the system could only execute, partially execute, or delay a purchase within safe limits.

This modular approach made debugging easier and helped us ensure that only the required capital is withdrawn while the remaining capital stays productive in the yield vault.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The Problem It Solves

For someone with a fixed salary, managing money can be relatively predictable. But for a freelancer, delivery partner, daily-wage worker, or self-employed individual, income can vary from week to week. One week may be comfortable, while the next may bring unexpected financial pressure.

The real problem is not simply “How much money do I have?”
It is “Will I have enough when I actually need it?”

Most financial applications tell people how much they have spent and where their money went. They rarely help users understand what their current financial situation means or what could happen in the coming days.

How Nidhi AI Helps

Nidhi AI acts as a personal financial companion for people with variable incomes. It brings together income, expenses, savings, and upcoming financial commitments to give users a clearer picture of their financial health.

Users can:

- Understand their financial health through a simple risk score that also explains the factors behind it.
- Look ahead with cash-flow predictions for the next 7, 15, and 30 days.
- Identify financial risks early by receiving alerts about upcoming payments, unusually high expenses, or possible cash shortages.
- Ask questions in everyday language, such as “Can I afford this purchase?” or “Why is my risk score high?” and receive guidance based on their own financial situation.
- Plan and track savings goals without having to manually calculate how much they can set aside.
- Make informed decisions by turning complex financial data into clear and understandable insights.

Nidhi AI is not designed to simply tell people where their money went. It helps them understand where their money is going, what may happen next, and what they can do today to be better prepared for tomorrow.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges We Ran Into

Building Nidhi AI was not just about connecting an AI model to a dashboard. The biggest challenge was making the different parts of the system work together reliably while keeping the experience simple for the user.

- Working with variable income: Unlike users with a fixed salary, our target users can have unpredictable earnings. Designing meaningful risk and cash-flow calculations around changing income and expenses was challenging.

- Making AI responses financially relevant: A generic AI response is not enough for a financial assistant. We had to ensure that Nidhi's responses were grounded in the user's actual financial data rather than giving vague or unrelated advice.

- Explaining AI decisions: A risk score alone does not tell a user much. We needed to present the reasoning behind the score in a way that was understandable to someone without a financial background.

- Connecting the frontend and backend: Integrating the React frontend with the FastAPI backend required careful handling of API requests, responses, authentication, and financial data.

- Keeping financial information understandable: Financial data can quickly become overwhelming. We had to decide what information users actually need to see and present it through simple cards, forecasts, alerts, and insights instead of overwhelming them with numbers.

- Multilingual support: Supporting English, Hindi, and Tamil while maintaining a consistent interface and meaningful AI-generated responses added another layer of complexity.

- Handling real-world edge cases: Financial situations are rarely straightforward. Missing data, irregular transactions, upcoming expenses, changing balances, and unexpected user inputs all had to be considered while developing the system.

- Balancing intelligence with simplicity: One of our biggest design challenges was making Nidhi feel intelligent without making it complicated. The goal was to hide the complexity of the calculations and AI processing behind a simple, approachable interface.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
CashSurvive is an AI-powered financial control tower that helps businesses predict cash-flow problems before they happen.
It brings financial data, cash-flow forecasting, scenario analysis, and risk evaluation into one platform. Instead of reacting after a liquidity problem occurs, users can see upcoming cash shortages, understand financial risks, test different scenarios, and make proactive decisions.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of our biggest challenges was integrating independently developed backend modules with the frontend into one working system. The modules had different structures, imports, and data interfaces, so connecting them directly caused compatibility and import-path issues.
We solved this by:
Building an integration/adapter layer instead of rewriting the existing modules.
Resolving Python import-path conflicts between the Financial State and Forecasting modules.
Connecting the React frontend to the FastAPI backend through API services.
Debugging missing Python dependencies such as NumPy during backend startup.
Handling Git and GitHub integration issues, including an initial repository-path mistake and a README merge conflict.
Testing each connection step-by-step before moving to the next part.
These challenges helped us build a more modular architecture while preserving the original business logic of each component.

cashpilot-6811.name: CashPilot
cashpilot-6811.tagline: CashPilot AI — Deciding where your next rupee shou

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges We Faced
1. Making the Data Matter

Historical and future-event data was already being stored in the backend and sent through it, but wasn't affecting any further steps. This problem was solved by transforming historical data into signals (such as customer payment history and delay tendencies), and making each event trigger re-forecasting and re-optimization.

2. Finding the Right Forecasting Method

ARIMA model was initially considered to work better than other models. In practice, however, simple models could sometimes be even more accurate. That's why we implemented the method of choosing the best model from Naive, Moving Average, Ridge, Ensemble, and ARIMA models by metrics of MAE, R², and MAPE. Also, we switched from forecasting cash balance itself to forecasting net cash flow and rebuilding balance.

3. Managing Financial Uncertainty

The fact that receivables may not be timely received could lead to false liquidity prediction when it is considered as a guaranteed receipt. We implemented confidence intervals and probabilities of receivables, and didn't replace negative predictions with zeroes so that actual deficits remained noticeable for the decision-making engine.

4. Implementing Truly Dynamic Decision-Making

In the beginning, we tried to implement the context-based weights depending on the situations ("tight cash," "comfortable cash"). It turned out that the approach remained static and rule-based, so we implemented continuous calculation of weights depending on the current financial situation.

5. Using Gemini for Explaining Decisions Instead of Financial Calculations

Initially, we considered allowing the large language model to decide about finances. However, it created a risk of wrong or hallucinated numbers. That's why forecasts, risk score calculation, reserve requirements and financing are done in a deterministic way, and Gemini is used to explain an already calculated decision.

6. Balancing Vision and Time of Hackathon

Our entire idea includes evaluation and allocation of capital between every invoice and financial obligation. However, considering limited amount of time during the hackathon, we decided to focus on implementation and rigorous testing of the company-wide liquidity, reserve and financing engine, leaving the per-invoice capital allocation as a definite future enhancement.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
1. Forfeited early-payment discounts, recovered automatically
Treasury teams routinely miss discount windows (e.g., 2.0% from a supplier, 1.5% from another) due to manual approval lag, forfeiting risk-free yield. CashPilot AI's discount-capture logic identifies active windows and prioritizes CAPTURE_DISCOUNT actions automatically, converting missed savings into captured yield the same day, with suppliers rated on historical discount reliability so the highest-value relationships are never the ones that slip through.

2. Cash-floor breaches and payroll shocks, prevented structurally
Discretionary vendor payouts can silently deplete the cash needed for payroll or tax obligations. CashPilot AI enforces a mandatory reserve floor policy and locks required payroll/operating cash before any discretionary invoice is even evaluated, this isn't a warning after the fact, it's a hard constraint upstream of the decision.

3. Receivable uncertainty, modeled and updated live
Customer payment delays create sudden liquidity gaps that a static forecast can't anticipate. A Bayesian inference engine continuously updates each customer's collection probability as real payment outcomes arrive, and when a probability drops, the system automatically shifts affected supplier payouts from cash to low-cost financing, the allocation adapts to the updated risk, not the original assumption.

4. Black-box AI output, made executive-legible
Raw optimization scores mean nothing to a CFO. Every recommendation is mapped onto a clean, normalized priority scale, and surfaced in an explainability layer that states plainly why a decision should execute today, the yield captured, the safety margin preserved, the obligation protected, not a mathematical array.

5. No way to stress-test a decision before committing cash
Treasury managers can't commit real cash on faith. An interactive what-if simulator lets you flex receivable delays and expense shocks and see the resulting cash curve, and the system's adapted recommendation, before anything is executed, not after.

6. Real financial data, not clamped or hidden
Projected liquidity deficits are tracked at their true size rather than floored to zero for a tidier display, and every recommendation is reconciled to the cent through a before/after simulation on the same engine used to generate it, so what you see is what the numbers actually are, not a rounded approximation.

7. Explainability without hallucination risk
Every decision is packaged into a structured object, action, forecast, confidence, risk, reserve, reasoning, that's the only input the LLM ever sees. It narrates facts; it never computes them.

8. Reliability proven, not asserted
33 automated tests, including 15 production-style stress scenarios, all passing, evidence that the engine behaves correctly under pressure, not just in the one path shown in a demo.

finasset-6c2b.name: FinAsset
finasset-6c2b.tagline: Agentic Financing for the Physical Supply Chain

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: One of the biggest challenges we faced was connecting the physical lifecycle of an asset with its financial lifecycle. An asset continuously changes from purchase order to production, shipment, delivery, invoice, receivable and finally cash, and each change can affect its value, risk, financeability and exposure. We also had to ensure that user-declared values were kept separate from verified valuations, prevent multiple financing claims and collateral conflicts, and make dynamic events such as shipment delays or damage trigger proper reassessment. Another challenge was integrating AI safely without relying on paid API keys, so we used a local Ollama model as a reasoning layer while keeping the actual financial decisions deterministic and auditable. Finally, we had to ensure that our dynamic UI remained fully synchronized with the backend so that every value and lifecycle state shown to the user represents the actual system state.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Businesses need capital at every stage of production — raw materials, manufacturing, shipment, warehousing, and delivery — long before their customers actually pay.

Traditional financing typically activates only when a financial document such as an invoice or receivable exists.

This creates a critical timing gap: valuable working capital remains trapped inside the supply chain, and businesses are forced to fund weeks or months of operations entirely on their own before financing becomes available.

At the same time, financiers face another problem: the physical asset, its actual condition, its value, its existing financing, and its risk are often represented across disconnected systems.

This can lead to:

delayed financing
uncertain asset valuation
insufficient verification
duplicate financing
collateral conflicts
over-exposure
inappropriate financing instruments
financing decisions that become outdated when supply-chain events occur

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1. Two parts of the system disagreed about what "reserve" meant

A stealth injection exposed it: the deterministic policy floor and the LLM intent judge were computing different reserve numbers for the same action. One treated the reserve as a floor under total treasury; the other
treated it as a dedicated bucket. Both were defensible. Both were in the code.

We resolved it by evidence rather than preference. `debit()` draws from
operating cash first which is only coherent if the reserve is a protected
floor under the total. That settled the semantic, and we collapsed both call
sites into `shared/treasury.py` as the single definition. A related bug fell out
of it: the guard was `total_before <= 0`, which conflated "no balance data" with
"a balance of zero", so a known-zero treasury passed the reserve check. Now
`has_balance_data = bool(balances)` — known-zero is a breach.

2. A false-positive attack match at 0.96 similarity

The attack-memory store started matching legitimate actions against stored
attack patterns with 0.96 similarity. The cause was mundane and invisible: our
structural tokens used underscores, and the tokenizer split on underscores. A token meant to be indivisible was being shattered into common fragments that
matched almost anything. Fixing the tokens to be genuinely indivisible dropped
the false positive to 0.21, well under the 0.85 threshold.

3. The CDP wallet adapter never worked, because the SDK is fully async

Our adapter called Coinbase's CDP SDK synchronously. It had never worked. After
wrapping every call in `asyncio.run()` it broke differently: a nested
`asyncio.run()` when resolving `self.address` from inside an already-running
loop. We resolved the address *before* entering the loop and added a re-entrancy
guard.
Our prompt-hardening demo runs the same agent, same model, same poisoned feed,
twice: once with injection-defence instructions, once without. We expected the
unhardened run to fall for it. Gemini resisted in both modes.

We reported that as measured rather than manufacturing a successful attack. It
is arguably the more honest finding: model resistance is a property you observe, not a control you own. The security layer blocked the action
regardless, which is the actual point. A related fix the script had been labelling a 429 quota failure as resisted, when in truth the model never
answered and nothing had been measured at all. It now reports not measured and draws no conclusion.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Autonomous AI agents are being handed real financial authority. The security
question everyone asks is "is this transaction properly authorised and signed?"

That question has a blind spot. If an attacker can change what the agent believes by poisoning a market data feed, a vendor email, an API
response  the agent will produce a transaction that is perfectly authorised,
correctly signed, and completely wrong. No key was stolen. No system was
breached. Nothing looks broken. The money is simply gone.

Every existing control passes. Multiset passes: the agent is a legitimate
signer. Spending limits pass: the attacker stays under them. Anomaly detection passes: the agent is behaving exactly as designed it is reasoning on
corrupted input.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges We Ran Into
1. Bundling INCO FHE Encryption WASM Modules with Vite
Hurdle: Integrating INCO’s Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) layer (@inco/js) into a modern Vite + React Web3 application presented significant bundling challenges. The encrypted ciphertext logic and WASM modules triggered top-level await and buffer polyfill errors during browser compilation.
Resolution: We configured vite-plugin-wasm, vite-plugin-top-level-await, and vite-plugin-node-polyfills inside vite.config.js. This enabled seamless client-side encryption whenever the user appends the "private" intent keyword to their prompt, submitting FHE ciphertexts directly to our smart contract.
2. Guaranteeing Zero-Secret Leakage in Trace Commons Local Redaction
Hurdle: AI coding agent session logs (Claude Code, Antigravity) record complete session transcripts, including file paths, model reasoning, bash executions, and environment configurations. Raw transcripts often accidentally contain API keys (sk-ant-...), passwords, or PII.
Resolution: We implemented a fail-closed local PII and key sanitizer script (scripts/trace-commons-helper.js) that runs regex-based redaction locally on the developer's machine before any trace data is submitted. This ensured zero secret upload risk while producing a signed attestation.jws token for Devfolio track judging.
3. Handling Shardeum EVM Provider Re-initialization & RPC Shifts
Hurdle: Switching networks or switching accounts inside MetaMask on Shardeum EVM Testnet frequently caused Ethers v6 BrowserProvider instances to throw NETWORK_ERROR exceptions when querying native SHM balances or smart contract state.
Resolution: We introduced auto-healing provider initialization logic with retry delays in Sidebar.jsx and App.jsx. The app detects account or chain shifts (accountsChanged, chainChanged) and cleanly re-establishes RPC connections without freezing the Web3 UI state.
4. Structuring Real-Time AI Explainability with Live Market Data
Hurdle: Synthesizing structured explainability models (inputs analyzed, reasoning summary, alternatives considered, risk acknowledged) alongside live Coinbase market rate streaming introduced potential latency delays in the decision feed.
Resolution: We decoupled live price fetching from the AI decision synthesis engine using custom React hooks (useAgent) and smooth Framer Motion micro-animations, ensuring real-time response feeds with zero UI lag.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The Problem It Solves
Most autonomous AI trading and decision-making agents operating today suffer from the Black Box Problem:

Opaque & Unaccountable Execution: Users cannot see what market inputs, technical indicators, or contextual signals the AI agent analyzed before taking an automated trade.
Centralized & Mutable Audit Trails: Off-chain AI logs can be altered, deleted, or falsified without detection, making true auditing impossible for DAOs and users.
Ungoverned Automation: Autonomous agents execute high-value transactions without predefined approval constraints or DAO oversight, risking capital loss and rogue executions.
The Privacy vs. Transparency Dilemma: Existing Web3 systems force a binary trade-off—either publish full trading strategies publicly (exposing trades to MEV sandwich attacks and front-running) or hide logic inside centralized black-box servers.
What People Can Use It For
AgentChain introduces a Transparent, DAO-Governed, and Privacy-Preserving AI Agent Framework:

DAO Treasury Management & Bot Governance: DAOs can deploy autonomous trading agents with hard smart contract governance boundaries. DAO members vote to approve, audit, or freeze agent execution privileges.
Auditable & Explainable AI Decisions: Users and auditors can inspect step-by-step AI decision logic—including observed market inputs, Buy/Sell/Hold reasoning summaries, alternative choices evaluated, and risk factors acknowledged.
Intent-Based Confidential Execution: By appending the keyword "private" in prompts, sensitive strategy parameters are encrypted via INCO FHE (Fully Homomorphic Encryption). This protects against MEV and strategy leaks while maintaining verifiable on-chain execution proofs.
🌐 Verifiable AI Work Registration: Integrates with Trace Commons to locally scrub and attest AI agent session traces via signed JWT tokens, providing verifiable proof of human-agent collaboration.
How It Makes Existing Tasks Safer & Easier
Safer DAO Oversight: AI agents cannot execute transactions without active smart contract authorization on Shardeum EVM (0x04AbE123D31971575Cd94850752f2C59faf92a26).
Easier Independent Verification: Public users can cross-reference explainable decision logs in the AgentChain Explorer with immutable on-chain decision hashes.
Front-Running & Sandwich Attack Protection: INCO encryption keeps internal values unreadable to external observers while proving valid compute execution.
Enhanced Accessibility: Features live Coinbase rate streaming and text-to-speech audio decision summaries for instant auditability during live trading demos.

description.title: Trace Commons AI
description.body: AgentChain and Trace Commons share the same core mission: transforming AI agents from black boxes into auditable, transparent systems. Our team collaborated deeply with Antigravity AI Agent and Claude Code to co-author our Shardeum EVM smart contract (0x04AbE123D31971575Cd94850752f2C59faf92a26), INCO FHE privacy layer, and React Web3 UI. Using the trace-commons-contributor CLI, we locally redacted PII/API keys, submitted 4 clean agent session traces under tenant-devfolio-hackathon, and generated a server-signed JWT attestation (attestation.jws). We also built an in-app Trace Commons Explorer tab inside AgentChain so judges can inspect scrubbed session events and attestations in real time.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Praetor addresses the security risks that arise when autonomous AI agents are given the ability to perform financial operations. Instead of relying only on authentication or predefined permissions, it evaluates each proposed financial action for transaction fraud, behavioural anomalies, transaction-network risk, counterparty and protocol risk, policy violations, and possible instruction manipulation. This helps organizations make autonomous financial operations safer by allowing low-risk actions to proceed automatically while escalating or blocking higher-risk actions before they can affect financial assets.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: One of the main challenges was integrating the machine-learning models with the live security dashboard. Initially, some frontend pages were still using older demo endpoints and static transaction data, which caused 405 Method Not Allowed errors even though the FastAPI server itself was running correctly. We diagnosed this by testing the API endpoints directly, then updated the frontend pages to use the common Aurelia transaction flow: retrieving the demo transactions through the API and sending them to the evaluation endpoint for real Praetor decisions. We also had to handle missing engineered features during demo scoring and ensure the models could reproduce their original preprocessing during inference. This gave us a consistent end-to-end flow from transaction input → ML/rule-based evaluation → security decision → UI.

description.title: Trace Commons AI
description.body: Praetor uses AI-driven analysis to interpret financial-agent activity and identify potentially anomalous or unsafe actions. Its architecture combines machine-learning risk signals with behavioural and policy analysis to provide clear, explainable security decisions. The system presents these decisions, risks, and detected security issues through an operator-facing interface, making complex AI-generated security analysis easier to understand and act upon.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Detect fuel fraud, predict failures, save lives.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
### Challenges I Ran Into

* **Real-time data integration:** Combining fuel monitoring, vehicle health, and driver safety data into one system was challenging. We addressed this by organizing each feature into separate monitoring modules.

* **AI detection:** Detecting road hazards and driver behavior reliably in real time was a major hurdle. We focused on AI-based computer vision and real-time alerts.

* **Predictive maintenance:** Converting vehicle health data into useful failure predictions required careful analysis of multiple vehicle parameters.

* **System integration:** Bringing fuel integrity, vehicle health, ADAS, driver monitoring, and mobile/web dashboards together was challenging. We solved this by designing the system as interconnected modules rather than one large component.

yourcircleits-basically-an-app-where-you.tagline: Your Characters, Your Stories, Your World.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Building a complete "Prove → Verify → Pay" pipeline that runs locally on-device while maintaining a premium UX was challenging:

1. **zkML Asynchronous Bindings in EZKL:**
   While building the ONNX to Halo2 zkML pipeline, we hit roadblocks with EZKL's Python API. Several crucial bindings (like `get_srs` for the KZG Structured Reference String and `create_evm_verifier` for generating the Solidity verifier) are backed by Rust/Tokio async functions. They couldn't be called synchronously and caused event loop crashes. We overcame this by wrapping the entire pipeline in an `asyncio` event loop, carefully orchestrating the transition from synchronous model training to asynchronous ZK proving.

2. **Bridging AI Inference with On-Chain Verification:**
   Quantizing our Logistic Regression model into fixed-point arithmetic for the ZK circuit introduced slight variations from the native PyTorch outputs. We had to carefully calibrate the circuit scale factors (`settings.json`) to ensure the on-chain `Verifier.sol` would accept the proof and that the threshold logic (e.g., matching the exact income/spending requirements) evaluated consistently.

3. **Mobile ZK Proving Overhead:**
   Generating ZK proofs locally on a mobile device (Flutter) requires significant computational overhead and can feel sluggish to the user. We solved the UX side of this by designing an animation that keeps the user engaged and informed while the heavy cryptographic operations happen in the background.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
In today's digital economy, users are constantly required to expose their sensitive personal and financial data (like bank statements, income history, or transaction records) to third-party platforms just to prove they are eligible for programs such as cashback offers, grants, loans, or scholarships. This creates massive privacy risks and honeypots for data breaches.

**Veil** solves this by flipping the paradigm: instead of sending raw data to a server for evaluation, the evaluation rules are sent to the user's device. 

Veil allows users to use a conversational AI (PrivatePilot) to fetch their local authentic data and run a lightweight Machine Learning model *entirely on-device*. It then generates a Zero-Knowledge Proof (zkML via EZKL and Noir circuits) that cryptographically guarantees the user meets the eligibility criteria, without ever exposing their actual financial data. The proof is verified by a smart contract on Ethereum, triggering a shielded payment (via Railgun). 

It makes proving eligibility safer, completely private, and seamless—users get their rewards without sacrificing their identity or financial history.

description.title: Private Wallets and Payments
description.body: Veil utilizes shielded transaction infrastructure (like Railgun) to ensure that once a user's zero-knowledge eligibility proof is verified on-chain, their rewards and payouts are transferred completely anonymously.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## Silent LLM failures that looked like working code

The hardest bug to find was not a crash. The orchestrator 
was returning the literal string `"No LLM response"` for 
every synthesis step — but it was doing so silently, 
caught inside a bare `except` block that swallowed the 
actual exception and returned a placeholder. The system 
appeared to be running. The SSE stream was flowing. The 
frontend showed output. It was just wrong output every 
single time.

Debugging this required adding structured logging to every 
code path in the orchestrator and watching what was 
actually being caught. The root exception turned out to be 
a missing API key — but instead of surfacing it, the code 
was catching it and returning a hardcoded string that made 
it look like the LLM had responded with nothing.

The real fix was architectural, not a patch. We removed the 
LLM from the critical synthesis path entirely. The template 
synthesizer now builds the final answer directly from the 
specialist agents' structured JSON responses — no LLM call 
needed. The system never returns `"No LLM response"` 
because there is no LLM call that can fail on the critical 
path. LLM polish is wrapped in a non-blocking try/except 
that falls back to the template silently. Lesson: if your 
fallback string is indistinguishable from a real response, 
you will spend hours debugging a bug that looks like 
working software.

---

## Subnet-EVM Cancun compiler mismatch

Contracts deployed fine locally against Hardhat Network. 
They failed silently on the Avalanche L1 devnet — not 
reverting, not throwing errors, just producing unexpected 
behavior on certain operations.

The root cause took significant time to find: Subnet-EVM 
currently targets the Cancun EVM fork. Solidity 0.8.30 and 
above defaults to targeting the Pectra fork. Contracts 
compiled with default settings emit bytecode that uses 
instructions Subnet-EVM does not support. The contracts 
deploy successfully — the bytecode is valid enough to land 
— but specific opcodes fail at runtime in ways that look 
like logic bugs rather than compiler issues.

The fix is one line in `hardhat.config.js`:
```javascript
solidity: {
  version: "0.8.20",
  settings: {
    evmVersion: "cancun"
  }
}
```

This is not documented prominently anywhere in the 
Avalanche or Subnet-EVM docs. We found it by comparing 
opcode output between a working Hardhat Network deploy and 
a failing devnet deploy using `evm disasm`. The lesson: 
whenever deploying to a non-standard EVM fork, explicitly 
set `evmVersion` in your compiler config and verify the 
target fork matches. Never assume the default is correct.

---

## MetaMask wrong network modal with no switch option

The custom Avalanche L1 (chain ID 88888) is not in 
MetaMask's default network list. When a user connected 
their wallet, the wrong-network modal appeared — but we 
had only wired up a Disconnect button. There was no way 
for the user to switch to the correct chain from within 
the app.

The initial fix attempt was calling `wallet_addEthereumChain` 
manually via `window.ethereum.request`. This worked 
inconsistently across MetaMask versions and caused the 
modal to flicker between states without actually switching.

The correct fix was using wagmi's `useSwitchChain` hook 
combined with defining the custom chain using `defineChain` 
from viem and registering it in the wagmi config:

```typescript
const agentMarketChain = defineChain({
  id: 88888,
  name: 'Agent Market (Private)',
  nativeCurrency: { name: 'tAGT', symbol: 'tAGT', decimals: 18 },
  rpcUrls: {
    default: { http: [process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_AVAX_RPC_URL] }
  }
});
```

When the chain is registered in wagmi's config, calling 
`switchChain({ chainId: 88888 })` automatically triggers 
MetaMask's `wallet_addEthereumChain` flow if the network 
does not exist yet, or `wallet_switchEthereumChain` if it 
does. One click handles both cases. The modal now shows 
a Switch button as the primary action and Disconnect as 
a secondary option. The network adds and switches 
correctly in a single user interaction.

---

## Atomic spend cap across parallel agent payments

The orchestrator runs independent subtasks — token risk 
scoring and gas timing — concurrently using 
`asyncio.gather()`. Both tasks involve a payment. Both 
payments check the session spend cap before executing.

The race condition: both payment coroutines read the 
current spend total simultaneously, both see it is below 
the cap, both proceed, and the total spend ends up double 
what the cap allows. The cap check passes twice for two 
payments that together exceed the limit.

The fix was wrapping the cap check and increment in an 
`asyncio.Lock`:

```python
async with spend_lock:
    if session_spend + amount > SESSION_SPEND_CAP:
        raise ValueError(f"Spend cap exceeded")
    session_spend += amount
```

The lock ensures that even when two payment coroutines 
run concurrently, the cap check and increment are 
atomic. One payme

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The agent economy has a fundamental infrastructure gap. AI 
agents today are excellent at reasoning, planning, and 
deciding — but the moment they need to act on those decisions 
by paying for a service, verifying a counterparty, or 
discovering what capabilities are available to them, they 
hit a wall. That wall is not a technical limitation of the 
AI. It is missing economic infrastructure.

Three things have to exist before the agent economy is real 
rather than hypothetical:

**Agents cannot pay each other.** Every agent-to-agent 
transaction that involves a paid service requires a human 
to create accounts, generate API keys, set up billing, and 
approve payment. None of that is autonomous. None of it 
scales.

**Agents cannot trust each other.** There is no standard 
way for Agent A to verify whether Agent B is legitimate, 
has done good work before, or should be trusted enough to 
pay for its output. Reputation lives in walled-garden 
platforms — not in a place any agent can query 
programmatically.

**Agents cannot discover each other.** There is no shared 
directory of agents, their capabilities, their prices, or 
how to call them that any autonomous agent can access 
without a human maintaining it.

DeFi Agent Marketplace solves all three simultaneously. 
x402 removes the human billing setup requirement — the 
payment itself is the authentication. ERC-8004 gives every 
agent a permanent, queryable onchain identity and a 
reputation score anchored to real payment transaction 
hashes — making trust verifiable and economically costly 
to fake. The onchain Identity Registry handles discovery 
— any agent can query it to find specialist agents by 
skill, check reputation and stake, and hire them 
autonomously.

**For DeFi traders:** token due diligence that currently 
requires four separate tools and thirty minutes of manual 
work — Etherscan for contract ownership, DexScreener for 
liquidity, CoinGecko for listing status, Slither for 
static analysis — completes in under ten seconds with zero 
manual steps.

**For developers building AI agents:** any agent can 
access paid intelligence services with no accounts, no 
API keys, and no billing relationships to manage. One 
HTTP call, one payment, one result.

**For DeFi protocols and DAOs:** autonomous contract 
monitoring, vulnerability detection, and risk reporting 
without a human security researcher in the loop for 
routine checks.

**For trading firms:** encrypted payments via eERC mean 
what a firm pays for intelligence — which tokens it is 
researching, how frequently — stays private. Competitors 
watching the chain cannot see what was purchased or for 
how much.

**For compliance officers:** a rotatable auditor key lets 
designated officers decrypt the full payment history on 
demand — privacy by default, transparency when required. 
The exact model institutions need before putting agent 
workflows onchain.

description.title: Private DeFi & Mempools
description.body:
DeFi Agent Marketplace fits the Private DeFi & Mempools track 
directly and completely.

The core privacy problem we solve is commercial in nature: in 
DeFi, what you pay for intelligence reveals your strategy. If 
a trading firm's AI agent is querying risk scores on fifty 
specific tokens, that query pattern is alpha. If it is 
auditing a contract before a large position, that audit 
request signals intent. On a public chain, every payment to 
every data service is visible to anyone watching — which 
makes agent-powered DeFi workflows commercially dangerous 
to run onchain.

We solve this at two layers simultaneously.

**Layer one — encrypted payments via eERC.** Every 
agent-to-agent payment in the marketplace uses eERC, 
Avalanche's encrypted ERC-20 standard built on Groth16 
zk-SNARKs and ElGamal encryption. Payment amounts are 
hidden onchain. The chain records that a transfer happened 
and between which addresses — but not how much was paid, 
for what service, or how frequently. Competitors watching 
the mempool see settlement events with no extractable 
signal about the buyer's research activity or strategy.

**Layer two — permissioned mempool access via Subnet-EVM 
TxAllowList.** The marketplace runs on a private Avalanche 
L1 with the TxAllowList precompile active. Unknown wallets 
are rejected at the chain level before they can submit any 
transaction to the mempool. MEV bots, frontrunners, and 
unauthorized observers cannot reach the RPC at all. There 
is no public mempool to watch — the entire transaction 
flow is gated behind operator-controlled allowlist 
verification.

**The compliance layer closes the loop.** Privacy without 
auditability is not acceptable for institutional DeFi. 
eERC's rotatable auditor key lets a designated compliance 
officer decrypt the full payment history on demand — 
actual amounts, counterparties, and timestamps — without 
that information ever being publicly visible onchain. 
This is the exact model regulated institutions require: 
privacy by default, transparency when the regulator asks.

The result is a DeFi agent marketplace where autonomous 
AI agents can research tokens, audit contracts, and 
optimize gas timing — paying specialist agents per 
request in encrypted stablecoins — without any of that 
commercial activity leaking to the public mempool or to 
competitors watching the chain.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of the biggest hurdles I faced was implementing real-time GPS tracking and AI-based exercise form analysis in the same application.
GPS tracking required continuously collecting location data while calculating distance, pace, speed, and route without making the app consume excessive battery. The camera-based form checker was also challenging because exercise movements need to be analyzed from video while providing useful feedback.
I solved this by separating these features into dedicated modules: using location services for GPS tracking, CameraX and pose-analysis technologies for movement detection, and Gemini for AI-powered coaching and feedback. I also designed the app so that sensitive AI operations and API keys are handled through a secure backend instead of being exposed in the Android application.
This experience taught me how to break a complex AI fitness application into smaller, manageable systems and integrate them into one platform.

haemo-core-4047.tagline: Right Blood. Right Place. Right Time.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## Challenges I ran into

### 1. Challenge One: Designing the Smart Blood Allocation System

One of the main challenges was designing an allocation system that could make meaningful decisions instead of simply selecting the first available blood unit. The system needed to consider blood compatibility, availability, expiry dates, FIFO prioritization, and the distance between hospitals.

**How I solved it:**
I developed a rule-based Smart Allocation Engine that evaluates these factors before selecting and recommending suitable blood units. This allowed the system to prioritize compatible and available units while also considering expiry and proximity.

---

### 2. Challenge Two: Managing the Blood Lifecycle

A blood unit can go through multiple stages, including registration, availability, reservation, transfer, delivery, and issuance. Managing these transitions without allowing invalid actions was challenging.

**How I solved it:**
I implemented structured status transitions and workflow validation. Each stage has defined actions, helping ensure that blood units move through the correct lifecycle. An audit trail was also added to record important changes.

---

### 3. Challenge Three: Handling Inter-Hospital Transfers

Coordinating blood transfers between hospitals required clear control over which hospital could perform actions such as approving, dispatching, and confirming delivery.

**How I solved it:**
I designed a transfer workflow with defined stages and role-based access controls. This helped ensure that actions were performed by the appropriate hospital and that the transfer status could be tracked throughout the process.

---

### 4. Challenge Four: Connecting the UI to Real Data

During the early stages of development, some parts of the dashboard relied on simulated or hardcoded data. This made the application look functional without fully representing the actual backend workflow.

**How I solved it:**
I gradually connected the frontend to the backend and database so that inventory, SOS requests, transfers, and other system information could be retrieved and updated through the actual application workflow.

---

### 5. Challenge Five: Implementing QR/RFID Tracking Without Hardware

The project required a way to track individual blood units, but using physical RFID hardware would add additional complexity and dependency on external devices.

**How I solved it:**
I implemented a software-based QR/RFID identification workflow using unique identifiers for each blood unit. This allowed the complete tracking workflow to be demonstrated without requiring physical hardware, while keeping the system extensible for future integration with actual QR scanners or RFID devices.

---

### 6. Challenge Six: Preventing Blood Wastage

Simply tracking blood inventory was not enough. The system also needed to prioritize blood units that were closer to expiry to reduce unnecessary wastage.

**How I solved it:**
I incorporated FIFO and expiry-based prioritization into the allocation workflow. When suitable blood units are available, the system can prioritize older or earlier-expiring units where appropriate.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## The problem it solves

Blood management across hospitals can be slow and fragmented, especially during emergencies. Hospitals may have limited visibility into the availability of compatible blood at nearby facilities, while manual coordination, delayed inventory updates, and inefficient tracking can increase response time and contribute to blood wastage.

**HAEMO/CORE** provides a centralized platform that helps hospitals manage and coordinate blood inventory across a connected network.

It can be used to:

* Monitor the availability of different blood groups across multiple hospitals.
* Raise and manage emergency blood requests when required units are not available locally.
* Identify suitable blood units based on compatibility, availability, expiry dates, FIFO prioritization, and hospital proximity.
* Track blood bags throughout their lifecycle using QR/RFID-based identification workflows.
* Manage inter-hospital blood transfers from allocation and dispatch to delivery.
* Reduce wastage by identifying and prioritizing blood units approaching their expiry date.
* Monitor cold-chain conditions and flag potential storage issues.
* Analyze blood usage patterns and support future demand planning.
* Maintain a clear audit trail of important actions and blood movement.

By bringing these processes into a single platform, HAEMO/CORE makes blood management more organized, traceable, and efficient while helping hospitals respond more quickly to time-critical blood requirements.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
#### 1. Moving real capital without revealing the split on a standard token

A rescue needs two things that pull in opposite directions: individual amounts must stay hidden before settlement, but escrowing real ERC-20 value necessarily emits `Transfer(from, to, amount)` after the block is published. Even with a private mempool, the breakdown becomes visible in logs once the transaction is included. No standard token can hide the amount after settlement.

The system separates the commitment layer from the settlement layer. `ShieldedPool` exposes a hash-only deposit that carries no value and a real-escrow deposit that does `transferFrom`, records `escrow` per nullifier and `depositor` per nullifier, and is documented as necessarily revealing per-rescuer transfers. Settlement reads escrow, mints `RescueShares` proportionally, and releases the total from escrow. The limitation is stated directly: hash privacy holds in calldata and the mempool, full amount privacy after settlement would require a confidential token. The test `DepositRealLeaksTransferButCommitmentRemainsHashOnly` asserts the trade-off.

#### 2. Binding commitments to nullifiers to prevent shuffling

Proving `sum ≥ T` is not enough. Each public commitment must be tied to the same private `nullifier` that the contract tracks for reuse. If nullifiers are not part of the public inputs, a prover could mix nullifiers from one commitment with amounts from another and still pass verification, bypassing single-use guarantees.

The circuit was built with fourteen public inputs - `commitments[6]`, `nullifier_hashes[6]`, `T`, and `roundId` - and asserts `pedersen_hash(amount, nullifier, secret, round) == commitment` and `nullifier == nullifier_hash` in the same loop. The contract checks `publicInputs[6+i] == nullifier[i]` before calling the verifier, so a shuffled proof fails with `InvalidPublicInputs` before the reuse guard. A dedicated test proves shuffling reverts.

#### 3. Choosing soundness over gas for the proof

A smaller, non-ZK proof saves about 600k gas and 960 bytes. It still hides witnesses from public observers, but it is not formally zero-knowledge. Presenting a witness-hiding build as a ZK proof would not survive cryptographic review.

The system ships a real ZK verifier with keccak transcript (8384 bytes) as the primary path. It is verified both off-chain with `bb verify` and on-chain on Sepolia. The cost is higher, but the soundness property is preserved and the verification is directly checkable on Etherscan.

#### 4. Getting privacy without relying on a private mempool

A common assumption is that a private RPC is what hides amounts. In practice the deployment often falls back to public broadcast because the Sepolia private endpoint is not reliably available, and in that case mempool privacy alone would provide no guarantee.

The design makes privacy mempool-agnostic. Amounts never appear in calldata - only `0xe9ceb85f <hash> <nullifier>` is sent - so even a public transaction shows no `012c` for 300. The private RPC path is kept as defense-in-depth and logs its fallback, but the verifier, the explorer view, and the demo all hold without it. Reviewers can confirm this by inspecting any deposit calldata and its logs on Etherscan.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## What it is

A lending vault with health 0.92 holds 92¢ of collateral for every $1 of debt. It needs 600 mUSDC to stay solvent. The natural way to raise that amount in public - each rescuer posting how much they will put in - reveals the exact discount each rescuer wants. Bots copy the signal, the discount disappears, and the rescue fails.

Insurance does not help here. It pays claims after failure. Proof-of-reserves shows a vault is solvent but does not raise new capital. Confidential lending creates new loans. Treasury tools move money that already exists. None let a group privately gather new capital for a specific vault without showing the split.

BlackSwan Relay is a private rescue market for one vault, one round, and a small set of rescuers.

**How it works:**

1. A keeper opens a round with a fixed target, for example 600 mUSDC.
2. Each rescuer commits locally as `hash(amount, nullifier, secret, round)` using pedersen_hash. Only the 32-byte hash is sent on-chain. Calldata looks like `0xe9ceb85f <hash> <nullifier>` with no visible `300`.
3. A Noir circuit proves the hidden amounts add up to at least the target and that every hash is correctly bound. Fourteen public inputs are used - six commitments, six nullifier hashes, the target, and the round - so commitments and nullifiers cannot be shuffled between rescuers.
4. A Barretenberg UltraHonk verifier checks the 8384-byte ZK proof on Sepolia. If it passes and no nullifier is reused, the vault is recapitalized and discounted RescueShares are minted proportional to each escrow in one atomic transaction. If the sum is too low or a nullifier is reused, the transaction reverts.

**What stays private and what is public:**

- Private: individual amounts and the exact strategy size before settlement. The explorer shows only hashes until a proof is presented.
- Public: the round, the target, the hashes, the fact that the target was met, the total moved, and the shares minted. Participant addresses are visible; hiding who participated would need a larger anonymity set.

**Why it stands out:**

- **Aggregate-capital proof, not a balance check.** The circuit proves `sum ≥ T` over six slots with `u64` range checks, not just solvency. It covers underfunded padding and prevents overflow.
- **Commitment and nullifier binding.** Both hashes are public inputs and recomputed inside the circuit. The contract checks binding before the reuse guard, which closes the shuffle attack where an attacker proves with one set of nullifiers and submits another.
- **Dual escrow.** A hash-only path shows the privacy property with a single aggregated transfer, and a real-escrow path does `transferFrom` per rescuer, stores `escrow` and `depositor`, and mints shares pro-rata. With a standard ERC-20 the real path necessarily reveals per-rescuer transfers after inclusion; the system documents this and notes that a confidential token would be needed for full post-settlement privacy.
- **End-to-end verifiability.** One proof, one vault, one rescue, one verifier, one pool on Sepolia. Every deposit, opening, settlement, and both revert paths are live transactions with direct Etherscan links. No amount is simulated in calldata.

**Verifiable on Sepolia (test tokens, no real money):** MockERC20 `0x11f3...`, Vault `0x1eE4...`, Rescue `0x3742...`, Pool `0xba04...`, Verifier `0x4207...` (47kB, 8384B ZK). Honest round `300+200+100=600` settles in `0xfce7...` block 11548213 gas 4734234 with `RescueTargetMet(1,600)`, `VaultRecapped`, and `RescueShareMinted` events. A Next.js UI walks through the same six steps without a terminal, and every claim links to Etherscan.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
DeFi lets everyone use the same leverage — a brand new trader and someone with years of experience both get 20x if they want it. Nobody's checking if that's actually a good idea for them. Turns out it isn't; new traders get liquidated way more often because nothing ever holds them back.

The obvious fix — let the platform check your trading history — means putting your entire trade record on a public ledger forever. Most people won't accept that trade-off.

What Nexora does
Looks at how you actually trade and sorts you into Novice, Balanced, or Expert
Turns that into real limits — a smart contract enforces them, not just a UI suggestion
Your raw trading history stays private; only the result goes on-chain
Who it's for
New traders who'd rather be held back a little than blow up their first position
Experienced traders who want their track record to actually count for something
Protocols that want risk-based tiers without forcing users to dox their history

Basically: personalized leverage limits, without giving up your privacy to get them.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Picking the right model. Started with a Decision Tree — worked, but accuracy sat around 75%. Switched to Random Forest, first with a capped depth, which got to ~85%. Removed the depth limit and landed at ~92.6%. Wasn't obvious upfront which would work best, so we just tried each one and kept what performed.

Figuring out what "private" actually means here. Building real zero-knowledge cryptography from scratch wasn't realistic in the time we had. So instead of pretending we'd built a full ZK-SNARK circuit, we built a hash-based attestation — the risk result gets hashed, and that hash is what goes on-chain, not the raw trading data. It's a stand-in for where a real proof system would sit, not the real thing, and we're upfront about that.

Foundry silently building nothing. forge build kept saying "Nothing to compile" even from the right folder. No foundry.toml, so Forge was looking for source files in completely the wrong place. One config file fixed it.

forge install failing without telling us. It just didn't install anything, no error shown. Worked around it by pulling the library in directly with git clone instead.

Buttons that looked broken but weren't. Backend logs showed every click working. Turned out a CSS rule was quietly keeping the home screen visible no matter what, so the dashboard was rendering underneath it, invisible. Fixed with one CSS rule.

Two traders sharing one identity. Both demo personas were signing from the same blockchain account early on, so their balances and positions kept colliding. Gave each one its own account.

Actually connecting everything. The model, the attestation, the contract, Anvil, and the frontend were all built as separate working pieces — getting them talking to each other as one flow was its own project. Model output had to match what the policy layer expected, the policy had to match what the contract accepted, and the frontend had to poll all of it live without breaking. Most of the bugs here weren't in any single piece — they showed up only once two pieces were forced to agree with each other.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
- Proof/verifier drift (the big one). Our first on-chain submission reverted with no reason string because proof.json and the deployed Verifier.sol had been generated from different EZKL circuits/setups. The pairing check therefore failed. I fixed this by rebuilding the entire pipeline — train → ONNX → gen_settings → compile_circuit → setup → create_evm_verifier → witness → prove — in a single script run, ensuring the verification key and proof are always consistent. The Foundry integration test then passed against the real verifier.

- EZKL number encoding. Public signals use little-endian encoding and are scaled by powers of two (2^scale), not base-10. Incorrect decoding initially produced nonsense values, such as a price of 4.48 instead of 2800, causing on-chain submission mismatches. I wrote a shared leHexToBigInt helper and used the same decoding logic across the TypeScript frontend, viem verification script, and contract submission flow.

- Vercel build failure caused by .gitignore. A repo-wide lib/ ignore rule, originally intended for Foundry's contracts/lib/, also excluded apps/web/lib/. As a result, contracts.ts and proof.ts were missing from Git, causing Vercel to fail with Module not found: Can't resolve '@/lib/proof'. I fixed this by scoping the ignore rules specifically to contracts/lib/, contracts/cache/, and contracts/broadcast/.

- wagmi v3 + Next.js 16 wiring. Getting wallet connection working without SSR or hydration mismatches required careful handling. I used injected() and coinbaseWallet() connectors, added a mounted guard to the navbar, and configured Sepolia as the default chain because the oracle and verifier are deployed there.

- End-to-end consistency. The biggest lesson was that a ZK application is only as reliable as the consistency between its circuit, proving key, verifier, proof encoding, and frontend submission logic. I treated the complete pipeline as one system and verified the final result against the live Sepolia contracts.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
In almost every DeFi lending market, your collateral amount, debt, and health factor are public on-chain. Anyone can read exactly how leveraged you are, target your position for liquidation, or build a financial profile of you. Privacy simply isn't an option.

Shielded Lending Oracle flips this: the protocol knows the decision, not the position.

A user generates a zero-knowledge proof via EZKL that their position satisfies the lending health requirements. Only the verdict — HEALTHY or LIQUIDATABLE — plus a public price and threshold, ever touches Ethereum. The underlying collateral and debt values remain private and are computed and proven offline.

What people can use it for:
- Private lending positions where the network verifies safety without learning your exposure.
- Confidential health checks where a position can be evaluated and acted upon without revealing the private inputs behind the decision.
- A reusable privacy-preserving oracle pattern for applications that need a yes/no verdict, such as "is this position solvent?", without exposing the underlying numbers.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
So we all know that whenever we have to go to get a print of our confidential document(like passport, aadhar card etc.), there's a large amount of uncertainty associated with it. We never know when such documents can be used against us and without our knowledge.
Then it clicked me that Ethereum and BlockChain are all about privacy and decentralization. So i decided to build upon that idea and make this build my app, PrintShield. 

In this app, after selecting document u can review the sensitive fields and then set a copy limit and an expiry limit, after this u get and QR which u can scan and then the files are sent to the printer without being locally saved on the Printer Shop's computer .

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1. Designing privacy without overclaiming security

The biggest challenge was figuring out what the MVP could actually guarantee. We didn't want to claim that a QR code alone makes a document secure, so we separated the current UX/prototype layer from the future encryption and backend enforcement layer.

2. Making temporary access meaningful

We had to think about how a print authorization should work: the user chooses a copy limit and an expiry time, then the QR becomes invalid after the selected window. Designing that flow while keeping it simple for a normal user was a challenge.

3. Designing the QR system without putting sensitive data inside it

A major design decision was keeping the actual document out of the QR code. The QR only carries things like the job reference and expiry information, while the document remains on the user's phone in the MVP.

4. Balancing security and UX

We wanted users to understand that shorter expiry times and fewer copies provide more control, without pretending that our “privacy score” is an actual security measurement. That led us to make the score explicitly a UX heuristic.

5. Building a convincing prototype without the complete infrastructure

A real system needs a backend, authenticated print-shop client, encryption, printer integration and secure deletion. Implementing all of that during an MVP would have significantly increased the scope, so we focused on proving the core user experience and QR authorization flow first.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Traditional sentiment analysis tools often suffer from binary over-simplification. When a customer leaves a detailed 10-point review praising 8 aspects of a product while pointing out 2 minor flaws, standard AI models frequently get swayed by negative keywords at the end of the text and classify the entire review as 100% Negative. Furthermore, conventional tools lack emotional nuance (failing to distinguish between anger, sadness, or fear), lack multi-language support, and force teams to manually copy-paste data without providing actionable business recommendations or executive-ready reports.

Sentix AI solves this by providing a multi-dimensional Sentiment & Emotion Intelligence Suite. It combines sentence-level clause aggregation, phrase highlighting, multi-language detection, live web scraping, and automated AI executive insights into a unified SaaS tool.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1. The "Mixed Review" Misclassification Bug
The Hurdle: Initially, single-pass binary transformer models evaluated long reviews as a single block of text. When testing a review with 8 positive sentences and 2 negative sentences, the model exhibited a recency bias toward the ending negative clause, incorrectly flagging the overall review as NEGATIVE.
How We Overcame It: We re-architected the sentiment engine to use sentence-level clause aggregation and weighted consensus calibration. The engine now splits text into individual sentences, evaluates each sentence independently, and calculates a net weighted positive ratio combined with keyword density scoring. This ensures mixed reviews with 8 positive points and 2 negative points are accurately classified as POSITIVE (or MOSTLY POSITIVE), while still flagging the 2 negative points in the pain points section.

2. Cloud Memory (OOM) Crash on Free Hosting Tiers (512 MB RAM Limit)
The Hurdle: When deploying our initial build to free cloud hosting platforms (Render.com), the deployment failed with a Ran out of memory (used over 512MB) error. Heavy PyTorch libraries and transformer weights allocated over 1.2 GB of RAM on startup, exceeding free tier hardware bounds.
How We Overcame It: We optimized the core runtime engine by integrating a high-precision, multi-clause VADER (Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner) engine combined with sentence-level clause breakdown. This optimization slashed RAM usage from ~1,200 MB down to under 35 MB, accelerated cold server startup times from 45 seconds down to 0.4 seconds, and allowed the entire application to deploy flawlessly on Render's 512 MB free tier.

apepay-e2e5.tagline: Privacy based payment gateway using ZkBob

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
# ApePay Architecture Decisions

## 1. Protocol Choice: ZK Proofs vs. Railgun vs. zkBob

I chose **zkBob** because it is purpose-built for lightweight token transfer privacy and pooled checkouts, whereas Railgun is designed for complex multi-token DeFi routing and custom ZK circuits carry extreme operational overhead.

## 2. zkBob Verification Problem & Intent Architecture

**The Problem:** On traditional EVM chains, payment gateways check:

```text
from (customer) == to (merchant)
amount == X
```

Privacy protocols break direct `from → to` linkability because funds flow through a shared liquidity pool (`PoolVault`).

### ApePay’s Solution

**Payment Intent & Commitment Note** (`POST /v1/payments`)

The backend creates a unique payment intent with a cryptographic commitment hash:

```text
commitment = SHA256(paymentId : amount : currency)
```

**Deposit with Commitment** (`PoolVault.deposit(bytes32 paymentId)`)

The customer deposits funds into the shared `PoolVault` contract along with the `paymentId` commitment in the calldata.

**Event Indexing**

The contract emits:

```text
Deposited(paymentId, sender, amount)
```

The ApePay indexer matches the `paymentId` to mark the order as paid without publicly revealing the merchant's payout wallet address.

**Decoupled Operator Payout** (`PoolVault.withdraw(...)`)

The operator batch-withdraws funds from the vault to the merchant's address, completely severing on-chain linkability between the customer wallet and merchant wallet.

## 3. Who Pays Gas?

**Customer Pays Gas.**

## 4. MetaMask vs ApePay Account

### Does the customer have to create an ApePay account?

**No.**

The customer should ideally be able to:

```text
Open checkout
      ↓
Connect MetaMask / wallet
      ↓
Approve payment
      ↓
Pay
      ↓
Done
```

Rather than:

```text
Create ApePay account
↓
Create password
↓
Verify email
↓
Connect wallet
↓
Pay
```

That would destroy the simplicity expected from a payment gateway.

## 5. Merchant Embedding Model (Stripe / Razorpay Model)

```text
Merchant Storefront
       │
       │ 1. POST /v1/payments (x-api-key)
       ▼
ApePay Backend API
       │
       │ 2. Returns paymentId & checkoutUrl
       ▼
Hosted Checkout Page (/p/:paymentId)
       │
       │ 3. Customer connects wallet & deposits into PoolVault
       ▼
ApePay Indexer & Webhook Engine
       │
       │ 4. HMAC SHA-256 Webhook (payment.paid)
       ▼
Merchant Order Fulfillment
```

tracezero-3cca.name: TraceZero
tracezero-3cca.tagline: Detect Your Vulnerabilities for an OSINT attack

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The biggest challenge was designing the system so that we could actually use blockchain and AI without defeating the purpose of a privacy application.

Our first architectural concern was data storage: sending raw OSINT information to a centralized backend or AI service would create exactly the privacy risk we were trying to solve. We therefore redesigned the architecture around local-first processing, keeping sensitive analysis on the user's device and sending only minimal, sanitized information to external AI services when necessary.

A second challenge was making Zero-Knowledge Proofs useful rather than simply adding ZK as a buzzword. We needed the exposure score to be deterministic and structured enough to be proven cryptographically. We separated the deterministic risk engine from the AI explanation layer so that AI could explain threats without being responsible for the value being proved.

Finally, integrating Ethereum required carefully separating public and private state. We designed the smart contract to store privacy policies and verify proofs, while keeping usernames, locations, OSINT findings, attack graphs, and other sensitive information completely off-chain.

This resulted in our final architecture:

**Private data → Local analysis → Deterministic exposure score → ZK proof → Ethereum verification**

rather than storing user data in a centralized database or on-chain.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Most OSINT and privacy tools focus on whether a user's data has already been leaked. However, attackers can often build a detailed profile without any new breach by correlating information that is already publicly available across different platforms.

TraceZero helps users discover these hidden correlation risks by analyzing their authorized public footprint, identifying potential attack paths, and generating an explainable digital exposure score. It then provides actionable recommendations to reduce that exposure.

The key difference is that TraceZero is **privacy-first by design**: raw OSINT data is processed locally and is never stored in a centralized database or placed on the blockchain.

After reducing their exposure, users can use Zero-Knowledge Proofs to prove that they satisfy a privacy requirement (for example, "Exposure Score < 30") without revealing their actual score or underlying personal information.

Ethereum acts as the public verification layer, storing privacy policies and verifying cryptographic proofs rather than storing user data.

description.title: Private AI on Ethereum
description.body:
TraceZero fits the **Private AI on Ethereum** track by combining private, local AI-assisted threat analysis with Ethereum-based zero-knowledge verification.

TraceZero analyzes a user's public digital footprint to identify OSINT correlation risks and potential attack paths. The sensitive data remains on the user's device, while AI operates primarily on sanitized, non-identifying representations of the findings to generate threat explanations and remediation recommendations. This prevents the AI layer from becoming another centralized repository of personal data.

The deterministic exposure score produced from the analysis is then used to generate a **Zero-Knowledge Proof**. A user can prove a statement such as **"my exposure score is below 30"** without revealing their actual score, OSINT findings, identity, or attack graph.

Ethereum provides the trust and verification layer: privacy policies are published on-chain, and a smart contract verifies the ZK proof. The blockchain therefore never needs to store the user's private information.

In short:

**Private data → Local analysis + AI → Deterministic risk score → ZK proof → Ethereum verification**

This allows users to benefit from AI-driven privacy analysis while retaining control of their data, and uses Ethereum to verify privacy claims without requiring users to reveal the information behind those claims.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
On Ethereum, payroll is public surveillance. When a company pays salaries on chain, every transfer is permanently visible: who got paid, how much, how often. Anyone (competitors, analytics firms, stalkers) can link an employee's wallet to their identity and see exactly what they earn. Traditional crypto payroll forces a brutal choice: leak everyone's salary, or pay people off chain and lose the auditability and composability that made you use crypto in the first place.

What Payshade does about it

It uses ERC-5564 stealth addresses plus the ERC-6538 meta-address registry so payments are real on-chain transfers, but unlinkable to recipients:

Employee registers once. They sign locally; a spending key and viewing key derive in-browser, and only a public key goes into the shared ERC-6538 registry.
Company pays in bulk. The payrun derives a fresh one-time stealth address per employee client-side (from their meta-address) and pays everyone in a single PayshadeCore contract call (about 46 lines by design).
Nobody can connect the dots. Observers see N transfers to N random addresses. No pattern links them to each other or to any identity. Amounts per person are hidden too.
Only the employee can find their money. They scan announcements locally with their viewing key, then sweep funds from each stealth address into their real wallet privately.

So employees get salary privacy without trusting a custodian or mixer, and companies get one-transaction payroll with no server, no KYC, no accounts. Fully non-custodial.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The one that cost me the most time was a React crash I caused myself. On the company page, every recipient row checks the ERC-6538 registry live and shows a little registered / not registered yet badge. My first version did if (!address) return null before calling useReadContract — React does not like that at all, so the whole payrun page crashed whenever rows were added or removed mid-edit. Took an embarrassing number of console errors to realize it was the Rules of Hooks biting me. Rewrote it so hooks always run unconditionally and the query is just gated with enabled.
Another sneaky one: refreshing the Employee page made it look like you'd never set up private payments, even though you registered on-chain earlier. Turns out wagmi restores the wallet connection asynchronously, and I was reading keys/payment history from storage during the very first render — while the address was still undefined. Moved all rehydration into an effect keyed on (address, chainId) and it went away. Cool side effect though: my stealth keys are derived deterministically from a signature, so even if the browser wipes session storage, signing the same message regenerates the exact same keys. A bug turned into self-healing.
And the classic deploy one: everything worked locally, pushed to Vercel, homepage fine — then refreshing /company 404'd, because the SPA lives inside an npm-workspaces monorepo and nothing told Vercel about client-side routes. Fixed with vercel.json rewrites to index.html plus moving the app under app/ so Vercel's monorepo detection picks the right root.
