avtarai-5341.name: Avtar.ai
avtarai-5341.tagline: Meter every call. Settle once on Base.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Agent-to-agent API payments have no workable settlement layer at the volume agents actually operate at.

On-chain per call is too expensive. An agent buying weather data, a price feed, a translation is each call is worth fractions of a cent, but a Base transaction costs real gas regardless of what it's for. Settling every call on-chain means the fee dwarfs the price. Nobody does that.

Off-chain invoicing has no enforcement. The alternative is meter calls, bill monthly, trust the total — works between humans who have relationships and recourse. It doesn't work between autonomous agents transacting with counterparties they've never dealt with before and have no legal claim against. There's nothing stopping either side from disputing the number afterward, and no cheap way to prove who's right.

What exists in between (x402) only solves discovery and per-call authorization — a provider quotes a price, a consumer presents payment, the call proceeds. It doesn't solve the settlement problem: paying per call is exactly the on-chain-cost problem above, restated.

Avtar.ai closes that gap. The consumer locks escrow once. Calls are metered locally against it — no transaction, no signature, no gas per call. When the channel closes, one Groth16 proof establishes exactly what's owed, and one transaction pays the provider and refunds the rest. The proof is what replaces trust: the amount is provably correct without either party needing to believe the other's ledger, and without publishing the call count, the rate, or what the calls were for.

So the shape of the problem is: agents need to pay each other at machine speed and machine volume, with cryptographic settlement instead of either prohibitive gas costs or unenforceable trust 

## Disclosure

The settlement design which is meter off-chain, prove the total with Groth16, settle
once was first built and proven out on Stellar/Soroban before being adapted for Base. Everything in this repository is a from-scratch implementation for Base: new Solidity contracts, a new TypeScript SDK, a new Foundry test suite, and a rewritten circuit
address-binding scheme (BN254 hi/lo limbs in place of 32-byte Stellar
strkeys). No Soroban code, dependency, or artifact is present here.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1.⁠ ⁠A stale proving key silently broke every settlement. The verifier is deployed immutably into the escrow's constructor, generated from a specific proving key. When the local key got regenerated, every proof came back a bare InvalidProof() — no clue why. We traced it to a bytecode diff between the committed verifier and what was actually deployed, then redeployed the full stack from the matching key.

2.⁠ ⁠Public RPC endpoints disagreed on account state mid-transaction. sepolia.base.org load-balances across nodes that don't agree on nonces, so opening a channel (three transactions in a row) would fail partway with nonce too low — a transient infra issue that read like a client bug. Fixed by switching to a steadier endpoint and adding a retry that reads the nonce the chain's own rejection names, instead of re-querying an inconsistent source.

3.⁠ ⁠Solidity and TypeScript had to encode addresses identically, with no automatic check that they did. BN254 field elements can't hold a full address, so each one is split into hi/lo limbs on both sides of the stack independently. A one-character drift between the two implementations would fail silently at settlement, not at compile time. Solved with a shared test vector that pins both implementations to the same expected output, so a mismatch fails in CI.

4.⁠ ⁠The escrow contract has no per-channel balance — only per-depositor. A dashboard trying to show "how much is locked for this channel" was actually reading the depositor's total pooled balance across every channel they'd ever opened, which looks right until two channels are open at once. Fixed by sourcing the per-channel figure from the agent's own session state, since the chain genuinely doesn't track it.

description.title: Private Wallets and Payments
description.body:
## Why this track

Paying per API call on-chain would leak how often an agent is used, what it costs, and how much moved. avtar.ai hides that traffic:

- Open: approve USDC, pin terms, deposit escrow.
- Meter: thousands of HTTP calls, none of them a transaction.
- Settle: one USDC payout, capped by escrow. Call count and rate are not public signals in a way that reconstructs the session log. Usage volume and pricing never go on-chain.

Sender, recipient, and amount of each call are not published. Observers see a channel open and a later settlement, not the commercial graph between agents. That is the payment-privacy property this track asks for, applied to agent-to-agent APIs rather than a retail wallet UI.

description.title: Private AI on Ethereum
description.body:
## Why this track

Avtar.ai is an AI agent commerce stack whose settlement is a Groth16 proof on Base.

A consumer agent picks tools (weather, crypto price, translation, or real function-calling when an OpenAI key is set), meters each call off-chain over x402, then produces a cryptographically verifiable close: `settle(a, b, c, publicSignals)` checks the proof, the registry confirms the parties, a nullifier stops replay, and the escrow pays out.

The model never has to leave a device for the privacy claim to hold. Prompts, tool names, and call count stay off-chain. What Ethereum sees is a proof of what is owed, matching this track's requirement for an output that is cryptographically verifiable on-chain.

Deployed on Base Sepolia with a working dashboard that shows the live meter and the thirteen public signals.

description.title: Overall
description.body:
## Why overall

This is a shipped privacy app, not a slide deck:

- Solidity escrow, agent registry, and Groth16 verifier on Base Sepolia

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: When an AI agent executes critical operations accessing funds, signing transactions, or managing sensitive data there is no trustless way to verify that its code hasn't been tampered with, that it's running on genuine secure hardware, or that its security posture is current

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The hardest bug was invisible to every unit test.

Our AgentRegistry contract calls Automata's DCAP verifier to validate TDX hardware quotes. We had 20 passing Foundry tests but the first real deployment silently failed every time with "execution reverted for unknown reason" and zero decodable error data.

The root cause: we had declared verifyAndAttestOnChain as view in our interface. Automata's real function is external payable  it writes state. Solidity compiled our call as a STATICCALL, which the EVM silently reverts the moment the callee touches storage. No revert data. No useful error. Three different RPC providers, same result.

We diagnosed it by splitting the call: calling verifyAndAttestOnChain directly from an EOA (no STATICCALL restriction) succeeded; calling certify() from our contract failed every time. One word change removing view fixed it. We then made the mock's callCount actually increment, so this class of bug fails a unit test if it ever regresses.

Getting TDX attestation right on real hardware was the second challenge. The report_data mode (raw vs sha256), the exact byte offset of report_data in the quote (568), and whether Automata's verifier would actually accept a real quote none of these could be confirmed from documentation alone. We had to spin up a GCP c3-standard-4 TDX Confidential VM, pull a real quote via configfs-tsm, and verify each assumption empirically against the live on-chain verifier

description.title: Private AI on Ethereum
description.body:
Rime is built across five interconnected tracks:

Shared Core (packages/shared) Defines the canonical manifest schema, deterministic hashing, and thereport_data commitment encoding that every other layer depends on.

Scanner (packages/scanner) Walks the dependency tree, runs six security heuristics, and wraps OSV/npm-audit to produce an AuditManifest with a tamper-evident auditHash.

Contracts (contracts) On-chain enforcement via AgentRegistry (TDX quote verification + report_data binding + freshness window) and GatedVault (access gating), deployed on Base Sepolia.

Agent Runtime (packages/agent) Runs inside a TDX enclave, performs a boot-time self-check against the baked-in manifest, and heartbeats certify() on-chain every 25 minutes.

Web Dashboard (web) React status page showing live certificate freshness countdowns and client-side audit hash re-verification against on-chain state

aegis-2a33.name: Aegis
aegis-2a33.tagline: Private by Design. Relentless by Nature.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
### 1. An attestation proves what was decided, not what was done

We realized that proving an AI decision doesn't guarantee the executor actually follows it. Our allocation was correctly hashed, attested, and recorded on-chain, but the trading code was still executing a fixed swap.

We fixed this by making `plan_rebalance` derive the trade directly from the attested allocation. It compares current holdings with the target and closes the largest gap. The caller can cap the trade size, but cannot choose the trade direction.

### 2. Finding a model small enough, but good enough

One of the harder parts was finding a model that was small enough to run comfortably inside the enclave while still being capable of making reasonable trading decisions. Larger models gave better reasoning, but increased memory usage and inference time, which isn't ideal for a constrained environment.

We tested smaller models and found that some struggled with basic allocation and reasoning tasks, while larger models were more capable but harder to fit within our constraints. We eventually settled on **Qwen 2.5 3B**, which gave us a good balance between model capability, inference time, and the resource constraints of the enclave.

### 3. Making private settlement observable enough to debug

Shielded transactions are great for privacy but make debugging much harder because you can't simply look at a public wallet balance and see what happened. We had to build our own execution checks around transaction receipts, events, and shielded-state updates so the system could verify that a trade actually settled without exposing the portfolio itself.

### 4. Testnet has no private mempool to hide in

We built private transaction submission to prevent swaps from sitting in the public mempool, but found it wasn't useful on Sepolia because there are effectively no MEV builders there. We sampled **60 blocks and found zero MEV-builder blocks**, while mainnet had **22 of 30**.

So Aegis chooses the submission route based on the chain: **private on mainnet, public on Sepolia**, while reporting the actual execution price and surrounding swap activity instead of claiming protection that the network can't provide. The **unshield → swap → reshield** process remains atomic either way.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## What Aegis is

Aegis is an **automated crypto trading agent**. You deposit funds, and on a schedule it reads market data, decides how to split your portfolio across five assets, and makes the trade that moves you closest to that target. A robo-advisor, essentially.

Two things make it different from every other trading bot:

- It runs inside a **secure enclave**, a hardware-isolated part of the processor that can produce a cryptographic receipt proving exactly which code and which AI model produced a decision. That receipt gets written to a smart contract before any money moves.
- It trades inside a **shielded pool (Railgun)**, where balances are encrypted commitments rather than public numbers. Your positions never appear on the blockchain.

## Why that combination matters

Most trading bots are a black box with a Twitter account. You hand over funds, get a performance chart, and take the operator's word that the strategy is what they claimed. Nothing stops them from swapping the model out or rewriting the story after a bad week.

The obvious fix is to put the bot on-chain, where everything is public and verifiable. But that trades one problem for a worse one: your entries, your sizing, and eventually your whole strategy become a public document that anyone can read and trade against.

So you're stuck picking between **trustworthy but exposed** and **private but unverifiable**.

**Aegis gets both. You can verify the agent did what it said. You can't see what it holds.**

## Who'd use it

- **A DAO or small fund** whose members need the treasury strategy to be auditable, without publishing every position to competitors.
- **Anyone delegating to a bot without handing over custody.** The agent signs with a key restricted to one function on one contract with zero ETH attached — and that contract has no ability to move a token. It's not that we trust it not to steal; **it structurally can't.**
- **Users who need compliance without surveillance.** Every trade passes a sanctions-list check before it can execute, proving the funds aren't tainted without revealing which funds they are.

patchproof-5137.name: PatchProof
patchproof-5137.tagline: Trust your AI? Trust your AI.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
AI can write code incredibly fast, but it can also confidently make a change that looks correct without actually being correct.

ProofPatch makes that process safer. Developers can ask an AI to fix a bug, add a feature, or make a security change, while ProofPatch independently checks what actually changed, makes sure protected tests were not tampered with, runs the tests, and records the evidence.

Instead of asking “Can I trust what the AI said?”, developers can ask “Can I verify what actually happened?”

For teams, this means safer AI-assisted development, easier code reviews, and a permanent cryptographic record of verified changes that can be anchored to Ethereum for later verification.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The hardest part was making sure the AI couldn't simply change the tests to make itself look correct.

At first, the verification loop treated a newly created test file differently from an existing one. That created an edge case where an AI could potentially introduce or modify test code and then pass verification.

I had to rethink the baseline: what existed before the AI started making changes had to be captured first and protected throughout the entire run. I also added checks to make sure the actual files on disk matched what the AI originally proposed.

Another hurdle was making the system handle failures honestly. If the AI claimed that everything worked but the independent test run failed, the evidence had to win over the AI's claim.

I eventually built the verification flow around a simple rule:

The AI can propose. It cannot decide whether its own work is correct.

That became the foundation of PatchProof.

description.title: Private AI on Ethereum
description.body:
ProofPatch is built around a simple problem: AI can make changes to private codebases, but the result still needs to be independently trusted.

The AI runs locally through Ollama/Qwen, so the source code being analyzed and modified does not need to be sent to a cloud AI provider. This makes ProofPatch useful for proprietary code, internal tools, and sensitive repositories where privacy matters.

ProofPatch then creates a cryptographic SHA-256 commitment over the verification evidence. That commitment can be anchored to Ethereum, along with metadata about the verification run.

Ethereum does not decide whether the code is correct. Instead, it acts as a public, tamper-evident timestamp and verification anchor for the proof.

So the flow is:

Private code → Local AI → Independent verification → Evidence → SHA-256 commitment → Ethereum

This gives us the combination the track is looking for:

Private AI: the coding agent can run locally without exposing the repository to a third-party AI service.
Verifiable AI actions: ProofPatch checks what the AI actually changed rather than trusting its response.
Ethereum: the resulting proof commitment can be anchored on-chain so it can be referenced and verified later.
Long-term trust: even after the AI run is over, there is a cryptographic record showing what was verified at that point in time.

In short: ProofPatch keeps the AI work private, but makes the proof of that work publicly verifiable.

veilswap-c01f.name: Veilswap
veilswap-c01f.tagline: A live searcher bot attacks a real trade, on chain

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
A swap on Ethereum is public before it settles. A searcher reads it in the mempool, buys
ahead, lets it fill at the worse price, then sells back. the trade succeeds, the trader
just gets less. VeilSwap makes that cost visible, then removes it.

Same 10 WETH trade, one live pool, two ways:
- Public mempool trader gets 82,816 MEME (quoted 90,909), bot takes 0.9707 WETH.
- Sealed commit-reveal trader gets the full 90,909. Bot takes nothing.

A third route, batch clearing, hides the settled trade too: offsetting orders net against
each other and never touch the pool — 71% of submitted order flow produces zero on-chain
swaps. Nothing is mocked; every number comes from Solidity on a live chain, and the
sandwich matches the Session 1 workshop lab to the wei.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Our own bot broke the design twice. The commit is opaque, but reveal() has to publish the
order in calldata — the bot read it and front-ran the reveal itself for 0.6977 WETH.
Fixed by anchoring execution to the price at commit time.

Batch settlement was worse: settleBatch() read the live price, so whoever called it could
move the pool and settle in the same transaction. One run took 2.965 WETH and cost an
honest buyer 30% of their fill. Fixed by anchoring to the price when the batch opened.

The fuzzer caught a wrong claim too — we said the pool never sees more than the buy side;
it broke that in 12 runs. The real bound is the imbalance between both sides, not either
one.

Hosting was its own problem: the demo needs instant blocks, funded signers, and
evm_revert to reset state, which no public testnet gives. Solved by running the same
Anvil chain in a container behind a URL instead.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Ethereum is a fully public ledger — every transaction, balance, and wallet address is permanently visible to anyone. Once a wallet is linked to a person's identity even once, their entire financial history (salary, donations, business payments) is exposed forever. This is a major barrier to using Ethereum for everyday, business, or sensitive payments.

BEARS solves this by letting users send and receive ETH through one-time stealth addresses (ERC-5564) instead of their real wallet address. The sender generates a fresh, one-time address tied to the recipient's public stealth meta-address; on-chain, it looks like a payment to a random new address with no visible link to the recipient. The transaction remains fully valid and verifiable by the network — blockchain's core trust guarantees are untouched — but no outside observer, chain analyst, or advertiser can trace the payment back to the recipient's identity or spending history.

People can use BEARS to receive salaries, donations, or business payments privately, without exposing their full financial history to anyone who looks up their wallet address.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
We started this hackathon as complete beginners to blockchain development, with no prior Solidity experience. Our biggest early challenge was deciding how to implement stealth addresses without deep cryptography knowledge — we initially considered writing our own privacy contract from scratch, which would have been unrealistic in the timeframe.

We solved this by discovering and integrating the canonical, already-deployed ERC-5564 Announcer and ERC-6538 Registry contracts on Sepolia, along with the official @scopelift/stealth-address-sdk. This let us focus our limited time on correctly integrating a proven, audited standard rather than reinventing cryptographic primitives.

On the frontend, we hit a bug where our "Disconnect Wallet" button only appeared on the home page and disappeared when navigating to other screens, due to the header being duplicated across pages without the button included everywhere. We traced this to the page-routing logic and fixed it by adding the disconnect handler consistently across all page views.

We also ran into a payment-scanning issue where the app initially failed to detect real stealth payments due to block-range and RPC timing issues, which we resolved by adjusting the announcement scanner's block range logic.

As a 3-person team of blockchain beginners, coordinating git workflows, environment setup, and debugging Windows-specific PowerShell issues alongside the actual privacy tech was itself a real challenge — but it taught all three of us practical, end-to-end Web3 development in under a week.

description.title: Private Wallets and Payments
description.body: BEARS is a wallet application built specifically for the Private Wallets and Payments track. It lets users send and receive ETH such that sending and receiving money does not leak the sender, recipient, or amount — using stealth addresses (ERC-5564), where every payment goes to a fresh, one-time address that only the intended recipient can detect and claim. The transaction remains fully valid and verifiable on-chain, but no outside observer can link it to the recipient's real identity or wallet history, directly addressing the track's goal of private wallets and payments.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## Issuer key vs address
We first stored a **wallet address** as `ISSUER_PRIVATE_KEY`. Signing failed until we used the real 64-character hex key on Vercel.

## Unique vs alias URLs
CLI deploys created one-off Vercel URLs that never updated. We always demo **https://silent-council-six.vercel.app**.

## One mock email for every wallet
Early mock verify used the same demo email, so the second wallet hit `already_verified` without being registered. We switched to a unique mock email per wallet.

## Onchain vs database
The UI could show verified from the contract while `/api/vote` only checked Supabase. Vote now recovers the nullifier from chain if the row is missing.

## Honest ZK vs OTP
Live demo uses a fast verify path plus OTP fallback. OTP is **not** zero-knowledge. We say that in the README and in the pitch.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## Problem

proofchain-8386.name: ProofChain
proofchain-8386.tagline: Prove it existed. Keep it private.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
### Keeping Proof IDs Correct After Filtering

The smart contract stores proofs in a single array, while the dashboard only displays proofs belonging to the connected wallet. Initially, filtering the list could cause the displayed array index to differ from the actual on-chain proof ID. This created a risk of generating verification links for the wrong proof.

We solved this by preserving the original contract index before filtering:

```ts
allProofs
  .map((proof, index) => ({ ...proof, contractId: index }))
  .filter((proof) => proof.owner.toLowerCase() === address.toLowerCase());
```

Every dashboard item now links to its original on-chain ID, ensuring that verification always opens the correct proof.

### Handling Incorrect Wallet Networks

Users may connect their wallet while being on Ethereum Mainnet or another network instead of Sepolia. Transactions would fail or be sent to the wrong network.

We added network detection before submission. When the connected wallet is on the wrong network, ProofChain requests a switch to Ethereum Sepolia and prevents the transaction from continuing until the correct network is selected.

### Uploading Files Without Exposing API Credentials

Pinata requires API credentials, but exposing those credentials in frontend code would create a security risk. We solved this by routing uploads through a server-side Next.js API endpoint. The browser sends the file to `/api/pinata`, and the server forwards it to Pinata using credentials stored in environment variables.

This keeps the credentials off the client while still providing upload progress and clear error states in the interface.

### Handling Blockchain and Upload Delays

IPFS uploads and blockchain confirmations are asynchronous and can take different amounts of time. We added separate loading and status states for uploading, transaction submission, network switching, and confirmation. This makes the workflow clearer and prevents users from accidentally submitting duplicate transactions while a previous action is still pending.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Important digital documents can be modified, replaced, or disputed after they are created. Proving that a specific contract, design, research file, invoice, or creative work existed at a particular time usually requires trusting a centralized service or sharing the entire document.

ProofChain makes this process easier and safer by storing only a document’s fingerprint, title, wallet address, and timestamp on Ethereum. The original file remains off-chain, while anyone with the proof link can independently verify that the registered fingerprint matches the document.

People can use ProofChain to:

- Prove authorship and priority of creative work, designs, code, manuscripts, or research.
- Record versions of contracts, NDAs, invoices, and compliance documents.
- Timestamp intellectual property disclosures and confidential business files.
- Verify that a document has not been altered since it was registered.
- Share tamper-resistant proof without relying on a central authority.
- Replace manual email trails, screenshots, or third-party timestamping services with a transparent on-chain record.

ProofChain does not publish the document contents on Ethereum. It anchors the document’s identity and existence, allowing users to prove **when** a file existed without unnecessarily exposing **what** is inside it.

description.title: Overall
description.body:
ProofChain is a privacy-focused proof-of-existence dApp built on Ethereum Sepolia.

It allows users to upload a document to IPFS and register its fingerprint, title, wallet address, and timestamp on-chain. The document itself is not stored on Ethereum, so users can prove that a specific file existed at a particular time without unnecessarily exposing its contents.

ProofChain makes existing workflows safer and easier for contracts, NDAs, research, creative work, invoices, and compliance documents. Instead of relying on email histories, screenshots, or a centralized timestamping service, users can share a verification link that anyone can independently validate through Ethereum.

The project demonstrates how Ethereum can act as a trusted, tamper-resistant anchor for real-world documents while following a minimal-disclosure approach.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
*For the demo video, please check the README file in the GitHub repo linked.*[](url)
2-demo videos
https://youtu.be/QFrrM6-IdZQ
https://youtu.be/aC4ShfRYFS0

**Problem Statement**

Freelancing platforms like Upwork solve a basic trust problem between clients and freelancers: the client doesn't want to pay before seeing the work, while the freelancer doesn't want to work without knowing they'll be paid. For fixed-price work, Upwork addresses this by having the client fund a milestone upfront and holding those funds until the freelancer submits the work and the client approves it.

However, this model introduces a centralized intermediary. For example, if a client hires a freelancer for $500, the platform sits between both parties, holds the funds, manages the release process, and handles disputes. The platform also charges service-related fees.

There is a second problem when these interactions move to public blockchains: financial activity becomes highly visible. If a client pays a freelancer 0.5 ETH, the transaction can expose the wallets involved, the amount transferred, and potentially allow anyone to study their broader on-chain financial activity.

**Our Solution**

VeilEscrow combines the familiar idea of freelance escrow with blockchain-based automation and privacy.

Imagine a client hires a freelancer to build a website for 0.5 ETH.

Instead of sending the money directly to the freelancer:

Client → VeilEscrow Smart Contract → Freelancer

the client deposits the 0.5 ETH into a smart contract. The contract holds the funds and enforces the job's rules:

Create Job → Submit Work → Approve → Release Payment

If the freelancer submits the work and the client approves it, the contract releases the payment automatically according to the predefined rules. If there is a dispute, the funds remain locked while the dispute process takes place.

This removes the need for a traditional platform to manually control the escrowed funds.

But VeilEscrow also addresses the privacy problem.

Alongside the escrow system, we integrate a Railgun-powered private payment module. Users can shield public ETH into private WETH, transfer it privately using zero-knowledge proofs, and later unshield it back to a public address.

So instead of exposing a straightforward public transaction like:

Client wallet → 0.5 ETH → Freelancer wallet

the private payment layer demonstrates how the financial movement can occur without exposing the normal sender-recipient-amount relationship.

In short, VeilEscrow combines two properties that traditional freelance platforms and ordinary public blockchains handle separately:

Escrow: "The money is protected until the agreed conditions are met."
Privacy: "The financial activity does not have to be publicly exposed."

The current hackathon version demonstrates these two systems independently—JobEscrow on Anvil and private payments through Railgun on Sepolia—with the next step being to cryptographically connect private payments to individual escrow jobs.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges Faced
Connecting two very different blockchain systems
The biggest architectural challenge was keeping the freelance escrow logic and private payment system separate while figuring out how they could eventually work together. The escrow contract runs on Anvil, while Railgun operates on Sepolia, creating a clear network and integration boundary.
Designing the escrow state machine
We had to carefully define how a job moves through Created → Submitted → Approved/Disputed → Resolved, while ensuring that only the correct party can perform each action. This included handling edge cases like repeated approvals, unauthorized actions, and disputes raised at different stages.
Building a fair dispute mechanism
Escrow becomes more complicated when the client and freelancer disagree. We implemented a response window, allowed the other party to submit a response, and added an owner-based resolution mechanism. Handling the case where the other party doesn't respond required a separate claim flow.
Integrating Railgun's client-side ZK system
Getting private payments working wasn't simply a normal blockchain transaction. We had to initialize the Railgun WASM engine, synchronize private balances, generate zero-knowledge proofs in the browser, and handle shield, private transfer, and unshield operations.
Managing privacy without losing usability
The private wallets are deliberately ephemeral for the demo. This means their keys cannot simply be persisted like a normal wallet, while the UI still needs to clearly communicate balances, addresses, transaction states, and the risk of losing access after a page reload.
Handling multiple networks in one application
The same frontend operates across Anvil for escrow and Sepolia for Railgun. We therefore needed network-aware UI and safeguards so that users don't accidentally attempt an escrow transaction on Sepolia or a Railgun operation on Anvil.
Understanding what should actually be public vs private
A major design challenge was deciding what the escrow contract should know and what Railgun should hide. The contract needs to know things like the job status and who can approve or resolve it, while the actual payment movement should remain private.
The hardest unresolved challenge: linking private payment to escrow
The current system demonstrates escrow and private payments independently. The difficult next step is proving that a specific private Railgun payment actually funds a specific escrow job, without revealing the payment amount or parties publicly. This is where the commitment/verification architecture becomes necessary.

description.title: Private Wallets and Payments
description.body: We use Railgun’s client-side ZK system to enable private payments: public ETH is shielded into private WETH, transferred privately between Railgun wallets, and later unshielded back to a public 0x address, with zero-knowledge proofs generated locally in the browser using WASM. For the demo, we generate two disposable Railgun wallets (A and B) in memory using RailgunSigner.random(). Their private keys are never stored in localStorage or environment variables, and each wallet gets its own 0zk... address.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**Technical/integration challenges**

*Reconciling two independently-designed pieces.* Person A's real ZK circuit used a different public-input structure than the contract originally assumed, 5 values instead of 4, hospitals identified by BabyJubJub public keys instead of Ethereum addresses, payouts in paise instead of wei. HealthInsurancePolicy.sol had to be substantially rewritten to match, while preserving a backward-compatible legacy path for the old test suite.
*Bridging an off-chain currency to on-chain value*. The circuit proves amounts in Indian paise (integer math, no oracle dependency inside the proof itself), but settlement happens in ETH. Solved with a Chainlink price feed doing the paise→wei conversion after verification, so the proof never depends on live price data.
A soundness gap in the circuit itself. The deductible, co-pay, and coverage-limit values used inside the ZK proof are private circuit inputs, the contract has no public signal to check them against the policy's actual on-chain terms. This means a proof could currently be built against fabricated deductible/coverage numbers and still verify. Not yet fixed, needs either exposing those values publicly or committing to them cryptographically.
*A front-running vulnerability in the legacy settlement contract*. ClaimPayoutChainlink.sol's settleClaim let any caller name an arbitrary beneficiary address, meaning a public proof sitting in the mempool could be front-run by someone else redirecting the payout to themselves. Turned out to be dead code (not called from anywhere in the deployed path), but was a real design flaw caught during review.
*Constructor signature drift breaking the test suite.* Adding the Chainlink price feed changed HealthInsurancePolicy's constructor from one argument to two, and the existing test fixture wasn't updated, all 13 tests failed at the deploy step until the fixture was fixed.
*Non-ceremony trusted setups on both ZK pipelines*. Both the claim circuit's Groth16 zkey and the premium pipeline's KZG SRS were generated locally rather than via a real multi-party ceremony, a known, disclosed limitation rather than a "real" trust-minimization guarantee.

**Team/scoping challenge**

*Correctly framing what problem is actually being solved*. The initial instinct, that ZK proofs prevent an insurer from secretly overcharging on premiums, turned out to be legally redundant (contract law already covers that). The real, sharper insight (from Aditya) was that the actual value is on the claims side, removing an insurer's discretion to deny a legitimate claim. That reframing changed the whole pitch.
Tracking what's actually built vs. designed-but-missing. At one point the premium/underwriting side looked completely unbuilt, no model, no proof pipeline, nothing. A later delivery (the EZKL FastAPI backend) closed that gap.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
**Health insurance has a trust problem that costs people their privacy, their money, and their time.**

Today's system forces an impossible trade-off, i.e., to get coverage at all, you must surrender your raw medical records to insurers, data that then sits in centralized databases vulnerable to breaches, and can be used to price against you. Then, when you actually need care, claims crawl through weeks of manual adjudication, where legitimate claims get rejected behind non-transparent processes no patient can audit. The entire industry runs on the mistreated assumption that someone must see your private data in order to trust you.

**ProofSure removes that assumption entirely by replacing trust with cryptographic proof.**

On the **underwriting side**, the pricing model runs locally in the client's browser via ONNX runtime, user's sensitive health inputs never leave the device, and are never persisted anywhere. A zero-knowledge ML proof (EZKL) then demonstrates to the insurer that the premium was computed honestly using their exact approved model, bound on-chain by its hash so neither side can cheat ensuring patients don't fake inputs and insurers don't secretly swap pricing models.

On the **claims side**, hospitals sign itemized invoices with EdDSA keys authorized on-chain, and a Groth16 circuit proves five facts simultaneously: the hospital is authorized, the treatment is covered, the expense sum is correct, the deductible/co-pay formula was applied honestly, and the payout respects coverage bounds. Zero medical details touch the chain.

Finally, **settlement is automatic** because, the smart contract verifies the proof, enforces nullifier-based replay protection so no invoice can ever be claimed twice, converts INR to ETH through a price oracle, and pays out instantly.

The result is that no medical data breaches because there's no central trove of medical data; no opaque rejections because verification is mathematical; no waiting weeks for payouts. Payouts now happen in seconds.

description.title: Private AI on Ethereum
description.body: ProofSure's premium underwriting pipeline uses AI in a privacy-preserving way that satisfies both paths this track allows. Client-side, the risk model runs entirely locally in the browser via ONNX Runtime Web, so a user's health and financial data never has to leave their device to get an inference. For a determination that needs to be trusted by the insurer, the same model is run through an EZKL proving pipeline, which produces a zero-knowledge proof that the model was executed correctly on the claimed inputs, without revealing the underlying personal data. This proof can be independently verified, giving a cryptographic guarantee of correct AI inference rather than requiring trust in the party running the model.

description.title: Overall
description.body: Beyond the AI component, ProofSure's core claims-settlement system is built entirely on zero-knowledge proofs deployed and verified on Ethereum (Sepolia). When a policyholder submits a claim, they submit a Groth16 proof that the hospital's invoice is authentic, the treatment is covered, the expense math is correct, and the payout matches the policy's deductible/co-pay terms, all without revealing the underlying medical or financial details on-chain. A nullifier prevents the same claim from being paid twice while revealing nothing about the claim's contents. This directly uses Ethereum's privacy primitives to remove a specific, real point of friction in insurance: the discretionary language insurers use to deny valid claims. Rather than privacy as a feature layered on top, it's structural to how the contract decides whether to pay out. Thus, the insurer has no ability to override a proof that verifies correctly.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges Faced

The biggest challenge was implementing privacy-preserving verification within a limited development timeframe while understanding and integrating unfamiliar blockchain and cryptographic concepts. We had to work through the interaction between zero-knowledge proofs, Ethereum smart contracts, wallet authentication, and frontend verification.

Another challenge was ensuring that sensitive identity information was never unnecessarily exposed or stored on-chain, while still making the verification process simple enough for users to understand and use.

We also faced challenges with Ethereum Sepolia testnet transactions, wallet connectivity, smart-contract integration, and debugging cryptographic verification flows**.

Working under the hackathon time constraint required us to prioritize the core privacy and verification functionality and build a working proof-of-concept rather than attempting to implement every feature at production scale.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The Problem We Solve
Traditional KYC or human verification services (like Persona, Jumio, or Stripe Identity) require users to upload passport photos and biometrics to centralized databases. This model presents critical flaws:

Centralized Data Leaks: Storing database copies of passports, driver's licenses, and biometrics creates high-value targets for hackers, leading to massive identity leaks.
Lack of User Ownership: Users lose control of their personal information the moment they upload it to a server.
Linkability & Sybil Attacks: Web3 applications need a way to verify unique humans (Sybil resistance) without linking their real-world identities across different dApps.
User Friction: Having to go through full document uploads for every individual website is repetitive and slow.
The SECUREID Solution
SECUREID introduces a Zero-Storage SSO Gateway that verifies identity parameters entirely on the client-side:

Zero Raw Data Storage: Biometrics and government ID scans are captured, cropped, and immediately hashed locally using Keccak256 inside the browser canvas. The raw files are wiped from memory and never uploaded.
On-Chain Soulbound Identity Passes (SBTs): Verifying the local hash creates an on-chain registry of unique nullifiers. Successful checks mint a non-transferable SBT representing a verified identity to the user's wallet.
Private Age Gating (zk-SNARKs): The user generates a ZK proof proving their birth year meets age criteria (e.g. Age $\ge$ 18) without disclosing their exact date of birth or name.
🛠️ The Tech Stack
Smart Contracts & Blockchain: Solidity (v0.8.24), Hardhat, and OpenZeppelin ERC721.
Zero-Knowledge Circuit: Circom (for ZK arithmetic constraints) and SnarkJS (Groth16 proving in the browser).
Frontend SSO Engine: Vite, React, Lucide-React, and Tailwind/Vanilla CSS.
Web3 Integration: Ethers.js (v6) for MetaMask connection and Sepolia testnet transaction pipelines.
⚙️ How It Works (Step-by-Step)
Decoupled Redirect: A gated portal (e.g. PulseTV Premium) requires verification and redirects the user to the SECUREID gateway.
Local Camera Scanning: The user takes a Face Liveness scan (in a circle crop) and an Aadhar ID card scan.
Canvas Hashing: The webcam frames are processed inside an HTML5 <canvas> and hashed locally. The raw biometrics are destroyed in memory.
ZKP Witness Generation: The browser generates a ZK-SNARK proof verifying that:
The user possesses a credential signed by an authorized issuer public key.
The age calculated from the credential timestamp satisfies the condition.
A unique nullifier hash is computed to block double-KYC attacks.
On-Chain Validation: The ZK proof is verified by the IdentityRegistry.sol contract on Sepolia, minting an SBT to the user's wallet.
Decryption & Access: The callback unlocks access to the calling dApp, unblurring the premium interface.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The biggest challenge was making STICK feel like a continuous conversation instead of a one-shot AI prompt.

At first, it was easy to generate a slide from a request, but things became complicated when users started changing their minds. We had to make sure STICK remembered what was already created, understood the current slide, and didn't accidentally overwrite or break the presentation.

We also ran into reliability issues. LLM calls, memory/database connections, and PowerPoint generation can all fail independently. We solved this by adding retries for temporary failures, graceful fallbacks, atomic state updates, and duplicate-event handling. A failed planner, for example, should never destroy a presentation that was already working.

Another challenge was integrating PPT Master into our realtime workflow. Instead of building another PowerPoint renderer, we connected STICK to PPT Master's SVG quality checking and native PPTX export pipeline. We also had to create isolated workspaces for different presentation sessions so files from one session couldn't leak into another.

Finally, keeping the system fast meant avoiding unnecessary LLM calls. We added execution policies so simple slide updates can skip the critic, while more complex transitions go through additional validation.

The result is a system that is more reliable, context-aware, and genuinely conversational, rather than just another prompt-to-PPT generator.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Making a presentation usually takes longer than actually figuring out what you want to say. You've got the idea, but then comes the annoying part: turning it into slides, writing prompts for AI tools, hunting for the right images, fixing layouts that never quite look right, and redoing half of it the moment you change your mind about something.

STICK is built to skip most of that. You just talk through your idea — the same way you'd explain it to a teammate or a friend. It follows the conversation, remembers what's already been built, and puts the presentation together as you go, instead of making you write out one long, perfect prompt upfront.

A few things it's actually good for:

Building a deck just by talking, no need to script out detailed prompts
Tweaking or improving slides mid-conversation, no restarting from scratch
Picking layouts that actually fit what you're explaining, not a generic template
Turning raw ideas, processes, numbers, or systems into something visual
Putting together decks fast for projects, pitches, demos, classes, or meetings
Exporting the whole thing as an editable PowerPoint at the end

The whole point is that you focus on the story you're trying to tell, and let STICK handle the part where that story becomes slides.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Cyber threats such as "phishing links, malicious files, suspicious login activities, and online scams" are becoming increasingly difficult for ordinary users to identify. Existing security tools may detect threats, but they often provide technical alerts without clearly explaining Why something is dangerous or what the user should do next.
"CyberShield AI – Detect. Explain. Protect." solves this problem by providing an easy-to-understand cybersecurity platform that:

Detects threats such as suspicious URLs, phishing attempts, and unusual activities.
Explains threats in simple language so users understand why an activity is considered risky.
Suggests protective actions to help users respond safely to detected threats.
Provides a security dashboard to monitor alerts, threat types, and security history.
Assists users through an AI security assistant  that answers basic cybersecurity questions.

This makes cybersecurity more accessible, understandable, and proactive, helping users make safer decisions instead of relying only on technical security warnings.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
While building **CyberShield AI – Detect. Explain. Protect.**, we faced several technical and design challenges:
Threat Detection Accuracy: 
It was difficult to distinguish between genuinely malicious and legitimate URLs or activities. We improved this by combining rule-based checks with machine-learning features and testing the system with different examples.
AI Explanations: 
Generating explanations that were both technically correct and easy for non-technical users to understand was challenging. We designed the output to show the reason for detection, risk level, and recommended action  in simple language.
False Positives: 
Some legitimate activities were initially flagged as suspicious. We refined the detection rules and adjusted the criteria to reduce unnecessary alerts.
Backend–Frontend Integration: 
Connecting the Flask backend with the dashboard and displaying detection results in real time required careful handling of API responses and data formats. We solved this by creating clear API endpoints and validating the data before displaying it.
Testing Different Threat Scenarios: 
Finding enough realistic examples for testing was challenging. We created controlled test cases representing different threat levels and used them to evaluate the detection workflow.
User-Friendly Interface:
Presenting cybersecurity information without overwhelming users was another hurdle. We simplified the dashboard and organized results using risk levels, alerts, explanations, and recommended actions.

Overall, these challenges helped us improve the project's accuracy, usability, reliability, and security awareness value.

# What Makes Zentrix Unique

This document explains what genuinely sets Zentrix apart from existing database tools, AI assistants, and monitoring platforms.

---

## 1. Evidence First, AI Second

**Most AI tools:** "Ask the AI a question, get an answer."

**Zentrix:** "Collect evidence. Analyze evidence. Reason over evidence. Recommend based on evidence."

The LLM in Zentrix never sees the database directly. It sees structured evidence — metrics, statistics, plan diffs, lock chains — that were collected by deterministic tools. The AI reasons over facts, not guesses.

```
Traditional AI:    User Question → LLM → Answer (may be wrong)
Zentrix:           User Question → Evidence Collector → ML Scoring → LLM → Answer (backed by data)
```

This is why Zentrix can say "94% confidence" — it knows exactly what evidence supports its conclusion and what contradicts it.

---

## 2. No Hallucination by Design

**The problem with LLMs and databases:** If you ask GPT-4 "why is my query slow," it will give you a plausible-sounding answer. It might even be right sometimes. But it has no way to verify its own claims. It cannot check whether statistics are actually stale, whether an index is actually missing, or whether a lock is actually blocking.

**Zentrix's approach:**
- Tools return structured data (JSON), not natural language
- ML models score anomalies using mathematical models, not intuition
- The LLM receives evidence as structured inputs, not free-form text
- The skeptic agent specifically challenges weak conclusions
- Statistical verification requires p < 0.05 before any recommendation

The LLM is a reasoning layer, not an oracle. It cannot make claims without evidence.

---

## 3. The Safety Pipeline Does Not Exist Anywhere Else

Most database optimization tools follow this pattern:

```
Detect problem → Suggest fix → Apply fix
```

Zentrix follows this pattern:

```
Detect problem → Collect evidence → Investigate root cause → Generate hypothesis →
Simulate on shadow DB → Statistical verification → Human approval →
Canary deployment → Monitor outcome → Feed back to ML
```

No existing tool:
1. Clones your database to a shadow environment
2. Runs the optimization in isolation
3. Measures actual before/after performance
4. Requires statistical significance (p < 0.05)
5. Has an adversarial agent challenge the result
6. Requires human approval
7. Deploys to a canary (10% of traffic) first
8. Auto-rollbacks if regression detected
9. Records the outcome for future learning

This 9-step pipeline is unique to Zentrix.

---

## 4. Closed-Loop Learning Is Rare in Database Tools

**Most tools:** Detect → Alert → Human fixes → Done.

**Zentrix:** Detect → Investigate → Recommend → Test → Deploy → Measure outcome → Update ML models → Better future recommendations.

Every optimization Zentrix recommends produces a data point:

| Input | Prediction | Actual Outcome | Model Update |
|-------|-----------|----------------|--------------|
| Stale stats detected | ANALYZE will reduce latency 80% | Latency reduced 75% | Prediction error: 5% |
| Plan regression detected | Reindex will fix plan flip | Reindex had no effect | Prediction error: 100% |
| Lock contention detected | Kill idle transaction will resolve | Latency dropped 90% | Prediction error: 10% |

Over time, the ML models learn:
- Which optimizations work for which workload patterns
- When the system should be confident vs. conservative
- Which indicators are reliable vs. noisy
- How to translate metrics into dollars

No other database tool has this feedback loop.

---

## 5. Multi-Agent Investigation Is Not a Gimmick

**The hype:** "We use 6 AI agents!"

**The reality:** Most multi-agent systems are just one LLM calling itself multiple times with different prompts. The "agents" share context, contradict each other, and produce inconsistent results.

**Zentrix's approach:**
- Each agent has a **specific, narrow domain** (plan, I/O, locks, vacuum, schema)
- Each agent has **exclusive access to specific tools** — it cannot investigate another agent's domain
- Each agent produces **structured evidence**, not free-form text
- The supervisor **reconciles contradictions** using evidence weighting, not voting
- The skeptic agent **actively challenges** the consensus

The agents are not a chat room. They are a structured investigation pipeline where each agent does one thing well, and the supervisor ensures consistency.

---

## 6. Deterministic Evidence + ML Scoring = Trustworthy Results

**Pure ML approach:** "The model says this is anomalous."

2. Statistical engines compute derived metrics (cardinality error, plan diff, lock chains)
3. ML models score the results (anomaly detection, root cause classification)
4. LLM reasons over the scored evidence
5. Skeptic challenges the conclusion

# The Problem It Solves

## The Pain

PostgreSQL is the world's most popular open-source database. It powers startups, banks, hospitals, and everything in between. But when it slows down, the consequences are real:

- **Sleepless engineers** — 3 AM pages because a query went from 40ms to 8 seconds
- **Expensive consultants** — senior DBAs charge $200-$400/hour to investigate
- **Guesswork** — most teams add indexes or restart services without understanding the root cause
- **Recurring incidents** — the same problems come back because nobody learns from past fixes

The core issue: **database monitoring tells you what broke, not why it broke.**

A dashboard might show "query latency increased 600%." But it will not tell you that a bulk import at 2 AM invalidated planner statistics, causing the planner to abandon an index scan in favor of a sequential scan on 1.8 million rows.

That "why" requires a senior database engineer — and there are not enough of them.

## Problem

AI agents can be manipulated by prompt injection and indirect instruction attacks hidden in documents, web pages, or tool output. These attacks can cause an agent to leak data, take unsafe actions, or follow instructions that conflict with the user's intent.

## Solution

INTENTFENCE is a local-first cybersecurity prototype that visualizes how an AI request is inspected before execution. It combines intent analysis, threat classification, policy checks, and an explainable decision timeline so a reviewer can see what happened at every phase.

## Trace Commons AI

IntentFence was built with Codex as an active engineering collaborator. Codex helped translate architecture into implementation, create typed security contracts, drive TDD cycles, debug CI and integration failures, design fail-closed authorization boundaries, verify persistence, integrate the frontend and backend, and prepare the judge-facing evidence dashboard.

Every model-proposed tool call passes through the IntentFence gateway. The system records the active Intent Contract, source context, policy decision, matched rules, execution status, receipt ID, risk score, and latency.

External web content is treated as untrusted data. The controlled attack fixture demonstrates a web page attempting to induce a .env read; the web fetch may be allowed, while the subsequent secret-file request is blocked before execution.

For the Trace Commons submission, 12 project-scoped Codex sessions were sanitized and submitted through the contributor CLI. The current signed attestation contains the privacy-backstop results for 6 scored submissions and is stored in the organizer's private JWT field.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Modern software can be built faster than it can be understood. Large GitHub repositories contain thousands of lines of interconnected code, APIs, databases, dependencies, and services, making repository-level understanding difficult and highly manual. This creates four connected challenges: hackathon judges struggle to evaluate the engineering behind polished demos; developers struggle to understand unfamiliar codebases and predict the impact of changes; security risks remain hidden inside complex repositories; and beginners struggle to learn from real-world open-source software.

CodePriya AI addresses these challenges through a unified AI-powered “Software MRI for GitHub repositories.” Given a repository, it combines LLMs, multi-agent analysis, AST/static analysis, Git intelligence, and repository-aware context to construct an intelligent model of the software. This model powers four perspectives: Judge Intelligence for evidence-driven hackathon evaluation; Developer Intelligence for repository understanding and change-impact simulation; Security Intelligence for risk detection with traceable evidence; and Learning Intelligence for project-specific, multilingual explanations.

For judges, CodePriya AI provides a 100-point AI-assisted evaluation framework covering Innovation & Impact, Architecture & Scalability, Code Quality & Engineering, and Feasibility & Readiness. A Repository DNA profile summarizes architecture, security, code health, scalability, testing, and engineering readiness, while Git Intelligence provides insight into project evolution and development activity.

Its key innovation is the Change Impact Simulator, which answers “What happens if I change this?” by analyzing repository relationships and identifying potentially affected components and risks. Its Evidence Engine connects important AI findings to repository context, making analysis more transparent and auditable. Architecture Intelligence transforms complex repository relationships into an understandable system view rather than forcing users to manually trace thousands of files.

Rather than building another AI code generator, CodePriya AI creates an intelligence layer over existing software — allowing judges, developers, security reviewers, and learners to understand the same repository from different perspectives.

One Repository. Four Perspectives. One Software Intelligence.

CodePriya AI — The Software MRI that reveals what is happening inside software.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Here is some content you can use for the "Challenges we ran into" box, tailored perfectly to the complex architecture of CodePriya AI. You can just copy and paste this right in:
### Challenges we ran into

Building a "Software MRI" for entire GitHub repositories meant dealing with massive amounts of data and complex AI orchestration. Here are the main hurdles we faced and how we overcame them:

Handling LLM Context Limits with Massive Codebases:
The Hurdle:Feeding an entire repository into an LLM for analysis is impossible due to strict token limits. We initially struggled with getting the AI to understand the full context without losing details.
The Fix: we implemented a smart AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) parsing and chunking strategy. Instead of sending raw text, we generate an architectural graph of the repository and only feed the most relevant, compressed code snippets to the LLMs based on the specific "Perspective" (Judge, Security, etc.) being requested.


Multi-Agent Synchronization:
The Hurdle:Coordinating the four different AI intelligence layers (Judge, Developer, Security, and Learning) simultaneously led to race conditions and inconsistent states.
The Fix:We designed a centralized state-management system using our PostgreSQL database to act as a single source of truth. We separated the agents into asynchronous workers (using Node.js and Flask), allowing them to process their specific tasks independently and report back to a unified "Evidence Engine."


Performance Bottlenecks in Git Intelligence:
The Hurdle:Analyzing deep commit histories and calculating the "Change Impact Simulator" in real-time caused severe latency, making the web interface freeze.
The Fix:We shifted the heavy Git analysis to background queues and introduced aggressive caching for repository relationships. We also optimized our Python processing scripts, cutting down the analysis time significantly so the user gets near-instant feedback.

hackmate-dc58.name: Hackmate
hackmate-dc58.tagline: Don't Hack Alone. Build the Right Team.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The main problem we identified is that finding a hackathon team is often very unorganized. Students usually search through WhatsApp groups, Discord, or their existing friend circles. Because of this, teams may end up having similar skills while missing important roles.

For example, a team might have three frontend developers but no backend or UI/UX person.

So the problem is not just finding people — it is finding people with the right complementary skills.   
 
**Our solution is HackMate**.

First, a student creates a profile and adds their skills, preferred role, experience, and interests.

Then they can create or join a project and define the skills and roles required for that project.

**HackMate analyzes the project requirements and the existing team, identifies the missing skills, and then recommends suitable students.**

For every recommendation, we can show a compatibility percentage, for example, “92% Match”, based on how well the student's skills and role fit the project requirements.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
While building HackMate, one common issue was that the frontend was not able to communicate with the backend API.

For example, when the frontend tried to fetch user or project data, the request failed with an error like “Network Error” or “Failed to fetch.”

Why it happened:

Backend server was running on one port, while the frontend was trying to access another.
The API URL was incorrect.
CORS configuration was missing or incorrect.

How we solved it:

Checked whether the backend server was actually running.
Verified the API URL and port.
Configured CORS in the Express backend to allow requests from the frontend.
Tested the API separately using Postman.
Then tested the complete frontend-to-backend flow again.

wavesafe-9469.name: WaveSafe
wavesafe-9469.tagline: Platform for Smarter Coastal Travel and Safety

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
# 🌊 Wave-Safe

> **A Unified Platform for Smarter Coastal Travel and Safety**

Wave-Safe is a unified web-based coastal safety and intelligence platform that combines real-time ocean and weather intelligence, trip planning, emergency coordination, and rescue tracking into one coastal travel experience.

## 👥 Team

**Team Name:** LazyCoders

- **Arvind Kumar** — Team Leader
- **Om Kushwaha**
- **Rishabh Pal**

---

## 🚨 Problem Statement

India has over **7,500 km of coastline**, but there is no unified digital platform that provides tourists with real-time beach safety intelligence and coordinated emergency response.

### Current Challenges

- No simple real-time **Safe / Caution / Unsafe** signal for beaches.
- Visitors may lack current information about ocean conditions, rip-current risks, and official hazard advisories.
- Emergency assistance can depend on a chain of separate phone calls.
- Hospitals, lifeguards, police, coast guard, rescue posts, and jurisdictions operate through disconnected records.
- There is no single system to automatically identify and coordinate the appropriate responder for an incident.
- Existing ocean and weather data is available, but it is not converted into one simple decision for a beach visitor.

---

## 💡 Solution

**Wave-Safe** bridges the gap between **real-time risk awareness and emergency response**.

The platform is designed as a travel website first, with safety intelligence integrated throughout the user's journey.

### Predict → Plan → Protect → Track

- **Predict:** Calculate a live beach safety verdict from ocean and weather data.
- **Plan:** Identify risky travel windows and suggest safer alternatives.
- **Protect:** Provide one-tap SOS with location sharing and coordinated emergency dispatch.
- **Track:** Provide live rescue tracking, acknowledgements, and ETAs.

---

## ✨ Features

### 🟢 Live Beach Safety

Provides a live:

- **SAFE**
- **CAUTION**
- **UNSAFE**

verdict for beaches using real ocean and weather data.

### 🗓️ Smart Trip Planning

- Evaluates risk across planned time windows.
- Flags potentially dangerous slots.
- Suggests safer alternative beaches.

### 🆘 One-Tap SOS

A single SOS trigger can share the user's exact location with:

- 112 / emergency response
- Nearest hospital
- Coast guard / marine police
- Lifeguard post

### 🚑 Emergency Dispatch & Tracking

Tracks an incident through:

```text
Created → Dispatched → Acknowledged → En Route → Arrived → Resolved
```

### 🗺️ Hospital & Authority Routing

- Capability-filtered hospital matching.
- Jurisdiction-matched authority routing.
- Defined response roles.
- Parallel emergency dispatch.

### 📍 Live Rescue Tracking

- Location pings.
- ETA tracking.
- Stale-session detection.
- Rescue progress visibility.

### 🔔 Notifications

- SMS notifications.
- Web Push notifications.
- Localized templates.
- English fallback.

### 📴 Offline Support

- Offline-capable Progressive Web App.
- Local action queue.
- Automatic synchronization after reconnect.

### 🔐 Authentication

- Phone + OTP login.
- Defined OTP expiry.

### 🏢 Admin & Operations

- Beach management.
- Jurisdiction management.
- Hospital management.
- Incident dashboards.
- Acknowledgement dashboards.
- Risk-rule tuning.
- Log export.

### 🌊 Data Ingestion & Risk Engine

- INCOIS + SACHET connectors.
- Manual beach closures.
- Data normalization and unit conversion.
- Redis-based deduplication.
- Risk scoring.
- Time-series hazard outlook.

---

## 🧠 Risk Engine

The Risk Engine combines multiple inputs into an explainable risk score.

### Inputs

- Wave height
- Current speed
- Wind
- Tide
- Water quality
- Forecast trend
- Lifeguard coverage

### Risk Formula

```text
R = σ( Σ wᵢzᵢ + Σ wᵢⱼzᵢzⱼ + λ₁Δtrend + λ₂Δtide )
```

### Risk Classification

| Risk Score | Verdict |
|---:|---|
| `R < 0.33` | 🟢 SAFE |
| `0.33 – 0.66` | 🟡 CAUTION |
| `R ≥ 0.66` | 🔴 UNSAFE |

Active **tsunami, storm surge, or evacuation** conditions override normal scoring and force:

```text
R = 1 → UNSAFE
```

---

## 🛠️ Tech Stack

### Frontend

- **React**
- **Next.js (SSR)**
- **Mapbox GL JS / Google Maps API**
- **Progressive Web App (PWA)**

### Backend

- **Python**
- **FastAPI**
- **REST APIs**
- **WebSockets**
- **Celery**

### Database & Storage

- **PostgreSQL 16**
- **PostGIS**
- **Redis 7**
- **S3-compatible object storage**

### Infrastructure & DevOps

- **Docker**
- **Kubernetes**
- **Kafka / RabbitMQ**
- **GitHub Actions CI/CD**
- **AWS / GCP**

### External APIs & Data Sources

- **INCOIS** — Ocean & advisory data
- **SACHET** — CAP / RSS alerts
- **112 ERSS** — Emergency di

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
# The Bug That Almost Slipped Into Production

**Project:** WaveSafe — Coastal Safety Platform
**Where it hit:** `POST /v1/admin/beaches`
**Found during:** Final Swagger E2E testing, hours before deployment

## The Crash

```
psycopg2.errors.InvalidParameterValue:
Geometry type (Point) does not match column type (Polygon)
```

A clean 500. Not a validation error — a raw database exception leaking straight
to the client.

## Why It Happened

Swagger's auto-generated example payload showed a generic GeoJSON `Point`.
Following it felt natural — but the `beaches` table stores each beach as a
**Polygon** (a boundary, not a pin drop). The API had no validation layer
checking the GeoJSON `type` before handing it to PostGIS. The request sailed
straight through FastAPI → SQLAlchemy → Postgres, where the *database*
finally said no — the hard way.

## The Fix

**Immediate:** Rebuilt the payload as a proper closed-ring Polygon
(5 coordinate pairs, first == last). Confirmed the endpoint logic itself was
fine — it was purely an input-shape problem.

**Real fix (queued, non-blocking):** Add a Pydantic validator on the GeoJSON
`type` field so bad input returns a clean `422` before it ever touches the DB.

## The Pattern

This wasn't a one-off. The same root cause — **the database was the only
validation layer** — surfaced twice more in the same session:

| Endpoint | Expected | Got |
|---|---|---|
| `admin/beaches` | 422 (wrong geometry) | 500 crash |
| `admin/activity-thresholds` | 409 (duplicate key) | 500 crash |
| `safezone/guidance` | 422 (empty-string UUID) | 500 crash |

All three: the app layer trusted the input and let Postgres be the bouncer.
Postgres did its job perfectly — data integrity held. But the *caller*
got a stack trace instead of a sentence.

## The Takeaway

> A database constraint enforcing correctness is not the same as an API
> validating input. One protects your data. The other protects your users
> from a 500 page.

None of the three were blockers — all admin/internal-only, zero impact on
the core user flow (SOS trigger → dispatch → tracking), which stayed clean
through every test. But they're first on the list for the next patch.
