replate-193c.tagline: Save a Meal, Share the Feel.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Large amounts of safe, surplus food from restaurants, events, and other sources can go to waste because there is no simple system to coordinate availability, verification, pickup, and redistribution. RePlate aims to connect surplus food sources with organizations that can redistribute it, making the process more organized, traceable, and time-sensitive.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: One of our main challenges was turning the idea into a usable prototype while keeping the food-rescue workflow simple enough for different users. We also had to iterate on the interface and navigation so that the core journey—from identifying surplus food to coordinating redistribution—was easy to understand. We tested the prototype repeatedly and refined the structure and user flow based on those issues.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of our biggest challenges was combining Machine Learning, rule-based detection, and graph analysis into a single meaningful risk score without making the system misleading.

We also had to handle large transaction graphs efficiently. Dense transaction networks can quickly become difficult to visualize, so we introduced bounded graph traversal, deterministic layouts, depth controls, and optimized frontend rendering.

Another challenge was making the system reliable for demonstrations. We added API validation, parameterized SQL queries, request cancellation, loading/error states, account search, transaction sorting, deterministic graph layouts, and extensive backend tests.

We also discovered an important limitation during evaluation: a high risk score does not automatically mean an account is fraudulent. Our synthetic dataset produced only 20% mule recall in the top 25 accounts, which we documented instead of hiding. This helped us keep the system honest and distinguish anomaly detection from confirmed fraud.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Financial fraud such as money mule activity is difficult to detect because suspicious transactions are often hidden within large and complex networks of legitimate-looking accounts.

Traditional rule-based systems may detect simple suspicious patterns, but they can struggle to identify unusual behavior, coordinated money movement, fan-in/fan-out activity, and multi-account transaction chains.

MuleGuard solves this by providing an investigation console that analyzes account behavior from three perspectives: Machine Learning anomaly detection, behavioral rules, and transaction-graph analysis. It combines these signals into a risk score and allows investigators to explore suspicious accounts, inspect their transactions, visualize money flows, and trace how money moves between accounts.

This helps investigators move from simply asking "Which accounts look suspicious?" to understanding "Why is this account suspicious, and how did the money move?"

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
***

### 1. Vector Map Clutter & Frame Drops
* **Hurdle:** Loading raw national boundaries drew 700+ internal district lines, creating a messy "spiderweb" mesh that lagged WebGL and obscured the satellite map.
* **Fix:** Built a custom TopoJSON parser (`topo2geo.cjs`) to extract only the 36 clean State/UT boundaries, eliminating clutter and boosting performance.

### 2. Balancing Satellite Visibility with Heat Waves
* **Hurdle:** Solid thermal fills completely blocked the satellite terrain (mountains, rivers, greenery), while point dots failed to show regional heat flow.
* **Fix:** Engineered a translucent WebGL heatmap layer (`opacity: ~0.18`) with Gaussian radial blending so satellite terrain textures remain visible under the glowing heat wave.

### 3. Preventing AI Hallucinations in the Scenario Lab
* **Hurdle:** Standard ML models gave unrealistic temperature drops (like -15°C from minor tree planting) when dragging intervention sliders.
* **Fix:** Constrained the XGBoost model with **physical surface energy-balance equations**, keeping counterfactual predictions scientifically accurate within **$\pm 0.42^\circ\text{C}$ RMSE**.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
### The Problem
ISRO captures massive Earth Observation (EO) data, but it sits in raw raster formats that State Municipal Corporations cannot easily interpret or use. Without in-house GIS teams, city administrations still rely on delayed field surveys and blanket advisories during deadly heatwaves.

---

### How State Municipalities Use It

1. **Automated Ward-Level Telemetry:**  
   Converts raw space telemetry into live thermal stress grids across all 36 Indian States and UTs with zero manual GIS processing.

2. **Automated Root-Cause Diagnosis:**  
   Uses physics-guided AI to tell municipal engineers exactly *why* a specific ward is overheating (+1.7°C concrete density, +0.8°C roof materials, +0.7°C canopy loss).

3. **Pre-Budget Policy Simulation:**  
   Allows municipal planners to simulate cool roofs and urban forestry before spending funds instantly projecting temperature drops (up to **-3.3°C**), required CapEx (₹ Cr) and citizens protected.

4. **1-Click Heat Action Plans:**  
   Automatically generates executive municipal briefs with ranked ward priorities and budget allocation ready for administrative sign-off.

---

### Impact
* **Bridges Space to City Hall:** Directly connects ISRO telemetry to Municipal Commissioners' decision pipelines.
* **Targeted Disaster Relief:** Directs emergency heat shelters and water resources to the most vulnerable wards.
* **Optimal Public Spending:** Ensures every municipal cooling rupee delivers maximum, scientifically verified temperature reduction.

description.title: Trace Commons AI
description.body: HeatWise AI fits Trace Commons because it addresses urban climate resilience through accessible, high-impact public-interest technology. It fits Trace Commons AI because we use a machine learning pipeline to predict land-surface temperature and hotspot probability, then translate those predictions into actionable insights through maps, intervention simulations, and municipal-style reports for heat mitigation planning.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
As AI agents become increasingly autonomous, they will need to interact, collaborate, hire services, and exchange value with other AI agents without constant human supervision. However, there is currently no reliable trust layer for these interactions. An AI agent may not know whether another agent is legitimate, what capabilities it actually has, whether it can be trusted, whether it is authorized to perform a particular action, or whether a payment will be safely handled. Traditional centralized platforms create a dependency on intermediaries to verify identities, manage permissions, process payments, and maintain reputation.

AgentChain solves this problem by creating a decentralized trust infrastructure for AI agents. It gives every agent a verifiable on-chain identity, programmable permissions and spending limits, a transparent reputation history, and secure escrow-based payments. This allows agents to discover, verify, hire, and transact with other agents autonomously while keeping important trust and financial operations transparent and tamper-resistant.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: While developing AgentChain, we faced several technical and design challenges. The biggest challenge was deciding where blockchain should actually be used without turning the application into a blockchain-only system. We had to carefully separate on-chain responsibilities such as agent identity, permissions, escrow, payments, and reputation from off-chain data such as AI responses, task details, and application state. Integrating AI agents with blockchain was another challenge because an LLM cannot be allowed to directly execute financial transactions or bypass permissions, so we designed a controlled workflow where the AI proposes actions and deterministic backend logic validates them before interacting with smart contracts. We also had to handle smart-contract security, including unauthorized transactions, spending limits, escrow failures, and incorrect reputation updates. Connecting the frontend, FastAPI backend, PostgreSQL database, wallet, and blockchain into one reliable workflow introduced additional integration challenges. Finally, because this is a hackathon prototype, we needed to balance real blockchain functionality with demo reliability, leading us to design a Demo Mode that can simulate blockchain interactions when a wallet, RPC, or testnet is unavailable while clearly distinguishing simulated activity from real on-chain transactions.

cyberfirst-68a1.tagline: CyberFirst turns panic and scattered evidence into

sheharsaathi-43e4.name: SheharSaathi
sheharsaathi-43e4.tagline: Move cities, not through twenty tabs.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Moving to a new city shouldn't require twenty tabs and ten different platforms.

SheharSaathi brings the entire relocation journey into one intelligent workspace. Users can discover housing, evaluate localities, find compatible roommates, understand commute options, plan monthly expenses, and check suspicious listings without piecing everything together themselves.

What makes it useful is not just having these features in one place, but connecting them. A cheaper house may mean a longer commute. A good locality may push the budget higher. A suitable roommate can reduce both rent and expenses. SheharSaathi helps users understand these trade-offs before making a decision.

Instead of simply giving more options, SheharSaathi helps users make safer, faster, and better-informed relocation decisions.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of our biggest challenges was making different relocation features feel like one connected product instead of a collection of separate tools. Housing, roommate matching, budgeting, locality insights, scam detection, and AI assistance all work with different kinds of data and user context.

We also faced several technical hurdles while integrating our Next.js frontend, FastAPI backend, authentication, APIs, and AI-powered features. API integration, CORS issues, deployment environment variables, authentication configuration, and keeping the frontend state consistent with backend data caused problems during development.

Another challenge was integrating AI meaningfully. We did not want to add a generic chatbot just for the sake of using AI. We structured the AI around relocation-specific tasks and context so that its responses could actually support the user's next decision.

We overcame these challenges by building and testing the platform module by module, debugging integrations independently, standardising our data flow, and continuously testing the complete user journey after connecting each feature.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of the hardest parts was getting the model to behave the same way during training and when it was actually running. At one point, the training pipeline was processing the data differently from the live system. The model could look good on paper, but the moment we connected it to live telemetry, the numbers did not line up the way we expected.

We had to go back through the pipeline piece by piece and figure out where the mismatch was coming from. We eventually made the feature processing the same for both training and inference, including how CPU, GPU, memory, disk and network data were normalized and how the heat proxy was calculated.

Another challenge was the sensor free part. We could not simply look at a temperature sensor and say that a rack was getting hotter. We had to work out how much thermal pressure could be inferred from the workload itself. That led us to using CPU and GPU activity to build a heat proxy and then using neighboring racks to understand the wider thermal context.

The last thing we struggled with was explainability. Getting a model to output a risk score is one thing, but being able to answer an operator asking “why did the cooling just increase?” is much more useful. We built the XAI layer around the actual changes in workload, thermal risk and neighboring rack activity so the system can explain its decisions instead of just giving a number.

A lot of the work ended up being less about writing the model itself and more about making all the pieces behave consistently. We now have 34 automated tests covering the pipeline, inference, feature processing and XAI, and all 34 are passing.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Every day, the digital world depends on thousands of servers working quietly behind the scenes. But keeping them running comes at a cost. Data centers use enormous amounts of energy to keep machines cool, often cooling systems react only after heat has already become a problem.

Thervo takes a different approach. It looks at the signals servers already generate, such as CPU, GPU, memory, disk and network activity, to understand how workloads are changing and predict thermal risk before it becomes critical. It does this without adding physical temperature sensors.

What makes Thervo different is that it does not simply make a cooling decision and leave operators wondering why. It explains what changed, why the risk increased or decreased, and what influenced the cooling decision.

This can help protect critical computing infrastructure, reduce unnecessary cooling, and give operators more confidence in AI driven decisions. It can also support the growing demands of AI workloads and modern data centers without requiring additional physical sensing infrastructure.

At its heart, Thervo is built around a simple idea.

Don't wait for machines to become hot to protect them. Understand what they are doing, anticipate what comes next, and act before it is too late.

description.title: Trace Commons AI
description.body: Thervo was developed iteratively with Gemini CLI across architecture, feature engineering, predictive modeling, testing, XAI, debugging, and validation. Our Trace Commons submission contains 12 authentic Gemini CLI sessions and 2,575 development steps, with reasoning excluded and the traces privacy-sanitized.

precursor-ff34.tagline: See small problems before they become incidents.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Integrating three independently-built pieces (AI/ML, backend, frontend)
Preventing report volume from drowning out severity*
Early in scoring design we realized a widely-reported minor issue could out-rank a rarely-reported serious one under a simple count-based formula — a real design flaw, not just a demo bug, that needed explicit fixing (severity weighting, per-user/per-location report caps) rather than trusting the naive math.
No photo hosting infrastructure*
Locally-selected photos only exist as browser-local blob URLs — the backend/AI literally can't fetch them over the network. Fixed by sending images as base64 directly, avoiding a dependency on any third-party hosting service that could fail mid-demo.
Merge conflicts and environment drift across a distributed team*
Parallel branches (AI/ML, backend, frontend) hit real git conflicts when merged, plus classic environment issues (Windows vs Mac terminal differences, PATH/venv setup) that ate real time close to the deadline.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
THE PROBLEM

Many physical-world problems begin as small, isolated signals:

A flickering light
A water leak
An overflowing bin
A damaged staircase
Increasing crowding
A minor safety hazard
Individually, these observations may not appear urgent. However, when similar observations start appearing from multiple people in the same area, they can indicate a developing problem.

Traditional reporting systems generally react after an incident is recognized.

Precursor aims to detect the pattern before the incident.

💡 Solution
Precursor allows users to submit lightweight observations containing:

📝 Description
📷 Optional photo
📍 Location
👤 User ID
The system then:

Receives the observation through FastAPI
Uses Gemini's multimodal AI to identify issue tags and severity
Stores the observation in PostgreSQL

Calculates an Emergence Score

Displays observations and alerts through the dashboard

aegis-5afb.name: AEGIS
aegis-5afb.tagline: When the world cannot hear her, Aegis listens.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
### 1. Steganography Data Loss via Image Compression
**The Hurdle:** 
The core of our covert SOS feature relies on Least Significant Bit (LSB) steganography to hide encrypted text within the pixels of an image. During testing, we discovered that if a user shared the SOS image via standard messaging apps (like WhatsApp) or if they took a screenshot, the platform's native JPEG compression completely wiped the hidden LSB data. The message would be destroyed, and the decoder would crash silently.

**How We Overcame It:** 
We couldn't bypass third-party compression algorithms, so we re-engineered the user flow and error handling. 
*   **Engineering:** We implemented a robust magic header (`AEGIS01`) and a 4-byte payload length check before the actual hidden message bits. Now, if an image is corrupted by compression, the decoder instantly throws a clear "Corrupted/Compressed Image" error rather than failing silently. 
*   **UX Pivot:** We restricted the output strictly to lossless PNG formats and utilized the browser's native Web Share API to send the image as a raw file attachment, bypassing platform compression. We also added explicit UI warnings against taking screenshots.

### 2. The Next.js URL History Trace (The Disguise Problem)
**The Hurdle:** 
The app is disguised as a calculator. Initially, we used standard Next.js routing (`/calculator` to `/dashboard`). However, we realized that navigating between pages leaves a trail in the browser history. If a monitor checked the phone's history, they would clearly see the user was not just doing math. 

**How We Overcame It:** 
We abandoned standard URL routing for the core stealth transition. We architected the frontend so the calculator and the actual safety dashboard share the exact same root route (`/`). Entering the secret PIN (`2580 =`) triggers a client-side React state change that dynamically mounts the dashboard *over* the calculator without ever updating the URL or pushing to the history API. When the "Quick Exit" (Escape) is triggered, it simply unmounts the component and purges all local state, leaving zero digital footprints.

### 3. Hallucination Control within a "Zero-Cost" RAG Pipeline
**The Hurdle:** 
To provide legal advice, we needed an AI that strictly cited the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (PWDVA) and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) without hallucinating. To keep the project zero-cost, we had to use MongoDB Atlas's free M0 tier for our Vector Store, which has a strict 512MB limit—far too small for a massive legal embedding database.

**How We Overcame It:** 
Instead of relying on large cloud embedding APIs, we ran `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` locally within our FastAPI backend. We ruthlessly curated and chunked only the most relevant, high-impact sections of the Indian legal codes rather than indexing the entire constitution. By keeping the corpus hyper-focused, we created a highly dense, incredibly accurate Vector Search index that easily fit within the free tier limits. We then strictly prompted the Groq LLM to *only* answer using the retrieved MongoDB context chunks, entirely eliminating hallucinations.

### 4. Overcoming Free-Tier API Rate Limits & Cold Starts
**The Hurdle:** 
Operating on a completely free stack meant dealing with Groq API rate limits (Too Many Requests) and 30-50 second cold-starts on our Render-hosted FastAPI backend. During rapid testing or multi-turn emotional support chats, the AI would frequently time out.

**How We Overcame It:** 
We built a resilient, offline-capable fallback architecture. The backend catches API rate limit exceptions or network timeouts and instantly routes the request to a pre-configured local fallback mechanism so the user is never left hanging. For the Render cold starts, we built an explicit loading state sequence in the UI to manage user expectations during the initial boot, ensuring the app feels responsive even when the server is waking up.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
# 🚨 The Problem It Solves

When individuals face domestic abuse, intense monitoring, harassment, or severe isolation, **the simple act of seeking help is often the most dangerous thing they can do.** Current digital safety solutions fail because they assume the victim has unrestricted, unmonitored access to their own devices. Aegis is built for the reality where they do not.

---

## 🔍 The Core Problem

1. **The Digital Trail of Trauma:** Openly searching for a domestic violence helpline, browsing legal rights, or downloading a "safety app" leaves a visible digital footprint. If an abuser or monitor sees this, it can trigger immediate, severe retaliation. 
2. **Fragmented Support:** In a crisis, support is scattered. Victims must use a web browser for legal rights, a dialer for SOS, and a separate platform for emotional guidance. This requires immense cognitive bandwidth during moments of peak stress.
3. **The Risk of Intercepted SOS:** Sending a panicked "help me" text is highly visible and easily intercepted by a monitor checking the victim's phone.
4. **The Stigma Barrier:** Many victims are initially too terrified or ashamed to speak to a human operator, leaving them completely isolated during the crucial early stages of abuse.

---

## 🛠️ What People Can Use It For (Concrete Use-Cases)

Aegis is a multi-tool disguised as a simple calculator. People use it to covertly access resources they would otherwise be too afraid to search for:

*   **Covert SOS Signaling:** A user can type a short, desperate phrase (e.g., "locked in, scared"). Aegis's AI expands this into a coherent distress message, hides it invisibly inside a normal-looking generated image (like a sunset), and allows the user to send it to a trusted contact.
*   **Accessing Legal Rights Without a Trace:** Users can ask an AI RAG Bot about their legal options regarding domestic violence (e.g., "What does the PWDVA say about eviction?"). The bot provides cited, hallucination-free answers based purely on verified Indian law.
*   **Judgment-Free Emotional Support:** Users can chat with a warm, always-available AI companion for grounding techniques and coping strategies when they are alone and panicked.
*   **Health and Medical Guidance:** Users can safely ask intimate health, reproductive, and safety questions without fear of judgment or browsing history exposure.

---

## ⚡ How It Makes Existing Tasks Easier

**The Old Way:** A victim has to open a browser in Incognito mode, desperately search for legal rights, try to parse complex government PDFs on a small screen, find a hotline number, write it down on a piece of paper, and remember to close all tabs before their abuser walks in.

**The Aegis Way:** The victim opens what looks like a stock calculator. They type `2580 =`. They instantly have access to an AI that parses the legal jargon for them, provides emotional support, and offers a one-click SOS workflow. Everything is centralized, offline-resilient, and instantly accessible. 

---

## 🛡️ How It Makes Existing Tasks Safer

*   **Stealth by Design (The Disguise):** Seeking help is infinitely safer because the app fundamentally does not look like a safety app. It functions perfectly as a standard calculator to survive casual scrutiny. 
*   **The "Panic Exit":** If a monitor suddenly enters the room, pressing the "Quick Exit" button (or hitting Escape) instantly reverts the app back to the calculator and wipes the active session from memory.
*   **Invisible SOS (Steganography):** Instead of a text message saying "Help me, he's angry," which can be read by anyone holding the phone, the victim shares a picture of a flower. To the monitor, it's just a photo. To the trusted contact using the Aegis Responder Dashboard, it decodes into a severe distress signal with an AI-assigned urgency score.
*   **No "App Download" Suspicion:** Because Aegis is a web application, it doesn't require an App Store download that leaves an email receipt or shows up in the phone's purchase history. 

---

## 🌍 The Broader Impact
Aegis doesn't just provide a tool; it shifts the balance of power. It gives people in zero-trust environments the ability to educate themselves on their rights, process their trauma, and formulate an escape plan securely and invisibly. It is not a replacement for 911—it is a discreet bridge that helps victims survive long enough to safely make that call.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
***1. Primary Use Cases***

**A. Rapid Developer Onboarding**
The Problem: New developers often spend 2–4 weeks reading code, asking senior engineers questions, and guessing how different folders and services connect.
With ARCHITECH: An engineer pastes a repository URL or local folder and immediately gets:
An automated Architecture Overview (Macro, Meso, and Micro design explanations).
An interactive File Dependency Graph and Function Call Map.
A clear breakdown of the system’s design style (Layered, MVC, Hexagonal, Event-Driven, etc.).
Result: Slashes onboarding time from weeks to hours.

**B. Pre-Refactoring "Blast Radius" & Impact Simulation**
The Problem: Modifying or deleting a core file (e.g., utils.py, auth_middleware.js, database.py) often causes catastrophic, unexpected runtime errors in distant parts of the application.
With ARCHITECH: Before touching a single line of code, developers run a Blast Radius Simulation:
Modify Simulation: See all 1-hop direct and 2–3 hop indirect dependent files that will be affected.
Delete Simulation: View every function that will break and calculate an objective risk score (0–100).
Move Simulation: Identify all import paths that will require rewriting.
Result: Eliminates "refactoring anxiety" and prevents broken builds in production.

**C. Eliminating Circular Dependencies & Spaghetti Coupling**
The Problem: Over years of development, modules start importing each other in circular loops ($A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$), making code tightly coupled, hard to test in isolation, and prone to memory leaks.
With ARCHITECH:
Uses Johnson’s Cycle Detection Algorithm to list the exact circular dependency chains.
Measures Fan-In (dependents) and Fan-Out (dependencies) to pinpoint "God objects" and fragile modules.
Result: Clear, prioritized refactoring targets to decouple the system.

**D. Architectural Drift & Snapshot Comparison (PR Auditing)**
The Problem: Architectural erosion happens gradually. A junior developer or tight deadline introduces a shortcut that violates layer separation, and no one notices during code review.
With ARCHITECH:
Take a snapshot before and after a major feature branch or refactor.
The Snapshot Comparison Engine detects:
Did coupling score increase or decrease?
Were new circular dependencies introduced?
Did the pattern integrity degrade (e.g., domain isolation dropped below 70%)?
Result: Automated architectural guardrails for PR reviews and release milestones.

**E. Monolith-to-Microservices Decomposition**
The Problem: Breaking a large monolith into microservices or separate packages is notoriously difficult because hidden inter-module calls are invisible in text editors.
With ARCHITECH:
The Function Graph and Transitive Call Chains reveal exact boundary clusters.
Developers can isolate domain boundaries that have low coupling to extract them cleanly into independent services.

**F. Technical Due Diligence & Open-Source Evaluation**
The Problem: When evaluating an open-source library or an M&A target codebase, reading thousands of files manually is impossible.
With ARCHITECH:
Instantly discover whether the codebase follows clean separation of concerns, has hidden circular traps, or relies on high-risk spaghetti modules.

***👥 Who Benefits Most?***
Software Engineers: Safely plan changes, discover functions and callers, and understand unfamiliar modules without getting lost.
Tech Leads & Staff Engineers: Enforce architectural boundaries, review structural impacts of major PRs, and guide refactoring efforts.
Engineering Managers: Track technical debt trends, reduce developer ramp-up time, and prevent architectural erosion across releases.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Here is the formatted text, optimized to copy-paste directly into Devfolio:

---

### **Challenges We Ran Into**

**1. Resolving Dynamic OOP Calls in Static ASTs**
* **The Hurdle:** Standard AST parsers only capture direct function calls (`func()`). They fail on common object-oriented patterns like `self.service.execute()`, where the receiver class is defined elsewhere.
* **How We Solved It:** We engineered a **two-pass parsing protocol**. *Pass 1* traverses constructor `__init__` assignments (`self.service = PaymentService()`) to map instance attributes to their concrete types. *Pass 2* uses this symbol table to resolve cross-file method dispatch directly in our graph database.

**2. Cross-Platform Path Inconsistencies (`\` vs `/`) & Node Duplication**
* **The Hurdle:** Windows backslashes, Unix forward slashes, and relative import differences caused Neo4j queries to fail or create duplicate orphan nodes.
* **How We Solved It:** We implemented a **multi-strategy path resolution layer** that indexes canonical absolute paths alongside normalized forward-slash suffixes, using `ENDS WITH` Cypher matching to ensure seamless cross-platform resolution.

**3. Preventing LLM Token Overflow & Generic Summaries**
* **The Hurdle:** Sending raw file trees to the LLM quickly exceeded token context windows and caused hallucinations or surface-level file summaries.
* **How We Solved It:** We offloaded structural heavy lifting to **NetworkX & Neo4j first** (detecting circular cycles, fan-in/fan-out metrics, and hub orchestrators algorithmically). We then fed only high-signal structural evidence into **Groq (Llama 3.3 70B)**, reducing token consumption while dramatically improving architectural insight depth.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of our biggest challenges was finding the right balance between cost, latency, and response accuracy. Routing every query to a cloud LLM gave us strong responses but increased API cost and latency, while relying only on a local model reduced cost but affected accuracy on complex queries.

We solved this by building a hybrid routing and verification pipeline. Simple queries are handled locally, while complex or low-confidence responses are escalated to a cloud model.

We also faced challenges with semantic caching and false cache matches. Exact string matching could not identify similar queries with different wording. We addressed this using embeddings and cosine similarity with a configurable threshold, allowing semantically similar queries to reuse cached responses.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
TriForge solves the problem of high cost, latency, and unnecessary cloud dependency in LLM applications. In traditional AI systems, every query is often sent to a powerful cloud model, even when the task could be handled locally or retrieved from cache.

TriForge introduces an intelligent hybrid routing layer that:

🚀 Routes simple queries to local LLMs for faster responses.
💰 Reduces cloud API and token costs by avoiding unnecessary remote inference.
⚡ Uses semantic caching to reuse responses for repeated or similar queries.
🧠 Escalates complex or unreliable local responses to stronger cloud models.
🛡️ Uses a Verify-Draft loop to detect low-confidence or potentially hallucinated local responses.
📊 Adapts routing decisions using feedback and performance metrics.

This makes LLM-powered applications more cost-efficient, responsive, and reliable, especially when handling large volumes of user queries.

description.title: Trace Commons AI
description.body: TriForge fits the Trace Commons AI track as a hybrid AI inference routing system that intelligently decides whether a query should be handled locally, served from semantic cache, or escalated to a cloud LLM. It uses intent-based routing, semantic similarity, local Ollama inference, cloud LLMs, and a Verify-Draft loop to reduce unnecessary cloud computation while maintaining response quality.

secagent-hub-16b6.name: SecAgent Hub
secagent-hub-16b6.tagline: A Security Digital Twin for Cloud Infrastructure

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Building meaningful infrastructure relationships: Converting Terraform resources into a security-aware model required understanding networking, IAM, dependencies, and resource access.

Keeping the analysis deterministic: Attack paths needed to be based on actual infrastructure relationships rather than AI assumptions.

Controlling AI hallucinations: Ensuring the AI only reasons from verified security findings and infrastructure relationships, instead of inventing resources, attack paths, or vulnerabilities.

Simulating changes safely: The What-If engine needed to modify a virtual copy without affecting the original infrastructure, then recalculate and compare attack paths.

Integrating multiple components: Connecting Terraform parsing, security scanning, Digital Twin, attack analysis, AI remediation, and verification while preserving the existing prototype.

Verifying AI-generated fixes: AI-generated Terraform changes cannot simply be trusted; they need to be validated, rescanned, and re-evaluated against the attack paths.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Modern cloud infrastructure generates hundreds of unprioritized security findings every day, yet most existing tools treat each vulnerability in isolation — leaving developers buried under a relentless flood of alerts with no clear sense of what truly matters. SecAgentHub was built to solve exactly this problem. Rather than simply cataloging disconnected findings, SecAgentHub understands how individual vulnerabilities interact and chain together to form real, exploitable attack paths across your infrastructure. It cuts through the noise by intelligently prioritizing critical risks based on actual exploitability and business impact, not just severity scores. But discovery is only half the battle — SecAgentHub goes further by empowering developers to apply AI-guided remediations and then verify, through a live Digital Twin simulation of their infrastructure, that the fix genuinely closes the attack path before a single line of code ever reaches production. The result is a security platform that doesn't just tell you what's broken — it shows you the path an attacker would take, guides you to the most impactful fix, and proves the door is locked before you deploy.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
As AI agents move beyond answering questions to taking the real world actions like reading files, querying databases, sending emails, processing invoices or even triggering transactions. A compromised agent can misuse the permissions it was legitimately given.

**Leash** is a runtime security layer for AI agents that detects when an agent's behavior starts drifting from its intended task and intervenes before a risky action is executed.

It continuously evaluates proposed tool calls using:

- **Semantic drift** — Is the action still relevant to the original task?
- **Behavioral anomalies** — Does the action deviate from the agent's normal behavior?
- **Tool sensitivity** — How risky is the requested action?

Based on these signals, Leash can allow, review or block an action and generate an explainable incident report.

### What can Leash be used for?

- **Finance & Procurement** — Prevent unauthorized payments or bank-account changes caused by malicious documents.
- **Document Processing** — Detect prompt injection hidden inside invoices, PDFs, emails, and other files.
- **Database & Enterprise Agents** — Prevent unexpected access to or export of sensitive data.
- **Coding Agents** — Detect suspicious attempts to execute commands or access resources outside the assigned task.
- **Customer Support & Email Agents** — Stop compromised agents from sending unauthorized emails or exposing sensitive information.

Instead of only asking **"What is this AI agent allowed to access?"**, Leash asks:

> **"Does what this agent is about to do still make sense for the task it was assigned?"**

**Leash watches what an agent is about to do—not just what it said.**

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
### 1. Securing the Agent–Tool Interaction
The biggest challenge was ensuring that a compromised AI agent couldn't directly execute a dangerous tool. We solved this by placing Leash between the agent and the tool layer, making every action pass through risk evaluation first.

### 2. Reliable Hackathon Demo
Depending completely on a live LLM/API could cause failures during the demo. We implemented an offline replay mode with controlled attack scenarios so the core security demonstration works reliably even without an API connection.

### 3. Detecting Behavioral Drift
Simple keyword checks aren't enough to identify agent hijacking. We combined semantic drift, behavioral anomalies, and tool sensitivity to calculate a risk score for each proposed action.

### 4. Limited Real-World Agent Data
Real agent execution logs are difficult to access, so we created synthetic agent-behavior traces representing normal and suspicious workflows for our initial anomaly-detection baseline.

### 5. Explainable Security Decisions
Instead of simply showing "BLOCKED", Leash shows why an action was considered risky and generates an incident report, making the system easier to investigate and trust.

sentra-0559.name: sentra
sentra-0559.tagline: Detect the drain before the deposit

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Crypto users can unknowingly send funds to compromised wallets monitored by sweeper bots. These bots can automatically drain incoming assets within seconds, leaving users with little or no warning before an irreversible transaction.

Sentra is a blockchain security layer that analyzes a wallet's real on-chain behavior before funds are sent. It detects patterns associated with sweeper activity, generates an explainable risk score, and warns users when a wallet shows signs of compromise. Users can also monitor wallets continuously and receive alerts when suspicious behavior emerges.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Same-transaction sweeps — Funds could enter and leave a wallet within the same transaction, so we had to add internal/token transfer detection.

Different drain speeds — Our initial detection could miss slower sweeps, so we adjusted the detection logic to catch different deposit-to-drain time gaps.

Live Polygon data — Alchemy's API introduced rate limits and delays, so we optimized our blockchain data fetching to make Sentra more reliable.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: In safety-critical industries — aviation, healthcare, industrial operations — the standard pre-shift fitness check is a worker answering "yes" to "are you fit for duty?", a question that is least reliable precisely when the answer should be "no": fatigue and impairment actively suppress awareness of themselves. Hours-of-service rules address this by counting hours rather than measuring the person, which means a pilot who slept eight fragmented hours or a nurse on their third consecutive night shift can be fully compliant and functionally degraded at the same time. Dusk replaces that broken self-report loop with a two-minute objective screening — reaction time and working memory, physiological hand tremor via webcam, and speech prosody — scored against each worker's own baseline rather than a population average, because drift from your norm is what matters, not whether you outperform an average stranger. The verdict is deterministic and auditable: a rules engine computes it, Claude narrates it in plain language, and a tamper-evident hash anchored to a Polygon blockchain contract means any auditor can verify a record was never quietly revised — without having to trust Dusk's own database.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: The tremor module broke us for a while — and the frustrating part was that it didn't look broken. The readings came out, the numbers made sense, everything compiled and ran, and we were genuinely proud of it until we held a perfectly steady hand in front of the camera and watched it report moderate tremor. That sent us back to basics. It turned out MediaPipe's hand-detection box shifts slightly between frames, and that inter-frame jitter lands right in the physiological tremor band — so what we'd built was a very accurate, very confident tracker of camera noise. The fix sounds simple in hindsight: instead of measuring fingertips in absolute coordinates, measure them relative to the palm centroid, so when the whole detection box drifts, the relative positions stay clean. One change, and the module went from fabricating tremor to resolving a real signal within 0.01 Hz of ground truth. There was a smaller version of the same lesson with amplitude — we almost expressed it in millimetres because that felt intuitive and professional, until someone pointed out that a 2D webcam has no depth calibration and we'd essentially be making the number up. So it's a fraction of the subject's own hand span instead, which is both honest about what the camera can actually know and weirdly more robust in practice. Both fixes came from the same uncomfortable realization: the system was telling a convincing story with bad data, and the only way to catch it was to go looking for failure rather than waiting for it to announce itself.

chainshield-sentinel-36d6.name: CHAINSHIELD SENTINEL
chainshield-sentinel-36d6.tagline: ChainShield Sentinel — Know What You're Signing Be

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Web3 users can unknowingly interact with fake dApps, malicious contracts, or dangerous token approvals—and once a transaction is signed, the consequences can be irreversible.

ChainShield Sentinel provides a pre-transaction security layer that helps users understand what they are about to interact with and authorize before signing. It analyzes the target URL, domain, contract context, transaction intent, and available threat intelligence to generate an explainable 0–100 risk score with specific reasons behind the assessment.

Instead of simply saying “Unsafe”, ChainShield Sentinel explains why something is risky and what action the user should take.

It also generates a cryptographic fingerprint of the security assessment and can anchor that evidence on an EVM testnet, allowing its integrity to be independently verified later.
ChainShield Sentinel helps Web3 users make informed decisions before connecting, signing, or authorizing potentially dangerous transactions.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The biggest challenge was making the project more than a simple Web3 security dashboard. We wanted the system to provide a real, explainable security decision before a transaction is signed, while still keeping the MVP reliable within a limited development window.

1. Transaction intent is difficult to interpret

A URL can be suspicious, but that alone doesn't tell a user what they are actually authorizing. We had to bridge the gap between technical transaction data and something a normal user could understand.

We solved this by separating transaction decoding from intent analysis. The system extracts actions such as token approvals, spender addresses, allowance values, and contract context, then compares the observed authorization with the expected user action to identify potential intent mismatches.

2. Avoiding a black-box risk score

We initially considered using more complex intelligence models, but an opaque score would make it difficult to explain why a transaction was considered dangerous.

Instead, we implemented a transparent weighted-rule engine. Each signal contributes to the final score, allowing the report to show exactly which indicators increased or reduced the risk.

3. External intelligence can be unavailable

Threat intelligence APIs and blockchain RPC endpoints can fail, rate-limit requests, or become temporarily unavailable.

Rather than making the entire scanner dependent on external services, we designed the architecture with modular intelligence adapters and a local analysis fallback. This allows the core assessment to continue when an optional external source is unavailable.

4. Evidence verification and blockchain reliability

We also had to ensure that putting evidence on-chain did not mean storing sensitive information on a public blockchain.

We solved this by generating a deterministic cryptographic fingerprint of the selected non-sensitive assessment data. Only the fingerprint and minimal proof metadata are anchored on the testnet. The original sensitive data remains off-chain.

5. Keeping the scope realistic

With a limited hackathon development window, it was easy to over-scope the project with ML, multiple chains, wallet integrations, and advanced threat intelligence.

We prioritized the core workflow:

Target → Analysis → Intent → Explainable Risk → Evidence Hash → Verification

This allowed us to focus on making the central security decision actually useful rather than building many incomplete features.

fix-bot-c2ee.name: Fix Bot
fix-bot-c2ee.tagline: Live Windows monitor in your terminal. Real system

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## Inspiration

Everyday PC problems are simple to *say* and hard to *fix*: slow Wi‑Fi, broken installs, “where is that file?”, “push this to GitHub.” Most tools either give static FAQ answers or dump raw terminal output. We wanted a **local AI support engineer** that understands plain English, reads the real machine state, and can act—with permission—instead of only chatting.

That idea became **FixBot**: a Windows CLI agent that diagnoses and repairs using live OS data, not memorized scripts.

## What it does

FixBot turns natural language into supervised actions across:

- **Network** — Wi‑Fi status, passwords, DNS/adapter repairs, speed tests  
- **Install / Update / Uninstall** — winget-driven package lifecycle with retries  
- **Files** — search (including typos), delete with shortcut cleanup  
- **Local RAG** — explain and answer questions over folders already on disk  
- **GitPilot** — guided + autonomous git (commit, push, recover from upstream errors)

Each serious action follows: **inspect → plan → permission gate → execute → verify → analyze errors → retry or escalate**.

## How we built it

- **Python** CLI with **Rich** for live agent streams and progress  
- **Gemini** for reasoning and plans; **Groq** for fast intent / classification  
- **LangGraph + LangChain** for multi-agent domain graphs (network, install, RAG, git)  
- **Windows APIs / CLI** — winget, netsh, git, psutil, WMI  
- **RAG stack** — loaders, chunking, embeddings, FAISS for local documents/code  
- **GitPilot** — allowlisted `git_ops` + tool registry so the LLM never gets free shell  

Architecture rule we stuck to: **the model plans; tools execute; the verifier decides success.**

## What we learned

- “Autonomous” only feels real when **failure is part of the loop** (e.g. push fails → no upstream → set upstream → push again).  
- **Permission gates** matter more than clever prompts for user trust.  
- Offline / rule-based fallbacks beat waiting forever on an LLM for network repair.  
- OAuth “localhost callback” auth is fragile; **PAT / SSH / a guided auth helper** is kinder to users.  
- Good UX is a **live stream of steps**, not walls of git tips.

## Challenges

1. **LLM hangs & timeouts** on network planning → offline telemetry ladders.  
2. **False verification** (e.g. DNS check fails while internet works) → softer health checks.  
3. **Install/uninstall edge cases** (user-scope apps, admin elevation, “already installed”).  
4. **LibreSpeed public servers** far from India → CDN fallback for speed tests.  
5. **Git auth UX** — browser redirected to dead `127.0.0.1` ports → auth helper + sanitized remotes (never show embedded tokens).  
6. Keeping **many domains** (network, install, RAG, git) isolated so one graph doesn’t break another.

## What’s next

Deeper Git conflict coaching, safer high-risk actions, richer speed-test UI, and tighter shared memory between FixBot and GitPilot—so the same repo context follows you from chat to coach menu.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## Challenges we ran into

### Making a Windows monitor feel like a real TUI
We wanted a **btop-style** view in a Windows CLI (live CPU/RAM/net/process), not a one-shot “scan and print.” Rich tables and `Live` look fine in a fixed window, then break when the user **resizes**: rules span 200 columns, the prompt jumps to the far right, and the welcome panel stretches instead of wrapping.  
**Fix:** cap content width, `expand=False` on panels, and treat the terminal as a **column**, not “use every pixel.”

### Live graphs vs. shallow numbers
A speed/net panel that prints “12 Mbps” once is not monitoring. Public LibreSpeed servers from India were **1–3 s away**, so download/upload showed **0 Mbps** and random city names. A static bar also isn’t a graph.  
**Fix:** measure against a nearby edge (Cloudflare), multi-stream with warmup discarded, and drive the UI from **real callbacks / NIC counters** (`psutil.net_io_counters`) the way btop samples bandwidth—not random numbers.

### Process list that actually works on Windows
Listing processes with `psutil` + `open_files()` **hung** the CLI (had to Ctrl+C). Killing “everything” is dangerous (csrss, lsass, explorer).  
**Fix:** skip `open_files()`, sort by CPU/RAM quickly, then **close all (safe)** vs **close some by index** vs **close by name**, with a confirm step.

### Admin vs. real machine state
The tool needs adapter, storage, process, and registry access; skipping those at startup means the monitor is **blind**. Running as Administrator then breaks **user-scope** apps (install/uninstall).  
**Fix:** permission gate at boot, and treat “what Windows reports” (winget, netsh, taskkill) as the source of truth—not FAQ text.

### Don’t confuse chat with a dashboard
Natural language (`process running`, `my wifi`, `speed test`) kept falling into a **planner/LLM graph** instead of opening the live view. Gemini `function_call` with empty text crashed the planner.  
**Fix:** route monitor phrases **straight to the dashboard**, keep the LLM for diagnosis, and never block the live UI on a model timeout.

**Lesson:** a Windows monitor CLI is hard because the OS is slow, scoped, and inconsistent—the UI has to stay live, safe, and width-aware while numbers come from the machine, not the model.

zerotrust-exam-engine-2f0d.name: ZEROTRUST EXAM ENGINE
zerotrust-exam-engine-2f0d.tagline: Zero-trust offline exams with forensic tracking

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Educational integrity is currently failing at the distribution layer. When instructors dedicate their time to preparing educational materials and structuring precise assessments, a single leak in the paper supply chain renders the entire evaluation meaningless. Traditional cloud-based software fails to prevent corrupt test centers from intercepting materials early or candidates from photographing screens.

Project Nivasha (ZeroTrust Exam Engine) treats examination security as a zero-trust supply chain problem. We eliminate the "Master Question Paper" vulnerability entirely through an offline-first, mathematically verifiable architecture that makes leaks computationally impossible to execute and trivial to trace.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Building an enterprise-grade, offline-first security product in a single weekend pushed our technical limits, especially regarding isolated state management and invisible data tracking.

1. Cross-Encoding Steganography (ZWSP) & Data Tracking:
Implementing Tri-Layer Steganography required injecting Zero-Width Spaces (ZWSP) and dynamic synonym tokens into the exam text. However, preserving these hidden Unicode characters from the FastAPI backend to the Electron frontend—without text sanitizers stripping them—was difficult. We developed automated Python tracking scripts to continuously monitor the payload's integrity as it passed through the IPC bridge, ensuring the forensic watermarks remained intact.

2. Strict Air-Gapping & IPC Communication:
To make the Electron kiosk genuinely "zero-trust," we had to disable all external network interfaces and rely entirely on strict loopback and IPC (Inter-Process Communication). Securing this without breaking the internal state-saving loops required precise architecture. We heavily utilized our AI coding agents to rapidly model secure IPC bridges and refactor the backend constraints.

3. Offline Cryptographic Handshake (T-5 Protocol):
Synchronizing the decryption of the exam payload exactly 5 minutes before the start time—without relying on an internet-connected NTP server—required building a localized, time-drift-resistant HMAC-SHA256 verification sequence.

4. Tooling & CLI Integration under Pressure:
While submitting our session logs for the Trace Commons track, we hit severe MSYS2 toolchain and Rust compiler errors on Windows. We had to manually bypass standard build processes, fetch the GNU compiler, and build the Rust CLI from source under extreme time pressure to successfully generate our cryptographic JWT attestation token.

description.title: Trace Commons AI
description.body: Project Nivasha fits into the Trace Commons AI track through its deep integration of AI coding agents and automated CLI workflows. During development, we utilized advanced AI agents via CLI to architect our T-5 dual-key cryptographic handshakes, design our Python-based Tri-Layer Steganography engines (ZWSP/semantic fingerprinting), and build secure Electron/FastAPI IPC bridges under tight constraints. Furthermore, our entire submission is cryptographically verified and attested using the Trace Commons CLI toolchain and JWT attestation pipeline, aligning with the track's core mission of verifiable, transparent software supply chains.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
⚠️ Challenges We Ran Into

During the development of CrashAid, we faced several technical and design challenges while trying to build a real-time, reliable emergency-response system.

 🔧 1. Sensor-Based Crash Detection

One of the biggest challenges was accurately detecting crashes using mobile sensors like the **accelerometer, gyroscope, and GPS**.
It was difficult to differentiate between actual accidents and normal sudden movements like braking or speed breakers.

**How we solved it:**
We implemented a **multi-factor approach**, combining speed changes, motion patterns, and a **confirmation countdown** to reduce false positives.

---

📱 2. Real-Time Location Tracking

Maintaining **accurate and continuous GPS tracking** was challenging, especially with fluctuating network conditions and device limitations.

**Solution:**
We optimized location updates and ensured that **last known location** is always available, even in low-connectivity scenarios.

---

🗄️ 3. Offline Data Availability

Emergency situations often occur in areas with poor internet connectivity, making it difficult to fetch nearby services.

**Solution:**
We integrated a local **SQLite database (`places.db`)** containing emergency service data, allowing the app to function **offline**.

---

🗺️ 4. Map Integration & Routing

Integrating maps, showing routes, handling markers, and visualizing real-time updates was complex.

**Solution:**
We used optimized mapping libraries and focused on **clear route visualization, markers, and efficient updates** for better performance.

---

🚦 5. Traffic Signal Priority (Simulation)

Implementing real-world traffic light control is not feasible in a hackathon environment.

**Solution:**
We designed a **simulation-based approach** that identifies signals along the route and demonstrates an **emergency priority corridor**, making the concept practical and demo-friendly.

---

🤖 6. Lightweight AI Implementation

Running AI features like **driver monitoring and first-aid assistance** on mobile devices without heavy processing was challenging.

**Solution:**
We used **lightweight and optimized AI approaches**, focusing on feasibility and performance rather than complex models.

---

🔄 7. System Integration

Combining multiple features like **crash detection, SOS, routing, AI, and offline data** into one smooth workflow was difficult.

**Solution:**
We designed a **modular architecture**, ensuring each component works independently but integrates seamlessly into the overall system.

---

🎯 Conclusion

These challenges helped us improve CrashAid into a **more practical, reliable, and scalable solution**, ensuring it performs effectively even in real-world emergency situations.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
# What Problem This Project Solves

Most adaptive traffic signal control today runs on reinforcement learning (RL) 
policies trained to optimize traffic flow. These policies are fast and 
efficient for everyday traffic, but they're fundamentally reflexive — they 
react to patterns they've seen before, without actually understanding **what's 
happening** in a scene.

When something unusual occurs — an ambulance approaching, a pedestrian caught 
mid-crossing, an accident blocking a lane — a policy trained purely on 
historical traffic data has no way to reason about the situation or judge the 
right response. It just keeps optimizing for the metric it was trained on, 
which can make emergencies worse (for example, holding a green light for 
maximum throughput exactly when an ambulance needs the intersection cleared).

## How VLMLight Solves This

VLMLight combines two decision-making systems instead of relying on one:

- **A fast RL policy** handles routine traffic — everyday queuing, cycle 
  changes, normal flow — where speed and efficiency matter more than deep 
  reasoning.
- **A vision-language reasoning branch** takes over for safety-critical or 
  ambiguous scenes. It actually *looks* at the intersection through a 
  multi-view visual simulator (bird's-eye view plus four directional camera 
  feeds), uses a vision-language model to understand what's happening, and a 
  language model to reason step by step about the right signal response.
- **A meta-controller** decides in real time which branch should be driving 
  the signal — deferring to the RL policy when traffic is normal, and 
  escalating to the deliberative reasoning branch when the situation calls 
  for judgment rather than pattern-matching.

## Who This Is For and How It Helps

### City Traffic Authorities & Researchers
Explore next-generation adaptive signal control that doesn't trade safety for 
efficiency.

### Emergency Response Optimization
The system is built to detect and prioritize scenarios like emergency 
vehicles needing right-of-way, instead of treating every vehicle the same.

### Interpretable Traffic AI
Because the reasoning branch produces actual language explanations for its 
decisions rather than a black-box output, it's more auditable than a pure RL 
policy — which matters when city planners and regulators need to trust 
safety-critical infrastructure.

### Cross-City Generalization
The system has already been validated across genuinely different traffic 
environments (Hong Kong, France, South Korea), showing it isn't overfit to 
one city's driving patterns or road layout.

## In Short

VLMLight gives traffic signals the ability to act fast when conditions are 
normal, and stop to actually think when they're not — addressing the core 
blind spot of today's purely reactive, RL-based traffic control systems.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
### Environment & dependency hell on Windows
Getting the simulation + RL stack running locally was harder than expected. 
The project's dependencies (TransSimHub, which wraps SUMO for traffic 
simulation, plus PyTorch/RL libraries) assume a fairly standard Python setup — 
we were initially on Python 3.14, which is too new for several packages in 
the stack. Sub-dependencies like `tinyscaler` (used by the multi-agent RL 
wrapper `supersuit`) don't ship prebuilt wheels for 3.14, so pip tried to 
compile it from source — which then failed because the Windows build tools 
were missing the Windows SDK (`io.h` header not found).

**Fix:** Rebuilt the environment in a Python 3.11 virtual environment instead 
of fighting the 3.14 compatibility gap. That gave us prebuilt wheels for 
everything, no local compilation needed, and a clean, isolated dependency set.

### Flaky large-file downloads
One dependency, `sumo_data` (a ~130MB wheel bundling SUMO's simulation 
network data), kept timing out mid-download on a slower connection. 

**Fix:** Increased pip's default timeout and retry count 
(`--default-timeout=120 --retries 10`) rather than relying on pip's default 
15-second read timeout, which was too aggressive for the file size.

### Regional API access restrictions
The project's default LLM/VLM config points at Alibaba's DashScope API — 
but DashScope has stopped accepting new signups from India, which blocked 
us from using the intended hosted backend entirely.

**Fix:** Since the underlying models (Qwen2.5-Instruct and Qwen2.5-VL) are 
open and hosted by multiple providers, we swapped to an OpenAI-compatible 
provider (OpenRouter) that exposes the same models without geographic 
signup restrictions — a small config change since `qwen-agent` already 
supports generic OpenAI-compatible endpoints, not just DashScope.

### Local hardware constraints
The reference setup assumes self-hosting a 72B LLM and 32B VLM, which needs 
serious multi-GPU VRAM we don't have access to.

**Fix:** Used a hosted inference API instead of local serving, which let us 
run the full decision pipeline without needing a GPU cluster.

description.title: Road Safety
description.body: VLMLight fits strongly into the Road Safety domain because it is designed to make traffic signals respond not only to normal traffic conditions but also to potentially dangerous situations in real time. Traditional traffic signals generally follow fixed timings or fast reinforcement-learning decisions, but VLMLight adds an intelligent reasoning layer that can recognize safety-critical events such as an approaching ambulance, a pedestrian still crossing the road, an accident or blocked lane, and dangerous traffic congestion. For example, if an ambulance is approaching from the North, VLMLight can detect it through camera feeds, prioritize its movement, extend the appropriate green signal, and keep conflicting directions stopped so the emergency vehicle can pass safely. Similarly, when one road has a very long queue and high waiting time while another direction has very little traffic, the system can intelligently redistribute green time instead of giving equal time to both directions, reducing unnecessary waiting and the possibility of congestion and queue spillback. The system can also protect pedestrians by extending crossing time when necessary and prevent vehicles from entering a blocked or accident-affected lane. Therefore, VLMLight is not simply an intelligent traffic optimization system; its main purpose is risk-aware traffic management, where safety, emergency response, pedestrian protection, congestion prevention, and efficient traffic flow are considered together. In simple terms, traditional signals react to traffic, while VLMLight reacts to traffic risk, making it a strong fit for the Road Safety domain.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
DodsEye is a multi-drone autonomous surveillance and defense system designed to detect, track, and coordinate responses to multiple aerial targets in real time.

It can help protect critical areas such as borders, airports, military installations, industrial facilities, and other restricted zones from unauthorized drones. Instead of requiring a human operator to manually monitor every target, DodsEye uses computer vision and autonomous coordination to detect and track multiple targets simultaneously.

A key problem it solves is multi-drone coordination. When several defense drones detect targets, the system helps prevent multiple drones from unnecessarily selecting the same target. If one drone is already assigned to a target, other available drones can identify and respond to different targets dynamically.

The system combines perception, target tracking, geolocation, real-time information sharing, and autonomous decision-making to improve response time, situational awareness, and scalability. DodsEye is designed with decentralized communication concepts so that drones can share important mission and target information even in environments where continuous internet connectivity may not be available.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of our biggest challenges was multi-drone coordination. We needed to ensure that multiple drones did not select or respond to the same target unnecessarily. Each drone had to know which targets were already being handled while still being able to react immediately when new targets appeared.

Another major challenge was maintaining a real-time shared view of target information. Target ownership, status, location, and updates needed to remain synchronized across multiple drones. We also had to consider situations where two drones detected or attempted to claim the same target at nearly the same time, which could create race conditions and inconsistent assignments.

Communication was another challenge, especially for scenarios where internet connectivity may not be available. We explored decentralized and mesh-based communication concepts to allow drones to exchange critical information directly rather than depending entirely on a central cloud connection.

Running multiple PX4 drones simultaneously also introduced simulation challenges, including managing separate drone instances, communication channels, vehicle spawning, and system resources. Integrating perception, tracking, geolocation, and autonomous decision-making into one coordinated system required extensive debugging and testing.

We overcame these challenges through modular system design, structured logging, simulation-based testing, and continuous debugging. By separating the project into perception, tracking, communication, behavior, and resource-allocation components, we were able to test individual systems independently and gradually improve end-to-end multi-drone coordination.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
### 🛠️ Challenges We Ran Into

Building **SmartVendor AI** for real-world retail environments presented several tough engineering hurdles:

#### 1. Specular Glare & Letter Distortion on Reflective Foil Packaging
* **The Hurdle**: Real Kirana store items (like *Maggi* yellow foil, *Snickers* wrappers, and *Lays* chips bags) reflect bright overhead lights. This created specular whiteout glare on camera frames, causing the OCR engine to extract garbled or duplicated letter noise (e.g., reading `"maazza"` instead of `"maaza"`).
* **How We Solved It**: We engineered a custom YUV frame processor in Kotlin (`OcrScannerManager`) that calculates pixel luminance ($Y$) and filters out whiteout glare spots ($Y > 235$) before sampling colors. We also added a regular expression character compressor (`replace(Regex("(.)\\1+"), "$1")`) to normalize glare-duplicated letters back into clean text before candidate evaluation.

#### 2. Phonetic & Visual Brand Cross-Match Confusion (*Maggi* vs. *Maaza*, *Soya Sticks* vs. *Snickers*)
* **The Hurdle**: Short FMCG brand names with overlapping letter counts produced high Levenshtein fuzzy similarity scores under fast camera motion. Scanning a *Maggi* packet would occasionally misidentify as *Maaza*, while *Soya Sticks* would cross-match with *Snickers*.
* **How We Solved It**: We created a multi-layered verification engine combining an explicit **Anti-Confusion Guard Matrix** (hard-blocking known negative brand pairs) with a **Packaging Color Classifier** (YUV $\rightarrow$ HSV hue mapping: Yellow for *Maggi*, Blue for *Oreo*, Red for *KitKat*). This ensured a +20% score boost on correct packaging colors while immediately dropping conflicting pairs.

#### 3. Camera Scanner Re-Triggering & User Interaction Ergonomics
* **The Hurdle**: When a vendor tapped **Add to Bill**, holding the packet in front of the lens while putting it into a customer's bag caused the camera to continuously spam duplicate item cards. Conversely, tapping **Cancel** on a misread item caused the camera to freeze up.
* **How We Solved It**: We built a dual-state interaction engine in `ScanViewModel`:
  - **Add to Bill**: Triggers a **5-second duplicate suppression cooldown** for that item ID.
  - **Cancel**: Records the rejected candidate in an ignored set and **instantly displays candidate #2 (the next highest-ranked alternative recommendation)** without interrupting the live camera stream.

#### 4. Cold-Start Camera & ML Native Binary Latency
* **The Hurdle**: Initializing Google ML Kit C++ native libraries and fetching store inventory from the database on first camera render caused a noticeable 2.8-second cold-start lag.
* **How We Solved It**: Implemented an application-level pre-warming pipeline (`SmartVendorApplication.kt`) that asynchronously pre-loads inventory products into an in-memory RAM cache (`InventoryCache`) and executes a dummy 0ms ML Kit initialization pass on app startup, dropping startup latency down to **under 0.4 seconds**.

NEURAL_EYE addresses the gap between traditional surveillance and real-time safety awareness. Conventional CCTV systems mainly record events or require continuous human monitoring, which can delay the recognition of potentially dangerous situations.

NEURAL_EYE uses AI-powered real-time computer vision to analyze camera feeds, detect and track objects, estimate proximity, and identify predefined critical conditions that may require attention. It can provide alerts to authorized users, reducing dependence on continuous manual monitoring and helping improve response awareness.

For women's safety, it is designed as an early-warning and decision-support system, helping authorised personnel recognise potentially concerning situations faster while keeping human judgement in the loop.

In simple terms: NEURAL_EYE turns passive CCTV footage into actionable, real-time safety awareness, helping people notice potential risks earlier and respond more quickly.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of our main challenges was designing the system to provide **real-time detection and alerts without relying entirely on continuous cloud processing**. We focused on processing the visual data close to the user to reduce latency and make the system more practical for real-world use.

Another challenge was proximity and context awareness. Detecting people alone is not enough for a safety system, so we worked toward combining object detection, tracking, and relative proximity to identify situations that may require attention.

We also had to consider privacy and responsible AI. Instead of automatically labelling people as threats, NEURAL_EYE is designed to provide alerts based on predefined conditions while keeping an authorised human in the decision-making loop.

Finally, integrating real-time detection, tracking, alert generation, and monitoring into a single platform required careful system design. Our approach is to continuously improve contextual detection, multi-person tracking, location-aware alerts, and emergency communication capabilities.

Women in distress often face a critical gap between recognizing danger and being able to call for help. Conventional safety apps depend heavily on smartphones, cellular connectivity, battery, and active user interaction—exactly the things that may fail during an emergency.

NAARI SHAKTI addresses this gap through a discreet, wearable safety system designed to provide help even when a phone or cellular network is unavailable.

📍**Real-time location**: During an emergency, the user's location can be shared with trusted contacts/responders.
🛡️ **Multi-layer protection**: Beyond alerting, the system incorporates active deterrence mechanisms to help the user create distance and escape.
🎙️**Automatic distress detection**: Sensors can help identify abnormal movement, falls, or distress sounds, reducing dependence on manual interaction.
🗺️ **Safer navigation**: Risk-aware route information can help users avoid reported unsafe or high-risk areas.

In short, NAARI SHAKTI transforms women's safety from a phone-dependent emergency action into a discreet, multi-layer wearable safety network—designed to Detect, Alert, Locate, and Protect when it matters most.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**Challenges We Ran Into**

Building **NAARI SHAKTI** involved several challenges because we wanted the system to remain useful even when the user's smartphone or cellular network becomes unavailable.

**Reliable emergency communication**: Our biggest challenge was designing an alert mechanism that does not depend entirely on cellular connectivity. We explored an off-grid communication approach so that an SOS can still be transmitted in low/no-network environments.
**Discreet SOS activation**: We had to make the emergency trigger quick and intentional without requiring multiple interactions with a phone. We refined the wearable interaction so that an SOS can be activated discreetly during a stressful situation.
**Hardware–software integration**: Connecting the wearable, location tracking, emergency alerts, and dashboard into one workflow required repeated testing and debugging of communication between the different components.
**Real-time location handling**: Maintaining accurate location information and passing it through the emergency pipeline while keeping the system lightweight was another challenge.
**Power and reliability**: Since a safety device needs to work when it is actually needed, we had to consider power consumption, response time, and reliable triggering rather than building a feature-heavy but impractical prototype.
Testing under realistic scenarios: We tested the complete flow—from *SOS activation → alert transmission → location sharing → response*—and iterated whenever one component introduced delays or failed to communicate correctly.

These challenges helped us move from a simple safety-app concept toward a multi-layer, wearable-first safety system designed around the realities of an emergency.

description.title: Women Safety
description.body:
### Women Safety

**NexTrack is built around one simple idea: a woman’s safety should not depend on having her phone in her hand or a network on her screen.**

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:

Added image preprocessing (resizing, grayscale, thresholding, denoising)

Used manual product detection for known brands

Created fallback mechanisms for failed OCR

The Problem: Every time we restarted the backend, all scanned products disappeared because we used in-memory database.

How We Fixed It:

Added sample products that load on startup

Made the app work seamlessly without MongoDB

Displayed clear error messages when products not found

Users can scan again to regenerate data

The Problem: AI Nutritionist wasn't giving real responses. The chatbot kept showing fallback replies instead of using Ollama.

How We Fixed It:

Fixed the /api/generate endpoint call

Added proper error handling with fallback responses

Displayed "Source: 🧠 AI" to show when Ollama was used

🧩 Challenge 4: 422 Errors on Donations
The Problem: Donation form kept failing with "422 Unprocessable Content" because the backend expected different data format.

How We Fixed It:

Added Pydantic models to validate data

Fixed the food_items array structure

Added proper error messages for debugging

🎨 Challenge 5: React Rendering Errors
The Problem: "Objects are not valid as a React child" error because we were passing error objects instead of strings.

How We Fixed It:

Converted all error objects to strings before rendering

Added type checking for all error messages

Used typeof error === 'string' ? error : error.message

Made penalties more aggressive for calories, fat, sugar

Balanced the weights properly

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Women often face safety concerns while travelling alone, especially at night or through unfamiliar areas. Existing navigation systems mainly focus on finding the fastest or shortest route based on distance, time and traffic, but they do not provide sufficient safety context for comparing different routes.
At the same time, many existing safety applications are reactive and become useful only after a person feels threatened or an emergency has already occurred.
NIRBHAYA AI addresses this gap by introducing safety-aware navigation. The platform analyzes multiple safety-related factors such as time of travel, area risk indicators, historical incident patterns, route conditions and proximity to emergency resources to generate a safety assessment for available routes.
Instead of only answering “Which route is the fastest?”, NIRBHAYA AI helps users make a more informed decision by asking “Which available route may be safer right now?”
Our goal is to shift personal safety from a purely reactive approach toward proactive and informed travel decisions.

Since accurate safety information requires verified datasets and responsible handling, we focused our prototype on a modular approach that can work with available data and be improved through verified data sources and partnerships.
We also faced the challenge of balancing safety and travel convenience. A route that has a potentially better safety score may take more time, so the system needs to present clear comparisons rather than simply recommending the longest or shortest route.
Finally, designing emergency features required careful consideration of privacy and responsible location sharing. Our approach focuses on user consent, trusted contacts, and transparent handling of safety-related information.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Signature-based intrusion detection can only catch attacks someone has already seen and written a rule for, leaving networks blind to zero-days, insider misuse, and novel behaviour — and the commercial tools that do more cost more than most small organisations can justify.
