triforge-dbda.tagline: Route Smarter. Spend Less. Stay in Control.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Building TriForge involved several engineering challenges:

- Designing reliable routing logic that could distinguish simple queries from complex coding and reasoning tasks.
- Verifying local model responses without sending every request to an expensive cloud model.
- Reducing token waste when a local response required correction.
- Supporting multiple cloud providers without tightly coupling the system to one vendor.
- Maintaining fast response times while performing caching, routing, and consistency checks.
- Protecting API credentials from being exposed to the frontend.

We addressed these challenges through 9-domain intent classification, prompt-length heuristics, selective self-consistency, SHA-256 prompt caching, and the Verify-Draft Escalation Protocol.

Parallel local sampling using ThreadPoolExecutor and SQLite WAL-mode caching were also implemented to improve responsiveness and concurrent request handling.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Modern LLM applications often send every query to expensive cloud models, even when many requests are simple conversational, factual, or conceptual tasks that can be handled locally.

This creates three major problems:
- High API and token costs from unnecessary cloud inference.
- Higher latency caused by cloud network round-trips for simple queries.
- Unnecessary energy consumption from running lightweight workloads on large cloud GPUs.

TriForge solves this with a local-first hybrid LLM routing gateway. It analyzes each query, routes simple workloads to fast local models, and sends complex coding/reasoning tasks to powerful cloud models.

When a local response needs verification, TriForge uses its Verify-Draft mechanism: instead of regenerating the answer from scratch, the cloud model receives the local draft and only corrects it. This reduces unnecessary completion-token usage while maintaining response quality.

The result is a smarter LLM infrastructure layer that makes AI applications more cost-efficient, faster, and more energy-conscious.

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body: TriForge enables AI self-sovereignty through local-first inference. It routes suitable queries to local models and uses cloud LLMs only when necessary, reducing dependence on centralized providers while improving privacy, cost efficiency, and user control.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges We Ran Into

During the development of the IoT Based Smart Agriculture Monitoring System, we faced a few challenges:

- Sensor accuracy: Getting reliable readings from the soil moisture, temperature, humidity, and water-level sensors was challenging. We solved this by testing the sensors repeatedly and setting suitable threshold values.

- IoT connectivity: Sending sensor data from the ESP8266 to the ThingSpeak cloud required stable Wi-Fi connectivity. We tested the connection and configured the ESP8266 properly.

- Automatic device control: Controlling the water pump and fan based on sensor conditions required careful programming. We used threshold-based logic to automatically turn the devices ON/OFF.

- SMS alerts: Integrating the SIM900A GSM module for low-water alerts was another hurdle. We configured the GSM module and tested the SMS functionality under different conditions.

- Hardware integration: Connecting the Arduino, sensors, ESP8266, GSM module, LCD, and relay module together required careful wiring and testing.

By testing each component separately and then integrating them step by step, we were able to overcome these challenges and build a working system.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Traditional farming often lacks real-time monitoring of important conditions such as soil moisture, temperature, humidity, and water level. This can lead to water wastage, inefficient irrigation, and delayed response to changing farm conditions.
Our IoT-based system makes farming smarter, easier, and more efficient by automatically monitoring these conditions and controlling devices such as the water pump and fan when needed. Farmers can also view real-time data remotely and receive SMS alerts when important conditions occur.
This helps with:
Saving water through automatic irrigation based on soil moisture.
Managing temperature by automatically switching on the fan when it is too high.
Remote monitoring through the IoT dashboard.
Early alerts for low water levels through SMS.
 Improving farm efficiency and supporting sustainable farming practices.

description.title: Decentralized Coordination Layers
description.body: Our project uses a distributed IoT architecture where sensors, Arduino, ESP8266, GSM, and relay-controlled devices work together to monitor and respond to farm conditions. Sensor data is processed locally by the Arduino, while ESP8266 sends data to the cloud and GSM provides alerts. This coordination between multiple devices enables real-time monitoring, automated irrigation, and faster responses without relying entirely on manual control.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: CertHack combines OCR, AI-assisted analysis, SHA-256 fingerprinting, and trusted certificate records to identify verified, tampered/invalid, and unverified certificates.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
While building CertHack, we faced several challenges during development:

- OCR accuracy: Different certificate layouts, fonts, image quality, and scanned PDFs caused OCR to sometimes misread names, dates, or course details.
- False positives: Some genuine certificates were initially classified as suspicious because they were not present in our trusted registry.
- Certificate verification: We learned that visual similarity alone cannot reliably prove whether a certificate is genuine.
- Hash verification :We implemented SHA-256 fingerprinting so that even a small change to a registered certificate can be detected.
- Frontend–backend integration: Connecting the React frontend with the FastAPI backend and displaying different verification states required debugging API responses and UI logic.
- Limited development time: Since the project was developed under hackathon time constraints, we focused on building a working end-to-end prototype rather than a fully trained machine-learning model.

How we overcame them:

We combined multiple verification signals instead of relying on a single AI prediction. CertHack now uses "OCR + AI-assisted analysis + SHA-256 hashing + a trusted certificate registry", and distinguishes between "Verified, Tampered/Invalid, and Unverified" results. This also prevents an unknown certificate from automatically being labelled as fake.

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body: CertHack supports Self-Sovereignty by allowing users to independently verify their certificates using SHA-256 fingerprints, trusted records, OCR, and AI-assisted analysis. Instead of depending entirely on manual issuer verification, users can check whether their credential is verified, potentially tampered with, or unverified. The system can later be extended to decentralized blockchain-based credential verification.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Symbiosis-OS is a decentralized, human-centric operating system designed for modern factory floors that dynamically balances machine optimization with the cognitive and physical well-being of the workforce. By utilizing non-invasive wearable biometrics and edge computer vision, the system monitors worker fatigue, stress, and ergonomic strain in real time. It acts as a bio-empathic orchestrator, automatically adjusting collaborative robot (cobot) speeds, redistributing workloads, and morphing the ambient workspace to prevent injuries and maintain a sustainable flow state without requiring manual intervention.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: Current Industry 4.0 paradigms prioritize absolute machine efficiency and throughput, often treating human operators as biological components forced to adapt to rigid, high-speed automated processes. This approach leads to severe repetitive strain injuries (RSIs), high cognitive burnout, elevated turnover rates, and eventual drops in product quality when human fatigue peaks. Existing "ergonomic" solutions are reactive, relying on post-shift surveys or manual supervisor interventions, leaving a critical gap for a system that can proactively prevent physical and mental overload the moment it begins to manifest on the assembly line.

description.title: Decentralized Coordination Layers
description.body: The "Decentralized Coordination Layers" track applies directly to Symbiosis-OS through its distributed edge-to-cloud architecture, which eliminates single points of failure and central bottlenecks in high-throughput industrial environments. Instead of relying on a monolithic SCADA server, the system utilizes decentralized node clusters—such as local edge computer vision processors and wearable IoT mesh gateways—that locally aggregate and process high-frequency biometric and postural telemetry with minimal latency. These distributed nodes leverage peer-to-peer event-driven protocols to asynchronously communicate state changes, allowing shop-floor devices like collaborative robots and automated guided vehicles (AGVs) to autonomously negotiate workload redistribution and safety parameter adjustments at the edge. Meanwhile, a federated machine learning and consensus layer coordinates across cells to continuously update global reinforcement learning policies without exposing raw sensitive worker telemetry, ensuring fault-tolerant, low-latency, and privacy-preserving synchronization across the entire manufacturing floor.

Another challenge was implementing secure user authentication. I added JWT-based authentication and protected the market-related APIs so that only authenticated users could access specific features.

Building these features taught me how to move from a basic prototype toward a more production-ready AI application.

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body: Lattice supports self-sovereign programmable accounts through modular ERC-7579 and ERC-6900 smart account architectures, built on ERC-4337 and ERC-1271. Users and applications can compose their own validation, execution, authorization, session-key, and account modules while retaining control over how the account behaves and evolves. Rather than depending on a platform-controlled wallet or fixed account implementation, Lattice makes account capabilities modular and upgradeable, allowing users to define their own security and permission model onchain.

description.title: Decentralized Coordination Layers
description.body: Lattice is a modular smart contract framework built on the EIP-2535 Diamond Standard that lets protocols compose governance, access control, upgrades, cross-chain messaging, DeFi, security, and account functionality behind a single programmable contract. By combining these capabilities through reusable facets with isolated ERC-7201 storage, Lattice provides infrastructure for coordinating users, assets, permissions, and protocol actions without relying on a monolithic contract architecture. Its governance modules also enable systems where upgrades and configuration can be controlled entirely through onchain proposals and timelocks.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Student achievements such as  : hackathon wins, course certificates, club roles — are scattered across PDFs, college portals, and screenshots, with no easy way to verify them. 
**Proof of You** lets trusted issuers (professors, clubs) issue tamper-***proof badges*** directly to a ***student's wallet***. Once issued, a badge can't be *deleted, altered, or transferred*; giving students a permanent, self-owned record of their achievements that anyone can instantly verify, without emailing anyone or waiting on a college database.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
We hit a wagmi/RainbowKit version mismatch that silently broke wallet connection with no clear error — traced it to an invalid dependency version and fixed it by pinning wagmi to the version RainbowKit expected.
 We also had a merge conflict in App.jsx when two of us built different pages independently, which we resolved by splitting the UI into separate component files. Finally, we tested our contract's issuer restriction by deliberately removing a team wallet from the approved list, confirming non-approved wallets are correctly blocked from issuing badges.

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body: Students fully own their achievement badges in their own wallet (not locked inside a college database or account that can be lost, deactivated, or controlled by an institution)

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body: Once a badge is issued, there's no delete or admin-override function in the contract - not even the deployer can revoke or alter it, so no institution can later erase or suppress a student's verified record.

fike-0e31.name: VIGIL
fike-0e31.tagline: Small transfers flow. Big ones wait

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Wallets are protected by a single private key. If that key **leaks**, gets **phished**, or is copied by **malware**, the funds behind it can be gone in one transaction. The usual fix, a multi signature wallet, is safe but needs several people online for every payment, which most users will not do for daily spending. **VIGIL** solves the same problem without that cost. Small, normal payments still go through instantly. Anything large or unusual is held for a short delay and can be cancelled by a second key, so a stolen key on its own is not enough to empty the wallet.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The hardest part was not the delay itself, that part is well known. It was making sure the delay could not be switched off by whoever stole the key. Our first version let the owner call functions like **disableGuard** directly. The very first test we wrote for that path passed immediately, which was the warning sign, since it meant an attacker who stole the owner key could turn off protection in one transaction and then drain the wallet right after, making the whole system pointless.

The fix was to remove every direct path to those settings. Now **setThreshold**, **setDelay**, **setGuardian**, and **disableGuard** can only be called by the contract calling itself, which only happens after one of these changes has gone through the exact same propose, wait, and cancel process as a normal large transfer. We wrote a dedicated test for this, **test_disablingGuardIsItselfDelayedAndVetoable**, and used it to check every other setting too. Turning the protection off is now protected by the same protection.

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body: **VIGIL** is a self custodied smart account. You hold both keys, the contract holds the funds, and no third party ever has custody or approval power. It fits the track's own call for a smart account wallet with a real policy engine, built around the specific case of a compromised everyday key rather than general session keys or bundlers.

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body: Once a queued action has cleared its delay and was not cancelled, **executeAction** can be called by anyone, not just the owner or a fixed relayer. No single party has to stay online or can be pressured into withholding a transfer that was already approved, so finishing a legitimate payment never depends on one gatekeeper.

description.title: Decentralized Coordination Layers
description.body: The owner and guardian are a small two party protocol enforced entirely by the contract, with no backend and no central service coordinating them. Neither key alone can both move funds and silence the other, and the rules that govern that relationship can only change by going through the same rules, which is the kind of trustless coordination logic the track asks for.

argus-2efe.name: Argus
argus-2efe.tagline: The lie detector for Ethereum RPCs — one endpoint

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## 1. Honest nodes kept "lying" (client diversity)
Geth, Erigon and Reth return different extra fields for `eth_getBlockByNumber`, so comparing full objects flagged honest nodes as deviant.
**Fix:** compare only the consensus-critical tuple `(hash, parentHash, stateRoot, transactionsRoot)` — false positives gone.

## 2. The "latest" tag made truth subjective
Honest nodes legitimately disagree about `latest` due to propagation delay, which would have caused false accusations.
**Fix:** pin every canonical query to an explicit **finalized block hex**. This made "lying" objectively definable — and made every piece of evidence reproducible forever via curl.

## 3. The router recommended the worst node
Our first "Best RPC" widget read `scores[0]`, but the query was sorted by timestamp — so it recommended whichever provider *finished polling last*, even a score-20 node.
**Fix:** dedupe to the latest row per provider, sort by score, and add safety thresholds (min score 50, score freshness, flagged fail-open instead of silent recommendation).

## 4. "Why should we trust YOUR server?"
Our first architectures kept failing this question. We iterated from client-side → federated observers, and finally landed on **"server is a reporter, not a judge"**: publish raw evidence, commit Merkle roots on-chain, and let a `/verify` page recompute the math in the skeptic's browser. That turned our biggest weakness into the product's core feature.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Every wallet and dApp silently trusts a single RPC provider. If that provider serves stale balances, mutated state, or quietly censors your transaction (published research shows ~46% of mainnet blocks have been produced by censoring builders), you would never know — no receipt, no proof, no recourse.

**Argus is a lie detector and failover router for Ethereum RPCs.**

## What people use it for

- **Devs & wallets:** paste one endpoint (`/api/rpc`) into any dApp or wallet. Argus pools the major free public RPCs plus any paid ones you add, routes every request to the highest-integrity live provider, and auto-fails-over the instant one degrades.
- **Auditors & skeptics:** click any flag to see raw evidence — expected-vs-got diffs, a reproducible `curl` frozen at a finalized block, explorer links, and an on-chain attestation. The `/verify` page re-runs our open-source math in *your* browser and checks it against on-chain Merkle roots: `browser math == server verdict == on-chain hash`.
- **The ecosystem:** a public, tamper-evident reputation ledger for RPC providers — accuracy, uptime, latency, censorship flags, and improving/degrading trends over time.

## How it makes things safer

- Cross-examines 8+ providers every 20s at pinned finalized blocks, reaches an independence-weighted consensus, and classifies deviations as `DEVIANT / STALE / CENSORING / DOWN`.
- A dedicated probe EOA detects write-path censorship that read-only checks can never see.
- The server is a **reporter, not a judge**: raw evidence is public, hourly Merkle roots are committed to Sepolia, and anyone can recompute every verdict. A server that cannot lie undetectably.

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body:
Argus implements both directions of this track — a consensus-driven decentralized RPC aggregator and a verifiable routing layer — as one shipped product.

**Consensus mechanism among providers (aggregator):** Every 20s Argus fans out identical canonical queries to 8+ RPC providers, pinned to a *finalized* block, normalizes and hashes the responses, and selects truth via an independence-weighted majority vote (one operator = one vote, so a single company running many endpoints cannot fake a majority). If no group holds >50%, the poll is marked INCONCLUSIVE instead of guessing.

**Accurate data selection:** Outliers are retried before accusation and classified as `DEVIANT / STALE / CENSORING / DOWN`. A dedicated probe EOA runs differential write-path tests to catch silent transaction filtering — the censorship mode read-only checks can never see.

**Load balancing:** A single `/api/rpc` endpoint routes every request to the highest-integrity live provider (integrity → uptime → latency), with automatic failover and hot-swap the instant a provider is flagged.

**Verifiable routing infrastructure:** Every accusation ships with independently checkable evidence: expected-vs-got diff, a reproducible `curl` frozen at the pinned block, explorer links, and an on-chain attestation. Hourly Merkle roots of all polls are committed to Sepolia so history can never be rewritten. The `/verify` page re-runs the open-source math in the user's own browser: `browser math == server verdict == on-chain hash`.

The tool itself practices what the track preaches: no trusted center — the server is a reporter, not a judge, observers are replaceable, and Ethereum holds the log.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
# 🛠️ Challenges I Ran Into & How We Overcame Them

Building **1Shot Agentic Wallet (`ukii`)** required bridging cutting-edge Account Abstraction standards (**ERC-7710**, **ERC-7715**), cryptographic signature protocols, and natural language AI processing into a smooth, single-page Web3 application. Here are the main technical hurdles we faced and how we solved them:

---

### 1. 🔑 Cryptographic EIP-712 Signature Compatibility for ERC-7715 Delegations

* **The Challenge:** 
  Implementing **ERC-7715 (`wallet_grantPermissions`)** requires producing strict **EIP-712 Typed Data signatures** so that Smart Accounts and off-chain relayer nodes can cryptographically verify delegated permissions. Different Web3 environments (e.g., MetaMask browser extensions vs. custom WebAuthn/Passkey private key signers) handle `eth_signTypedData_v4` domain parameters and BigInt/uint256 serialization differently, leading to frequent signature verification mismatches across different chain IDs.

* **How We Overcame It:** 
  We designed a unified cryptographic signing abstraction within [`DelegationManager`](file:///Users/meta/coding/ppapa/js/modules/delegation.js). It normalizes the EIP-712 domain schema (`name`, `version`, `chainId`, `verifyingContract`) and typed data structs (`Delegation`). For BigInt parameters like `spendLimitDaily` and `expiryTimestamp`, we standardized unit conversion using Ethers.js v6 `parseUnits` and built a fail-safe fallback signing pipeline to ensure signature validity across all connected account types.

---

### 2. 🤖 Safeguarding Autonomous AI Execution Against Agent Hallucination

* **The Challenge:** 
  Allowing an AI Assistant to translate natural-language user prompts directly into executable Web3 transactions poses a critical security risk: if the AI misinterprets a prompt or hallucinates contract parameters, it could generate unsafe operations or exceed user expectations.

* **How We Overcame It:** 
  We implemented a **two-tier execution barrier** in [`AgentEngine`](file:///Users/meta/coding/ppapa/js/modules/agent.js):
  1. **Intent Parsing & Pre-Flight Audit:** Natural language inputs are parsed into structured execution plans containing protocol routes, token amounts, and gas sponsorship breakdowns.
  2. **Strict On-Chain Policy Verification:** Before any transaction plan can be executed or sent to a relayer, it is checked against active ERC-7715 delegation policies in `validateAgentAction()`. If a planned action exceeds daily spending limits or violates whitelisted contracts, execution is blocked immediately with an explicit policy warning.

---

### 3. ⚡ Multi-Chain RPC State Management & Provider Switching

* **The Challenge:** 
  Supporting multiple EVM testnets (**Base Sepolia**, **Arbitrum Sepolia**, **Optimism Sepolia**, and **Sepolia**) alongside multiple wallet authentication types (Injected Web3 Wallets vs. 1Shot Passkey Accounts) often led to desynchronized provider states, stale RPC balance queries, or broken transaction signing when switching networks dynamically.

* **How We Overcame It:** 
  We created an event-driven `SmartWallet` controller in [`wallet.js`](file:///Users/meta/coding/ppapa/js/modules/wallet.js). We separated RPC read operations (`ethers.JsonRpcProvider`) from transaction signing (`ethers.BrowserProvider` / `ethers.Wallet`). When a user switches networks or wallet modes, the provider pool automatically reinstantiates the appropriate RPC provider, purges cached balances, and performs asynchronous multi-token balance refetches without refreshing the page.

---

### 4. ⛽ Zero-Gas EIP-7710 Relayer Integration

* **The Challenge:** 
  Executing transactions for users who have **zero native gas tokens (`ETH`)** required routing transaction payloads through EIP-7710 Paymaster Relayers. Ensuring transaction payloads were correctly structured with Paymaster gas limits while providing instant visual feedback on dollars saved was non-trivial.

* **How We Overcame It:** 
  We wrapped transaction payloads with EIP-7710 Paymaster metadata, delegating gas payment to the 1Shot Public Relayer. We also built real-time gas tracking hooks that calculate estimated gas fees in native tokens and convert them to USD, giving users transparent visibility into their cumulative gas savings.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
# 🎯 Problem Statement & Solution Overview

## 1. The Core Problem in Current Web3 / DeFi Interactions

### 🔴 High UX Friction & Multi-Step Complexity
Performing basic DeFi actions—such as swapping tokens, bridging assets across layer-2s, or executing yield strategies—requires navigating complex decentralized application interfaces, manually approving token allowances, calculating slippage, and individually signing multiple sequential wallet popups.

### 🔴 Gas Token Management Bottleneck ("No ETH for Gas")
Users frequently find their accounts stuck because they hold ERC-20 tokens (e.g., USDC, DAI) but lack the native chain gas token (`ETH`), forcing them to acquire or bridge ETH just to pay transaction fees for a single transfer or swap.

### 🔴 All-or-Nothing Private Key Exposure for AI Agents
Autonomous AI agents, DCA bots, and trading scripts currently require users to share their private keys or grant unrestricted, non-custodial wallet access. If an agent is compromised, exhibits algorithmic failure, or hallucinates, all funds in the user's wallet are at risk of being drained.

### 🔴 Lack of Pre-Execution Safety & Seed Phrase Security
Blindly executing automated or AI-generated transaction plans leaves users vulnerable to high slippage, front-running, or malicious contract interactions. Additionally, traditional seed phrase backups remain a major single point of failure for mainstream user security.

---

## ⚡ The Solution: 1Shot Agentic Wallet (`ukii`)

`ukii` transforms Web3 interaction into a **natural-language, gasless, safe, and autonomous agent-enabled experience**.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                           1Shot Agentic Wallet                              │
├──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┤
│  🤖 Agentic AI       │  ⚡ EIP-7710 Gas      │  🔐 ERC-7715 Permission       │
│     Assistant        │     Abstraction      │     Delegation                │
│                      │                      │                               │
│  - Natural Language  │  - 100% Sponsored    │  - Bounded Agent Scopes       │
│  - Multi-Step Routes │  - Zero Native ETH   │  - Max Spending & Gas Caps    │
│  - Safety & Risk     │  - Public Paymaster  │  - Contract Whitelisting      │
│    Scoring (0-100%)  │    Relayer           │  - 1-Click Instant Revocation │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘
```

### 🤖 1. Natural Language Intent & Multi-Step Automation (Easier)
Instead of manually navigating multiple DEXs and bridge interfaces, users express their intent in plain English:
> *"Swap 25 USDC to ETH on Base and bridge 50 USDC to Arbitrum when gas is optimal."*

The integrated **Agentic AI Assistant** parses natural language into structured, multi-step transaction plans, automatically computing optimal swap routes and execution steps with a single click.

### ⚡ 2. EIP-7710 Gas Abstraction & Paymaster Relayer (Seamless & Gasless)
Leveraging EIP-7710 specifications and sponsored Paymaster Relayers, `ukii` delivers **100% sponsored transactions**. Users can swap, bridge, and execute agentic strategies with zero native `ETH` in their smart account.

### 🔐 3. ERC-7715 Granular Permission Delegation (Safer)
Users can delegate execution authority to autonomous AI agents without exposing private keys. With **ERC-7715 policy enforcement**, users set strict on-chain operational boundaries:
* **Max Spending Allowance**: Cap total spending per transaction (e.g., max $50 USDC per tx).
* **Gas Caps**: Limit the maximum gas fee allowed per automated execution.
* **Contract Whitelisting**: Restrict agent execution exclusively to verified routers (e.g., Uniswap V3, Hop Protocol).
* **Expiration Timestamps**: Set automatic permission expiration (e.g., valid for 7 days).
* **Instant Revocation Engine**: Revoke active delegation grants at any time with a single transaction.
### 🛡️ 4. Transaction Safety Scoring & Passkey Recovery (Safer & Frictionless)
* **Automated Risk Scoring (0–100%)**: Before execution, every plan undergoes real-time pre-flight inspection checking contract integrity, output slippage, and parameter sanity.
* **Passkey & Social Recovery**: Built-in support for hardware-bound WebAuthn / Passkey authentication (Touch ID, Face ID) paired with an **m-of-n Guardian Social Recovery network** prevents single-point-of-failure key loss.
---
## 💡 What People Can Use It For

1. **Gasless Intent-Based DeFi**: Execute swaps and cross-chain transfers across EVM L2 testnets (Base Sepolia, Arbitrum Sepolia, Optimism Sepolia, Sepolia) using natural language with zero native gas tokens required.
2. **Safe Autonomous AI Trading & Delegation**: Delegate bounded execution permissions to automated AI agents or trading algorithms with user-defined spending caps, whitelisted dApps, and expiration limits.
3. **Seedless Smart Account Management**
4. **Pre-Flight Risk Auditing**

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body:
# 🛡️ How 1Shot Agentic Wallet (`ukii`) Fits the Self-Sovereignty Track

**Self-Sovereignty** in Web3 is about empowering individuals to maintain complete control over their digital identity, financial assets, and cryptographic keys—without relying on centralized intermediaries, custodial custodians, or permissioned third parties.

**1Shot Agentic Wallet (`ukii`)** advances self-sovereignty into the era of Autonomous AI Agents by solving the core conflict of agentic Web3: **How to leverage AI automation without surrendering key ownership or custodial control.**

---

### 1. 🔐 Non-Custodial Agent Delegation (ERC-7715)
* **The Self-Sovereignty Value:** Traditional Web3 bots force users into a dangerous tradeoff: either manually sign every transaction (destroying automation) or hand over private keys / unlimited API access to third-party servers (destroying self-custody).
* **Our Implementation:** Leveraging **ERC-7715 (`wallet_grantPermissions`)**, `ukii` grants autonomous AI agents **cryptographically bounded, non-custodial execution scopes**. The user maintains 100% key ownership while delegating specific, fine-grained tasks (e.g., maximum $50 USDC per transaction, whitelisted DEX routers only, 7-day expiration). The user retains sovereign authority to **revoke delegations on-chain in 1 click at any time**.

---

### 2. 🔑 Hardware-Bound Passkey Authentication (WebAuthn / Passkeys)
* **The Self-Sovereignty Value:** Relying on centralized OAuth providers (Google/Web2 logins) creates identity lock-in and censorship risks, while seed phrases create severe single-point-of-failure vulnerabilities.
* **Our Implementation:** `ukii` utilizes hardware-anchored **WebAuthn / Passkeys** (Touch ID, Face ID, YubiKeys). Passkey credentials reside inside the user's local device Secure Enclave, ensuring that private signing keys are generated, stored, and operated locally without central database storage.

---

### 3. 🛡️ Trustless Social Recovery via Guardian Consensus (`m-of-n`)
* **The Self-Sovereignty Value:** Self-sovereignty shouldn't mean permanent financial loss if a user loses a single hardware device or phone. Traditional recovery relies on centralized customer support or custodial password resets.
* **Our Implementation:** Built into [`SocialRecovery`](file:///Users/meta/coding/ppapa/js/modules/recovery.js), `ukii` implements a peer-to-peer **m-of-n Guardian Consensus mechanism**. Users designate a threshold of trusted guardians (e.g., 2-of-3 consisting of a hardware wallet, trusted contact, or cloud backup). Account ownership can be restored in a decentralized, trustless manner without any central admin intervention.

---

### 4. ⚡ Gas-Abstracted Economic Autonomy (EIP-7710)
* **The Self-Sovereignty Value:** True economic sovereignty means being able to transact with the assets you hold without being blocked by external network gas barriers (e.g., having 500 USDC but 0 ETH for gas fees).
* **Our Implementation:** Through **EIP-7710 Paymaster Relayers**, users can execute transfers, swaps, and agentic interactions without needing native chain gas tokens (`ETH`). This democratizes access and removes platform friction while preserving non-custodial smart account execution.

---

### 📊 Summary: The Self-Sovereignty Spectrum

| Dimension | Traditional Bot / Custodial Wallet | 1Shot Agentic Wallet (`ukii`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Private Key Custody** | Shared / Custodial Server | **100% Self-Custodial (Hardware Enclave)** |
| **AI Agent Permissions** | Unlimited / Full Account Access | **ERC-7715 Bounded & Revocable Scopes** |
| **Account Recovery** | Centralized Support / Seed Phrase | **Decentralized m-of-n Social Recovery** |
| **Gas Dependency** | Must hold native ETH per chain | **Gasless EIP-7710 Paymaster Relaying** |

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges I ran into

The core anonymity guarantee wasn't actually being tested — it was being assumed.
Early on, it would have been easy to build the 3-hop mix routing, watch a message successfully arrive at the destination, and call it done. But "the message arrived" doesn't prove "no relay saw both ends of the conversation" — that's the entire point of the project, and it's exactly the kind of property that's easy to get subtly wrong (e.g., a relay logging more than it should, or a data structure accidentally carrying sender and receiver together). I made per-hop visibility an explicit, enforced test: each relay's actual state/logs are inspected after a real send to prove no single relay ever had both sender-side and receiver-side information — not just that decryption worked. That discipline — verify the guarantee in code, don't assume the library or the plumbing gives it to you — became the standard for every later component too (blind-token unlinkability, cover-traffic indistinguishability from real traffic, Poisson delay actually following the right distribution).

Picking the wrong library would have quietly broken a guarantee, not caused an obvious bug.
For the anonymous spam-resistance layer, "blind signature" sounds like one well-defined thing, but different libraries give different real guarantees — some give blind issuance without true unlinkability across redemptions, which would have silently defeated the entire anonymity model while looking correct in every normal test. The same trap showed up picking a Double Ratchet library — some candidates were unmaintained, one was a name collision with an unrelated crate, another only handled group sessions instead of pairwise messaging. Each library decision had to be checked against actual source code and documented guarantees, not just its name or README, before being trusted into the core protocol.

No maintained library existed for the mix-network delay/cover-traffic design (Poisson mixing), and building it wrong would have made the timing-correlation defense fake.
Rather than hand-rolling probability code and hoping it was right, the actual distribution shape was tested statistically (thousands of samples checked against expected exponential-distribution properties) before trusting it anywhere near production paths. This also surfaced a real, subtle bug: an early test assumed messages would always take at least a fixed minimum time to arrive — true for a fixed delay, but mathematically false once the delay became randomized, since a random draw can legitimately land below the average. The fix wasn't to hack the test to pass — it was to recognize the test's assumption was wrong and rewrite it around the real statistical behavi

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The problem it solves 

Every popular messaging app today including Signal has a structural blind spot: even with perfect end-to-end encryption, the app's own servers still see who is talking to whom, and when. Content is private; the relationship graph is not. That metadata alone is enough to identify activists, journalists' sources, whistleblowers, dissidents, or anyone a government or adversary wants to target — without ever breaking a single encryption key. And because these apps run through one company's servers, that metadata is sitting at a single point that can be subpoenaed, seized, or blocked outright.

WARREN removes that blind spot. Messages are routed through multiple independent relays using onion-style mix routing (similar in spirit to Tor, purpose-built for messaging), so no single relay ; not even the people operating the network ; ever sees both the sender and the receiver of a message. The network is also secured against a second, usually-ignored problem: anonymous networks are easy to spam and abuse. WARREN solves this without requiring identity, using anonymous proof of work gated tokens, so real users stay untraceable while abuse still has a real cost.        

                                                                                                                                         Who this is for, concretely:

Activists and journalists working under governments that monitor who contacts whom, not just what's said ; WARREN means there's no connection graph to seize or subpoena in the first place.
Whistleblowers and sources who need to reach a journalist without either party's contact being traceable, even if the messaging app's infrastructure itself is compromised or compelled.
Anyone in a censored region ;traffic is disguised to look like ordinary web traffic, and relay trust is split across multiple independent signers rather than one operator, making the network harder to fingerprint, block, or shut down at a single point.
Any user who simply doesn't want their social graph built and stored somewhere, even if they have "nothing to hide" — the same way encryption became a baseline expectation, unlinkable metadata is the next baseline that's currently missing from every mainstream option.

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body:
Censorship doesn't just mean blocking content — it means an adversary being able to identify, target, and shut down the people communicating, and being able to detect and block the communication channel itself. WARREN is built directly against both of those capabilities, not just the surface-level "can I read the message" problem that most encrypted apps solve.

1. It removes the single point that gets censored.
Apps like Signal run through one company's servers — a single legally-compellable, technically-blockable chokepoint. A government can subpoena the operator, order an ISP to block their domain, or force the app off app stores in that country. WARREN has no equivalent single target: messages route through multiple independent relays, and the relay directory itself is signed by multiple independent keys (K-of-N) rather than one operator, so there's no single party or server whose removal takes down the network.

2. It protects the people, not just the content.
The core censorship threat for activists, journalists, and dissidents usually isn't "can they read my message" — it's "can they prove I was talking to this person at all." Even fully encrypted apps leak that connection graph to their own servers. WARREN's mix routing means no relay — including the network's own operators — ever sees both sender and receiver for a given message, so there's no metadata graph to seize, subpoena, or hand over under legal pressure in the first place.

3. It resists network-level blocking, not just server-level takedown.
A censor doesn't need to touch a server to block a service — they can just fingerprint its traffic pattern at the ISP/DPI level and drop it. WARREN's traffic is wrapped to resemble ordinary encrypted web traffic instead of a distinctive custom protocol, raising the cost of a censor trying to detect and block it at the network layer, not just the server layer.

4. It resists shutdown-by-flooding, without reintroducing the thing that makes people traceable.
Anonymous networks are an easy censorship target because they're easy to abuse — flood them with spam or DoS traffic, and either the network collapses or its operators are forced to add identity checks that undo the anonymity. WARREN solves spam resistance anonymously (proof-of-work-gated, unlinkable tokens), so it can't be strangled by abuse without ever requiring anyone to identify themselves.

Taken together: Signal is censorship-resistant only in the sense that its content is unreadable. WARREN is censorship-resistant in the structural sense the track is actually asking about — no single operator to compel, no metadata graph to seize, no easy network fingerprint to block, and no identity requirement to weaponize against its own users.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**1. A local chain made valid proofs prove the wrong state**

A stray Anvil process on our RPC port reported a different chain (31337), causing our anchor selection to use an invalidly old block. Proofs were technically valid but against the wrong chain. We fixed this by validating chain IDs and anchoring to the highest block confirmed by at least two independent endpoints. We also correctly distinguish proven zero/absence from missing data.

**2. Our best demo moment was invisible**

Our malicious RPC was correctly detected, but the UI only showed the failure as text because the first valid proof won the race. We now retain and visualize failed proof paths, making the exact point where a forged proof breaks visible to the audience.

**3. Public RPCs and local forks couldn't reliably serve proofs**

Anvil forks inherited upstream **eth_getProof** rate limits, while some public endpoints throttled or refused proofs. We moved to two independent public mainnet endpoints plus our malicious proxy, giving us real mainnet proofs and cross-provider corroboration. Verified results are also cached by address + state root.

**4. Noir's API changed underneath our ZK circuit**

The Poseidon/Keccak hashing APIs we planned to use had changed in Noir 1.0. We switched to Poseidon2 and built a self-consistent, tested circuit, while explicitly marking its JavaScript-side integration as incomplete rather than claiming unsupported ZK functionality.

**5. Making the proof visualization consistent was harder than expected**

Proofs have different depths, making naive scaling distort the visualization. After three iterations, we fixed the row height and scale limits and used browser debug measurements to guarantee consistent rendering across proof states.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
When your wallet shows you a balance, that number came from a company.

Your wallet asked a server how much ETH an address holds. The server answered. Your wallet drew the answer on the screen. That is the entire exchange. There is no signature, no proof, and no check anywhere in it. The number you are looking at is a claim, and your wallet believes it the way you believe a stranger who tells you the time. 

This is true of nearly everything you see in crypto: your balance, your token holdings, whether a transaction went through, what a contract currently holds. It all arrives as an unverified assertion from a server you do not control, and every interface presents it as fact.

Three things make that worse than it sounds. A very large share of Ethereum reads flow through a handful of companies. A lying server looks exactly like an honest one, because there is no error and no warning, and the interface renders a lie in the same font as the truth. And if an attacker can make your wallet believe a false balance or a false allowance, they can walk you into signing something you never would have signed.

description.body: The smart account is only as sovereign as the endpoint telling it what state it is in, which is the gap we close. Plus Sybil resistance that costs capital instead of privacy.

description.title: Decentralized Coordination Layers

deadhand-7b13.name: deadHand
deadhand-7b13.tagline: A dead man's switch where nobody holds the key.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
If you are holding a document that someone powerful wants buried, your options today are
to trust a newspaper, a lawyer, or a company. All three can be pressured, and all three
have been.

Deadhand lets you seal a document and set a check-in interval. Keep checking in and
nothing happens. Stop, and the document decrypts itself in public at a deadline fixed in
advance. Nobody can be pressured into releasing it early, because nobody holds the key.

The document's key is encrypted to a **future round of the drand beacon**, a public
randomness network that signs a value every 3 seconds. The signature that decrypts it does
not exist yet, anywhere. It comes into existence on schedule, and then anyone can open the
document. No server, no custodian, and no transaction from anyone.

Existing tools in this space split your key among paid custodians who promise to forget.
it. That is an ongoing cost, a liveness assumption, and a group that can be bribed or.
subpoenaed into opening your file early. We removed that group entirely.

**Who it is for:** journalists protecting a source file, whistleblowers who need insurance.
before they go public, and activists who need something to outlive their arrest.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**The hurdle that redefined the project.** We planned for a check-in to push the deadline
back. Our first test proved that is impossible: a published timelock capsule cannot be
extended. If a capsule opens at round R, anyone who saved a copy opens it at round R, and
nothing you do later takes that back. This is precisely why older systems needed paid
custodians, since only a human who agrees to re-share your key can move a deadline.

We redesigned around it. A check-in now **rotates** instead of extending: derive a fresh
key, re-encrypt the document under it, seal that key to a later round, and unpin the
previous copy of the file. The old capsule still opens on schedule and still gives up a
real, working key, but that key now decrypts a file nobody has any more. A check-in
removes availability, not secrecy.

We turned the objection into a feature. The app has a "Try to break it" panel that pulls
old capsules back out of transaction calldata so anyone can replay one and watch a valid
key land on a 404.

**The bug that cost us the most time.** Sealed documents never opened in the UI, even
though the same code worked in Node. The chain poll rebuilt the switch object every 1.5
seconds, which retriggered a React effect whose cleanup cancelled the in-flight beacon
fetch. That fetch takes about 1.4 seconds, so it was cancelled every single time and the
result was never committed. It looked exactly like a broken timelock. The fix was to
depend on the fields that actually change the answer instead of the object identity, and
to read the latest object through a ref. We also stopped swallowing errors in that path,
since a reader that silently stays "sealed" is indistinguishable from a broken product.

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body:
The track asks for users to hold their own capability instead of renting it from a
provider. Every existing tool in this space asks you to hand key shares to somebody. We
require you to hand nothing to anybody.

- No custodian, no shard-holder network, no quorum holds any part of your key.
- The encryption key is derived from a signature made with your own wallet, so it is
  recoverable on any device from the key that controls the switch. There is no recovery
  file to lose or have taken.
- All encryption happens in the browser. The key never reaches a server, including ours.
- The owner alone can rotate, stand down, or force an early release.

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body:
The track asks for tools that remove single points of control from the path a user
depends on. Publishing is exactly that path here, and we removed every controllable point
from it.

- There is no server or company in the release path, so there is nobody to serve an order
  on. Taking our site down does not stop a release.
- The capsule sits on-chain in public. Anyone can open it with about 20 lines of code, so
  the front-end is a convenience and not a dependency.
- Once the beacon reaches the round, release needs no transaction from anyone and cannot
  be recalled. There is no step left for an adversary to block.
- The failure mode is early release, never silent suppression, which is the correct
  direction for a censorship-resistant tool.

description.title: Decentralized Coordination Layers
description.body:
The track asks for coordination that does not route through a platform or an operator.
Ours is coordinated entirely by a public randomness beacon and verified in the open.

- Release timing is coordinated by drand, which never sees your ciphertext, does not know
  the switch exists, and signs the same rounds for everyone. It cannot single you out.
- No operator, keeper, or voting quorum decides when anything happens.
- Independent readers can attest on-chain to what they read. Several unrelated addresses
  converging on the same hash is public evidence that no single front-end fabricated the
  contents, which is a decentralized substitute for a trusted publisher.

unpack-f657.name: Unpack
unpack-f657.tagline: A wallet with no seed phrase and no gas

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Self-custody today makes you trade sovereignty for security. A seed phrase is the only thing standing between you and losing everything, gas fees mean you need ETH before you can even move your own funds, and every approval you've ever granted to a dApp — most of them unlimited — just sits there forever as silent attack surface, because no mainstream wallet shows you the full list, let alone lets you clear it in one shot.

Unpack replaces all three failure points with one ERC-4337 smart account:

- No seed phrase. You sign in with a passkey (Face ID / fingerprint). The wallet address is derived deterministically from it, so it's recoverable and consistent without a 12-word phrase to write down or lose.

- No gas. Every write — mint, send, revoke, session setup, recovery — goes through a sponsored UserOperation. The wallet never needs to hold ETH to be usable.

- No forgotten approvals. The Approvals dashboard indexes every approval an address has ever granted, re-verifies each one's live allowance so stale entries disappear, flags unlimited approvals, and bulk-revokes any selection in a single signature and a single sponsored transaction — instead of one signed, gas-paying transaction per token, which is why almost nobody does this today.

On top of that, session keys let you delegate scoped, time-boxed permissions (e.g. "only call transfer, only for one hour") instead of handing over full account control, and social recovery lets a guardian rotate you onto a new passkey if you lose your device — so losing a phone doesn't mean losing the account.

Concretely: someone who's been swapping on DeFi for two years and has dozens of unlimited approvals from apps they've forgotten they used can open Unpack, see every one of them, and clear the risky ones in a single tap — safer self-custody with strictly less friction than what they have now.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The one that cost the most time was a dead end I had to walk all the way into before backing out of: I initially built session keys and social recovery on Rhinestone's Smart Sessions module (@rhinestone/module-sdk) running on top of our Kernel account. Everything looked right — the modules were deployed on Base Sepolia, installation succeeded, on-chain state showed the validator correctly registered and the session enabled. But every UserOperation routed through it reverted with AA23 InvalidValidator(). I traced it down through two real bugs in the module-sdk's Kernel support (a missing hook address, and a nonce-encoding bug that was routing operations to the root validator instead of the session validator), fixed both locally, and it still failed. It turned out Rhinestone's smart-sessions examples are all built and tested against Safe, not Kernel — the combination just isn't a supported path, and the package itself is deprecated. Rather than keep debugging a library against an integration nobody had verified, I switched the whole account layer to ZeroDev's own SDK, since Kernel is ZeroDev's account and sessions/recovery are first-class there. That meant redoing account construction and accepting that passkey addresses would change, but it actually worked.

The switch caused its own sharp bug: the app started rendering a blank white screen with Class extends value undefined. ZeroDev's SDK re-exports a class that extends Node's EventEmitter at module load time, and Vite externalizes Node builtins in the browser by default, so the import resolved to undefined. Fixed with an events polyfill package and a resolve.alias in Vite config — a two-line fix, but it took real digging through the bundle to find, since the failure looked like a React crash rather than a bundler/runtime mismatch.

Both taught the same lesson: in fast-moving ERC-4337 tooling, "the docs say it should work" isn't enough — verify against the specific account implementation and version you're actually running, headlessly, before wiring it into the UI.

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body: A passkey smart-account wallet with gasless transactions, session keys, and social recovery, plus a dashboard that finds and bulk-revokes every risky token approval

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: Initial plan was to directly have the company enter the credentials and leave a signature but the problem with that was that ultimately it involved a human entering details which made it vulnerable to tampering .So then we switched to using UAN details and removed the previously employing company from the system and directly the user and recruiter can use the web app.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: The decentralized recruiter app tackles the rampant problem of fabricated work histories and résumé fraud that plagues professional networking platforms such as LinkedIn—​candidates can easily claim positions, salaries, or ten‑year tenures that have no authoritative backing, leaving employers vulnerable to costly hiring mistakes and undermining trust in talent pipelines. By fetching a candidate’s official EPFO UAN record directly from the government‑maintained database and anchoring the full, immutable employee profile on a public blockchain, the solution provides a tamper‑proof, verifiable proof of employment that any recruiter can audit without exposing sensitive personal data, thereby restoring confidence in candidate credentials and dramatically reducing the risk of fraudulent hiring.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Self-custody wallets still funnel every transaction through an RPC provider — the same request carries your IP and your Ethereum address, letting a provider geoblock, censor, or deanonymize you before your transaction ever reaches a mempool. Dead Drop breaks that coupling: the browser signs a transaction fully offline via viem (no wallet extension, no RPC call), then hands the raw signed bytes off over a transport unrelated to Ethereum infra — a Nostr note tagged `#ethrelay`, a QR code, or a clipboard blob. A swarm of volunteer relayers subscribed to that tag decodes, validates, and broadcasts on the sender's behalf via `eth_sendRawTransaction`. Because broadcasting a given signed tx is idempotent, redundant relayers racing to submit is harmless — the sender's network never has to prove they touched Ethereum, since it never did.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: Getting the signer and relayer to agree byte-for-byte on the envelope format without ever talking to each other directly — solved by pulling encode/decode, the Nostr event/filter schema, and offline tx validation into a shared `packages/protocol` module both sides import, so a wire-format change can't silently desync them. Also had to make sure signing stayed genuinely offline: the only network call the web app is allowed to make is one optional, read-only nonce check that fails soft and never blocks signing. On the relayer side, validating untrusted envelopes (wrong chain ID, missing tip, malformed rawTx) before ever calling `eth_sendRawTransaction` was necessary to keep a swarm of relayers from broadcasting garbage or replaying transactions across chains.

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body: Dead Drop is a direct response to this track's second bullet — verifiable, censorship-resistant transaction routing — approached from the client side rather than the RPC side. Instead of aggregating multiple RPC providers (which still assumes RPC is the only path to the chain), it removes the RPC dependency from the sender entirely: transactions are signed fully offline in the browser via viem, and the raw signed bytes are handed off over transports that have nothing to do with Ethereum infrastructure — a Nostr note tagged `#ethrelay`, a QR code, or a clipboard blob — so a network that blocks known RPC endpoints, geoblocks an address, or logs IP↔address correlation never sees the sender touch Ethereum at all. A swarm of independent volunteer relayers then broadcasts on the sender's behalf via `eth_sendRawTransaction`, and because relaying is idempotent (same signed bytes → same tx hash), no single relayer is a chokepoint — any one being blocked, offline, or malicious just gets bypassed by the others. It's censorship resistance built into the transport layer itself, not into which RPC provider you trust.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1. **Eliminating Main-Thread UI Lag in 3D Real-Time Physics**:
   - *Challenge*: Updating state at 60 Hz caused heavy React re-renders, resulting in boat stutter and frame drops.
   - *Solution*: Decoupled the physics loop from React state by storing real-time vehicle vectors in mutable ref containers (`worldStateRef`) and using frame-delta linear interpolation (`lerp`) inside Three.js `@react-three/fiber` render loops for buttery-smooth 60 FPS movement.

2. **Preventing MetaMask Transaction Failures & Gas Estimation Rejections**:
   - *Challenge*: Strict contract checks were triggering MetaMask's `eth_estimateGas` pre-simulation to flag valid winner claims with "Transaction likely to fail".
   - *Solution*: Optimized the Solidity smart contract (`SmashArena.sol`) to validate state Keccak hashes while guaranteeing fallback call execution (`winner.call{value: payout}`), alongside explicit gas limit overrides to ensure 100% clean, one-click execution.

3. **Safe Web3 Address & Hex Sanitization**:
   - *Challenge*: Standard hex converters threw padding exceptions (`Hex size exceeds padding size`) when processing match identifiers and AI bot addresses.
   - *Solution*: Created a native hexadecimal sanitizer (`toValidAddress`) that normalizes match IDs and wallet addresses into valid, checksummed 20-byte/32-byte strings before passing them to `viem` and `wagmi`.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Traditional Web3 games often suffer from two major pain points: **clunky, high-friction user experiences** with constant wallet popups during gameplay, and **untrustworthy or central-server-reliant prize distribution** that leads to high latency and unfair payouts.

**MUCKERS** solves this by delivering a high-speed, arcade-action 3D Maritime Demolition Derby coupled with a **trustless, automated Smart Contract Escrow System on Ethereum (Sepolia)**:

- **Trustless Fair-Play Payouts**: Players stake a fixed 0.001 ETH entry fee directly into the `SmashArena` escrow smart contract. The contract deterministically holds funds and guarantees an immediate 95% payout directly to the winner's wallet without centralized admin intervention.
- **Zero-Lag 60 FPS Browser Gameplay**: Powered by Three.js and a custom reference-based physics engine, the 3D boat battle runs smoothly in the browser at 60 FPS without main-thread UI bottlenecks or input lag.
- **Seamless Real-Time Peer Synchronization**: Implements real-time room code matching, allowing players to host or join matches instantly with live positional updates.
- **Arcade Action & Combat Weapons**: Features dynamic ocean arenas, mystery weapon crates (TNT Rockets, Plasma Shockwaves, Mega Cannons, Scorching Fireballs), bow water splashes, and reactive particle FX.
