description.body:
TokenShield: 88/100 - Clear winner that actually solves a real $100M+ problem with an MVP buildable in 24 hours and clear monetization from day one.

This is the hackathon project that becomes a company. 🚀

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Track 1 - Self-Sovereignty:

Smart Wallets: 60/10 (crowded, hard to differentiate)
Sybil Resistance: Niche, limited users
TokenShield: 88/100 ✅ Real problem, MVP-ready, high demand

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Every real bug came from running against live Sepolia, not from reading code. Anvil hid all of them.

We accused innocent providers of censorship. Early on, one endpoint got named a silent dropper twice  it was merely lagging a few seconds behind its peers. For a censorship-resistance tool that is the worst possible bug: a false accusation is more damaging than a missed one, and it goes on-chain permanently. Fixed by requiring sustained denial four confirmation rounds over ~20 seconds, while peers already report the transaction mined and by exempting verification reads from quarantine so a quarantined provider can't skew its own trial.

The attestation raced the chain head. blockhash(block.number) returns zero, so the contract requires minedBlock < block.number. Anvil simulates against the pending block and accepted it; live Sepolia reverted. Unconditionally waiting a block would stall on an idle chain, so: attempt, and only on failure wait one block and retry once.

One key signed both the user's transaction and commitIntent, consuming the nonce every provider then rejected the broadcast. Fixed with an explicit nonce reservation for the commit.

nonce too low was misclassified as fatal. It means either "already mined" (benign) or "stale nonce" (fatal). Resolved by outcome now, never by string-matching the error.

Unbounded provider calls. A single hanging endpoint stalled block-pinning and receipt polling forever — the whole point is surviving one bad provider. Every call is now wrapped in a timeout, with retryCount: 0, since a silent retry would hide the failure and skew latency.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Every dApp talks to Ethereum through one RPC provider and trusts whatever comes back. That single connection fails in two invisible ways: a provider can lie about what it sees there is no second opinion to check it against or it can quietly drop the transaction you sent, returning a valid-looking hash and never relaying it. From your side that is indistinguishable from a slow network. Neither failure leaves a trace, so neither costs the provider anything.

Quorum makes the answer a vote and the silence a receipt.

Reads fan out to six independent providers, pinned to one explicit block, and are accepted only when ⌈2/3⌉ return the same result hash. A wrong answer is flagged as a dissenter and quarantined; a timeout is recorded as a non-vote, because a node that is down has not lied.

Writes commit their intent on-chain before broadcasting that ordering is the whole mechanism then go to all six at once. If it mines, any provider still denying it is named a silent drop. If nothing mines by the deadline, anyone can write a permanent CensorshipDetected event to Ethereum.

Honest about its limits: the oracle records a liveness attestation, not a receipt-trie inclusion proof. ATTESTED and VERIFIED stay two separate states throughout.

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body:
Censorship at the RPC layer is the cheapest and least visible attack on Ethereum. Everything below it is well defended consensus is decentralized, blocks are validated by thousands of nodes but almost every user reaches that chain through a single company's endpoint. A provider that refuses to relay your transaction doesn't need to break cryptography or bribe a validator. It just returns a hash and does nothing. You are censored, and you cannot prove it happened.

Quorum attacks that layer directly, on both axes:

Resistance the censorship fails. A transaction broadcast to six independent operators simultaneously survives any one of them refusing to carry it. Reads survive too: no single endpoint can feed you a false view of the chain, because an answer needs ⌈2/3⌉ agreement to be accepted at all. Censorship by one provider stops being effective.

Accountability the censorship is recorded. This is the part the track is actually missing. Today, withholding is invisible and therefore free. Quorum commits intent on-chain before broadcasting, so when the deadline passes with nothing mined, anyone can write a permanent CensorshipDetected event to Ethereum. The silence becomes evidence. A provider that suppresses transactions now leaves a public, timestamped, unretractable record which changes the incentive, not just the outcome.

Resistance without evidence lets censorship stay deniable. Quorum makes it cost something.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The problem it solves

Nexora makes group coordination and decision-making more transparent, verifiable, and wallet-native.

Traditional online groups often rely on centralized accounts, private databases, and trusted administrators to manage membership and voting. This makes it difficult to independently verify who joined, who voted, what was decided, and whether records were changed.

Nexora moves these core coordination actions on-chain:

Verifiable membership: Group membership is recorded on the blockchain and tied to a user's wallet.
Transparent governance: Members can create proposals and vote YES/NO directly through their wallets.
Tamper-resistant records: Group creation, membership changes, proposals, and votes are recorded as on-chain events.
Wallet-based identity: Users interact through their Web3 wallet instead of relying on a centralized username/password system.
Auditable decisions: Anyone can verify the history of important group actions through blockchain transaction records.
Simpler coordination: Instead of combining separate tools for membership, proposals, and voting, Nexora brings them together in one workspace.

In short: Nexora provides a decentralized coordination layer where membership, governance, and decision history can be verified rather than simply trusted.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges we ran into

One of our main challenges was handling on-chain state correctly across wallet changes and page refreshes. Initially, a user could successfully join a group, but after refreshing the page the UI could incorrectly show “Join Group” again.

We solved this by making the frontend re-fetch membership directly from the deployed smart contract using isGroupMember(groupId, walletAddress) instead of relying only on local UI state. We also added optimistic updates after successful transactions so the interface responds immediately while remaining synchronized with the blockchain.

Another hurdle was wallet and smart-contract transaction errors, particularly custom Solidity errors during gas estimation. We debugged these by checking the deployed contract state, verifying the connected wallet and network, and mapping common contract errors into clear messages for users.

We also experimented with Push Protocol for persistent group chat. Due to initialization and dependency/API compatibility issues, we reverted to a simpler chat implementation for the demo rather than allowing an unreliable feature to affect the core on-chain governance experience.

Key takeaway: building a Web3 application required us to treat the blockchain as the source of truth while carefully handling asynchronous wallet, transaction, and frontend state.

description.title: Decentralized Coordination Layers
description.body:
How Nexora fits the Decentralized Coordination Layers track

Nexora directly addresses decentralized coordination by providing an on-chain coordination layer for groups to organize, make decisions, and maintain verifiable records without relying on a centralized administrator.

The core flow is:

Wallet → Group Membership → Proposals → Voting → Verifiable On-Chain History

Decentralized membership: Users join groups using their Web3 wallets, with membership stored and verified by the smart contract.
On-chain governance: Group members can create proposals and vote directly on-chain, making decisions transparent and auditable.
Shared source of truth: The smart contract maintains the authoritative state of groups, members, proposals, and votes instead of a centralized database.
Verifiable coordination: Important actions generate blockchain events, allowing participants to independently verify what happened.
Permissionless participation: Anyone with a compatible wallet can participate in eligible groups without needing a centralized account or administrator to approve every action.
Composable foundation: The same coordination primitives—groups, membership, proposals, and voting—can serve communities, student organizations, DAOs, hackathon teams, clubs, and other decentralized communities.

Why this fits the track:
Nexora isn't just putting an existing social feature on-chain. It uses the blockchain as the coordination and trust layer itself: the rules for membership and decision-making are enforced by a smart contract, while the frontend provides an accessible interface for interacting with those rules.

Nexora turns “trust us, this is what the group decided” into “verify it on-chain.”

sentinel-9ee0.name: Sentinel
sentinel-9ee0.tagline: A live watchtower for RPC censorship and relay com

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**Challenges I ran into**

Architectural bugs that only surface once you actually run the code. Early prompts for the divergence engine assumed server-side state could persist a rolling window of "3 consecutive lagging checks" across polls — but Next.js API routes are stateless serverless functions that can cold-start between requests, silently dropping that memory. Caught this before it became a live-demo bug and restructured so the classification logic lives client-side in React state, while the API routes stay pure single-shot snapshots.

CORS and rate-limiting on external relay data. The relay-compliance monitor needs live MEV-Boost bid-trace data from third-party relay APIs. Fetching that directly from the browser hits CORS failures and risks getting rate-limited during a demo with multiple polls per session. Solved by routing all external calls server-to-server through our own API routes, with fetch-level caching so repeated client polls don't hammer the upstream relays.

Preventing AI-hallucinated endpoints and fields from silently breaking the build. Since most of the code was AI-assisted, the real risk wasn't bad logic, it was confidently wrong specifics — an invented RPC URL, a guessed JSON field name from a relay API. Addressed this by forcing a verify-before-build step for every external endpoint (a standalone script that hits the real API and prints the real response) before any parsing code got written against it.

A deployment trap in the demo fault-injection node. The mock "misbehaving RPC node" used to demo censorship detection live was originally built as a separate process on localhost — which would silently break the moment the app got deployed, since localhost inside a cloud container doesn't point to your laptop. Rebuilt it as a pure in-process function derived from timestamp math instead, so it behaves identically locally and deployed.

Switching AI tools mid-build without breaking either half. Built the dashboard logic with Claude, then hit a usage limit partway through integrating a separately-built landing page (done with Gemini Pro in Antigravity). Two AI tools independently touching the same repo meant the real risk was one agent assuming it understood code the other one wrote. Handled this with a strict audit-first process — reading actual file contents and exported shapes before writing any integration code, rather than trusting either build matched its original spec

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
**The problem**: Ethereum's neutrality isn't guaranteed by the protocol alone — it depends on the RPC providers and MEV-Boost relays that sit between users and the chain actually behaving well. Most people interact with Ethereum through 2-3 RPC endpoints they never think about, and since the Tornado Cash sanctions in 2022, a significant and fluctuating share of Ethereum blocks are built by relays that proactively filter sanctioned addresses' transactions — a real, ongoing, currently-measurable phenomenon, not a hypothetical. On top of that, individual RPC providers can lag, silently drop transactions, or diverge from the rest of the network without any user-facing signal that something's wrong.

Why it matters: censorship resistance is one of Ethereum's foundational value propositions, but it's currently a black box to the average user — you have no way to know whether the infrastructure you're using right now is behaving neutrally, lagging, or actively filtering.

What **Sentinel** does about it: a live dashboard that (1) polls multiple public RPC providers in parallel, detects and flags divergence patterns that suggest an unhealthy or misbehaving node, and automatically reroutes away from flagged providers, and (2) pulls real bid-trace data from MEV-Boost relays to show, in real time, what share of recent blocks came from OFAC-compliant vs. non-compliant relays — the same category of transparency tool that projects like MEV Watch have shown there's real demand for, built here as a from-scratch, live, self-contained monitoring layer.

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body: Sentinel builds both bullets in the track. It aggregates multiple public RPC providers, flags any that diverge from consensus, and auto-reroutes around them — directly matching "distribute requests, validate through consensus, balance traffic." It also monitors MEV-Boost relays in real time to show what share of recent blocks come from OFAC-compliant vs. non-compliant relays, giving users visibility into censorship at the relay layer — matching "verify network path integrity, route to avoid censorship." In short: it makes the two layers that actually determine censorship resistance — RPC providers and relays — visible and actionable, not just theoretical.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Right now, almost every wallet and dApp connects to the blockchain through one RPC provider — a single company's server acting as your only door onto the network. That's a hidden single point of failure:

The provider can silently drop your transaction and you'll never know why.
It can be slow or unavailable during peak load or an outage.
It can selectively block a specific wallet address or destination.
You get a "submitted successfully" message that doesn't actually prove your transaction reached a real node.

Users have no way to detect this, prove it happened, or route around it — they just retry and hope.

CensorMesh removes that single point of failure and gives you proof.

What people can use it for
Everyday wallet users who want confidence their transaction actually gets delivered instead of silently vanishing into a blocked RPC.
Wallet developers who want a drop-in fallback layer instead of building and maintaining their own list of backup RPC providers.
DeFi apps, DAOs, and bridges sending time-sensitive or high-value transactions — liquidations, emergency withdrawals, governance votes — where a dropped transaction is costly, not just annoying.
Relayer operators who want to earn a reward for reliably delivering transactions other routes failed to deliver.
Researchers/infra teams who want visibility into which RPC providers are actually reliable versus which ones quietly fail.
How it makes things safer and easier
Automatic fallback — if one relayer fails or censors a transaction, another one picks it up without the user manually resubmitting anything.
Proof, not blind trust — every delivery attempt is signed and logged, producing a verifiable delivery certificate instead of a vague "transaction submitted" message.
Built-in accountability — a suspicion score flags relayers that repeatedly fail or drop specific transactions, without falsely claiming mathematical proof of censorship.
No vendor lock-in — users and apps stop depending on one company, region, or cloud provider to get their transaction through.
Incentive-aligned delivery — relayers are paid only when they successfully deliver, so honest, reliable relayers are rewarded directly.

In short: CensorMesh turns "I hope my transaction went through" into "here is proof of exactly what happened to my transaction."

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1. Signature verification mismatches between frontend and backend

Getting the wallet's signed message to actually verify correctly on the backend was harder than expected — small differences in how the intent object was serialized (key order, number vs string types, JSON formatting) meant the signature the wallet produced didn't match what the backend recomputed and tried to verify against. This silently failed every intent.

Fix: we standardized on ethers.js's typed data signing (eth_signTypedData_v4) instead of signing a raw string, so both sides hash the exact same structured data instead of relying on identical string formatting.

2. Race conditions in the relayer fallback logic

When simulating the censoring relayer, our first version tried all three relayers in parallel to save time — but that meant whichever relayer happened to be fastest (including the "honest" ones) sometimes returned before we'd finished logging that the censoring relayer had failed, so the timeline events showed up out of order on the frontend.

Fix: we switched to a sequential fallback loop (try relayer, wait, log the result, only then move to the next one) instead of racing them. This cost us a bit of speed but made the delivery story easy to follow and kept events chronologically honest.

3. Keeping the smart contract and backend in sync on intent hashing

The contract computed the intent hash one way (using Solidity's keccak256 over packed fields) while the backend was hashing the JSON object a different way — so the hash the backend tracked never matched the hash the contract emitted, which broke our ability to look up certificates by transaction.

Fix: we wrote a small shared hashing function based on the contract's exact encoding and reused that same logic on the backend, instead of letting each side hash independently.

4. Making "censorship" demoable without it looking staged

Simulating a relayer that silently drops a transaction is easy to fake so obviously that it stops looking like a real problem. We wanted the failure to look like a genuine network issue (timeout, no error message) rather than an obvious scripted rejection.

Fix: we made the censoring relayer just... never respond, instead of returning an explicit rejection — so the backend has to time out and infer failure, which is much closer to what real-world censorship actually looks like.

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body:
Here's how CensorMesh maps directly onto the track's requirements, point by point.

The track asked for two things

Decentralized RPC Aggregators: reduce dependency on centralized access points by distributing requests across various RPC providers, with consensus mechanisms, accurate data selection, and load balancing.

Verifiable Routing Infrastructure: client-side tools that let users verify network path integrity and route around censorship points.

CensorMesh is built primarily around the second bullet, with a piece of the first baked in.

How each track requirement maps to what you built
Track requirement	How CensorMesh satisfies it
"Reduce dependency on centralized access points"	Instead of trusting one RPC/relayer, the intent goes to multiple independent relayers — no single provider is a single point of failure.
"Distributing requests across various providers"	The intent is broadcast to 3 relayers (honest, slow, censoring) rather than one — that is the distribution mechanism.
"Consensus mechanisms among providers"	Your simplified version doesn't do formal multi-party consensus, but the witness-signed event log plays the same role: instead of trusting one relayer's self-reported status, you have independent signed records of what actually happened at each step. Worth being upfront about this being a lightweight stand-in, not full consensus.
"Accurate data selection"	The backend doesn't just accept the first response — it verifies signatures and only counts a relayer as successful once it's actually confirmed executed, not just "acknowledged."
"Load balancing"	Loosely covered — you have fallback/failover between relayers rather than true load balancing across healthy nodes, so this is the weakest match. Worth noting it as a future feature (route diversity scoring) rather than overclaiming it.
"Client-side tools to verify network path integrity"	The delivery certificate is exactly this — it lets the user verify, after the fact, exactly which relayer received, dropped, or executed their transaction, with signatures backing each claim.
"Manually or automatically route around censorship"	The automatic fallback (censoring relayer fails → backend retries with another relayer) is a direct, literal implementation of this line.

sovereignguard-a259.name: SovereignGuard
sovereignguard-a259.tagline: Zero-Trust Session Keys, Epoch Revocation & Caps

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## The Problem

Floating off-chain session key signatures often linger in mempools or with relayers even after a smart account owner initiates a standard revocation. This leaves ERC-4337 smart accounts exposed to front-running and paymaster gas-drain attacks from stale, still-valid signatures.

## The Solution — SovereignGuard

SovereignGuard is a zero-trust account abstraction security layer that adds:

- **Instant global epoch revocation** — a single `globalEpoch++` call instantly nullifies every outstanding off-chain session key signature, closing the window attackers rely on.
- **Granular spend caps** — per-transaction and rolling 24-hour daily spend limits, enforced on-chain, to contain the blast radius of a compromised session key.

## Tech Stack

- Solidity 0.8.28
- Foundry test suite (19/19 passing)
- Next.js + TypeScript
- Tailwind CSS
- Glassmorphic dashboard UI

## Key Security Primitives

- Instant global epoch revocation
- Micro-value spend tracking with daily resets
- Real-time on-chain execution audit logging

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
### 1. Off-Chain Signature Invalidation vs. On-Chain State Sync
* **The Challenge:** Standard session key revocation algorithms only flip a boolean flag on-chain. This leaves signed, floating off-chain UserOps lingering in relayers and mempools, exposing the account to front-running exploits before state synchronization completes.
* **The Solution:** We architected an atomic `globalEpoch` state variable in `SovereignAccount.sol`. Binding session key validation to the contract's active epoch allows triggering `emergencyRevokeAll()` to increment `globalEpoch++`, immediately invalidating all pending off-chain signed payloads in a single transaction.

### 2. Micro-Value Spend Limit Resets Without Bloated Gas Overhead
* **The Challenge:** Tracking 24-hour rolling spending caps (`dailySpendLimit`) usually requires expensive on-chain array iteration or gas-heavy storage updates on every execution.
* **The Solution:** Implemented a stateless timestamp window check (`lastResetTimestamp`). If `block.timestamp >= lastResetTimestamp + 1 days`, cumulative spend resets inline inside `executeWithSessionKey()`, keeping gas consumption minimal while guaranteeing strict limit enforcement.

### 3. Real-Time State Synchronization in Frontend
* **The Challenge:** Refactoring UI state smoothly to capture epoch increments, active limits, and real-time gas usage across Next.js components without inducing unnecessary re-renders.
* **The Solution:** Built a high-performance **Contract Security Audit Log** panel fed directly by structured `SessionKeyExecuted` and `EmergencyRevocationTriggered` event streams.

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body:
SovereignGuard directly advances Self-Sovereignity by restoring complete, uncompromised account ownership back to the user without sacrificing Web3 UX. 

While conventional account abstraction delegates execution authority to session keys, it introduces vendor lock-in and persistent vulnerability windows from floating off-chain signatures. SovereignGuard reinforces self-sovereignty through three core mechanisms:

1. **Absolute On-Chain Ownership:** The contract owner retains ultimate control via `globalEpoch` revocation, allowing instant invalidation of all active sessions and off-chain pending signatures without relying on centralized relayers or third-party indexers.
2. **Autonomous Policy Enforcement:** Users define non-custodial guardrails directly in the smart contract—including daily spend caps and per-transaction limits—ensuring automated apps operate within user-defined boundaries.
3. **Transparent Execution:** On-chain structured audit logging (`SessionKeyExecuted`) guarantees full visibility into account interactions, keeping key delegation fully verifiable and non-custodial.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Every "uncensorable publishing" tool has the same hole: someone is holding the material, and that someone can be reached. Publish now and you're the target before anyone has read it. Hand it to a journalist and the leverage
moves to them. Encrypt and distribute the key and any keyholder can be
compelled to open it early. Put it on IPFS and the pin lapses. Suppression works.
DEADLIGHT makes suppression
counterproductive. The document is armed to
release on SILENCE, so detaining the publisher doesn't prevent publication
- it causes it. The AES-256-GCM ciphertext lives entirely in contract state (no server, no pin, no host to subpoena) and the key is Shamir-split k-of-n across guardians who hold only shares, while the chain holds their commitments.

The load-bearing part: the embargo is enforced by the contract, not
promised by guardians. submitShare()
REVERTS while the publisher keeps checking in - every guardian could collude, or be served by the same court on the same morning, and it still wouldn't open a second early. In the demo we prove this on camera by submitting a genuine valid share and watching the chain refuse it with StillAlive.
Symmetrically, heartbeat() and
revoke() both stop working the instant the deadline lapses, so a captor who seizes the publisher's key afterwards can't bury the release either.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Getting the embargo semantics right - the first design let the publisher
heartbeat at any time, which quietly broke the whole guarantee: a captor
with the key could keep the switch alive forever. Both heartbeat and revoke now hard-revert past the deadline. Making the guarantee demonstrable rather than asserted, via a console that lets anyone attempt an early release with a real share. On-chain storage economics (~20k gas per 32 bytes) capping documents at 8KB. Stack-too-deep in the vault struct, resolved with via_ir.

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body:
DEADLIGHT gives the publisher control over the conditions under which their document is released without relying on a platform, publisher, journalist, or centralized intermediary.

The document is encrypted client-side with AES-256-GCM, while the decryption key is split using Shamir Secret Sharing and distributed across independent guardians. No single guardian possesses the complete key. The blockchain stores the ciphertext and share commitments, while the smart contract autonomously enforces the embargo and release conditions.

Most importantly, the release rules are not controlled by a third party. The publisher sets the heartbeat and silence conditions, and once the deadline passes, even the publisher can no longer revoke the release. This prevents an attacker, institution, or captured publisher key from overriding the predetermined rules.

DEADLIGHT therefore makes publication a cryptographic and on-chain right governed by rules chosen in advance, rather than permission granted by a centralized authority.

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body:
DEADLIGHT is designed so that censorship becomes counterproductive. The document is encrypted and committed on-chain before publication, while the decryption key is split across independent guardians using Shamir Secret Sharing.

The critical guarantee is enforced by the smart contract itself: guardians cannot release their key shares while the publisher is still alive and checking in. submitShare() reverts with StillAlive, even when a genuine valid share is submitted. Once the publisher goes silent past the deadline, the embargo expires and the contract allows the shares to be submitted and the document to be decrypted.

This means there is no single publisher, server, IPFS pin, journalist, or keyholder whose capture can suppress the document. Attempting to silence the publisher is precisely what activates the release mechanism.

DEADLIGHT therefore treats censorship not as something to resist after the fact, but as the trigger that causes publication.

description.title: Decentralized Coordination Layers
description.body:
DEADLIGHT uses the blockchain as a coordination layer between the publisher and a distributed set of guardians without requiring a trusted coordinator.

Guardians hold only individual shares of the decryption key, while the smart contract stores their commitments and enforces the rules for when those shares can be submitted. No guardian needs to trust another guardian, and no central server needs to coordinate the release.

The contract provides a shared, deterministic state that every participant can independently verify: while the publisher is alive, valid shares are rejected; after the silence deadline, the embargo expires and the required threshold of shares can be submitted to reconstruct the key.

This turns a group of potentially independent or mutually distrustful participants into a coordinated release mechanism whose behavior is governed by transparent on-chain rules rather than by a central authority.

lazarus-0427.name: Lazarus
lazarus-0427.tagline: Bring dead languages back to life

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
LAZARUS solves the legacy code modernization problem.

  An estimated 800 billion lines of COBOL still run the world's banks and governments — written by developers who are now retired or gone.
  Organizations need to migrate this code to modern languages, but existing tools either:
  - Use AI as a black box (no explanation of what changed or why)
  - Silently drop code they can't translate

  What it does: Takes code written in dead/legacy languages — COBOL, Pascal, VB6, retro BASIC — and transpiles it to modern Python 3 or JavaScript,
  with line-by-line "Necromancer's Notes" explaining every transformation. Anything it can't handle is preserved as a TODO comment, never silently
  dropped.

  The hardest sub-problem it tackles is GOTO resurrection: unstructured GOTO/GOSUB jumps in BASIC have no direct structured equivalent, so it
  rebuilds them as a program-counter state machine (a while + switch trampoline) that faithfully reproduces the original control flow.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1. GOTO resurrection
  Unstructured jumps (GOTO/GOSUB) have no direct structured equivalent in Python or JS. Solved with a program-counter trampoline — a while loop
  dispatching on line numbers that replays the original control flow faithfully.

  2. Inclusive loop bounds
  COBOL, Pascal, VB6, and BASIC all include the loop end value. A naive translation silently off-by-ones every loop. Had to explicitly adjust ranges
  in every transpiler.

  3. String literals vs keywords
  The BASIC translator was rewriting keywords found inside string literals — e.g. "T-MINUS" was becoming "t-minus". Fixed with literal-protection
  sentinels (placeholder tokens that shield string contents during transformation). This bug was caught by the execution tests, which is exactly why
  the test harness asserts on actual program output rather than just "it produced some code."

private-pass-406c.name: Private Pass
private-pass-406c.tagline: “Prove What You Need. Reveal Nothing More.”

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Problem Description 

Traditional identity verification often requires users to share complete personal documents even when only one specific fact needs to be verified. This leads to unnecessary data exposure, privacy concerns, and security risks.

For example, a platform may only need to know whether a person is an eligible student, but the user may have to reveal their name, ID number, photo, and other personal details.

PrivatePass addresses this problem by enabling users to prove specific eligibility claims while keeping unnecessary personal information private.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges We Faced

 Implementing the zero-knowledge verification workflow.

 Debugging proof generation and verification issues. 

Ensuring different eligibility criteria work correctly.

Integrating Web3 identity and wallet functionality. 

Deploying the application and resolving local vs. production environment issues.

Building and testing the project within a limited hackathon timeframe.

description.title: Self-Sovereignty
description.body:
How PrivatePass Applies Self-Sovereignty 

User-controlled identity: Users have control over their own identity information rather than relying entirely on a central authority. 

Selective sharing: Users choose which specific claim to prove, instead of sharing their complete identity.

Privacy: Unnecessary personal information remains private during verification. 

User-controlled verification: The user decides when and what information to present to a verifier. 

Reduced dependence on centralized databases: The concept supports identity verification without requiring all personal information to be stored in one central system. 

In short: PrivatePass applies self-sovereignty by giving users greater ownership, control, and choice over how their digital identity is used and verified.

proofroute-34c0.name: ProofRoute
proofroute-34c0.tagline: Don't trust the relay. Verify it.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
ProofRoute — Hackathon Submission Description
One-line pitch

ProofRoute is a decentralized accountability layer for blockchain infrastructure: stake-backed relays make cryptographic propagation commitments, independent peers provide handoff evidence, quorum produces verifiable coordination certificates, and relays that provably violate their commitments get slashed and automatically deprioritized — with cryptographic proof, not trust.

The Problem

When you send a blockchain transaction, you never talk directly to the chain. You go through a chain of infrastructure you don't control:

Wallet → RPC → Relay → Peer Network → Builder/Sequencer → Blockchain

If your transaction silently disappears somewhere in that chain, you have no way to prove who dropped it. A centralized RPC can censor you. A relay can quietly ignore your transaction. Different RPC providers can return conflicting information about the same chain state. And as a user, you're left with nothing but "trust me" — no cryptographic evidence of what actually happened to your transaction.

This is a foundational trust gap in how everyone interacts with blockchains today, and it sits exactly at the intersection of censorship resistance and decentralized coordination.

The Solution

ProofRoute creates a permissionless network of stake-backed relays that make cryptographically verifiable promises about transaction propagation — and then produces on-chain proof of whether they kept those promises.

Instead of trusting a relay's word, the user gets proof of what the relay actually did.

How it works, step by step
Relays stake collateral. Any address can permissionlessly become a relay by depositing ETH into RelayRegistry. This makes creating fake relay identities economically expensive and gives honest behavior a real financial incentive.
The user sends a transaction through multiple relays at once. The ProofRoute SDK routes it to several independent relays instead of trusting a single infrastructure provider.
Each relay signs an EIP-712 propagation commitment — a cryptographic promise of the form "I commit to propagating transaction X before deadline Y." Critically, this is not a promise that the transaction will be included in a block (that's outside a relay's control) — it's only a promise about the one thing a relay actually controls: propagation.
The relay proves propagation by handing the transaction to a registered peer, who returns a signed acknowledgement: "I received transaction X from Relay A." Together, the commitment and the acknowledgement form a verifiable handoff proof.
Independent relay observations are aggregated into quorum. If enough relays (e.g. 3-of-5) produce valid commitment + handoff pairs for the same transaction, the network issues an on-chain Coordination Certificate — cryptographic proof that multiple independent parties attest to the same event, rather than one server's word.
If a relay fails or goes offline, the SDK simply routes around it and quorum is still reached with the remaining relays — this is the censorship/failure-resistance property.
If a relay signs a commitment but never produces the handoff (i.e., it lied about propagating), anyone can submit a Fault Proof on-chain. The protocol verifies the relay's own signature against the missed deadline, then automatically slashes a portion of that relay's staked collateral — a bounty goes to whoever submitted the proof, and the rest goes to a treasury vault.
What ProofRoute deliberately does not claim

This boundary is core to the design's integrity: ProofRoute never claims a relay is guilty just because a transaction wasn't included in a block, or because its execution reverted. Inclusion is controlled by builders/sequencers, not relays, and reverts can be unrelated to propagation entirely. ProofRoute only ever enforces the one obligation a relay explicitly signs and actually controls — its propagation commitment. This scoping is what makes the slashing condition objectively provable on-chain, rather than a subjective judgment call.

Why it qualifies for both tracks

Censorship Resistance

Multi-relay transaction routing instead of single-provider trust
Automatic rerouting around offline or unreliable relays
Verifiable, signed propagation commitments
On-chain detection of protocol-defined relay failures
Economic penalties (slashing) for provable violations

Decentralized Coordination

Signed, independent observations from multiple relays and peers
Threshold quorum instead of a single source of truth
On-chain, verifiable coordination certificates
Permissionless participation (anyone can stake and become a relay)
Cryptographic attribution — you know exactly who said what
What We Actually Built

This isn't a slide-deck concept — the full stack is implemented and runnable end-to-end on a live local devnet:

Smart contracts (Solidity / Foundry)

RelayRegistry.sol — permissionless staking, restricted slashing entrypoint
CoordinationManager.sol — EIP-712 domain and signature

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Scoping what's actually provable on-chain. The hardest design problem wasn't cryptographic — it was philosophical. My first instinct was to slash a relay if a transaction wasn't included in a block. But inclusion is controlled by builders and sequencers, not relays, and execution can revert for reasons that have nothing to do with propagation. If I slashed on inclusion, I'd be punishing relays for something they don't control — which makes the whole system untrustworthy and un-auditable. I had to pull the scope back repeatedly until I landed on the one thing a relay actually signs and actually controls: the propagation handoff to a peer. That discipline — resisting the urge to make bigger claims than the cryptography can support — shaped almost every other decision in the project.

"Stack too deep" in Solidity. CoordinationManager.submitQuorumCertificate takes six parameters (transaction hash, relay list, deadlines, commitment signatures, peer list, handoff signatures) plus internal loop variables for verification. The default Solidity compiler ran out of stack slots and refused to compile with a Stack too deep error. Fixing it meant switching to the IR-based codegen pipeline (via_ir = true in Foundry config) rather than restructuring the function into something less readable — a good reminder that gas-optimization tooling and readability sometimes pull in different directions.

BigInt serialization silently breaking the API. The backend reads on-chain values like relay stake as native JavaScript BigInts (since Solidity's uint256 doesn't fit safely in a Number). The first version of the status endpoint spread that raw state directly into a JSON response — and JSON.stringify has no idea how to serialize a BigInt, so the endpoint returned a 500 on every single request. It's a small bug, but it's the kind that's completely invisible in casual testing and only surfaces once real values start flowing through the read path — every numeric field touching the chain had to be explicitly converted to a string before it could leave the backend.

Making time-based slashing demoable without lying about the mechanism. The fault-proof condition genuinely requires a deadline to pass — that's not optional, it's the whole point (a relay shouldn't be punishable before it's actually had the chance to fulfill its commitment). On a local Anvil devnet I could cheat time forward with evm_increaseTime and evm_mine to keep a live demo fast-paced. But that's an Anvil-only RPC method that doesn't exist on a real network — so making the same flow work on a public testnet meant reworking the fault-proof path to genuinely wait out a short real deadline instead, rather than assuming the time-travel trick would always be available.

Key management discipline. Anvil's ten default dev accounts are derived from a public, widely-known test mnemonic — perfect for a local demo (zero configuration, funds are meaningless), and actively dangerous anywhere real value is involved. Moving toward testnet deployment meant explicitly separating "local devnet mode" (mnemonic-derived, safe) from "real network mode" (freshly generated private keys the user actually controls), and refusing to start the backend at all if a non-local chain ID was configured without real keys supplied — making the unsafe path structurally hard to fall into by accident.

Environment friction across a fresh machine. A meaningful chunk of actual build time went into things with no cryptography involved at all: foundryup not being on PATH until a new shell session, forge install needing a git init first, a stray shell-escaping issue that silently truncated a contract address by one hex character when it was first typed out, and Node.js not being installed at all. None of these are exotic problems, but they're a good reminder that a genuinely reproducible hackathon demo has to survive someone else's clean machine, not just the one it was built on — small mistakes like a single dropped character in a 42-character address are exactly the kind of thing that's invisible until something breaks downstream.

description.title: Censorship Resistance
description.body:
Censorship in blockchain infrastructure rarely looks dramatic — it's not a chain halting or a wallet getting blacklisted. It looks quiet: a transaction that just... never shows up. An RPC that returns nothing. A relay that accepts your request and then does nothing with it. There's no error message, no explanation, and critically — no proof it even happened. That silence is what makes infrastructure-level censorship so hard to fight: you can't contest what you can't demonstrate.

ProofRoute is built specifically to attack that silence.

Redundancy that's structural, not optional. Instead of a user (or their wallet) depending on a single RPC or relay to carry their transaction, the ProofRoute SDK broadcasts to multiple independent, permissionless relays at once. No single relay is a chokepoint — if one refuses to act, or simply ignores the request, the transaction doesn't die with it. This is the most direct form of censorship resistance: removing any single point of failure or control from the critical path between a signed transaction and the chain.

Automatic failover, not manual intervention. When a relay goes offline or misbehaves, the system doesn't require the user to notice, complain, or manually switch providers. The SDK routes around the failure in real time — as demonstrated live in the project, killing one of five relays mid-demo still results in a successful transaction, because the remaining relays clear quorum on their own. Censorship resistance that depends on the victim noticing and reacting isn't real resistance; it has to be automatic.

Turning silent failure into provable failure. This is the core innovation for this track specifically. Most censorship-resistance designs stop at redundancy — "just use more providers." ProofRoute goes further: every relay signs an EIP-712 commitment before it acts, so if it drops the transaction anyway, that drop is no longer invisible. It's a broken promise with the relay's own cryptographic signature attached to it. A user (or anyone) can point to an exact, verifiable, on-chain artifact and say "this relay committed to propagating my transaction and did not." That converts censorship from an unfalsifiable claim into a provable fact.

Economic cost for censoring, not just workaround. Circumventing censorship is necessary but not sufficient — if there's no cost to the censoring party, the behavior just continues against the next victim. ProofRoute attaches real, enforceable consequences: a relay that's caught dropping a committed transaction gets a portion of its staked collateral slashed automatically, on-chain, the moment a fault proof is submitted. This is what separates resisting censorship from merely tolerating it — bad actors are actively priced out of the network over time, not just quietly routed around forever.

Permissionless relay entry keeps the network resistant to capture. Because becoming a relay only requires posting stake (no whitelist, no approval, no centralized operator), the network can't be quietly captured or narrowed down to a small set of relays that could later collude or be pressured to censor collectively. Anyone can join as a relay and add more independent paths to the chain, which keeps the "how many relays would need to censor you simultaneously" number high and permissionlessly growing.

Scoped narrowly enough to be credible. It's worth naming directly: ProofRoute doesn't claim to solve censorship at the builder/sequencer level — inclusion is still outside a relay's control, and the protocol is explicit about not slashing for that. What it does claim, and can prove, is resistance to censorship at the relay/propagation layer, where today there is zero accountability at all. A narrower, provable guarantee is more valuable to judges (and to users) than a broader, hand-wavy one — it's the difference between "trust us, we're decentralized" and "here is the exact cryptographic guarantee, and here is exactly where it stops."

In short: most censorship-resistance pitches are really just redundancy pitches — "use more than one provider." ProofRoute's contribution to this track is turning relay behavior itself into something that can be caught, proven, and economically punished — so censorship stops being a silent, cost-free action and starts being a detectable, expensive one.

description.title: Decentralized Coordination Layers
description.body:
Coordination is usually the hidden centralization point in systems that otherwise call themselves decentralized. You can have permissionless relays, open participation, and no single company running the show — and still end up with a system where the coordination layer itself is a single server saying "trust me, this happened." That single point of attestation is a centralization bottleneck wearing a decentralized costume. ProofRoute is built specifically to replace that bottleneck with something genuinely multi-party and verifiable.

Multiple independent observers, not one authority. In most infrastructure today, when you're told "your transaction was propagated," that statement comes from exactly one party — the relay itself, or a dashboard it controls. There's no second opinion. ProofRoute restructures this so that no single party's word is ever sufficient. A relay's commitment only means something once an independent peer signs off on the handoff — two separate, non-colluding parties have to agree before anything counts as valid. That's the smallest possible unit of decentralized coordination: an event isn't real until more than one independent party attests to it.

Quorum instead of a single source of truth. ProofRoute doesn't stop at pairwise agreement — it aggregates observations across the whole relay set and requires a threshold (3-of-5 in the current implementation) before it will issue a Coordination Certificate. This is the actual mechanism of decentralized coordination: instead of a centralized coordinator deciding "this happened," a quorum of independent, permissionless, stake-backed participants collectively decides it, and their agreement is the proof. No one relay, and no operator of ProofRoute itself, has the unilateral power to declare an outcome.

The coordination artifact is cryptographic, not administrative. A coordination certificate isn't a database row somewhere or an API response you have to trust the operator of — it's an on-chain object that anyone can independently verify by checking the underlying EIP-712 signatures themselves. This matters because decentralized coordination isn't really decentralized if verifying it still requires trusting the party who produced the summary. ProofRoute's certificates are self-verifying: you don't need to trust ProofRoute to trust the certificate.

Permissionless entry keeps the coordinating set genuinely open. Anyone can become part of the coordinating quorum by staking into RelayRegistry — there's no fixed validator set, no whitelist, no approval process gating who gets to participate in producing these certificates. This is what keeps the coordination layer decentralized over time rather than just decentralized at genesis: the set of parties capable of attesting to network events can grow permissionlessly, the same way anyone can join as a miner, validator, or relayer in other permissionless systems.

Coordination extends to disagreement, not just agreement. A meaningful coordination protocol has to handle conflicting observations, not just happy-path unanimity. The RPC-verification extension in ProofRoute's design shows this directly: when multiple providers return the same value for a read, you're done cheaply; when they disagree, the system escalates and samples more providers until quorum resolves the discrepancy. That's adaptive, decentralized coordination applied to disagreement resolution, not just event attestation — you don't need five signatures for the boring case, but you get real quorum-based arbitration the moment sources conflict.

Coordination with consequences, not just consensus theater. It's easy to build a system where independent parties "vote" on something and nothing follows from the vote. ProofRoute's coordination has teeth: if the quorum process reveals that a specific relay violated its commitment (signed but never handed off), that finding isn't just recorded — it triggers a real, automatic, on-chain slashing consequence. Decentralized coordination that doesn't feed into decentralized enforcement is only half the system; ProofRoute closes that loop.

Scoped honestly, which is itself part of good coordination design. The protocol is explicit that quorum certificates only ever attest to propagation, never to inclusion or execution outcomes — because those aren't things the coordinating relay set actually controls or can honestly observe together. Good decentralized coordination isn't about getting a quorum to agree on everything; it's about being precise regarding exactly which claims a given quorum is actually qualified to attest to.

In short: ProofRoute's contribution to this track isn't "we have multiple relays" — plenty of systems have that and still centralize the coordination step. The contribution is that the act of agreeing on what happened is itself decentralized: multi-party, threshold-based, cryptographically self-verifying, permissionlessly open to new participants, and directly wired into enforcement —

replicator-3255.name: Replicator
replicator-3255.tagline: Personal desktop utilities, built from a request.

description.title: What is the problem your project solves?
description.body:
A small personal workflow often falls between two bad options: adapt to a general-purpose app that does much more than needed, or build and maintain custom software. AI coding tools can produce source code, but source code is not a usable result for someone who wants a focused desktop tool. They still have to choose a framework, install dependencies, build the app, verify it, and repeat that work whenever the utility changes.

Replicator treats the application package as the output. The goal is to let someone describe a specific need, receive a desktop utility they can launch on Windows, macOS, or Linux, and revise it later with another request. This would make personal software practical for narrow tasks that are too specific for a mass-market product.

description.title: What is the deployed URL for this project?
description.body: https://github.com/somus/replicator

description.title: How Did You Use Claude?
description.body:
Claude is the planning and coding engine inside Replicator. Each Utility gets a persisted Claude Agent SDK session that stays with it through the initial request, clarification, build, and later revisions. Replicator saves the session as soon as it starts, so work can resume after a clarification or application restart without losing the Utility's context.

Replicator changes Claude's tools as the work progresses. During planning, Claude can inspect attached reference images and search a bundled index of official development documentation, but it cannot edit source. It returns either a structured clarification or a plan covering the Utility Format, requirements, implementation outline, documentation selection, and behavior scenarios. Replicator validates and locks that plan before giving Claude scoped editing tools.

During the build, Claude inspects the current source, reads only the approved documentation, edits files allowed by the selected format, validates the result, repairs specific failures, and runs the accepted behavior scenarios. Claude finishes by requesting finalization, but Replicator independently checks the source and binary digests, verification evidence, package, signature, and launch result before marking the Utility ready. Owner-visible progress comes from accepted tool calls rather than Claude's private transcript, so users can follow the work without exposing prompts or internal reasoning.

description.title: How you are solving it?
description.body:
Replicator is a cross-platform desktop builder with a persistent library of personal utilities. An owner submits a Build Request in plain language and can attach reference images. Replicator uses Claude to plan the utility, asks a structured clarification when a decision would materially change the result, and locks the work to one of three controlled formats: bounded Native, multi-module Native, or React inside a protected WebView shell. It is designed to produce standalone utilities for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

The host controls the build state and acceptance rules. It limits file access, validates the chosen format, runs a short behavior contract, packages a standalone app, and keeps the previous verified artifact available if a revision fails. Each utility also keeps an Owner Timeline, so the user sees requests, clarifications, plans, and verification evidence without exposing Claude's private transcript.

During the hackathon we built the native builder shell, the worker protocol and persistent registry, Claude Agent SDK session initialization and persistence, protected templates for all three formats, and the first validation and WebView test harness pieces. The complete request-to-packaged-app path is still being integrated. The repository began as planning and design work for this hackathon; the implementation described above is the work completed here.

description.title: How you are solving it?
description.body:
CiteSprout answers the visibility question with evidence instead of a bare number.

- Prompt matrix: generates realistic buyer prompts (informational, transactional, navigational) for a brand's niche and competitors, weighted to match GEO-bench's real-world query distribution (Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024).
- Orchestrator: fires every prompt at Claude and GPT with web search/grounding enabled, with retry-then-FAILED handling so one bad call never blocks the run.
- Parser: extracts brand mentions, sentiment (positive/neutral/negative), citations, and competitor mentions per response.
- Classifiers: prompt-category and sentiment classification were designed around a ColBERT-style late-interaction matcher and a hosted RoBERTa sentiment model. What ships is a single-vector embedding classifier (Hugging Face or OpenAI) standing in for the ColBERT-style matcher, with RoBERTa used for sentiment when HF_API_KEY is set and a Claude-based classifier as the fallback otherwise — the code reports which backend actually ran rather than assuming one.
- Store: persists every raw response verbatim to SQLite the moment it returns — nothing derived is kept without the transcript behind it.
- Score engine: a counted-mention rate per intent category, combined as a weighted average (80/10/10), with categories under 3 successful records reported as "insufficient data" rather than a misleading rate.
- Viewer: the score, a per-category breakdown, a diagnostics tab for failed/unparseable calls, and a methodology explainer — click any number to the exact model response it came from.

All of this was built during the hackathon window. The plan/architecture docs were drafted first, then implemented end-to-end against real Claude and GPT API calls. No prior-hackathon code was reused.

description.title: How Did You Use Claude?
description.body:
Claude is a core part of the intelligence layer, not a bolt-on:

- Grounded provider calls: Claude (with web search) is one of the two LLMs actually being measured for brand mentions — it's both a subject of the audit and, via the Anthropic SDK, the audited caller.
- Prompt generation: the prompt matrix engine uses Claude to expand a small set of hand-written seed prompts into the full realistic buyer-prompt matrix.
- Fallback sentiment classifier: when the optional Hugging Face RoBERTa backend isn't configured, sentiment classification of "was the brand mentioned favorably?" falls back to a Claude-based classifier.
- Suggestions engine: paper-backed improvement suggestions are derived from each run's own transcripts using Claude to reason over the parsed evidence, not a canned template.

description.title: What is the problem your project solves?
description.body:
CiteSprout solves for Generative Engine Optimization in verifiable, retracable and transparent way.

If Claude or ChatGPT never names your brand in the answer, you are invisible to that buyer. There is no analytics tab for this. The tools that do measure it hand you a score with nothing behind it, so you cannot tell whether a low number means "the model dislikes us," "the model has never heard of us," or "the tool made it up."

CiteSprout answers the question with evidence: 15-20 realistic buyer prompts, fired at Claude and GPT with web search enabled, every raw response persisted before anything is derived from it. Click any number in the viewer and you get the response text, the model snapshot that produced it, the citations it returned, and whether the call needed a retry.

iplayd-00ff.tagline: Track what you play, rate and review games, build

description.title: How Did You Use Claude?
description.body:
Two different things, kept distinct on purpose rather than blurred into one "we used Claude" claim.

**Claude Code, at build time — the actual mechanism by which this exists.** The entire hackathon build ran through Claude Code as the engineering agent: reading the pre-existing codebase to find the real boundary, designing the abandonment heuristic in `lib/claude/play-history.ts` (a single earned trophy with no recent activity as proof of a dropped session — PSN's API exposes no playtime, so this was the only way to get real signal), building GAME's deterministic retrieval and baseline-relative ranking in `lib/claude/game-engine.ts`, writing the migration and verification scripts, wiring the retrieval pass into the live home page (`app/home/page.tsx`, `lib/data.ts`, the "For You"/"Surprise me" UI), sourcing and implementing the real brandbook logo from Figma, and writing the README this answer is consistent with. This is a build-time tool, not a runtime feature — disclosed as exactly that rather than left implicit or reframed as an API integration it isn't.

**The Claude API itself — designed, not wired in.** Three modules sketch a judgement layer on top of the deterministic retrieval, each on a `.md` system prompt loaded from disk (`prompts/`, never inlined):

- **Taste-spec compiler — Opus** (`prompts/taste-spec.md`). Would read a player's full labelled play history and compile it into stated behavioural principles, each citing the exact titles that support it (e.g. "abandons crafting-heavy RPGs past hour 9, 3 of 3 titles"). The hardest reasoning in the design — inferring a pattern nobody stated, across dozens of titles, while staying honest about thin samples.
- **GAME slate — Opus** (`prompts/game-match.md`). Would take the taste spec plus GAME's 36-game shortlist and pick one game per lane, arguing it. The `blind_spot` lane is adversarial by design — it would have to argue *against* the player's own revealed preference using evidence from their own library, and is allowed to reject a weak candidate rather than force-fill the slot.
- **Verdict — Sonnet** (`prompts/verdict.md`). Would predict finish-or-abandon for any single game against an already-compiled spec — bounded, cheaper reasoning for the interactive, called-repeatedly path, with the spec sitting in a cached prompt prefix so repeated verdicts pay only for the per-game delta.

We chose not to wire these in for this submission and to say so plainly rather than demo a mocked call: the code is real and typechecks, but none of it has executed against the live API, and the product that's actually live at app.iplayd.games doesn't depend on it. What shipped is the deterministic half, built end-to-end with Claude Code, and honest about exactly where the line sits.

description.title: What is the deployed URL for this project?
description.body: https://app.iplayd.games/home

description.title: How you are solving it?
description.body:
**Disclosure, upfront.** This repository is the pre-existing iPlayd codebase — a live product with real users, built before this hackathon. Organiser permission to build on it was confirmed. The git tag `hackathon-start` marks the exact boundary; `git diff hackathon-start..HEAD --stat` is the complete, verifiable hackathon diff. No pre-existing file was refactored — every change is additive: two new Postgres tables, new `lib/claude/*` modules, a new `mcp/server.ts`, a real brandbook logo/wordmark, and purely-additive wiring into `app/home/page.tsx` and `lib/data.ts` (new imports, new functions appended — nothing existing was touched).

**What we built in the window:**

1. `lib/claude/play-history.ts` — reads the existing PSN/Xbox/Steam sync tables and labels every game `completed` / `abandoned` / `playing` / `untouched`. The hard part was abandonment: PSN's trophy API exposes no playtime, so a single earned achievement with no recent activity is treated as proof of a real, dropped session. That one heuristic took this account from 2 detectable abandonments to 40 — the difference between no signal and a usable model.

2. `lib/claude/game-engine.ts` — GAME (Gamers Algorithmic Match Engine). Deterministic retrieval scores every candidate on genre affinity, measured against the *player's own* baseline completion rate rather than a fixed prior — this account finishes 1 game in 9, so a naive 0.5 prior would rank their strongest genre as below average. Retrieval narrows the pool to a 36-game shortlist across three lanes: `backlog` (their own unfinished games), `adjacent` (unowned games inside their demonstrated taste), and `blind_spot` (a genre they've never touched, quality-gated, argued against their revealed preference).

3. Shipped to the actual product, not left as a script — `/home` on app.iplayd.games has a "For You" section (backlog + adjacent, ranked by affinity) and a "Surprise me" button (samples one `blind_spot` pick per click, shown in a modal with real cover art, genres, and rating, plus a "surprise again" resample action). Both call the same verified retrieval function, `previewCandidates()`, live in production right now.

**A deliberate constraint: the shipped product makes zero calls to the Claude API, anywhere, at build time or runtime.** Every recommendation is 100% deterministic — real trophy and playtime data in, statistics out, no external dependency, no key required, fully auditable. Three further modules (a taste-spec compiler, a GAME reasoning pass, and a verdict engine — all designed to call Opus/Sonnet on top of this same retrieval layer) are written and typecheck, but were deliberately left unwired for this submission rather than half-demoed. See the next answer for why that's still a real, disclosed use of Claude.

Full README with real command output against production data: https://github.com/priyanshuratnakar/iplayd

description.title: What is the problem your project solves?
description.body:
Storefronts rank games by what sells — pre-orders, wishlist adds, launch-week revenue. None of that signal survives the purchase, so nothing in gaming today ranks by what a player actually *finishes* versus quietly abandons. Every recommendation engine in the industry is built from what publishers and storefronts can see: what you bought, what you wishlisted, what you clicked. None of them can see the thing that actually characterises a player — the hour they put a game down and never came back.

iPlayd is a live cross-platform tracker (PlayStation, Xbox, Steam) at app.iplayd.games, with real synced trophy and playtime data across thousands of games. That data already holds the signal nobody else has. This account alone — 252 games — has 40 abandoned titles against only 5 completed. An 8:1 ratio a fixed-genre or "similar users" recommender throws away entirely, because it has no concept of a player's *own* baseline completion rate, only a population average.

The problem: there is no demand-side signal layer in gaming. We built one — a taste layer that reads abandonment as data, not noise.

shortlist-f356.name: ShortList
shortlist-f356.tagline: Paste a job link — an agent applies for you

description.title: How you are solving it?
description.body:
## Disclosure of prior work

**Read this first.** Shortlist is an existing codebase, not a same-day build. The repository opened on 10 June 2026 and holds 545 commits and roughly 56,000 lines of Go. **The hackathon-day work is 15 commits, +6,758 / −99 lines**, described under "Built during the hackathon" below. Everything above that line predates today and is the platform the new work sits on. This project has not been presented at another hackathon.

## What already existed

A hexagonal Go apply engine. Every ATS is a `Submitter` implementation behind a port; `internal/core` imports nothing from adapters, so adding a portal is a new adapter, never an engine change.

- **Two browser frameworks, because CAPTCHAs decide the architecture.** A managed remote browser handles reCAPTCHA platforms (Greenhouse, Ashby); local headful Chrome on a clean residential IP handles hCaptcha (Lever), which cannot be cleared headless.
- **An answer chain** — saved answers, then deterministic rules over the profile, then an LLM for the subjective tail.
- **A preflight pass** that dry-runs the form and names every field it cannot answer *before* anything is submitted.
- **A pre-submit gate** that reads the rendered DOM and refuses to click until every required field is provably filled — ownership has to be earned from the fill trace, not assumed.
- **Idempotency keys on every submit.** A double-apply damages the candidate and our standing with the ATS, so it is designed out rather than guarded against.
- **Per-user email alias infrastructure**, so ATS verification codes route back to the engine and the run continues unattended.
- **It never fakes success.** If the engine cannot finish autonomously it returns `needs_action` and asks the human.

## Built during the hackathon

**The universal apply layer** (`docs/plans/0057`): applying to an ATS we have never written a connector for.

The governing idea is one line: **the LLM proposes, deterministic code disposes.** An LLM reads the rendered form and reports what the fields are. It never decides whether to submit. That decision stays in the same pre-submit gate as every hand-written connector — read-only, ATS-agnostic, and blind to who filled the form. Arranged this way, an LLM that is wrong produces `needs_action`, never a bad submit.

Landed today:

- **`FormReader` port + LLM adapter** — the seam that turns a rendered page into a field list.
- **`GenericSubmitter`** — fills the `default:` branch that previously returned `unsupported engine`. Shipped read-only first (preflight only, structurally incapable of submitting), then wired through fill → gate → submit.
- **Three DOM-probe faults fixed** — phantom single checkboxes, checkbox groups split across differing `name` attributes, and styled `[role=checkbox]` shells that bypassed grouping and duplicated required fields tenfold. On a live run this cut detected required fields from 27 to 17.
- **A Workable connector** — URL routing, canonicalization, and dashboard support.
- **Fields asked in their own words**, with widget chrome stripped, so a question put to the user reads like the question the form asked.
- **A verified live submission** end to end on a real Workable posting, confirmed by both the database record and the employer's confirmation email.

Every step followed the repository's rule: failing test first, minimum code to pass, then refactor. Connectors are tested against recorded fixtures; real submissions are gated behind an `e2e` build tag and run by hand, never in CI.

description.title: What is the deployed URL for this project?
description.body: https://shortlistapp.co/

description.title: What is the problem your project solves?
description.body:
Applying for jobs is the same forty fields, retyped forever.

A candidate running a real search fills in name, phone, location, work authorization, notice period, salary expectation, and a dozen screening questions — then does it again at the next company, because every employer sits behind a different applicant tracking system. Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby and Workable each render a different form, with different widgets, different required fields, and different names for the same question. 

**Why this can't be solved with an API.** Every live ATS gates the submit button behind a CAPTCHA and browser fingerprinting. The documented "apply" APIs need the *employer's* key, not the candidate's. So there is no integration path: the only way to actually submit is to drive a real browser, the way a person does.

That is why the existing tools stop short. Autofill extensions paste text into fields and still hand the click back to you. "One-click apply" products only work on the one portal they were built against. And an agent that guesses at a question it cannot answer does something worse than nothing — it submits a wrong answer under your name, to an employer, permanently.

**The impact.** For a candidate, this is hours a week of mechanical work standing between them and the jobs they're qualified for. For the ecosystem, the missing piece is infrastructure: nothing today can take an arbitrary job URL and complete the application end to end, safely, without a human finishing it. That layer is what everything else — job discovery, matching, agents that act on your behalf — has to be built on.

**Current Stage** Currently Shortlist have 3 paid users.

description.title: How Did You Use Claude?
description.body:
**Claude is the workflow layer: Claude Code wrote this engine, and wrote it test-first.**

That is the honest description, and I want to be precise about where Claude sits rather than overclaim.

## How Claude was used

Claude Code (Opus) is the author of essentially the entire codebase — 545 commits across the repository, including all 15 landed during the hackathon. Not autocomplete: the working loop is red → green → refactor, with Claude writing the failing test first, then the minimum code to pass it. The repository's `CLAUDE.md` encodes the architecture rules Claude works under — keep `internal/core` pure, never submit without an idempotency key, never fake success — and the numbered plan documents in `docs/plans/` are Claude-authored designs reviewed before implementation.

Specific work Claude did today:

- **Designed the universal apply layer** — including the constraint that makes it safe. The insight that the LLM must be allowed to propose fields but never to authorize a submit, so that a wrong model produces `needs_action` instead of a bad application, came out of a Claude Code design session and is the load-bearing idea of the whole plan.
- **Diagnosed three DOM-probe faults** that a live Workable run surfaced as a wall of duplicate required fields, and fixed each with a test that reproduced it.
- **Root-caused a class of bug we had been misreading for weeks** — an "unanswerable field" that looked like anti-bot defence turned out to be our own matcher querying the whole page instead of the field's own listbox.

Subagents are part of the loop too: a `go-reviewer` agent reviews changes before commit and has caught real defects, including two paths that would have lost user credits.

tracetalk-8629.tagline: Can make distributed systems dashboard talk !

description.title: How you are solving it?
description.body:
**TraceTalk** replaces query-builder UIs with conversation. An engineer asks a plain-language question ("why did payment latency spike at 2pm?") and an AI agent investigates live querying logs, metrics, and traces showing its reasoning trail alongside evidence-grounded answers.

## What We Built

1. **5 query tools** — `run_sql`, `list_streams`, `search_logs`, `get_metrics`, `get_service_graph` wrapping SQL queries against OpenObserve

2. **Claude agent loop** — Multi-step tool-use with streaming narration, evidence grounding, and 20-call budget cap

3. **SSE streaming backend** — Flask server streams investigation events in real-time via Server-Sent Events

4. **Interactive frontend** — Next.js chat interface with live investigation panel showing agent narrations and tool results as they happen

description.title: How Did You Use Claude?
description.body:
- **Tool-use loop**: Claude decides which tools to call based on the user's question, chaining calls across services to trace root cause
- **System prompt engineering**: Custom prompt instructs Claude to act as an SRE, ground every claim in tool results, emit narrations for the UI, and cap investigation at 20 calls
- **Multi-hop reasoning**: Claude autonomously chains evidence e.g., metrics → service graph → logs → traces to answer ambiguous questions without being told which service or time window to investigate
- **Streaming narration**: Each Claude turn produces narrations ("Checking payment-service latency...") that stream to the UI in real-time, making the investigation visible

description.title: What is the deployed URL for this project?
description.body: https://github.com/Omkar-Ghongade/Push2Prod

description.title: What is the problem your project solves?
description.body:
When something breaks in a distributed system, the person on call doesn't get a root cause they get a wall of dashboards. Debugging today means manually jumping between three or four disconnected tools a metrics dashboard for the symptom, a log search UI for the evidence, a tracing tool for the request path and hand-writing a different query language in each one, all while a service is actively degraded.

This has two costs:

Speed. Every minute spent translating "why is checkout slow" into the right PromQL query, then the right SPL query, then the right trace filter, is a minute the incident stays open.
Access. This workflow assumes deep, tool-specific expertise. An engineer who didn't build the system, or who's newer to on-call, often can't investigate as fast as the person who wrote the original queries so the same few people end up paged for everything.

TraceTalk removes the translation step. You ask what you actually want to know, in plain language "why did payment-service latency spike around 2pm?" and an agent investigates the way a senior engineer would: it queries the metrics, follows the evidence into the logs, checks the trace, and answers with the specific numbers and log lines that back up its conclusion. Nothing is asserted without a tool call behind it, and the side panel shows every step live, so the answer is verifiable, not just plausible.

The result isn't a smarter dashboard. It's a different way of interacting with observability data entirely closer to debugging with a colleague than querying a database.
