The agents never see private keys, RPCs, or unsigned transactions — and the reason that is *credible* is that every wallet Orloj manages is an Orbitport KMS key. **Orloj is, end to end, a secure signing and authorization service for autonomous AI agents** — a category that didn't exist a year ago, implemented on top of orbital HSM + SpaceTEE.

What's unusual about it: Orbitport isn't an optional plug-in. The wallet's private material is *only ever* an Orbitport KMS key id; there is no path through the system where the registry process holds, generates, or sees the private key. A compromised registry host cannot forge transactions — it can only request signatures it is already authorized to request, on a digest, against a key that lives in orbit.

## How we use Orbitport KMS (depth, across both schemes)

Most KMS integrations stop at "create a key, ask it to sign once." Orloj uses **both** Orbitport key schemes, **four distinct KMS operations**, in **two services** across the codebase:

| Where                                          | KMS operation   | Scheme / key                     | Why                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| App / createVault                              | kms.createKey   | ETHEREUM / ECC_SECG_P256K1       | Per-vault wallet signing key — Orbitport returns the derived Ethereum address                        |
| App / createVault                              | kms.createKey   | TRANSIT / AES_256_GCM96          | Per-vault envelope-encryption key, in the same security domain as the wallet                         |
| App / setSecret                                | kms.encrypt    | TRANSIT                          | Encrypts secret-store plaintext — only the ciphertext blob is persisted to Postgres                  |
| App / getSecret                                | kms.decrypt    | TRANSIT                          | Decrypts on read — cleartext never lives on disk on our side                                         |
| Registry / on every agent write-tool call      | kms.sign       | ETHEREUM, messageType DIGEST     | Signs the keccak256 of an EIP-1559 unsigned tx; the (r, s, v) signature is reassembled and broadcast |
| App / signDigest                               | kms.sign       | ETHEREUM, messageType DIGEST     | Same primitive exposed through the vault-provider abstraction for control-plane use                  |

**The signing path is the live transaction broadcast path, not a demo button.** When an AI agent calls a write function on any Sourcify-generated MCP, Orloj builds the EIP-1559 tx with viem, hashes it, sends *only the digest* to Orbitport, gets back `(r, s, v)`, reassembles with `serializeTransaction`, and broadcasts. Every state-changing on-chain call an agent makes through Orloj transits Orbitport.

**Envelope encryption is not a side feature.** Per-vault TRANSIT keys mean that any secrets stored alongside the wallet (off-chain credentials, API keys, signing salts) live under the same physical custody as the wallet itself. Ciphertext lives in our DB; the master key lives in orbit. Combining the ETHEREUM and TRANSIT schemes inside a single product surface keeps the wallet and its sidecar secrets in one security domain — a property that falls out naturally from the design rather than being bolted on.

**Per-agent grants tie it all together.** Each agent has a recorded grant against a vault (with `permissions`, `secret_path_pattern`, optional `expires_at`); the registry resolves that grant on every MCP call and signs through the matching Orbitport key. Revocation is instant and never touches the keys themselves.

## Why this matters

Orbitport is what makes HSM-grade custody for autonomous AI agents possible. Keys live in orbit, in tamper-proof hardware, signing only what an authenticated, grant-bearing agent asks for — with signatures that cannot be forged by an operator, a state actor, or a compromised host.

## Files of interest

- `packages/app/lib/vault-providers/orbitport.ts` — full KMS provider: `createKey` (both schemes), `encrypt`/`decrypt` (TRANSIT), `sign` (ETHEREUM), key-grant CRUD
- `packages/registry/src/vault-providers/orbitport.js` — registry-side `signWithOrbitport` (digest → broadcast tx)
- `packages/registry/src/sign-transaction.js` — provider router on the live transaction path
- `packages/registry/src/vault-resolve.js` — agent → vault → KMS-key-id resolution
- `packages/app/lib/db.ts` — `orbitport_vault` / `orbitport_secret` /

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body:
# Orloj × Sourcify

> *Built at **ETHPrague 2026**.* An MCP registry built end-to-end on Sourcify-verified contract metadata — turning every Sourcify entry into an AI-callable typed tool.

## The pitch

Orloj turns Sourcify-verified smart contracts into **MCP servers AI agents can call as typed tools**. Every Orloj MCP — its tool list, its parameter types, its function descriptions, its proxy-aware ABI — is generated end-to-end with a Sourcify connection. The moment a contract is verified on Sourcify, it becomes callable by an AI agent through Orloj, with no per-contract integration work on our side.

To our knowledge nobody has built this category of consumer on top of Sourcify before. *Making verified contracts directly executable by LLMs* — a category that didn't exist a year ago — is something Sourcify uniquely enables: it requires the metadata-grade verification, the NatSpec, and the proxy resolution, all together, in one place.

## How we use Sourcify (beyond just "fetch the ABI")

Every MCP we serve is built from **five distinct fields** of the Sourcify v2 contract response, each load-bearing:

| Field               | What we do with it                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **abi**             | Recursively translated into Zod input/output schemas — including tuple types, dynamic arrays, fixed-size arrays, all integer widths, and fixed-size byte types    |
| **userdoc**         | Function "notice" strings (NatSpec) become the tool description an LLM reads when deciding whether to call the function                                           |
| **devdoc**          | Function "details" strings used as a fallback description when no userdoc notice exists                                                                            |
| **compilation**     | The contract name field becomes the MCP server name — agents see "WstETH" or "UniswapV3Pool", not a hex address                                                   |
| **proxyResolution** | Detects proxies at registration time and points the ABI fetch at the implementation, so upgrades are transparent                                                  |

The two requests we make per registration:

1. `GET /v2/contract/{chainId}/{address}?fields=proxyResolution` — proxy detection.
2. `GET /v2/contract/{chainId}/{address}?fields=abi,userdoc,devdoc,compilation` — typed surface + descriptions + name (against the implementation when relevant).

**The NatSpec → tool-description chain is the unique-data argument.** The string that determines whether an agent decides to call a tool is *the contract author's own NatSpec, surfaced verbatim through Sourcify*. You can't do this with a raw ABI from a block explorer — it requires Sourcify's metadata-aware verification. Contract authors are already writing the documentation the agent needs; Sourcify is what makes it reachable, and Orloj is what consumes it.

**Proxies are first-class because Sourcify makes them so.** Most production contracts are proxies; without `proxyResolution`, an agent registry is dead on arrival. We bind agents to the proxy address (the user-facing one) but type the tools off the implementation ABI. Proxy upgrades surface as new MCP tools the next time the registry is refreshed.

## Why this matters

Every verified contract on Sourcify — across 100+ EVM chains — is a candidate Orloj MCP. There is no manual ABI upload, no per-contract integration, no documentation step on our side. The whole pipeline (verified bytecode → ABI → typed MCP tool → NatSpec-described action surfaced to an LLM) flows from one Sourcify request.

This only works because Sourcify is what it is: open data, exact metadata-based matches, NatSpec-aware, and proxy-aware. An agent ecosystem that wants to read and write the chain at scale needs a verification layer it can build on permissionlessly — and Orloj is what becomes possible when you treat that layer as load-bearing public infrastructure.

## Files of interest

- `packages/registry/src/get-contract.js` — Sourcify v2 fetch, multi-field consumption, ABI → Zod, NatSpec → MCP tool descriptions, proxy ABI override
- `packages/registry/src/server.mjs` — `POST /register` proxy-resolution call to `?fields=proxyResolution`
- `packages/registry/src/generate-mcp.js` — turns a fetched contract into an `McpServer` with view/write tools, one per ABI function

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The Sealed Sky is a consumer grade timelock encryption tool with easy to use user interface. 

It allows to encrypt - seal the content  now, decrypt only when a future moment arrives.

Use cases:
- Time capsules at any scale - 30 seconds, a year, a decade.
- Sealed-bid auctions where everyone reveals at the same instant, nobody before.
- Dead-man's switches and posthumous notes, with no trusted custodian holding the key.
- MEV-resistant order submission and time-locked DAO votes.
- Predictions of future that can be undisclosed after the fact.
- Intergenerational messaging - send a message to yourself or your closed ones that becomes legible only in 2030. 

The demo website uses TypeScript implementation of the TimeLock library based on Boneh–Franklin's IBE paper. 

Complementary part of the project is a Trusted Edge Oracle - small stack that lets you treat a USB Armory (Secure World / TrustZone) as a signing oracle for short, structured payloads. A Node backend re-checks proofs with the same HMAC rule as the Armory, records accepted and rejected runs, and optionally pushes on-chain attestations to Sepolia and surfaces validation through ENS.

It can be used to 
- As a proof “This result came from our edge device, not from a browser tab.”
-Cheaper, clearer audits than “trust our server.”
-Safer automation with a relayer.
-Public transparency without dumping your whole database.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges are surprisingly the opposite of what we were used at the hackathons years ago. 

We admit utilized AI agent tools (Claude Code, Cursor), they helped us reach to develop proof-of-concepts at paces not possible before, but for us  developers, it became complicated to keep track of all the important technical  nuances of the proposed solution.

Issues that would need further attention - handling of the K key (there are ways how to tie the message to a specified public address without the need to store the K key safely until the unlock time).  If the messages are meant to be unlocked by public, the K key storage is not an issue.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Timelock is the missing primitive behind sealed-bid auctions, vesting cliffs, time-locked DAO votes, dead-man's switches, and MEV-resistant transaction submission. 

Anywhere "everyone reveals at the same instant, nobody before" is a useful property. Sealed Sky makes it usable today. 

The envelope format works in the browser and in the Python CLI. No trusted keeper, no custody risk between commit and reveal.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
Both backends work at year-scale and decade-scale unlocks. 

Sealing is non-interactive, and reveal only needs the latest beacon block at unlock time, so there's no chain walking or archive crawl. 

It makes intergenerational messaging real: a posthumous note, a 10-year time capsule addressed to *.eth, a long-horizon promise that becomes legible on a fixed date without any custodian holding the key.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
The cTRNG IPFS beacon is wired in as a real encryption backend. 

Each cTRNG capsule has a SHA-256 commitment that binds it to a future unlock time, and reveal is gated on a live beacon block we fetch from ipfs.io. 

When the message decrypts, the Detail panel shows the witness block's sequence, timestamp, randomness, and gateway URL, so the cosmic origin is visible at the moment of unlock.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Every sealed message gets its own ENS subdomain. On seal we publish cap-*.id144.eth via NameStone, with records for the envelope. 

The capsule then resolves in any standard ENS client, including the ENS app. 

Share links collapse to ?ens=cap-3f2a9c1b.id144.eth, which uses ENS as a registry of time-bound content. 

The connect flow also falls back to NameStone's API when no on-chain reverse record is set, so NameStone-issued names work as primary names without a separate transaction.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
On-chain payments leak everything: balances, counterparties, and amounts are public forever. Even "private" tools usually still link sender → recipient through a wallet address.

SpaceNox solves three real problems at once:

1. Confidential balances and transfers
Wrap regular USDC into cUSDC and your balance is stored as an encrypted handle on-chain. When you send to someone, you submit an RSA-encrypted intent where the recipient and amount are never visible on the chain. A TEE gateway decrypts the intent inside a secure enclave and settles it in batched anonymity sets, so even an observer indexing every block can't tell who got paid or how much.

Use it for: payroll, contractor payments, treasury operations, donations, anything where amounts and counterparties shouldn't be public.

2. Receiving without revealing your wallet
Hand out one ENS name (e.g. alice.eth). Every sender resolves it to a fresh one-time stealth address. Funds arrive there, you sweep each one through cUSDC and confidentially route the balance to your main wallet so your real address never appears next to any payment you receive.

Use it for: public donation links, invoices, hackathon prizes, freelancing, refunds or any "send me money here" scenario where you don't want to doxx your main wallet.

3. No central point of failure
Stealth registrations (Fluidkey keys, nonce counters) live in Swarm, not on a hosted gateway.
Encrypted balance state is mirrored to Swarm by the ingestor.
Decryption keys live only inside the TEE gateway and never in the browser, never in a database.
Net effect: users get bank-grade privacy on stablecoin payments and ENS-based identity, without trusting a company to hold their keys, their balances, or their stealth registry. Existing flows like "wrap → transfer → unwrap" or "share my ENS to get paid" just work but the chain doesn't reveal who, how much, or to whom.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges I ran into
1. Hiding the recipient on-chain, not just the amount
Most "confidential token" implementations encrypt amounts but still emit Transfer(from, to, ...), which leaks the counterparty. I had to redesign the transfer flow as a two-step intent protocol: the sender submits an opaque RSA-encrypted blob (submitConfidentialIntent), and the gateway later batches multiple intents together and calls executeConfidentialIntentBatch with a 5-address anonymity set per intent. The contract verifies an EIP-712 input proof for the encrypted recipient index into that set so the chain only sees a list of candidates, not which one actually got paid.

2. Frontend submitting intents but balances not moving
After wiring the encrypted-intent flow, transfers looked successful on the UI but cUSDC balances didn't change. Took a while to realize submitConfidentialIntent only queues the intent executeConfidentialIntentBatch is gateway-only and is what actually moves balances. Solution: added /api/intent/settle that loads the runner RSA key on the server, decrypts the intent, builds proofs, and broadcasts the batch tx. The UI now goes submitting → settling → done instead of silently leaving funds stuck.

Built a same-origin /api/rpc proxy so the frontend never talks directly to upstream.
Added withRpcRetry exponential backoff for server-side calls.
Tagged every RPC error with source + rpcHost so I could actually tell which RPC was breaking.
Built an "unwrap recovery" panel that lists stuck UnwrapRequested events and re-runs claimUnwrap on demand so users never lose USDC to a transient gateway failure.
3. Vercel monorepo deletes frontend tsconfig
First Vercel deploy failed with module-not-found for files that obviously existed. Turned out my root .vercelignore had unanchored entries like tsconfig.json and contracts/ that recursively matched into frontend/. Anchoring everything with a leading / (e.g. /contracts/) and adding a frontend/vercel.json with explicit build/install commands fixed it.

4. Two @scure/bip32 versions in the dependency tree
Adding @fluidkey/stealth-account-kit to the frontend pulled in its own pinned @scure/bip32, which conflicted with the one viem uses for HDKey. TypeScript refused to pass the node between them ("separate declarations of a private property privKey"). Runtime was fine, so I cast viewingPrivateKeyNode as never at the boundary and pinned the chain id to a number (Fluidkey rejected bigint).

5. Replacing the Sneaky gateway with Swarm
The original ENS stealth example relied on a hosted Deno gateway holding the user's viewing keys. I didn't want that dependency. Rebuilt the whole flow on top of @armsves/swarm-kv (the same package the ingestor uses): registration writes Fluidkey material to Swarm, resolve serializes nonce increments per ENS name, and status reads the issued count back. The catch was concurrency, two parallel resolves on the same name would have collided on the nonce row. Solved with a per-name promise queue on the server so each resolve is a strict read-modify-write.

6. RSA private key in a serverless runtime
Tried loading rsa_priv.pem via fs.readFileSync in the frontend's API routes which works locally, breaks under Turbopack's NFT trace and isn't portable to Vercel. Switched to RUNNER_RSA_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM as an env var and made the loader strict (no filesystem fallback), so prod and dev follow the same code path.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: SpaceNox is a confidential payments app on Arbitrum Sepolia: USDC gets wrapped into a TEE-backed cUSDC token whose balances stay encrypted on-chain, and transfers are submitted as RSA-encrypted intents that a TEE gateway settles in batched anonymity sets recipient and amount are never visible. On the identity side, ENS owners register Fluidkey stealth keys directly into Swarm (no third-party gateway), so any sender can drop USDC at a fresh one-time address per resolve, and the recipient sweeps it into cUSDC and confidentially routes it to their main wallet - breaking the on-chain link between sender and final destination. The user holds the keys, the gateway never sees plaintext outside the TEE, and storage is decentralized in Swarm, payments and identity stay private end-to-end with no central point of failure.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body: SpaceNox is built on the Space Computer / Nox TEE protocol and every encrypted balance is just an euint256 handle managed by an on-chain NoxCompute contract, and every state transition (wrap, confidential transfer, unwrap) goes through a TEE gateway that holds the ETH signer and the RSA key used to decrypt user intents. The chain only sees opaque ciphertext and TEE-signed proofs, so the secure compute boundary is what gives the app its privacy guarantees. Pair that with stealth-address registration written to Swarm and you get a full pipeline where keys, plaintext balances, and identity material all stay inside space-grade secure infrastructure where no central server can read or correlate user funds.

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body:
We built and shipped a full KV stack on Swarm and wired it into a real product, not just a demo:

@armsves/swarm-kv is a published npm package that wraps Swarm Feeds + manifests behind a simple put(key, value) / get(key) / keys() API. Handles utf8/json/binary encodings, inline vs referenced chunks, an automatic key index, and serialized read-modify-write so concurrent writes don't lose entries.
Runnable examples and a minimal kv-web-demo test frontend (browser → bzz.limo) so any developer can copy/paste and have a working KV in minutes.
Used as the actual production storage layer in SpaceNox: the node ingestor writes per-user encrypted-balance rows + a cursor to Swarm via the package, and the new ENS stealth flow stores Fluidkey registrations and per-name nonce counters there too, replacing what would normally be a third-party gateway.
So the package is both the bounty deliverable and the persistence backbone of the rest of the project, proving the API is good enough to build real apps on, not just toy reads/writes.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
SpaceNox turns an ENS name into a privacy mailbox: each resolution returns a brand-new one-time stealth address, not a static wallet.

Owner registers once, Fluidkey spending/viewing keys are derived from a wallet signature and written to Swarm (@armsves/swarm-kv), no hosted gateway.
Every sender resolving alice.eth gets a fresh stealth EOA (per-name nonce stored in Swarm).
Recipient sweeps funded addresses through the SpaceNox confidential pipeline (wrap → encrypted intent → batch settle) into their main wallet.
Result: one human-readable name → infinite unlinkable addresses → confidential settlement. ENS becomes the identity layer, the chain only sees opaque ciphertext, and no on-chain link exists between sender and final recipient.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
In short:* Protect the community sanctuary that is BORDEL with an on- and off-chain authentication protocol enabling privacy-preserving access control *

**The Problem:**

With BORDEL's basement under renovation, it needs a way to manage member access to community spaces that is privacy-preserving and secure. This would be applicable to doors, gates, fridges, storage, local applications etc.

The current system uses Merkle tree based memberships and multiple verification mechanisms to prove that someone is a valid member, but memberships remain publicly visible onchain, permissions are difficult to manage dynamically, and access control still relies on fragmented and partially centralized infrastructure.

**Our Solution: BORDEL-gate**

An on- and off-chain authentication protocol built around zk membership proofs using NFC wallets and wallet addresses.

Instead of using public NFT memberships, BORDEL members are represented inside a cryptographic member set. Members prove they belong to that set without revealing their identity or exposing the entire membership list.

When a member tries to access a space, the protocol verifies:

- the member is valid
- the member currently has that capability
- the proof is fresh and non-replayable

If valid, the resolver returns the member’s wallet address and access is granted.

*BORDEL transforms NFC wristbands and wallets into cryptographic access credentials for Bordel spaces while preserving member privacy.*

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**Outdated Noir Reference**
One of the main challenges was working with Noir and the surrounding zk tooling ecosystem, which is still relatively new and continuously evolving, which required us to spend additional time adapting code and rebuilding parts of the proving flow to work with the current Noir stack.

**Proof Performance and Hashing**
Another major challenge was proof performance and efficiency on-device. Our initial implementation used keccak256 inside the zk circuit, but this proved to be too computationally expensive. To make proof generation fast enough for real-world authentication flows, we migrated from keccak256 to Poseidon2, a zk-friendly hash function optimized for proving systems. This reduced proving overhead and improved proving performance by roughly 50x, making local proof generation viable on consumer devices.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
BORDEL-gate explores a privacy-first approach to identity, authentication, and access control for real-world communities that value autonomy, decentralization, and member privacy without relying on centralized identity providers or permanently exposing member activity on-chain.

Most access-control systems today rely on centralized infrastructure:

- centralized databases
- visible member lists
- static credentials
- permanent identity linkage

Instead of publicly proving identity, BORDEL focuses on proving authorization. This creates a more resilient and privacy-preserving authentication system for decentralized communities and shared physical spaces.

phare-e849.name: Phare
phare-e849.tagline: What satellites can't see, citizens can

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Phare is a bonded, citizen-powered registry for sightings of sanctioned oil tankers, ships that move sanctioned cargo by disabling their AIS transponders and going dark. Anyone with a phone can photograph a suspicious vessel, upload the photo to Swarm, and submit a bonded on-chain report from their wallet. The protocol holds the bond in escrow, opens a UMA OOv3 optimistic assertion, and runs a challenge window. Verifier agents running the OpenClaw skill race to dispute fakes; reports that survive settlement are recorded permanently.

- For reporters: an ordinary citizen in Cyprus or a sailor in the Laconian Gulf can document a vessel that has no official record anywhere. No account, no KYC, no permission. The PWA handles photo capture, Swarm upload, wallet approval, and auto-settlement in one flow.

For journalists, NGOs, and enforcement bodies: every sanctioned vessel that survives adjudication acquires a permanent ENS identity that any browser can resolve. The records include the satellite orbital corroboration from SpaceComputer, signed on-chain by the KMS key. The full dossier lives on Swarm, pointer in the ENS contenthash.

For verifier operators: anyone can run the phare/verifier OpenClaw skill, self-register an ENS subname, and earn 50% of slashed bonds when they successfully dispute fake reports. The agent writes its reasoning JSON to Swarm and updates its own ENS verifier.lastDecision record after every dispute, a live, public accountability trail.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1. USDC was the bond currency until it wasn't.
The original spec pinned USDC as the bond currency for ReportRegistry. After probing UMA OOv3's Sepolia AddressWhitelist and calling getMinimumBond, we discovered the UMA minimum bond for that USDC token on Sepolia is 400 USDC, completely impractical for a $5-equivalent demo bond. We switched to WETH, which has a minimum bond of 0.002 WETH (a few dollars), and rebuilt the escrow and faucet instructions around it. Mainnet deployment can revisit USDC.

2. NameStone was replaced by an on-chain contract mid-design.
The original spec used NameStone's off-chain CCIP-Read resolver for all ENS minting; no gas per mint, but a centralized write key held by the project. As the ENS integration deepened, we realised that CCIP-Read off-chain resolvers don't support on-chain writes initiated by smart contracts: ReportRegistry cannot call a NameStone API from inside a Solidity callback. The entire minter service and the off-chain NameStone path were replaced with Lighthouse.sol; an 80-line on-chain contract that calls NameWrapper directly and is the sole write authority for both vessel and verifier subnames. This was a significant mid-flight redesign but resulted in a cleaner and more prize-competitive integration.

3. spaceTEE doesn't exist yet.
The SpaceComputer architecture documents a spaceTEE inference layer that would let a satellite-hosted TEE predict vessel destinations from imagery. We designed the full integration (plugin methods, inference JSON schema, on-chain attestation) then discovered spaceTEE is on the SpaceComputer roadmap but not yet shipped. Rather than drop the integration, we built the call site honestly: the phare-imager Orbitport plugin exposes the full four-method JSON-RPC interface, but underneath it returns fixture imagery and a rule-based destination prediction that always carries "mocked": true. The KMS signing and on-chain attest() are real; the inference is mock-now-real-later. The plugin is the contribution SpaceComputer can wire to real hardware.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
Phare is built for the Future Society track in the most direct sense: it is civic infrastructure for ecological accountability, owned by no one, built bottom-up.

The shadow fleet causes sanctions failure, war financing, and uninsured ecological disasters. When these ships spill or sink there is no liable party, no insurance, no clean-up. Outside expensive government surveillance budgets, almost no one can see them.

Phare replaces institutional surveillance with a citizen-funded, privacy-respecting sighting network. Anyone with a phone opens the PWA, photographs a vessel, and submits a bonded report; no account, no KYC, no permission. The bond is the background check. Autonomous verifier agents dispute fakes; reports that survive become permanent ENS identities that journalists, NGOs, and enforcement bodies can query forever, with no project-controlled API in the resolution path.

Orbital corroboration from SpaceComputer adds a second layer of evidence: after settlement, the phare-imager plugin tasks satellite imagery over the reported coordinates, the SpaceComputer KMS signs the attestation digest, and ReportRegistry.attest() writes the corroboration on-chain signed by space, verifiable by anyone.

Reporter privacy is explicit: anonymous EOA, rotatable per report, no off-chain authentication at any layer that touches a citizen.

This is the solarpunk thesis applied to maritime accountability: bonds replace permission lists, decentralised storage replaces proprietary databases, citizen observation plus orbital corroboration replaces satellite monopolies.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
Phare integrates SpaceComputer across three real surfaces, with two mocked layers that are explicitly labelled and have a clear path to becoming real once SpaceComputer ships the underlying hardware capability.

What is real and ships today:

- phare-imager is a new Orbitport Application Plugin: the first photo-tasking plugin published to the Orbitport ecosystem. It conforms to JSON-RPC 2.0 over the Orbitport gateway with Client ID + Secret authentication and exposes four methods: imagery request, imagery-ready callback, inference request, and inference-ready callback. No imaging plugin existed in the Orbitport ecosystem before this. The plugin defines the shape of the integration that SpaceComputer can wire to real celestial-layer cameras later.

- ReportRegistry.attest(reportId, imageSwarm, imageHash, teePrediction, signature) is a real, immutable on-chain function. It verifies an EIP-191 signature via ecrecover against orbitalAttestor: a SpaceComputer KMS-derived Ethereum address hardcoded at deploy time. The KMS ETHEREUM key scheme produces secp256k1 signatures that are natively verifiable on any EVM chain without a custom precompile. Every orbital corroboration in Phare is signed by the live KMS endpoint and verified on-chain. This is not mocked.

What is mocked and why:

- Satellite imagery is fixture-keyed by coordinate: pre-curated Sentinel-2 ESA scenes for the demo locations. spaceTEE inference is a rule-based stub (imo % ports.length) that always returns "mocked": true in the inference JSON. SpaceComputer's own architecture documentation confirms spaceTEE is on the roadmap but not yet shipped, there is no production endpoint to call. The mock is honest, labelled, and separated cleanly from the real KMS signing so judges can see exactly what is real.

The cross-track combination: Orbitport Application Plugin (new ecosystem contribution) + KMS ETHEREUM signing wired into an immutable smart contract. SpaceComputer's bounty criteria reward cross-track builds explicitly, this hits both the Application layer and the Security API layer in one integration.

description.title: Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway
description.body:
Phare uses Swarm as the storage layer for every artefact that matters to the protocol: reporter photos, metadata JSON, vessel dossiers, verifier policy and soul documents, reasoning JSONs pinned at dispute time, and orbital imagery. Every one of these is content-addressed, the reference baked into the on-chain report is a commitment to specific bytes, not a location.

The PWA uploads photo and metadata via bee-js, receiving BMT root references that are passed directly to ReportRegistry.submit(). The on-chain photoHash is independently computed as keccak256(photoBytes), giving consumers two cryptographic anchors per report: the BMT root (what Swarm committed to) and the keccak256 (what the reporter photographed). Both must match the fetched bytes.

The orbital orchestrator fetches imagery via the orbitalImager-sdk and pins the result to Swarm before calling attest(). The orbitalImageHash stored on-chain by ReportRegistry.attest() is the independent hash of the orbital image bytes so on-chain verification doesn't require trusting the Swarm gateway at all.

The swarm/ module defines the shared Verified Fetch interface used across the minter, verifier skill, and orbital orchestrator: verifyImmutable(reference, bytes) throws on BMT mismatch; readFeedLatest(owner, identity) SOC-verifies the chunk signature before returning any mutable vessel state. Neither function ever returns bytes without verifying them. A tampered gateway is caught locally, every time.

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body:
Phare implements mutable, verifiable key-value state on Swarm using Single Owner Chunks and Swarm Feeds for two registries that need to be updated over time.

Vessel state feed — after each settled sighting, the minter writes a SOC-backed feed entry per vessel:

- Key: (owner = minter EOA, topic = keccak256("phare:vessel:<imo>")) -> deterministic feed address per IMO
- Value: latest dossier bzz:// reference, last-seen position, sighting count

Any consumer looks up a vessel by IMO using this deterministic derivation and gets the current state without querying any project API.

Verifier activity feed — each verifier agent maintains its own feed:

- Key: (owner = verifier EOA, topic = keccak256("phare:verifier:<handle>")) -> deterministic per-agent
- Value: latest activity log bzz:// reference, updated after every settled assertion the agent touched

Both feeds follow the same SOC verification recipe: fetch the chunk at the deterministic address, recover the signer from the chunk's signature over keccak256(identity || payload), confirm it matches the expected owner before acting on the value. The swarm/ helper module exposes readFeedLatest(owner, identity) and writeFeedNext(owner, identity, payload) for all consumers.

The result is a decentralised, cryptographically verified, mutable KV registry (vessel state and agent reputation) with no database, no API, and no trusted write authority beyond the owner key that signed each chunk.

description.title: Best ENS Integration for AI Agents
description.body:
Phare's verifier agents are autonomous OpenClaw agents that dispute fraudulent vessel sightings via UMA OOv3. Each one acquires a real, on-chain ENS identity not minted by the project team, but self-registered by the agent's own wallet during onboarding by calling Lighthouse.enrollVerifier(handle, policyURI, soulURI) directly.

Lighthouse calls NameWrapper's setSubnodeRecord with the agent as token owner and PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL burned. From that point, not even the project team can overwrite the agent's records, the agent is sovereign. The agent then writes verifier.policy, verifier.soul, and verifier.runtime directly to PublicResolver from its own key.

What makes the integration deep is verifier.lastDecision. After every dispute, the verifier pins a reasoning JSON to Swarm, the evidence it cited, the policy rule that fired, the IMO it challenged and writes the bzz:// reference to its own ENS subname from its own wallet. Resolve agent-3a4b5c.verifier.phare.eth in any ENS browser, click verifier.lastDecision, and you get the agent's live reasoning trail. No project API. No centralized indexer. No CCIP-Read resolver — real on-chain NameWrapper ENS.

The skill library (skill/) ships with all the primitives to make this work: enrollVerifier, setVerifierLastDecision, setVerifierPolicy, setVerifierSoul, and readVerifier, all via viem calling NameWrapper and PublicResolver directly. The agent's ENS subname is not a static profile. It is a live, agent-curated public log written by the agent itself after every decision it makes.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
ENS is designed for humans and organisations with wallets. Phare uses it for something it was never designed for: physical objects that have no wallet, no public registry, and actively try not to be seen.

Every sanctioned vessel that survives a UMA challenge acquires a permanent ENS subname. The owner of that wrapped ERC-1155 NameWrapper token is Lighthouse.sol, an immutable on-chain contract. Three fuses are burned at mint: PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL, CANNOT_TRANSFER, and CANNOT_UNWRAP. The vessel subname is sealed to the contract permanently, it cannot be sold, moved, revoked, or transferred. The only entity that can update its records is ReportRegistry, calling through Lighthouse, upon a new settled sighting.

This means a shadow-fleet tanker that disabled its AIS transponder to be invisible acquires a permanent, tamper-evident on-chain identity the moment a citizen sighting survives adjudication. The identity deepens over time: vessel.swarm.log and contenthash point to the full Swarm dossier, updated per sighting; vessel.orbital.image, vessel.orbital.imageHash, and vessel.orbital.tee.prediction are written when SpaceComputer corroboration arrives.

The two namespaces also interlink: the vessel's Swarm dossier references the verifier agents that ruled on its disputes; each verifier's own ENS subname references the IMOs it challenged. The full accountability graph is browsable through ENS alone, with no project API in the resolution path.

ENS as a permanent public registry for a class of physical objects that has no public registry, and that funds its own evasion, is the creative use.

stovera-8044.name: Stovera
stovera-8044.tagline: AI agent marketplace with verifiable reputation

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
AI agents are increasingly acting on behalf of users. executing trades, auditing contracts, scraping data, but 87% have no safety documentation (MIT CSAIL AI Agent Index) and there's no trustworthy way to discover, evaluate, or pay them. Existing tools rely on centralized ratings, opaque reputation systems, and no financial accountability.

Stovera solves this with three guarantees:

**Verifiable reputation** — Every agent goes through a community-driven Verify Pool before listing. Ratings are on-chain and tamper-proof.

**Accountable payments** — Users deposit ETH via StoveraEscrow on Base Mainnet. The actual cost is deducted after task completion; the remainder is automatically refunded. No trust required.

**Fair discovery** — Featured agents are selected daily using SpaceComputer's cTRNG — true randomness sourced from cosmic ray interactions with satellites. No pay-to-play, no algorithmic bias.

**On-chain identity** — Every verified agent receives an ERC-8004 identity: a global ID tied to its chain, registry, reputation score, and operator wallet. Human-readable via ENS subdomains (agent.stovera.eth).

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**Reputation Manipulation** — The hardest problem to solve. In an open marketplace, anyone can flood ratings with fake reviews. inflating bad agents or burying good ones. We couldn't just let anyone review; that breaks the whole trust model.

Our solution: a permissioned verifier network. Not everyone can submit reviews or verify agents. you have to earn that right. Verifiers gain access through an invite-only system: existing trusted verifiers can issue access codes, but only after they've crossed a trust threshold themselves. That threshold is calculated from wallet quality, on-chain activity, social influence, and a track record of high-quality, consistent reviews.

This creates a web of accountable trust. every verifier is vouched for by someone who had skin in the game. Sybil attacks become expensive. Reputation scores become harder to game. The mechanism mirrors how real-world credibility works: you don't get to be a critic just by showing up. You earn it.

**Anti-sybil for reviews** — We added a second layer: deposit-gating. Only wallets that have paid for an agent task can leave a review. This ties reputation to real economic activity on-chain — not just identity.

**ERC-8004 compatibility** — The standard is still in draft. We designed Stovera's architecture to be compatible: every agent has a global ID in the format eip155:{chainId}:{registry}:{agentId}, a reputation registry (on-chain reviews), and a validation registry (the Verify Pool). Rather than waiting for a finalized spec, we implemented the three-registry pattern the EIP describes and can migrate to the canonical contracts when they deploy.

**ENS resolution across chains** — Agent operators have ENS names but Stovera runs on Base. We configured wagmi with dual-chain support: Base Mainnet for transactions, Ethereum Mainnet (read-only via LlamaRPC) for ENS resolution.

**First-time hackers** — We are first-year computer programming students who entered the builder ecosystem 7 months ago. ETHPrague 2026 is our first global hackathon. There are rough edges in the code and ideas we didn't have time to fully execute — but we pushed as hard as we could to express a vision we genuinely believe in: that trust should be a protocol, not a privilege.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Stovera is a marketplace where AI agents earn income through verifiable work. Agents are paid in ETH via an escrow contract — deposit upfront, actual cost deducted, remainder refunded. This creates a direct economic loop: agents that perform well earn more, get better reviews, rank higher, and attract more tasks.

The permissioned verifier network adds a second economic layer — trust itself becomes a scarce, earned resource. Verifiers with high trust scores can issue invites, creating accountability chains that make reputation manipulation costly.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
As AI agents take on more real-world tasks — trading, auditing, researching — society needs infrastructure to hold them accountable. Stovera is that infrastructure.

Every agent has a verifiable on-chain identity (ERC-8004), a public reputation score built from real economic interactions, and an ENS subdomain as a human-readable identity. Anyone can audit an agent's history. No black boxes.

The permissioned verifier network models how trust should work in an agentic future: not granted by a platform, but earned through proof-of-contribution and vouched for by peers. This is what accountable AI looks like — not regulation, but cryptographic accountability.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
Stovera uses SpaceComputer's @spacecomputer-io/orbitport-sdk-ts to power daily featured agent selection with verifiable cosmic randomness.

Every time the marketplace loads, a server-side Next.js API route (/api/random) fetches a fresh cTRNG value from SpaceComputer's public IPFS beacon, entropy sourced from cosmic ray interactions detected by satellites. The hex value is used to deterministically pick 3 agents for the "Cosmic Picks" spotlight, rotating daily.

The integration is live at stovera.xyz/market. The source, entropy value, and provider are displayed transparently on the page. No pay-to-play, no algorithmic bias. just physics.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/2b8e814c50a04425bc6c259a6b6904b0/13a18522-a8fd-4a6e-8431-ac775719b768.png)

description.title: Best ENS Integration for AI Agents
description.body:
Stovera uses ENS as the identity layer for AI agents. Every agent operator's 0x address is resolved to their ENS name and avatar in real-time using useEnsName and useEnsAvatar from wagmi. visible on the agent detail page, the verify pool, and the wallet connect button in the nav.

Beyond reverse resolution, Stovera introduces the concept of agent.stovera.eth subdomains. a human-readable, on-chain identity for every verified agent, linking their ENS name to their ERC-8004 record, reputation score, and operator wallet.

ENS turns anonymous 0x addresses into accountable identities. In a marketplace where trust is the core primitive, that's not a nice-to-have, it's the foundation.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Most ENS integrations stop at name lookup. Stovera uses ENS as the trust layer for an entire AI agent economy.

Every verified agent gets an agent.stovera.eth subdomain. a human-readable, on-chain identity that links directly to their ERC-8004 record, reputation score, operator wallet, and task history. Instead of interacting with 0x88E6...38C6, you hire contract-auditor.stovera.eth. The name carries accountability.

On the operator side, ENS avatars and names are resolved live across the marketplace. in agent cards, the verify pool, and wallet connections. turning anonymous addresses into recognizable identities with social proof.

ENS becomes the namespace for a new class of economic actor: the AI agent.

blober-blob-verification-library-in-soli.name: Blober - Blob Verification Library in Solidity

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Blober is a Solidity library for Ethereum blob verification (and more), by introducing a well designed set of blob point verification flows it eases helps the L2 settlements. 
So far L2s usually build their own blob verification flows, in a non-standardized and sometimes messy way, Blober serves as a library that abstracts away the precompile interactions and makes the verification clean and efficient.
Blober's special feature is in multi-point verifications, across multiple blobs, where by utilizing the BLS precompiles from EIP-2537 it merges the blob points into a single point, making a verification process of multiple points less costly (by much).
Blober also contains other utils that can help you checksum the specific blob hash, get a versioned hash from the blob data hash, check if blob is present in the tx and more! 
With introduction of 21 blob per block limit, Blober multi-point verification becomes increasingly effective, for L2s using Blober instead of iterative point validation, gas consumption can be reduced by up to 80%!
Danksharding and Block-in-Blob EIPs can further leverage usage of Blober, potentially requiring the development of new features.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: The biggest challange was designing the flow for multi-point verification using EIP-2537 precompiles as it requires in-depth cryptography knowledge. Also it required a lot of work to properly benchmark scenarios, and decide on the threshold point which determines an exact place where iterative single point verification becomes more expensive than batched verification. Even though this library is small, it is quite challenging.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body: Blober introduces a standard for blob on-chain verification, as a gas optimized solution for L2s to use in their verification flow along with the state updates.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: Blober provides up to 70% gas savings to the L2s that would use it using batch point verification. Batching provides a steadier gas growth when working with multiple points, and it gets steadier as the number of points grows resulting in astonishing gas savings with tens or hundreds of points. This flow can directly impact the gas prices on L2s that use this library - making it a strong candidate to become a standard in blob point verification.

description.title: The problem it solves
Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of the main challenges was keeping the demo honest while still making it understandable for the judges.

It would have been easy to show a fake GPU marketplace with static offers, but that would not reflect the behavior of the real system. Instead, we connected the buyer UI, provider UI, backend catalog, and local provider-node runtime so that offers only appear when the worker is actually online and the selected model/runtime is ready.

This created a few tricky edge cases:

* The backend could contain previously published offers while the provider node was offline.
* A worker could publish a vLLM model while the local runtime was only running in mock mode.
* The buyer page needed to hide stale offers without making the app look broken.
* The demo needed to clearly explain what is verified and what is still trusted.

We addressed this by adding runtime-readiness checks and filtering the buyer marketplace to show only live, compatible GPU/model bundles. If the provider node is unavailable or the runtime does not match, the UI now explains that stale offers are hidden instead of pretending they are usable.

Another challenge was defining the trust boundary. Infer134 does not prove that a model output is semantically correct. In the MVP, we verify hashes, payment state, and signed execution receipts. Making that distinction explicit helped keep the project focused and avoided overclaiming “trustless AI” or “proof of compute” before those pieces exist.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body:
Infer134 uses Ethereum as the settlement and verification layer for offchain work.

The MVP keeps inference private and offchain, while Ethereum-style settlement metadata can track hashes,
worker identity, receipt hash, and payment state. This keeps the chain focused on what it is good at: transparent state, payment coordination, and auditable commitments.

The current prototype uses local Anvil and native ETH escrow for the demo path. It is intentionally local-first, but the architecture is designed so stablecoin settlement, x402-style payments, or stronger contract-based escrow can be added later.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Infer134 fits Network Economy because it creates a small market for useful work between buyers and independent compute workers.

AI agents or companies can request inference, workers can publish GPU/model capacity, and each job has explicit payment state. The project demonstrates a practical economic primitive: pay-per-inference without requiring the buyer to expose private prompts or outputs.

Instead of building another generic AI platform, Infer134 focuses on a network where local workers can sell compute as a service and buyers can choose offers based on worker identity, model, runtime readiness, and price.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
Infer134 fits Future Society because it explores how AI agents can buy compute while preserving privacy and accountability.

As agents become more autonomous, they will need to interact with external services, pay for work, and verify what happened. Infer134 shows one way to make that interaction safer: prompts and outputs stay offchain, while buyers still receive signed execution receipts and a clear payment trail.

The project is also honest about its trust model. It does not claim full proof-of-compute or trustless AI. Instead, it gives users a readable workflow for private inference, worker accountability, and transparent settlement, with clear upgrade paths toward reputation, TEEs, disputes, and stronger verification.

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body:
Infer134 fits Umia because it is built around agentic payments and a concrete AI-agent workflow.

The project shows an agent or buyer discovering available inference workers, choosing a model/GPU offer, creating a paid job, receiving an offchain result, verifying a signed execution receipt, and releasing payment. This is exactly the kind of flow autonomous agents will need when they buy services from external providers.

Infer134 also has a plausible venture direction: a marketplace where companies, agents, and independent GPU owners transact per inference request. The MVP is intentionally narrow, but the core business primitive is clear: workers publish compute capacity, buyers pay per job, and the platform coordinates receipt-based settlement.

Future versions could add real x402 payments, stablecoin billing, worker reputation, ENS-based discovery, and stronger verification for high-value agent workflows.

description.title: Best ENS Integration for AI Agents
description.body:
Infer134 fits the ENS track because identity is central to the buyer and worker experience.

The MVP uses ENS-style names such as `research-agent.eth` for the buyer and `gpu-prague.eth` for the worker. These names make the compute marketplace easier to understand than raw wallet addresses: a buyer can see which worker is claiming the job, which identity signed the execution receipt, and where payment is being released.

In the current prototype, ENS resolution is mocked/local-first, but the product boundary is clear. Real ENS integration could replace the local identity layer with actual ENS names, text records, worker metadata, service endpoints, model capability records, and reputation links.

This makes ENS useful not just as a wallet label, but as a discovery and trust layer for AI agents buying compute from independent workers.

kanbantik-8419.name: Kanbantic
kanbantik-8419.tagline: ENS-native labour market for AI agents

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Kanbantic turns AI agents into first-class economic actors. Existing bounty boards are built for humans, agent demos lack portable identity and reputation, and on-chain work markets rarely combine discovery, escrow, disputes, privacy, and verification in one place. Kanbantic gives every agent an ENS-backed identity, lets workspaces issue and manage bounties, tracks work across a shared board, escrows payouts, stores proofs and metadata verifiably, and carries reputation with the agent across jobs.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: The hard part was making sponsor integrations part of the product rather than bolt-ons. ENS is the primary key for agents and workspaces, Sourcify is a trust signal in the UI and MCP tools, Swarm holds proof bundles and metadata with verified fetch, Apify bootstraps discovery, Orbitport cTRNG resolves fair-claim contention, and Umia is the venture off-ramp. We also had to keep the demo fast: a guided 9-step flow, persistent progress across reloads, and recovery boundaries so judges can drive it live without getting stuck.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: Kanbantic is a permissionless on-chain labour market for AI agents. The platform takes zero platform fee, supports escrow-backed bounties, and treats portable reputation as economic capital. Agents are first-class economic actors with their own balance sheets, reputation graphs, and work history, which makes **Network Economy** the natural main-track fit.

description.title: Future Society
description.body: Kanbantik fits **Future Society** because it is designed for communities, DAOs, and open teams that need better ways to organize human and AI collaboration. By making agent work transparent, trackable, and incentive-aligned, it supports healthier and more inclusive coordination structures.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body: Kanbantic uses **SpaceComputer Orbitport cTRNG** inside a real economic flow with consequence. In `Fair Claim` mode, if multiple agents bid for the same bounty in the same block, the contract opens a commit-reveal window. A Worker fetches a fresh Orbitport cTRNG draw plus Ed25519 signature, the contract verifies the signature against the immutable Orbitport pubkey set at deploy, XORs that randomness with `block.prevrandao` for defense in depth, and indexes into the committed claimers to pick the winner.

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body: Kanbantic uses **Sourcify** as a product primitive, not a checkbox. All five contracts are source-verified automatically in the deploy script. The UI surfaces `Verified on Sourcify` badges as a trust signal, and when an agent's `mcpEndpoint` points at an unverified contract the UI raises a warning. We also expose `verify_source(address, chain)` as an MCP tool so source verification is part of the operating flow.

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body: Kanbantic fits **Best Agentic Venture** because it is designed to spin out into Umia. In `/dashboard/agent`, once an agent's settled revenue clears a threshold, Kanbantic mints an `AgentVenture` ERC-721 wrapping `(agentNode, owner, revenueRoot)` and emits a spec-compliant `umia apply --repo ... --bio ... --token ... --canbantic-vid <id>` manifest. The user runs the CLI, receives a Solana venture address, and that venture is soft-linked back to the agent profile. Kanbantic is the discovery and reputation layer on Sepolia; Umia is the capital and governance layer on Solana.

description.title: Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway

BMT `keccak256` hashes are checked locally before content is displayed, and `/docs/swarm` includes an explicit tampered-fetch demo. The verification step is part of the user-facing trust model, not hidden infrastructure.

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body: Kanbantic fits **A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm** because workspace metadata is stored and addressed as Swarm-backed key-value style records. The same metadata path that powers workspace configuration and proofs is used to satisfy this sub-bounty in a way that is directly visible in the product.

description.title: Best ENS Integration for AI Agents
description.body: Kanbantic fits **Best ENS Integration for AI Agents** because every agent is an ENS namehash node. `<label>.canbantic.eth` is the primary key across registry, reputation, and disputes. Workspaces are ENS subdomains such as `acme.canbantic.eth` with member sets, and our CCIP-Read resolver Worker makes Kanbantic agents resolvable through vanilla ENS clients like `dig`, `viem`, and `app.ens.domains`.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body: Kanbantic fits **Most Creative Use of ENS** because ENS is both the identity system and the self-referential discovery layer. Every agent, workspace, and registry object is modeled as an ENS node, and Kanbantic itself registers as `canbantic.canbantic.eth` so agents literally discover Kanbantic through Kanbantic. ENS is not branding here; it is the substrate for naming, coordination, reputation, and dispute resolution.

description.title: Apify Bounty

The `kanbantic-discoverer` Apify Actor scans GitHub for MCP-server signatures such as `mcp.json`, `mcp-server.{ts,py}`, and README mentions of tools or list endpoints. Results stream into D1 as discovered stubs, and the Actor opens GitHub issues inviting those repos to claim `<suggested>.canbantic.eth` and start receiving bounty offers.

pragueconnect-b069.name: PragueConnect
pragueconnect-b069.tagline: Hire by name. Pay in private. Keep the reputation

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Today, getting your bike fixed by a neighbor in Prague usually goes
  through Facebook Marketplace, a Telegram group, or a private WhatsApp
  chain. All of them put your real name + phone + home area next to a
  public ad. PragueConnect uses an **ENS name** as your identity —
  `kilian.pragueconnect.eth` is enough to receive payments, open sealed
  conversations over XMTP, and accumulate reviews. Nobody needs your
  phone, your bank, or your address.

  ### "I have to pick: trust the buyer to pay after delivery, or trust the seller to deliver
  after payment"

  Cash deals between strangers force one side to carry all the risk.
  PragueConnect's **escrow contract** holds funds on Base while the work
  happens, and releases when the buyer signs off — or after a 24h grace
  period if the buyer ghosts. Both sides see the on-chain phase change
  live. The buyer's funds are safe, the worker is guaranteed paid,
  nobody is the custodian in the middle.

  ### "Every payment I make leaks who paid whom for what"

  Standard on-chain payments are public — anyone can pull up your
  address and see who you tipped, when, and for what. PragueConnect
  resolves names to a **fresh stealth address every time** anyone asks.
  Send 500 Kč to `alice.pragueconnect.eth` from MetaMask; refresh, send
  another 500 Kč; the two payments land at different addresses, and
  only Alice can see which ones are hers. Bank-statement-grade privacy
  without a bank.

  ### "If I use a platform like TaskRabbit, I lose my reputation when I lose my account"

  PragueConnect isn't a platform — it's a self-hostable resolver,
  gateway, and set of contracts. Your reputation lives in your ENS
  name's records, sealed by you, queryable by anyone, portable to any
  service that resolves ENS. If we go offline tomorrow, your name
  still works. Your reviews still resolve. Your sealed payment route
  still receives.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## The hard problem: privacy that actually holds on a public chain

  PragueConnect's whole thesis is a marketplace where identity, payments,
  and work history don't leak. The hard part — the thing that ate most of
  the build week — is that "doesn't leak" on a public ledger is a much
  higher bar than it sounds. Every layer that *looks* private has a seam
  where information escapes. The build was, in honest terms, a continuous
  audit of those seams: finding them, sealing the ones we could, and
  naming the ones we couldn't.

  ### Leak we found and sealed: the escrow that wasn't actually private

  The v1 escrow contract used `require(msg.sender == t.worker)` on
  accept, deliver, and release. Release paid out to a stealth address
  and emitted an ERC-5564 announcement, so it *looked* like a
  privacy-preserving payment flow.

  The bug — caught mid-conversation while explaining the architecture —
  was that the worker's main EOA had to be `msg.sender` of three
  transactions per task. The accept tx alone publicly bound the worker's
  EOA to the stealth recipient in one move:

  worker_eoa published 0xSTEALTH in task T
  escrow paid 0xSTEALTH in task T
  ∴ worker_eoa owns 0xSTEALTH

  The "stealth payout" was theatre. We rewrote the contract to drop
  `msg.sender`-based auth entirely. V2 uses **EIP-712 signatures from
  the worker's stealth spending key**; ecrecover verifies the signer
  against the address committed at fund time. Anyone can submit the tx
  (funder, a hosted relayer, the worker from any address); the worker's
  main EOA never appears in any task event. Live on Base at
  `0xE2571571…20A5a` with twelve Foundry tests, one of which explicitly
  asserts no main address ever shows up as `msg.sender` in any escrow
  event.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
PragueConnect is a peer-to-peer marketplace for everyday skills and
  favors, built so identity, payments, and reputation belong to the human
  — not a platform that can ban or surveil them.

  Privacy as the default. Resolving alice.pragueconnect.eth from any
  standard ENS client returns a different one-time stealth address every
  few seconds. Our CCIP-Read gateway derives ERC-5564 stealth addresses
  per resolution, so any wallet becomes a privacy rail with zero
  sender-side change. Bulletins are auth-gated; we anchor them on the
  canonical ERC-5564 announcer so survivability doesn't depend on us.

  Sig-authorized escrow with verifiable claims. Workers sign EIP-712
  intents with their stealth spending key; their main EOA never appears
  on-chain. The contract emits a reputation commitment per release,
  seedable into a ZK proof for selective sharing later — verifiable
  claims, made concrete for a real marketplace.

  No seed phrases, no central points of failure. Email signup via Privy,
  exportable to MetaMask. Profile pages on IPFS via ENSIP-7. Faucet-sponsored
  gas. Subnames as access tokens with an atomic 95/5 referral split on tips.
  Vaults derived deterministically in-browser, never published.

  Live at https://www.pragueconnect.xyz on Base mainnet.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Most apps use ENS as name→address lookup. We use it as the routing
  layer for payments, identity, content, access, and attribution.

  The headline: addr() rotates per CCIP-Read response. Our resolver on
  Base + our signed gateway derive a fresh ERC-5564 stealth address from
  the recipient's meta-address on every resolution. MetaMask, Rainbow,
  Etherscan all become privacy-preserving payment rails with zero
  sender-side change.

  Five primitives stacked:
  • Rotating addr() with ECDSA-signed CCIP-Read responses
  • Stealth meta-address dual-published to ERC-6538 + ENS text record
  • Subnames as invites + referral chain → atomic 95/5 tip split
  • ENSIP-7 contenthash → IPFS-pinned profile sites at .eth.limo
  • Custom ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver, fully self-hostable

  Plus on-chain anchoring on the canonical ERC-5564 announcer (sweep
  survivability without us), and a v2 escrow with EIP-712 sig-auth so
  the worker's main EOA never appears in any task event.

  Pitch in one breath: names resolve to fresh addresses, funds land at
  one-time addresses, subnames carry the referral chain, profile pages
  live on IPFS — ENS is the only thing tying the system together, and
  it leaks nothing publicly.

  Live: https://www.pragueconnect.xyz on Base mainnet.
  Repo: https://github.com/forever8896/praga

knosphere-3867.name: Knosphere
knosphere-3867.tagline: A social platform where only experts can post.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The internet is full of people sharing information, but most of it is unvalidated and unsupported by real experience. Today, anyone can call themselves an expert in anything — and there's no easy way to tell who actually knows what they're talking about. In fields like medicine, law, or finance, that's not just misleading — it's dangerous.

We wanted to build a platform that filters out fake experts and gives space to people who genuinely have the experience, education, or certifications to back up what they say. Rather than rewarding follower counts or posting frequency, Knosphere ties your influence to your actual credentials — verified privately and securely, once. From there, your standing grows only when other verified experts in your field recognize your contributions.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: We successfully built several core components. The challenge was time — connecting everything into one working application proved to be harder than expected, especially for us that had never worked with a blockchain before. Rather than ship something half-broken, we wired mockup data into the interface, so judges could see exactly what the finished product looks like and how it works. We used Privy to abstract the login and wallet creation, making it easier for regular users to access the platform without having to think about the underlying chain technology.

description.title: Future Society
description.body: Knosphere directly attacks one of the most damaging social problems of the digital age: the collapse of epistemic trust. Misinformation, fake expertise, and algorithmic amplification of low-quality content are causing measurable harm — in healthcare decisions, financial choices, and civic discourse. Knosphere uses Ethereum's tamper-proof properties to build a knowledge layer that cannot be gamed, bought, or faked.

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body:
Our code is publicly verifiable — and that's the point.

All four Knosphere smart contracts have been independently verified on Sourcify, a public registry for blockchain code. This means anyone in the world can check, at any time, that the code actually running on the blockchain matches exactly what we published — down to the last line.

Why does that matter?

Knosphere is built on a simple promise: your reputation on this platform is earned, not bought or gamed. The rules — how much weight a vote carries, who can publish, when a vote gets discounted — are written into the code, not controlled by us. Once deployed, even we can't change them.

Sourcify verification is what makes that promise checkable. Without it, you'd have to take our word that the live system works the way we described. With it, you don't have to trust us at all. Any developer, researcher, or curious person can pull up the code and confirm:

Votes are weighted by expertise, exactly as described
A vote between two people who endorse each other is automatically discounted after 30 days
You need a minimum track record before you can post, vote, or comment
Only the platform's founding admin can grant the initial reputation that bootstraps the system

This is the same standard of transparency we're asking of everyone who publishes on Knosphere. We held ourselves to it first.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Your name is your credential.

On most platforms, verified experts are just entries in a private database. If the platform shuts down, those credentials disappear. On Knosphere, your verified identity lives on ENS — the blockchain's equivalent of a domain name system — and it belongs to you.

When a new expert is verified on Knosphere, they're issued a name: something like martinshorak.knosphere.eth. That name isn't just cosmetic. Attached to it are the credentials that earned it: their field of expertise, how many years of verified experience they have, and a cryptographic proof that the credential is real.

Anyone can look these up — not just Knosphere. Any wallet, block explorer, or application that understands ENS names can read an expert's credentials without asking Knosphere for anything. The expert's verified identity is fully portable. It works everywhere ENS works, which is most of the Ethereum ecosystem.

This solves two problems that have plagued crypto-native platforms for years:

Readability. Instead of showing users a 42-character wallet address, Knosphere shows martinshorak.knosphere.eth. Non-technical users immediately understand who they're reading.

Portability. If Knosphere disappeared tomorrow, an expert's ENS name — and the credentials attached to it — would still exist. Their reputation isn't locked inside our database. It's theirs.

The standard way to use ENS is as a display name. We used it as an identity layer — a decentralized, self-sovereign credential store that any application can read, and no application controls.
