truthmarket-2eb3.name: TruthMarket
truthmarket-2eb3.tagline: Prediction for the Age of AI

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## The Problem It Solves

Prediction markets like Polymarket are powerful because they turn public belief into a live price. But they still have one major weakness: **someone has to decide what actually happened.**

That works for simple outcomes. But many of the most interesting markets are messy, subjective, probabilistic, or hard to verify:

- Did this DAO proposal achieve its stated goal?
- Was this AI agent’s decision correct?
- Did this creator actually hit the promised milestone?
- Was this prediction resolved fairly?
- Did the event happen according to the rules?

Today, these outcomes often depend on a centralized resolver, moderator, oracle, admin, or social consensus. That creates disputes, bias, pressure, and unclear resolutions.

**TruthMarket is a prediction market where the truth is resolved by the market itself.**

Every market starts with a locked claim and rules document, so everyone knows exactly what **YES** and **NO** mean before they stake. Voters commit their votes privately, so nobody can copy, influence, or pressure the outcome during the voting period. When voting closes, a randomly selected jury of staked participants reveals their votes and resolves the market.

This creates a fairer way to settle non-obvious outcomes. Instead of relying on one platform, one oracle, or one powerful moderator, TruthMarket lets communities resolve claims through staked, private, randomly selected judgment.

TruthMarket can be used for **DAO decisions, public predictions, creator promises, AI agent actions, community bets, impact claims, and any outcome that is too subjective, probabilistic, or non-verifiable for a normal oracle.**

**Polymarket shows what people believe. TruthMarket helps decide what is true.**

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
### The Core Design Challenge

Polymarket is great when the answer is obvious later.

But what about questions like:

- Was this AI demo real progress or just hype?
- Did a DAO actually deliver what it promised?
- Is this prediction still credible?
- Was a claim misleading, even if not technically false?

These are valuable markets, but they are hard to resolve.

Our biggest hurdle was making those markets feel fair without handing the final decision to one admin.

We solved it with a random staked jury:

> **Stake shows conviction. Random jurors decide the outcome.**

Votes stay private with commit-reveal, rules are locked before anyone stakes, and the final result comes from selected jurors instead of a centralized moderator.

That turned TruthMarket into something simple:

**Polymarket for questions too messy for a normal oracle.**

description.title: Future Society
SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
## Space-Powered Security: Fair, verifiable Jury selection

TruthMarket is applying under the **Space-Powered Security APIs** direction.

We use SpaceComputer cTRNG for the protocol’s most important security function:

> **selecting the jurors who decide the market outcome.**

TruthMarket is built for claims where truth is uncertain: AI forecasts, agent reputation, DAO accountability, public claims, model evaluations, and questions too messy for a normal prediction market.

For these markets, the game theory only works if jury selection cannot be predicted, manipulated, or front-run.

### Why randomness is core

TruthMarket uses private commit-reveal voting. Voters stake on a claim without revealing their vote during the voting phase. Only after voting closes does the protocol use SpaceComputer randomness to select a jury from the committed voters.

That timing matters.

If jurors were known early, voters could bribe them, copy them, intimidate them, or coordinate around them. If the operator could choose the jury, the market would collapse into a trusted moderation system. If large stakers could influence the draw, the outcome could be bought.

SpaceComputer randomness prevents that.

The jury is selected only after commits are locked, using external unpredictable entropy.

> **SpaceComputer is the fairness engine of TruthMarket: it makes the market game playable by preventing predictable, operator-controlled, or front-runnable jury selection.**

### Working prototype

Our prototype demonstrates the full core flow:

1. Voters privately commit their belief.
2. Stake is locked.
3. Voting closes.
4. SpaceComputer cTRNG provides randomness.
5. The protocol selects a random jury from committed voters.
6. Selected jurors reveal.
7. The market resolves.
8. Payouts are calculated from the outcome.

The randomness is directly tied to market settlement. It decides the selected jurors, the selected jurors decide the outcome, and the outcome decides payouts.

### Technical integration depth

This is not a cosmetic API call.

The cTRNG is in the critical path of the protocol:

- it protects juror selection from prediction;
- it prevents pre-selection coordination;
- it makes front-running the jury draw impractical;
- it keeps the operator from hand-picking resolvers;
- it gives every committed voter a fair chance to be selected;
- it supports the one-juror, one-vote resolution design.

We also store randomness evidence so the draw can be inspected and replayed:

- cTRNG value;
- randomness hash;
- beacon metadata;
- selected jurors;
- deterministic selection process.

### Why this matters

TruthMarket creates markets for uncertain truth:

- AI predictions;
- agent reputation;
- DAO accountability;
- disputed public claims;
- model evaluations;
- research forecasts;
- probabilistic questions.

These markets are only credible if participants believe the resolution process cannot be gamed.

SpaceComputer randomness gives the protocol the neutral entropy it needs for fair selection. Without it, the mechanism becomes vulnerable to manipulation. With it, humans and agents can stake, reveal, and resolve under a process no single party controls.

### Creativity

Most randomness integrations are lotteries, games, or NFT traits.

TruthMarket uses randomness for something more structural:

> **randomly assigning temporary judgment power in markets for disputed claims.**

That creates a new primitive: a random-jury market where the crowd provides the voter pool, SpaceComputer provides the entropy, and selected participants resolve uncertainty.

### Future direction

As SpaceComputer moves toward fully verifiable, space-signed randomness, TruthMarket can upgrade the jury draw into an even stronger system.

Future markets could prove not only that jurors were selected deterministically, but that the entropy itself came from a verifiable space-grade source.

That is the long-term vision:

> **space-signed randomness for public market resolution.**

### In one line

**TruthMarket uses SpaceComputer randomness as its fairness engine: the unpredictable draw that makes random-jury markets possible by enabling the game theory behind fair market resolution.**

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body:
## Sourcify: verified contract infrastructure for efficient market factories

TruthMarket uses a split contract architecture:

- one **MarketRegistry** as the public creation and discovery entry point;
- many lightweight **TruthMarket** instances, one per market, all referencing a core script

This is important for performance and scalability, future updates plus context isolation in case something goes wrong.

Instead of one giant contract trying to store and manage every market forever, each market gets its own isolated contract with its own immutable parameters, lifecycle, jury selection, reveal phase, slashing, and payouts. The registry stays thin: it creates markets, records them, and routes shared operational settings like treasury, admin, stake token, and jury committer.

That gives us a cleaner and more efficient architecture:

- markets are isolated from each other;
- per-market storage stays small and local;
- each market can resolve without touching unrelated market state;
- agents and humans use one simple `createMarket()` path;
- the registry gives the app one canonical place to discover markets;
- protocol fees from registry-created markets route consistently to the same treasury.

### Why Sourcify matters

The tradeoff with many contracts is trust.

If TruthMarket can create many market contracts, users need to know which ones are real, which ones follow the canonical logic, and which ones are modified forks.

Sourcify gives us the verified-contract infrastructure to check that.

We can use Sourcify data to verify:

- whether the registry is verified;
- whether a market contract is verified;
- whether a market’s bytecode matches the expected TruthMarket implementation;
- whether ABI and compiler metadata match the canonical contract family;
- whether a deployment is a trusted market, a verified fork, or an unknown contract.

### Why this improves UX

Before users stake, the frontend can show a simple trust status:

- **Canonical market from verified registry**
- **Verified market fork**
- **Unverified market**
- **Unknown deployment**

That means users do not need to trust our frontend, a market creator, or a random link. They can verify both the entry point and the individual market contract.

### Why this fits the bounty

TruthMarket uses Sourcify data as a real safety layer for a multi-contract protocol.

The registry gives us performance and clean scaling. Sourcify gives users confidence that the many contracts created through that registry are actually running the expected code.

This uses the most important parts of Sourcify’s dataset:

- verified source code;
- deployed bytecode;
- ABI;
- compiler metadata;
- contract identity across deployments.

### The full trust flow

For a user, trust comes from two checks:

1. **Swarm verifies the claim rules**  
   The app proves the rules document shown to the user is the one stored for the market.

2. **Sourcify verifies the contract code**  
   The app proves the registry and market contract are running the expected verified logic.

Together, this removes middleman trust.

The user can see the rules, verify the code, and stake into a market without trusting a centralized operator.

### In one line

**TruthMarket uses one verified registry for scalable market creation, and Sourcify proves every market it creates is running the code users expect.**

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway
description.body:
## Swarm Verified Fetch: trust no gateway

Swarm is great for storing public data, but there is one big problem for apps:

> If you read through a public gateway, how do you know the gateway gave you the real data?

Running a full Bee node is not realistic for every browser, mobile app, or lightweight agent. But trusting random gateways is not good enough either, especially when the data controls markets, claims, or user decisions.

That is why we built `@truth-market/swarm-verified-fetch`.

It lets any JavaScript/TypeScript app fetch Swarm data from a gateway and verify it locally before using it.

### Where we use it

TruthMarket stores market rules and claim documents on Swarm.

Those documents define important things like:

- what the claim means;
- what YES and NO mean;
- voting and reveal deadlines;
- jury size;
- payout and risk rules;
- metadata used by the app.

Before anyone stakes, the app needs to prove that the claim document shown in the UI is the same document referenced by the contract.

Swarm Verified Fetch makes that possible.

The contract stores the Swarm reference and hash. The frontend downloads the claim document from a gateway, recomputes the Swarm hash locally, and only enables staking if the bytes match.

So the gateway can help deliver the file, but it cannot quietly change the rules.

### What it verifies

- Immutable Swarm files using **CAC + BMT**
- Multi-chunk byte trees, reconstructed like Bee does internally
- Mantaray manifest paths from verified manifest bytes
- Mutable **SOC/feed updates** using Ethereum signatures
- Feed target content after the signed update is verified

### Why it matters

Without this, a malicious or broken gateway could show users the wrong claim rules, stale metadata, or modified app data.

With verified fetch:

> download from anywhere, verify locally, trust the hash.

That makes Swarm usable for real apps without requiring every user to run a full node.

### Features

- familiar `verifiedFetch()` API
- browser and Node.js support
- gateway failover and racing
- stream mode for large files
- progress callbacks
- retries, timeouts, and abort signals
- typed metadata and verification proofs
- manual verification helpers
- tests for corrupted chunks, bad manifests, feed tampering, and MITM-style gateway attacks

### In one line

**Swarm Verified Fetch lets TruthMarket store claims on Swarm and prove the rules users see are the rules they stake on.**

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body:
## Swarm KV: decentralized storage that feels like a database

Swarm has powerful primitives: content addressing, feeds, manifests, postage stamps, and SOCs.

But most developers do not want to think about all of that just to save app data.

They want this:

```ts
await store.put("settings", { theme: "dark" });
const settings = await store.getJson("settings");
```

`@truth-market/swarm-kv` gives them exactly that: a simple key-value database on top of Swarm.

### What we need it for

TruthMarket needs an easy way to store and update app data without falling back to a centralized database.

We use Swarm KV for:

- market discovery indexes
- creator market lists
- saved market references
- app read models
- user preferences
- agent memory and lightweight state
- registry-style metadata
- claim attachments and supporting market documents

This data changes over time, so it should not live in the immutable claim document. Swarm KV gives us a clean place for mutable storage while still keeping it decentralized and user-owned.

The important market rules stay immutable and verified separately. Swarm KV handles the storing, listing, updating, and deleting around the app.

### Why it matters

A lot of dApps still use normal databases for everyday storage because decentralized storage is too hard to work with.

Swarm already has the pieces, but developers should not need to understand feeds, topics, manifests, SOCs, and postage just to save a profile, setting, or app index.

Swarm KV wraps those pieces into a familiar interface:

- `put()` to save data
- `get()` to read it
- `list()` to list keys
- `delete()` to remove values
- `entries()` to iterate

### Features

- strings, JSON, binary, `ArrayBuffer`, and `Blob` support
- key listing and async iteration
- missing keys return `null`
- deletion with indexed tombstones
- large multi-chunk values
- postage batch reuse and optional Bee postage handling
- encrypted private mode
- stable latest-index feeds
- optional feed manifests for stable Swarm pointers
- serialized writes to avoid local lost updates
- optimistic write guard with `ifIndexReference`
- verified reads through `@truth-market/swarm-verified-fetch`
- fake Bee, live Bee, public testnet, deletion, concurrency, and large-value tests

### In one line

**Swarm KV makes decentralized storage feel as easy as `localStorage`, but persistent, user-owned, and built on Swarm.**

description.title: Apify Bounty
The problem it solves
description.body: To check if smart contracts are safe is often difficult, slow, and spread across many tools. Developers usually need to manually review code, compare trusted contracts, search for exploit history and verify that project claims actually match the code. Our project, SolidScan, simplifies this process by bringing everything into one workflow inside VS Code. It helps developers quickly spot compliance issues and security vulnerabilities before deployment, making smart contract reviews faster, easier and more trustworthy for both builders and users.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: One of our biggest challenges was choosing the right idea. We had many creative concepts, but we needed to focus on one that solved a real-world problem and could still be built within 48 hours. Another challenge was working with large datasets and combining many features into one smooth workflow during the fast-paced hackathon environment.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body:
SolidScan strengthens the Ethereum developer ecosystem by helping developers detect legal compliance risks, security vulnerabilities and unsafe patterns in Solidity smart contracts during development.
Instead of auditing contracts only after deployment, our tool shifts security and compliance checks left into the coding workflow, enabling safer Ethereum applications before they reach mainnet.

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body: **Sourcify** is the core tech stack for our vscode extension **SolidScan**. We used Sourcify dataset as the source of verified on-chain contract dataset for SolidScan. SolidScan takes the Solidity source code being audited then feeds it into embedding-based similarity search to compare against Sourcify dataset in order to find similar smart contracts on-chain (and related hash etc. by **BigQuery**). Then we leverage scraper agents to find known vulnerabilities by sourcing GitHub, Etherscan etc. All the information will be useful as anti-pattern **Few-shot Examples** to improve the security of our source solidity code.

description.title: Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway
description.body: **Swarm** is the core backend tech for our product vscode extension **SolidScan**. We implement the Swarm verified-fetch idea (the **JS libraries**) and then uses it as the trust layer for our legal knowledge base. SolidScan needs external compliance and exploit intelligence. In the workflow of our product, we create an LLM orchestra for continuous legal text scraping and we need to maintain a backend database to store these data series legal text. However, we did not want to blindly trust a random gateway response, and Swarm is used for it and serves as trustworthy JSON legal knowledge base. We use it during legal-risk analysis without depending on a full Bee node.

description.title: Apify Bounty
description.body: SolidScan qualifies for the Apify bounty by using an on-chain x402 USDC payment flow to dynamically orchestrate a fleet of specialized Apify Actors. When a developer runs our VS Code plugin, our system analyzes the context of the smart contract and programmatically triggers the most relevant Apify Actor for that specific sector. These Actors scrape live, timestamped regulatory sources, including ESMA, EBA, and MiCA frameworks. Apify serves as the core data layer of our architecture, compiling these diverse sources into a structured, time-series legal dataset. This fresh, verifiable intelligence is then ingested by our LLM Agent, allowing it to return a highly accurate, context-aware compliance audit directly to the developer's IDE.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## What Spacy is

Spacy is a Web3 wallet that lets users sign in with Google and immediately use crypto applications without a seed phrase, browser extension, or any prior wallet experience. Same product category as Privy or Dynamic, the embedded wallets behind tens of millions of consumer crypto accounts today. The difference is that Spacy is the only one in this category that lets anyone, on their own laptop and without trusting us, verify that every transaction was actually signed in the hardware we claim, with the safeguards we promise.

## The problem we are solving

When a user signs into a Privy-backed app, their private key is generated and stored inside a Trusted Execution Environment, or TEE: a special area of a server's processor that is supposed to be sealed off from everyone, including Privy itself. The user is asked to trust three things: that the TEE is real, that the randomness used to make the key was unpredictable, and that the operator has not been compromised. None of those claims can be verified independently. You take Privy's word for it.

This was always a fragile model. In 2026 it is breaking down on three fronts at once.

**The hardware was broken in October 2025.** Researchers at Georgia Tech and Purdue published the TEE.Fail attack: using under $1,000 of equipment, they extracted the cryptographic keys that prove a TEE is genuine, then forged fake TEE attestations that pass Intel's own verifier. The same primitives protect tens of millions of consumer wallets today. Privy, Turnkey, and Dynamic have published nothing about how they are responding.

**The cryptography has an expiration date that just moved closer.** In May 2025, a Google researcher showed that breaking RSA-2048 encryption now requires 20 times fewer quantum bits than estimated six years ago. Major roadmaps now point to capable quantum computers around 2030. Every embedded wallet today still signs transactions with ECDSA, the algorithm that quantum computers will break. None of the incumbents have a published migration plan.

**The proofs do not survive Q-day.** When quantum hardware breaks today's TEE attestation keys, every TEE proof ever issued can be retroactively forged. The proof that your wallet's transaction was actually signed inside a real enclave by a real user becomes worthless overnight. Existing wallets have no durable, independent record that can survive this collapse.

## How Spacy solves it

The signing key is held inside SpaceComputer's Orbitport KMS, a service running in Intel TDX (Intel's TEE technology). Our orchestration backend, the part that authenticates Google sessions and brokers the signing requests, runs on a real AWS EC2 instance with AMD SEV-SNP (AMD's TEE technology) enabled. This is not a roadmap claim, it is shipping today: every Spacy session produces a real SEV-SNP attestation report from real AMD silicon, exposed on a public health endpoint anyone can fetch and verify offline. Two different TEE vendors, two different operators, two different attestation roots. A single class of zero-day cannot reach both halves of the trust path.

Every signing operation is timestamped against a fresh sample of cosmic randomness from SpaceComputer's cTRNG service, recorded in the receipt and matchable against an IPFS public beacon archive. Every transaction emits an attestation receipt: a JSON document containing the transaction details, the SEV-SNP self-attestation including its certificate chain, the KMS keyId, and the cosmic entropy witness. The receipt is pinned to IPFS through Pinata, and its content-addressed identifier is emitted to a Sepolia smart contract as an on-chain pointer. Real receipts, real on-chain events, today.

To verify any Spacy transaction, you read the on-chain event, fetch the receipt from IPFS, walk the AMD certificate chain offline against AMD's root, and cross-check the cosmic entropy against SpaceComputer's public beacon. No step requires Spacy to be online. No step requires trusting us.

When SpaceComputer ships their published roadmap (orbital KMS, ML-DSA dual signatures for post-quantum), our SDK adopts each upgrade with a single parameter change. The wallet a user onboards into in 2026 should be the wallet that still works in 2032. Today, that wallet does not exist. Spacy is the bet that it should, built on SpaceComputer's open infrastructure, licensed AGPL-3.0.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## We started building threshold ECDSA, then realized the KMS would not let us

The original plan was a 2-of-3 threshold ECDSA wallet using cggmp21, with one share in the user's browser, one inside the SpaceComputer KMS, and one held by our coordinator. Full liveness across satellite, ground, and user, no single party able to forge a signature alone. We started wiring the protocol against the Orbitport KMS expecting it to participate in the threshold protocol.

The KMS does not work that way. It is a black-box signer: you create a key, ask it to sign a digest, get a 65-byte ECDSA signature back. There is no API for participating in MPC, no way to produce a partial share, no hook for any threshold scheme. The signing key never leaves the TEE in any form, including as a share, which is exactly what makes it a strong signer and exactly what makes threshold cryptography on top of it impossible without rebuilding the KMS itself.

We stopped, took stock, and rewrote the architecture around the actual primitive Orbitport ships. Instead of distributing trust cryptographically across multiple parties, distribute it structurally across multiple TEE vendors. Intel TDX for the signer (Orbitport), AMD SEV-SNP for the coordinator (our AWS instance), with the trust path crossing two heterogeneous hardware lineages. A single class of zero-day cannot reach both halves. The structural distribution we lost from threshold, we got back from vendor heterogeneity. SpaceComputer's roadmap moves to threshold KMS in phase 2, at which point the original plan slots in without architectural rewrite.

## The KMS attestation quote we expected was not exposed by the API

Spacy's pitch is that every signature comes with a verifiable Intel TDX attestation quote from the KMS. The receipt schema reserves a signer.quoteHex field for this. SpaceComputer's spec describes it, the SDK type declares it, we wired the call expecting it to be populated.

It was not. We tried kms.GetAttestation, kms.Attestation, plain GET and POST against /attestation and /kms/attestation, every variant the SDK type hinted at. All 404 or 405. The SDK's "expected one of" error listed every method it knew about and none was an attestation endpoint. The kms.sign response itself returned signature and metadata, but no quote.

We could have populated the field with a placeholder. Instead we kept it as an empty string, marked quoteVerified as the honest result of attempting verification on nothing, documented the gap, and structured the schema so it accepts the quote the day SpaceComputer ships the endpoint. The TDX side is reserved, not faked.

## The cTRNG response is missing fields its SDK type promises

Two related problems on the entropy side. First, the SDK type declares getRandom includes a signature object with value, pk, algo. We hit the raw ctrng.Get RPC directly and the wire payload was just src and value. No signature anywhere. The SDK was projecting a type the gateway does not currently fulfill.

Second, cTRNG offers two source modes: rng for the live satellite roundtrip, derived for the BIP32-derived fallback. We asked for rng. The API returned derived, because the live source is gated and not active for our token tier during the hackathon.

We left entropy.signatureHex empty and wrote the actual returned source value into the receipt verbatim. The verifier matches the entropy value against the IPFS public beacon archive, which is signed at the round level and is independent of our backend. The cosmic randomness witness still has a real verification anchor, just not the per-call satellite signature the SDK type promises. Nothing in the receipt claims a stronger source than the API actually provided.

## VLEK extraction from the kernel did not work, AMD KDS rescued us

The SEV-SNP attestation report is only meaningful if you can verify it against AMD's certificate chain (VLEK to ASK to ARK). The obvious approach is to pull the chain from the kernel: sev-guest -x should hand it back. It did not. The command returned an Input/output error, because the host had not been pre-provisioned with sev-host-set-cert-chain and the guest kernel does not expose VLEK by default.

We initially suspected a permissions issue and wasted time on chmod and dmesg. The actual fix was to bypass the kernel entirely. The SEV-SNP report contains a chip_id field at a documented offset. We read it out, fetched the VCEK directly from AMD's KDS at https://kdsintf.amd.com/vcek/v1/Milan/<chipId>, and concatenated it with the bundled ASK and ARK roots offline. Cleaner than the kernel path: verifiers need nothing from our host, only AMD and the trust anchor bundle we publish.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body:
Spacy is a practical Ethereum wallet that directly improves the security posture of self-custody on Ethereum. The signing key is held in a Trusted Execution Environment (Intel TDX, inside SpaceComputer's KMS), the orchestration backend runs in a second TEE (AMD SEV-SNP, on AWS), and every signature is paired with a verifiable attestation receipt pinned to IPFS with an on-chain pointer event on Sepolia.
Three concrete contributions to Ethereum's usability and security:
- Usability. Google sign-in to a working Ethereum wallet in under thirty seconds, no seed phrase, no browser extension, no chain configuration. The same UX as Privy or Dynamic, which together back over 120 million Ethereum-compatible wallets today. Spacy is the embedded wallet category, just with the trust model rebuilt.
- Security against the threat model that actually matters in 2026. The TEE.Fail attack disclosed in October 2025 demonstrated that attestation keys can be extracted from Intel SGX, Intel TDX, and AMD SEV-SNP enclaves with under $1,000 of equipment, and was demonstrated against Ethereum BuilderNet. Every embedded wallet on the market today, securing tens of millions of Ethereum addresses, runs on the same primitives. Spacy's response is structural: a heterogeneous TEE chain across two different vendor lineages, paired with public self-attestation that any third party can verify offline. A single class of zero-day cannot reach both halves of our trust path.
Native Ethereum integration. Standard EIP-1559 transactions, viem in the browser, public RPC for broadcast, Foundry-deployed Solidity contract on Sepolia. No custom chain, no L2 dependency, no proprietary RPC. Spacy is composable with every existing Ethereum tool.

The receipt format is open. The verification path runs offline. The license is AGPL-3.0. This is the wallet stack any Ethereum project can adopt, audit, fork, or self-host.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Spacy is a Web3 wallet that puts cryptographic user control above operator trust. Same UX as Privy (Google sign-in, no seed phrase, no extension), but every claim the wallet makes about itself is independently verifiable, with no Spacy infrastructure required in the verification path.
The fit with Network Economy lands on four axes:
- Identity. Spacy bridges Web2 identity (Google OAuth) and Ethereum identity with cryptographic provenance that wallet identity actually needs. Existing embedded wallets ask users to trust Privy or Turnkey that their key is real, generated correctly, and signed by the hardware claimed. Spacy makes the binding verifiable: any third party can fetch the on-chain AttestationPublished event for a given wallet, pull the IPFS receipt, walk the AMD VLEK certificate chain offline, and confirm the signing TEE is genuine without trusting us at any step.
- Privacy through deliberate separation. We split confidentiality and verifiability into different storage layers. Personally identifying information (Google identifier, email) lives in encrypted Postgres inside the TEE, GDPR-compliant and deletable, never on-chain or on IPFS. Verifiable artifacts (KMS keyId, SEV-SNP self-attestation, cTRNG entropy witness, transaction details) live on IPFS and on-chain, immutable and auditable. Two storage layers, two trust models, the right one for each kind of data. Privy stores both opaquely on the same backend.

User control as a structural property. Six-step verification walkthrough at spacy.computer/verify, fully offline, runnable on any laptop, with no Spacy infrastructure in the path. The architectural posture is "we don't ask you to trust us, verify it yourself." This is what user control looks like when it is built into the receipt format rather than promised in marketing copy.
Decentralized in a real way. AGPL-3.0 licensed, multi-vendor TEE chain spanning two operators (SpaceComputer for the signer, our own AWS account for the coordinator), Pinata pinning with multi-gateway IPFS retrieval, public Sepolia RPC for broadcast, on-chain event index for discovery. Every signed transaction produces a content-addressed proof artifact that survives even if Spacy disappears. The wallet a user onboards into in 2026 keeps working in 2032 because the verifiable provenance lives on Ethereum and IPFS, not on our servers.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
Spacy is built on the conviction that wallet infrastructure is becoming the infrastructure of cryptographic sovereignty. Where keys live, who can compel access to them, and whose randomness seeded them are no longer engineering details. They are political facts about whose hands hold the future of self-custody.
The current embedded-wallet stack normalizes a quiet concentration: three AWS regions, one TEE vendor lineage, US/EU jurisdictional reach, opaque entropy, no published quantum migration plan. Each individual provider is competent. The systemic posture is fragile and increasingly anachronistic against the threat landscape of 2026.

Spacy aligns with Future Society's mandate on three axes:
- Sustainability through durability. Self-custody infrastructure should outlast its operators, jurisdictions, and the cryptographic primitives it currently relies on. Spacy's attestation receipts are content-addressed on IPFS with on-chain Sepolia pointers, designed to survive even Q-day attestation forgery, when today's TEE certificate roots will become forgeable retroactively. The wallet a user onboards into in 2026 should keep working in 2032. We build for that horizon, not for the next funding round.
- Ethical infrastructure through verifiability. Privy and Turnkey ask users to trust their backend. Spacy proves the backend, with public health endpoints serving live SEV-SNP attestation reports any third party can verify offline against AMD's published certificate chain. Trust is a design choice. We choose the version that gives users power instead of taking it.

Inclusive sovereignty beyond corporate enclaves. AGPL-3.0 licensed from commit one, built on SpaceComputer's open infrastructure, with cosmic randomness drawn from a public IPFS beacon anyone can pull without authentication. We build on commons-grade primitives rather than walling them off. The codebase is auditable, the receipt format is open, the verification logic ships as a single fork-and-run package. This is solarpunk infrastructure: optimistic, durable, jurisdictionally untethered, verifiable down to the cosmic ray, open-sourced, built to be inherited.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
Spacy is a Web3 embedded wallet (Privy-class UX, Google sign-in, no seed phrase) whose entire pitch is built on three architectural commitments that no other infrastructure stack on the market today can deliver simultaneously: a TEE-backed signer, a publicly verifiable cosmic randomness witness on every signature, and a credible post-quantum migration path with zero rewrite cost. SpaceComputer's Orbitport is the only stack where these three commitments can coexist. Everything else we considered required us to give up at least one of them.

We use four SpaceComputer primitives directly.

**KMS as the signer**. Every Spacy wallet's private key is created with kms.createKey (curve ECC_SECG_P256K1, scheme ETHEREUM) and signed with kms.sign on a digest passed from our backend. The key never leaves Intel TDX. The alternative was building our own threshold ECDSA wallet on cggmp21, which we started and abandoned, because rebuilding a TEE-backed signer at consumer-grade reliability is not a hackathon project. It is also not where the value of Spacy lives. The value lives in the trust chain wrapped around the signer, and Orbitport gives us that primitive solid enough to wrap the rest of the architecture around.

**cTRNG** as the entropy witness. Every signing operation pulls a fresh sample with trng.getRandom. The sample is recorded in the receipt and matchable against the IPFS public beacon archive, giving every Spacy transaction a verifiable timestamp anchored to a physical event in low Earth orbit. The IPFS beacon fallback path works without authentication and is what turns cTRNG from a service we depend on into a public commons we participate in. No other randomness source on the market can be cross-checked against a publicly archived signed feed. CSPRNG outputs from Privy or Turnkey produce no auditable artifact at all.

Orbitport as the gateway. Every external call from our backend routes through op.spacecomputer.io with OAuth2 client-credentials. This means our credential surface is one stable endpoint instead of three separate vendor integrations, and it means our migration path to orbital signing (Q4 2026) is one URL change. The gateway abstraction is exactly the property that made the post-quantum story possible to claim honestly: when SpaceComputer ships ML-DSA in the KMS, our SDK migrates by changing one parameter on the same gateway call, with no architectural rewrite.

Space Fabric as the migration anchor. The pitch we make to users in 2026 is "the wallet you onboard into today is the wallet that still works in 2032." We can only make that claim because SpaceComputer has published a real architecture document (the Space Fabric paper, April 2026) committing to hybrid classical/PQC signatures using satellite TPMs as an independent root of trust. No other embedded wallet provider has anything equivalent. Privy, Turnkey, Dynamic, Magic have published nothing about post-quantum migration. We are not just building on SpaceComputer's primitives, we are building toward SpaceComputer's roadmap, with our SDK shaped to slot every phase-2 capability in as it ships.

Why this would not have worked anywhere else.

AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, and HashiCorp Vault all offer TEE-backed signers, but none publish satellite-witnessed entropy and none have a post-quantum migration path that lives in the same product surface. We would have ended up with three separate vendor integrations and no coherent verification story to give the user.

Privy or Turnkey as a backend would defeat the purpose. Their value proposition is operator-trust, ours is operator-removal.

A homegrown threshold ECDSA wallet on cggmp21 would have gotten us cryptographic distribution but not vendor heterogeneity. The TEE.Fail attack (October 2025) proved that homogeneous TEE deployments share a class of zero-day exposure. SpaceComputer's KMS in Intel TDX, paired with our coordinator in AMD SEV-SNP, gives us heterogeneity at the hardware layer that threshold cryptography on a single vendor lineage cannot.

Beyond direct primitive use, we built explicitly within the SpaceComputer development pattern. Our backend is structured against the patterns in kms_starter, our authentication flow draws from cosmic-siwe, and our receipt schema reserves fields for the KMS attestation quote and cTRNG satellite signature that are documented in the spec but not yet exposed by the public gateway. These reserved fields are the most important architectural commitment in the project: the day SpaceComputer ships them, every existing Spacy receipt schema accepts them with no migration. We are not waiting for a future version of Spacy to align with SpaceComputer's roadmap. The current version is already aligned, with explicit slots for what comes next.

Spacy is what an embedded wallet looks like when it is built natively on SpaceComputer's stack. That is the only place this project could have been built.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The Problem: High-Value Logistics is a "Black Box"

Shipping assets like luxury watches, electronics, or pharmaceuticals currently relies on blind trust. Centralized data can be faked, damages are only discovered after delivery, and insurance disputes take months of manual paperwork.
The Solution: Eliver Autonomous Intelligence Hub

Eliver turns logistics from a risky process into an autonomous agent that guarantees integrity.

    Trustless Truth: We use SpaceComputer for hardware-signed telemetry. Data is signed at the sensor level, making it physically impossible to spoof or manipulate the shipment history.

    Human-Readable Identity: Instead of complex hex codes, we use ENS (e.g., tracker-patek.eth) so operators can manage high-value cargo with intuitive identities.

    Forensic Investigation: Our Temporal Scrubber allows users to "time-travel" through the shipment's history, pinpointing exactly when and where a breach occurred on a real-world map.

    Autonomous Justice: If a breach is detected (e.g., temperature spike or 5G shock), the "Supreme Judge" AI instantly verifies the hardware-signed evidence and generates an automated Insurance Report PDF to trigger immediate refunds.

Eliver makes logistics safer, faster, and trustless—moving high-value assets with the certainty of code.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Building Eliver was a journey of cutting through noise to reach cryptographic truth. Here are the specific hurdles we cleared:

    The React Hook Sync: We initially broke the "Rules of Hooks" by trying to conditionally inject agentic events (like x402 payments) into the timeline. This caused render mismatches and crashes. We solved this by performing a "surgical refactor," moving all processing to the top level and handling empty states directly inside our memoized logic to ensure a stable render cycle.

    Temporal Scrubber Performance: Syncing a real-time map, high-fidelity charts, and monospaced AI logs while sliding through history was a performance nightmare. We overcame the lag by centralizing the playbackTime state and using heavy memoization to ensure that "time-traveling" through the data remains a smooth, 60fps experience.

    The Minimalist UX War: Our first version was cluttered with duplicate stats and long AI paragraphs. We fought back with Radical Minimalism—moving current values directly into chart headers and replacing bulky instructions with an interactive "Supreme Judge" chat. This kept the focus on the data breach, not the UI.

    Highway-Aligned Tracking: Standard map markers fly in straight lines, but trucks don't. We replaced "crow-fly" paths with road-accurate GeoJSON routes for the Prague-to-Malaga line, ensuring our Digital Twin reflects the physical reality of the asset.

    Forensic PDF Logic: Designing a report that looks professional enough for a court or an insurance adjuster was tough. We built a custom template that captures the "Hardware Signature" from SpaceComputer, turning raw telemetry into a legally-defensible document.

description.title: Future Society
description.body: Eliver provides a foundational blueprint for a future society where global trust is powered by autonomous code rather than slow bureaucracy. By replacing standard logistics with hardware-signed truth from SpaceComputer, we guarantee the integrity of critical high-value assets through unfakeable digital twins. We shift from weeks of manual paperwork to near-instant conflict resolution using AI-driven judges and smart contracts, proving a society can settle disputes fairly via cryptographic evidence instead of human bias. By integrating ENS, we transform complex decentralized systems into human-centric experiences, allowing businesses to interact through recognizable identities rather than machine-readable hex codes, ultimately removing the friction of trust to build a more efficient global economy guaranteed by the laws of mathematics.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
Eliver uses SpaceComputer’s hardware-grade security to create tamper-proof sensor logs for RWA logistics. Each telemetry packet, including temperature spikes and G-force shocks, is signed inside a secure hardware enclave before being sent on-chain.

We also extended SpaceComputer’s QEMU environment by adding post-quantum cryptography: Dilithium for signatures and Kyber for encryption/key exchange. This lets us simulate quantum-resistant telemetry proofs and encrypted payloads for future secure logistics.

Together, Eliver combines secure edge signing, post-quantum protection, and smart contract dispute resolution to create a verifiable logistics chain with real-world impact.

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body: Eliver is a high-fidelity Agentic Venture designed to automate the $30B luxury logistics and insurance market by replacing slow, manual paperwork with an AI "Supreme Judge" agent. Our project functions as an autonomous insurance engine that ingests hardware-signed telemetry from SpaceComputer to identify shipment breaches in real-time and trigger automatic smart-contract refunds without human intervention. This "Insurance-as-an-Agent" model has a clear path to revenue through a SaaS-plus-arbitration-fee structure, targeting high-value brands that require ironclad audit trails for Real World Assets. Built to scale into a fully on-chain organization on Umia, Eliver demonstrates how agentic workflows can protect capital and resolve global disputes trustlessly, making it a viable venture for a future tokenized ecosystem where decentralized integrity is the core product.

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body: Eliver implements a decentralized Key-Value store on Swarm to manage shipment-specific metadata and user dashboard configurations without relying on centralized servers. By leveraging Swarm Feeds to map keys like "alert_thresholds" or "shipment_notes" to persistent storage, we provide a simple `get/put` interface that keeps user data private and tied to their Ethereum identity. This integration ensures that all "soft" state in our logistics hub is just as resilient and decentralized as the hardware-signed telemetry, proving that complex dApps can maintain mutable state while preserving full data sovereignty for the user.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Eliver transforms the cold, machine-readable world of logistics into a trusted, human-centric ecosystem by using ENS as the primary identity and data layer for high-value Real World Assets (RWA). We move beyond simple name resolution to make ENS the root of a forensic audit trail.

    RWA Identity: Instead of tracking anonymous 0x... addresses, every stakeholder—from the shipment (tracker-patek.eth) to the payer (lvmh-vault.eth) and the carrier (brinks-eu.eth)—is a verifiable ENS identity.

    The "Audit Passport": We use ENS text records to store dynamic logistical parameters, such as sensor thresholds and hardware signatures. These records act as a decentralized "passport" for the cargo, which our system cross-references against hardware-signed telemetry from SpaceComputer.

    Reputation & Resolution: When a breach is detected, our AI "Supreme Judge" resolves the shipment’s ENS identity to fetch its specific audit rules and automatically stages a refund to the correct human-readable principal.

By replacing hex codes with trusted brand identities and using text records to power autonomous dispute logic, Eliver eliminates the "trust gap" in global trade, making blockchain-based logistics intuitive, accountable, and ready for the real world.

proof-of-reality-6a31.name: Proof of Reality
proof-of-reality-6a31.tagline: Cryptographic proof that physical things exist

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
AI can fake any photo in five seconds. That broke something basic: looking at a picture used to mean the thing was real. Now it doesn't.

  A lot of things depend on that:

  - **Used-car and used-goods sites** are full of fake photos. People fly across countries to inspect cars that turn out to be nothing like the ad.
  - **Insurance claims** rely on before/after pictures. Anyone with a laptop can make those.
  - **Tokens that represent a real-world asset** ("this NFT is a watch in a vault") have no way to prove the watch is still there.
  - **Smart contracts that care about the real world** (parametric insurance, supply-chain triggers, DePIN sensors) have to trust one central data source.
  - **Provenance for art, wine, watches** is paperwork. Paper can be forged.

  ## What we built

  A 30-second scan from an iPhone or an industrial camera, tied to a random number that came from a satellite seconds before, signed by a chip inside the device, and minted as an NFT on Base. Five separate signatures get checked on every scan. To fake one, you'd have to fake all five at once, and one of them comes from space.

  ## What people can use it for

  **Online marketplaces.** A listing with a Reality NFT was scanned right before posting, on real hardware, with a satellite timestamp on it. Listings without one start to look suspicious by default.
  
  **Rentals and insurance.** Scan the car when you hand over the keys. Scan it when you get them back. Both scans are on-chain. There's nothing to argue about.

  **Tokenized real-world assets.** A watch in a vault gets re-scanned every week by a camera with a hardware signer. The token now points at a real watch, not a PDF promising a watch.

  **Provenance for valuables.** Every time a painting changes hands, a fresh scan goes on-chain. The history is cryptographic, not a folder of certificates.

  **Smart contracts that care about physical things.** Any contract can ask "is this thing actually there, right now?" and get back a real proof.

  **Theft and warranty.** A bicycle, a power tool, a server in a data center all get a hardware identity. Stolen things stay traceable. Warranty fights have an answer.

  ## Why it matters

  Today, the proof that a physical thing exists is a photograph. Photographs broke. We're building a replacement that uses cryptography instead.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
While integrating with **SpaceComputer**'s gotee_starter, one line in scripts/armory-link.sh silently hung on Linux but worked fine on my Mac: ping -c 2 -W 2000 "$GATEWAY".

No output, no error, no timeout. We assumed it was something else: a routing issue, the **SpaceComputer** Armory not booted yet, a set -e interaction, the case "$OS" block picking the wrong branch. Then we lined up the man pages. On **macOS (BSD ping)**, -W is in **milliseconds**, so 2000 = 2 seconds. On **Linux (iputils ping)**, -W is in **seconds**, so 2000 ≈ 33 minutes. The script wasn't frozen, it was waiting half an hour for a host that hadn't finished booting.

**Fix:** set PING_W per OS inside the case "$OS" branch (2000 on macOS, 2 on Linux), then use $PING_W in the shared ping call.

**Lesson:** when a shared command behaves differently across OSes, the answer is usually in the man pages, not the script. Always diff flags with units before assuming they mean the same thing.

PR to **SpaceComputer**: https://github.com/spacecomputer-io/gotee_starter/pull/5

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Proof of Reality is itself a small network economy with three roles, each with a clear incentive.

**Capture operators** (organizations running B2B OAK4 stations or fleets of B2C iPhones) register their devices in a permissionless on-chain **DeviceRegistry.sol**. Registration is a public stake of reputation: every scan a device produces is signed by it, and every signature is traceable on-chain back to the registering org. There is no gatekeeper. A used-car dealership, a logistics company, an insurance adjuster, or a citizen-science collective registers under the same contract on the same terms.

**Verifiers** (marketplaces, RWA protocols, DePIN orchestrators, KYC officers) consume scans for free, but their economic question is no longer "do I trust the listing photo." It becomes "is the bundle hash committed on-chain, do the five signatures verify, is the signing device registered to an org I'm willing to credit." That moves the trust decision from human judgment about a stock photo to a deterministic check against public infrastructure.

**Asset holders** (the people who scanned the thing) get a transferable on-chain artifact, the Reality NFT, that travels with the object across marketplaces, custody changes, and protocol boundaries. The proof is durable independent of any single operator: bundle on Swarm, name on ENS, contract on Base, source on Sourcify.

The economic primitive we are adding is "proof of physical existence at a moment in time." Today's RWA and DePIN networks assume this primitive and outsource it to a single trusted operator. We make it a public good, secured by hardware and a satellite, and route incentives so capture operators are rewarded for honest scans and slashable (via on-chain registry revocation) for fraudulent ones. The backend is a thin economic proxy that collects gas, postage, and Orbitport quota, not value.

The result is the missing settlement layer for any network whose economic claims depend on something physical existing. That is the Network Economy contribution.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
A Solarpunk future needs cryptographic ground truth about the physical world. Which solar array exists. Which battery actually holds the capacity it claims. Which carbon-credit forest is a forest, and not a satellite-image overlay. Most of today's RWA, DePIN, and impact-finance protocols collapse onto a single trusted operator who promises the physical thing is real.

We replace that operator with a structural alternative: three independent hardware-rooted witnesses (satellite cTRNG, KMS co-sig, on-device key) plus a permissionless on-chain device registry where any organization can publicly stake reputation by registering its capture devices. No central authority issues the truth. The truth is a recomputable hash, signed by parties with public keys, anchored to a moment in time the operator did not get to choose.

The infrastructure stack carries the same values down to the bottom layer. Storage is Swarm (self-hosted Bee), not S3. Randomness is Orbitport, not a centralized RNG. Device identity is hardware, not a SaaS API. Contract source is verified on Sourcify, not a single-operator dashboard. A Reality NFT is durable in the strict sense: if we disappear tomorrow, the bundle is still on Swarm, the ENS name still resolves, the contract is still on Base, and the proof is still verifiable from a laptop.

The Solarpunk theme isn't a metaphor we borrowed for the pitch. It is the literal scope of the system.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
SpaceComputer is the spine of this project, not a logo on a slide. Every Reality NFT we mint embeds two independent SpaceComputer-rooted signatures, both verifiable client-side against pinned pubkeys.

The first is **satSig**. The iPhone (or the OAK4 station) pulls a cTRNG nonce from Orbitport before capture, the satellite signs it, and the device paints the value into the scene as a QR plus audio overlay. The signature pins the scan to a moment in time the attacker cannot precompute or roll back.

The second is **cosmoSig**. Every bundle hash gets co-signed by Space Fabric KMS in TEE. The order of operations is fixed in **apps/api/src/routes/upload.routes.ts**: verify the device signature, KMS co-sign the **deviceSigningHash**, embed the **spaceFabric** block, recompute the final **bundleHash**. The KMS pubkey is pinned in the viewer (**docs/trust-model.md**), so verification runs without trusting our backend at all.

Both signatures are committed on-chain via **RealityProof.mint(...)** on Base Sepolia, so they cannot be retroactively swapped. If our backend is fully compromised, the attacker can drain Orbitport quota, Swarm postage, and gas. They cannot forge a scan, because they hold neither the satellite's key nor the KMS's key.

We use Orbitport as the temporal anchor and Space Fabric as the integrity anchor, exactly as they were designed: cryptographic ground truth for an oracle that bridges the physical world onto Ethereum.

description.title: Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway
Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Each Reality NFT publishes its own ENS subname on Sepolia: **vin-<bundleHash[2:14]>.realityproof.eth**. The handle is not decoration. It is how the proof is shared.

Records on each subname carry the full commitment:

- **addr** resolves to the attestor wallet
- **contenthash** is an ENSIP-7 Swarm reference to the canonical bundle JSON
- text records hold **bundleHash**, **satSig**, **cosmoSig**, **capturedAt**, **tokenId**, **mode**, **url**, **avatar**

A verifier holding only the ENS handle can fetch the bundle (Brave, MetaMask, eth.link all resolve ENSIP-7 contenthash natively), recompute the canonical hash, and check the five signatures. They do not need our contract address, our backend, or our app to be online.

That is the creative use: ENS is not a vanity wrapper around an NFT URL. It is the canonical, wallet-native, infrastructure-agnostic sharing surface for an off-chain proof. The contract is a commit log. The bundle lives on Swarm. The ENS name is the human-readable handle that ties them together. If our company disappears tomorrow, the proof remains resolvable.

A demo script (**apps/api/scripts/verify-ens.ts**) walks any judge through resolving a live mint to its records, end to end, in one terminal command.

ethesis-b242.name: ETHesis
ethesis-b242.tagline: Fund research globally, verify progress onchain.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Research funding is often opaque and trust-based: funders can rarely verify whether milestones are actually delivered, and early-stage researchers outside legacy institutions struggle to access capital. ETHesis creates a transparent venture lifecycle where researchers launch tokenized research ventures, communities fund them, and an autonomous auditor agent continuously checks real outputs against declared plans. Every verification cycle produces a signed attestation anchored to ENS, so funders and teams share a public, tamper-evident record of progress.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: We had to connect several difficult pieces into one coherent flow under hackathon time pressure: server-side ENS provisioning, deterministic agent identity, source monitoring, and verifiable attestation publishing. The hardest parts were handling asynchronous onchain transactions reliably, designing resilient fallback behavior for external data providers, and keeping the product usable while complex background processes run. We solved this by separating integrations behind typed adapters, adding mock-safe modes for degraded dependencies, and building a launch flow that surfaces progress clearly while preserving verifiable outputs.

description.title: Ethereum Core

By turning core primitives into a live funding-and-accountability workflow, ETHesis demonstrates applied Ethereum infrastructure value.
