description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Web3 financial actions are still unsafe and hard to understand for normal users, and the risk becomes even higher when AI agents are allowed to prepare transactions.

Today, users often sign opaque wallet prompts without understanding the real calldata, token approvals, recipients, or contract risks. Browser wallets can be phished, hosted frontends can be compromised, and server-side signing creates dangerous hot-key custody risk. At the same time, AI agents are becoming useful for financial workflows, but giving an agent direct control over private keys is not safe.

Jimmy solves this by separating intent, reasoning, memory, and signing into different trust layers. The user creates intent locally, the AI agent explains and prepares the action, Swarm stores encrypted decentralized memory, ENS provides human-readable identity and agent discovery, and final transaction signing is handled by a satellite-backed SpaceComputer signing layer instead of a normal browser wallet or centralized hot server.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenge 1 — Reliable tool-calling for real transactions
Our supervisor uses LLM function calls for ENS checks and Sepolia market actions. The model often put fields like amount, recipient, or to next to the tool call instead of inside payload, which broke our market agent’s expectations. We fixed this in code by merging top-level fields into a single payload before dispatch, and we tightened the system prompt so the model follows a consistent quote → confirm → execute flow. That made swaps, sends, and ENS registration repeatable enough for a live demo.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Jimmy fits the Network Economy track because it builds a safer, user-controlled model for on-chain financial actions. The project combines satellite-backed transaction signing, AI-assisted wallet operations, ENS identity, and decentralized Swarm memory to reduce reliance on centralized backend custody and opaque browser signing.

Instead of giving an AI agent direct custody of funds, Jimmy separates intent, reasoning, memory, and signing into different trust layers. Users can perform swaps, sends, ENS-related actions, and agent-assisted financial workflows while keeping final transaction authorization in an isolated signing layer.

This directly supports the Network Economy theme by improving user control, wallet security, and decentralized identity for real on-chain economic activity.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
TL;DR: Private key and signing operations are on SpaceComputer satellite.

Jimmy fits the SpaceComputer track because the core wallet signing flow is built around the idea that financial actions should not be signed by a normal browser wallet or a hot backend server.
In our architecture, the local wallet UI and AI agent create transaction intent, but the signing authority is moved into a KMS Space Computer / satellite-backed signing environment. This means the agent can reason about actions, prepare swaps, sends, or ENS-related operations, but it does not directly custody the private key.
The SpaceComputer layer acts as the isolated trust boundary for transaction signing:
the interface creates intent, but does not own the key
the backend routes and builds transactions, but is not the custodian
the AI agent explains and prepares actions, but cannot directly steal funds
the SpaceComputer-backed signer is responsible for final transaction authorization
This fits the bounty because Jimmy demonstrates a real wallet use case for SpaceComputer: secure signing for autonomous Web3 agents or the users themselves. The project shows how satellite-backed compute can become a safer signing layer for AI-powered financial workflows.

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body:
Our project uses Swarm as a decentralized key-value memory layer for the Jimmy AI wallet agent.

Jimmy stores encrypted session history, transaction context, and agent decision logs in Swarm instead of keeping this data only in a centralized backend or local browser state. This gives the agent persistent decentralized memory: it can preserve previous wallet interactions, security context, and audit history across sessions.

In our architecture, Swarm is not just file storage. It acts as a simple decentralized KV store for agent memory:

key: wallet / agent session identifier
value: encrypted session history and transaction context
This fits the track because we use Swarm KV as a practical storage primitive for a real application: a satellite-backed AI wallet where the agent needs persistent, encrypted, decentralized memory.

description.title: Best ENS Integration for AI Agents
description.body:
Our project integrates ENS as an identity and discovery layer for AI agents inside Jimmy, our satellite-backed AI wallet.

Jimmy uses ENS in three ways:

ENS agent discovery
We implemented ENSIP-26-style metadata lookup for AI agents. The system can read ENS text records such as agent-context and agent-endpoint[http] to discover whether an ENS name represents an AI agent and where its agent metadata or endpoint lives.

ENS name checks and registration flow
The ENS Agent can check .eth name availability using ENS normalization, Blockscout BENS data, and on-chain Base Registrar reads. Availability checks use Ethereum mainnet sources; registration and sends resolve ENS on Sepolia for the demo. If a name is available, Jimmy can prepare a Sepolia ENS registration flow through the Market Agent.

ENS as human-readable recipients
For wallet actions, users can provide ENS names instead of raw 0x addresses. Jimmy resolves ENS names on Sepolia for actions like native ETH sends or swap output recipients.

This fits the track because ENS is not just displayed as a username. We use ENS as a practical coordination layer for AI agents: agent discovery, human-readable wallet actions, and domain-based identity for autonomous Web3 workflows. In our architecture, ENS helps users and agents understand who they are interacting with before any financial action is prepared or signed.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Jimmy uses ENS creatively as more than a human-readable wallet name. We use ENS as an identity and discovery layer for AI agents inside a satellite-backed autonomous wallet.

The project integrates ENS in three ways:

AI agent discovery: Jimmy can inspect ENS records for agent metadata, including ENSIP-26-style text records like agent-context and agent-endpoint[http].
Human-readable financial actions: users can send ETH or route swap outputs to ENS names instead of raw 0x addresses.
ENS domain automation: the agent can check .eth availability and prepare a Sepolia ENS registration flow when the user wants to claim a name.
The creative part is that ENS becomes part of the agent workflow: it helps the wallet understand who an agent is, where its metadata lives, and where assets should be sent. In Jimmy, ENS is not just a name label; it is a coordination layer for AI agents and wallet actions.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Semaphore gives any smart contract and autonomous agents access to real-time, verifiable market sentiment, something that currently doesn't exist on-chain. Today, protocols can react to price movements, but they cannot react to the social narratives and news events that often cause those movements in the first place.

We this by turning live social web sentiment from sources like Twitter/X, Reddit, Google News, and Telegram into a decentralized oracle feed that smart contracts can consume directly, just like Chainlink price feeds.

Semaphore’s oracle data enables smart contracts and on-chain applications to become more resilient, adaptive, and context-aware by allowing them to:

Detect panic, fear, or negative narratives before major market crashes
Automatically adjust risk parameters based on real-world sentiment
Trigger circuit breakers or emergency protections during extreme fear events
Power AI trading agents with pay-per-query narrative intelligence
Create prediction markets and financial products based on public sentiment trends
Help DAOs detect community backlash or governance instability
Enable wallets and consumer apps to surface narrative-risk warnings to users
Allow insurance protocols to dynamically adjust premiums based on ecosystem risk
Provide autonomous agents with machine-readable narrative awareness

Unlike centralized sentiment APIs, Semaphore is permissionless, composable, and auditable. Every data request is paid for through X402 micropayments, every scrape is verifiable, and every sentiment result is linked to an on-chain proof and data hash.

We also built a real-time web dashboard that showcases the oracle data in an an aggregated and intuitive interface. The dashboard visualizes:

Live sentiment scores and fear/greed signals
Narrative strength indicators
Asset-level trend tracking and momentum changes
Historical sentiment movements
Source-level signal breakdowns
Market-wide sentiment distribution
Search and filtering tools for specific assets, protocols, or blockchains
On-chain verification and transmission activity

This demonstrates how DeFi protocols, AI agents, trading systems, and risk-management platforms could directly integrate Semaphore’s oracle feeds into their own infrastructure and decision-making systems.

In short, Semaphore brings narrative awareness to blockchains: enabling protocols to respond not just to price changes, but to the information and emotions driving the market itself.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: Apify currently requires USDC on the mainnet, which involves 402 transactions. While this setup presents a usability challenge, it is a limitation of the underlying network rather than Apify itself

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Semaphore fits the network economy track by creating a decentralized marketplace for narrative data where value is exchanged autonomously between machines.

Autonomous Resource Exchange: It enables AI agents and smart contracts to purchase real-time intelligence directly from scrapers using X402 micropayments, removing human intermediaries from the economic loop.

Permissionless Data Monetization: By using Apify Actors, the project allows any participant to contribute scraping power to the network and get paid instantly for verifiable on-chain data.

Programmable Web Intelligence: It treats information as a liquid commodity, allowing protocols to dynamically price risk and adjust interest rates based on the "cost" and "value" of sentiment data within the ecosystem.

description.title: Apify Bounty
description.body:
Semaphore fits the Apify track by demonstrating a real-world, production-oriented use case for Apify’s x402-powered agentic payment infrastructure. Our project uses Apify Actors as the core data acquisition layer, enabling autonomous agents and smart contracts to pay for real-time web intelligence through X402 micropayments without relying on API keys or centralized subscriptions.

Every sentiment update requested through Semaphore triggers an off-chain agent that:

Pays for Apify services using X402 and USDC
Executes Apify Actors to scrape live social and news data
Aggregates and verifies the results
Publishes the processed sentiment feed on-chain for smart contract consumption

This directly aligns with the Apify bounty goals around:

Agentic payments via X402
Autonomous agents paying for services
Web3-native monetization of data infrastructure
Real-world usage of Apify Actors in blockchain applications
AI agents purchasing and consuming live web intelligence

Semaphore also expands the utility of Apify beyond traditional scraping use cases by transforming Apify-powered web data into programmable on-chain infrastructure. Instead of scraping data for dashboards alone, we use Apify as the real-time intelligence backbone for decentralized systems, enabling DeFi protocols, DAOs, AI agents, wallets, and other smart contract applications to react to live market narratives in a verifiable and permissionless way.

Our project showcases how Apify and X402 can power the next generation of autonomous, machine-to-machine economies where agents dynamically purchase external intelligence and immediately use it inside blockchain-native applications.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
1. This tool helps both retail and institutional users better understand a DeFi protocol before allocating capital. By simply pasting a vault or pool address, users receive an interactive dependency graph that maps all underlying smart contracts powering the protocol. This provides a better visibility into how funds move across the system, enabling users to make more informed risk management decisions.

2. The solution aggregates all protocol dependencies into a single unified interface and visually demonstrates how contracts are interconnected. Instead of manually searching through explorers and documentation, users get a complete structural overview of the protocol in one place, significantly simplifying due diligence and security analysis.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
- Dependency Graph Ordering
Getting the correct visual hierarchy in the dependency tree was tricky. Initially, governance contracts (curator, guardian, owner) appeared at the bottom of the tree after all markets and tokens, which didn't reflect their importance. The issue was in the manifest execution order - the system processed dependencies in the order they were defined in the protocol manifest. We solved this by reordering the directCalls array to prioritize governance contracts, ensuring they appear first in the visualization.

- Finding the correct approach how to explore the protocol dependencies. Initially we were using a separate TypeScript files which all logic related to the protocol. But we understood that this approach will become heavy very fast and we come up with an idea to describe protocol in manifest files.

- Collect risk related data from open source for each node. There is a lot of data in the web about smart contracts and a lot of resources. All this data should be somehow structured and after that managed to create a risk scoring engine. For this prototype we decided to move with the risk flags for the beginning. These flags can be quickly identified in the abi (e.g. "upgradeTo", "blacklist") of the smart contract and displayed in the node information.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body:
Panorama improves Ethereum's security and usability by giving developers, auditors, and DeFi users a practical tool to visualize and understand complex smart contract dependencies. By automatically mapping protocol architectures and revealing hidden connections, we make it significantly easier and safer to audit, integrate with, and build on top of Ethereum protocols.
Our tool addresses a critical infrastructure gap - the ability to quickly understand "what depends on what" in DeFi - which is essential for the security and resilience of interconnected decentralized systems.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: Panorama automatically visualizes smart contract architectures and protocol dependencies, giving users clear risk insight before deploying capital. By making deep protocol analysis accessible to everyone, it minimizes financial losses caused by knowledge gaps in DeFi workflows - creating a safer, more transparent ecosystem for all participants.

description.title: Future Society
description.body: Panorama promotes transparency and fair governance in DeFi by making protocol architectures visible and understandable to everyone. By revealing governance structures (curators, guardians, owners) and their relationships to protocol components, we empower communities to make informed decisions about which protocols align with their intentions and risk model

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body: We use Sourcify as the primary source for retrieving verified smart contract ABIs. When analyzing a contract, we query Sourcify's API to fetch the ABI, which enables us to identify the contract type and automatically discover dependencies by calling protocol-specific functions. If Sourcify doesn't have the contract, we fall back to Etherscan's API, ensuring maximum coverage.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Kowalski Market is an on-chain prediction market where the live trading price of every event is its real-time probability. Three distinct features set it apart: (1) permissionless market creation — anyone can deploy a market with custom rules by posting a bond, with a curator  validating before it goes live; (2) Kowalski, a voice- and text-controlled AI layer that lets users trade, place limit orders, navigate, and discuss markets in natural language while every transaction is signed by the user's own wallet; and (3) Central-Europe-first coverage of events legacy bookmakers and global prediction markets ignore — CE politics, weather, energy prices, regional sport, and culture.

Together these features unlock things today's prediction markets can't:

1. Niche markets get real liquidity. A user asks "Will US tariffs on European steel exceed 15% by Q3 2026?"  - user get a prediction on the probability of an event of his/hers interest

2. Standard prediction markets and their interfaces aren't intuitive — most users don't understand order books or CLOB mechanics. Through Kowalski's agentic interface, beginners interact by simply talking, and the agent explains whatever they need along the way.

3. Research happens in the same flow. "Why did this move 8% in the last hour?" — the agent surfaces the news behind the move. Voice works hands-free.

4. CE coverage that didn't exist finally does — politics, weather, energy, regional sport, and culture, in the region's own language and context.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The interesting part was designing the prediction market around the end user — improving on what existing prediction markets get wrong and rethinking how the trading surface should feel for someone who isn't already a crypto-native trader. 

On the technical side, ENS resolution was returning stale or near-match records, so Kowalski would confidently answer about a different market than the user named — solved by exact-match first, fuzzy only as a confirmation prompt, plus a sanity check that the resolved market's question matches user intent before any action. The other big opportunity was making a CLOB and an AMM coexist so liquid markets get tight order-book spreads while freshly created ones aren't dead on arrival; we routed every quote through a single pricing layer that aggregates both sources, with the AMM as implicit counterparty when the book is thin — fillable prices on day one, tighter book-driven prices once real makers arrive.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Kowalski Market puts the user — not the platform, not the agent — in control of every economic action. Three ways we address the track:

1. Non-custodial even with an AI in the loop. Most "AI agent" products quietly take custody to make UX work. Kowalski inverts this: the agent interprets intent, drafts orders, and chains multi-step trades, but the wallet stays with the user and every transaction is signed locally. No session tokens that can move funds, no bypass of the signing prompt — conversational UX without giving up self-custody.

2. No central point of failure. Markets are created on chain via bond, prices come from CLOB + AMM, resolution is protocol-enforced. No bookmaker can rewrite odds. Identity is wallet-native.

3. Real economic activity, privacy-respecting by default. Settlement is on-chain; positions and fills are auditable without exposing personal data. With no central account system, there's no honeypot linking trades to real identities — and agents acting on a user's behalf inherit that same boundary, so AI participation doesn't leak data into a centralized ledger.

Net effect: users keep their keys, their identity, and their data, while still getting AI-native UX and real on-chain economic activity — the "user control first" stack the track asks for.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
Kowalski Market addresses this by removing three concrete barriers that keep on-chain tools out of ordinary people's hands:

1. Onboarding is a conversation, not a learning curve. Most people never interact with Ethereum because the interface assumes you already understand wallets, gas, slippage, and order books. Kowalski's voice- and text-controlled agent translates all of that into plain language — "buy €5 of YES if it drops below 30¢" — while the user signs every transaction themselves. The agent never holds keys, so non-custodial self-sovereignty stays intact; the wall in front of it just disappears.

2. Anyone can price an event, not just the legacy bookmakers. Forecasting outcomes — elections, energy prices, regional weather — has historically been gatekept by centralized markets that ignore anything outside their commercial top tier. Open, bond-backed market creation means a community can mint a market on a question that matters to them (a Czech referendum, a Polish energy cap, a regional drought) and the crowd prices it transparently on-chain. Information that would otherwise live in opaque polls or paywalled reports becomes a public, verifiable signal.

3. AI-native participation expands who counts as a trader. When agents can trade on a user's behalf within the limits the user sets, liquidity stops being a function of how many humans happen to click through an order book. Niche, civically important markets that used to die from thin volume now get priced by agent participation, which means better forecasts on the long-tail questions communities actually care about — without sacrificing user custody, transparency, or on-chain auditability.

Together: a non-custodial, AI-native, community-creatable prediction layer that turns Ethereum into infrastructure for collective forecasting — open to anyone who can speak, not just anyone who can read a CLOB.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
We use SpaceComputer's cosmic-radiation true RNG (cTRNG) as the supplier of entropy for our project. There are two main uses of entropy in our project:
1/ Some actors’ utility function is maximized by betting on randomness. We have a prediction market where they can bet on verifiable randomness - the market is resolved based on a  modulo of randomness in a predefined (defined before the market is created) block in SpaceComputer. An optimistic oracle (UMA style) provides the data on-chain.
2/ For matching the orders, we use a 0x-like off-chain order book protocol. The holder of the off-chain order book can always abuse the situation and front-run their own put or call options. SpaceComputer provides randomness for the decision of which order should be executed first.


Demo: https://www.loom.com/share/9cbeabbc145f49299a8cb3c941ab0f9c

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body:
We have built an agent-agnostic backend protocol for a prediction market MCP server, featuring an x402 paywall for premium tools. Any AI agent—whether it is Claude Code, a Custom GPT, an autonomous Python bot, or any entity with httpx and a wallet—can fully interact with these markets.
While agents can operate independently, users can also utilize our agentic frontend when preferred. Our execution stack consists of three cleanly integrated layers:
* End-user agents place trades on behalf of humans.
* Our backend operations agent manages overhead, such as paying Apify for real-time scraping.
* Our public intelligence API monetizes data by selling up-to-date world news to other agents.

Potential Revenue Streams
Global betting is an approximately $500B annual category—encompassing sports betting, casinos, and lotteries. Online betting alone accounts for over $90B, with prediction markets being the fastest-growing segment (notably, Polymarket cleared multi-billion dollar notional volume in 2024).
Our potential revenue streams include:
1. Bond Slashing: Penalties for bad-faith or unethical market routes are captured as protocol revenue and distributed as curator rewards.
2. Trading Fees: A fee toggle can be activated per market once liquidity is sufficient. Implementation timing may be determined by a UMIA decision market.
3. Intelligence API: Earns $0.50–$0.75 per call via the x402 protocol.
4. Asset Yield: On-chain interest generated from liquidity locked within betting markets represents a significant secondary revenue source.

UMIA Integration
Integrating UMIA is optimal for our DAO token distribution and is essential for securing the financing needed to scale the project.
Furthermore, it strengthens company governance through decision markets. Our DAO is built on the core belief that markets are the ultimate predictors; therefore, implementing them into our own decision-making mechanisms is both a logical and strategic move.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Each prediction market gets a <slug>.kowalski.eth subname that AI agents discover, pay for, and consume — without API keys, accounts, or off-chain config.

 - Self-describing API contract on-chain. Text records api / api-input / price tell the agent where to call, what body to send, and how much to pay in USDC.
 - Cross-chain live state mirror. Indexer streams MarketCreated / Resolved events from Base Sepolia → ENS text records on Ethereum Sepolia (status, outcome, expiresAt) update within seconds. ENS is not just a snapshot — it's a real-time on-chain projection of market state.
 - Agent flow in 3 RPC calls. Resolve subname → POST endpoint → 402 challenge → sign USDC → retry → signed intelligence. No SDK, no docs, no allowlist. Wallet = identity, payment = auth.
 - Beyond name → address. ENS becomes the addressing layer for x402-paywalled data oracles. The pattern generalizes to any priced resource — ENS as the universal directory for the agent payment economy.
 - Live & functional. 9 markets registered on Eth Sepolia via custom MarketSubnameRegistrar + MarketResolver contracts. Verifiable end-to-end: cast call returns the URL → curl returns 402 → demo script ships with the repo.

description.title: Apify Bounty
description.body:
AI agents reasoning about prediction markets need real-time web data — tweets, news, Reddit, sentiment — but lack native payment rails for paid APIs, forcing manual API key provisioning, accounts, and invoices. We wrap Apify actors behind an x402 paywall: autonomous agents hit our /v1/intelligence/* endpoints, the server returns HTTP 402 with payment requirements, the agent signs a USDC transferWithAuthorization on Base Sepolia, retries, and receives fresh scraped data within seconds ($0.50 USDC per call, $0.75 for premium tools, settled via the public x402.org facilitator). The novel piece: we chain two x402 hops in a single user flow — the agent pays us on Base Sepolia, then we pay Apify on Base mainnet, both via x402, producing two visible 402sign200 across both layers. 
Effect: agents become first-class data consumers without manual API key provisioning, accounts, or invoices.

nexora-57a5.name: Nexora
nexora-57a5.tagline: Freelance Platform entirely on DeFi  DAO  AI

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Nexora solves the trust gap at the heart of every online freelance transaction. When a client and a freelancer who have never met agree to work together, there is no neutral, transparent system guaranteeing fairness for both sides. Centralised platforms like Upwork or Fiverr act as judge, jury, and fee collector simultaneously — charging up to 20% in fees while making opaque, unappealable decisions about disputes behind closed doors. Freelancers face delayed payments and subjective rulings. Clients struggle with vague deliverables and limited recourse when work falls short.
Nexora replaces the middleman with a verifiable, trustless stack.
For Clients

AI-assisted task creation — instead of writing a vague brief and hoping for the best, Nexora's AI co-pilot structures your task into a precise specification with measurable acceptance criteria, milestone breakdowns, and deliverable formats. Both sides know exactly what "done" means before work begins.
Funds locked in smart contract escrow — your payment is secured on-chain from day one. No platform can freeze it, redirect it, or charge hidden fees. It releases only when work is verified — automatically, transparently, and on your terms.
Verified freelancer ratings — every freelancer's skill level is represented by an AI-evaluated Elo rating, not self-reported experience. You see a verified track record, not a curated portfolio.

For Freelancers

Guaranteed payment — once you complete work that meets the agreed spec, the escrow releases automatically. No chasing invoices, no waiting on client goodwill, no platform deciding to hold your funds.
Fair dispute resolution — if a client disputes your work unfairly, a decentralised jury of qualified community members reviews the evidence and decides — not a customer support agent with no accountability.
Portable reputation — your Elo rating and work history live in your ENS identity, not inside Nexora's database. Take your reputation with you to any platform that reads it.

For the Ecosystem

DAO-governed disputes — contested work is resolved by a community jury using a blind voting system that prevents groupthink. Jurors stake tokens on their verdicts and are rewarded for honest participation, creating a self-sustaining court system with real skin in the game.
Newcomer discovery incentives — clients who hire new freelancers earn token rewards, solving the cold-start problem that locks talented newcomers out of traditional platforms.
Zero platform lock-in — no company controls your account, your reputation, or your funds. Nexora is a protocol, not a gatekeeper.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges We Ran Into
Making the AI evaluator trustless
Our first approach called the OpenAI API from the frontend and passed results directly to the contract — anyone could fake an evaluation. The fix was giving the evaluator its own Ethereum wallet that signs every Completion Report. The escrow contract only accepts results signed by the registered evaluator address. A security constraint turned into the core design feature that made the agent real.

Preventing jurors from influencing each other
We built the dispute screen showing a live vote tally — standard DAO behaviour. Testing immediately revealed the problem: late voters just copy early voters. We fixed this at two levels simultaneously: commit-reveal voting in the contract makes it cryptographically impossible to see others' choices early, and the UI deliberately hides all juror reasoning until after you've committed your own vote. The frontend information sequencing mirrors the on-chain cryptographic guarantee.

ENS reputation update costs
Writing every Elo change directly to ENS text records on L1 cost more in gas than most task values. Solution: reputation changes live in our ReputationStore contract on L2 (cheap per update), with ENS records updated in batches via a CCIP-Read offchain resolver. Reputation stays portable and readable from ENS — just not updated on every single action.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: At its core Nexora is on-chain economic infrastructure. The smart escrow system handles programmable milestone payments between pseudonymous parties without any intermediary holding funds. The DWK token creates a self-sustaining incentive loop — jurors stake to participate, earn for honest verdicts, and lose for bad ones. Freelancer Elo ratings are AI-evaluated and stored on-chain, creating verifiable economic identities that travel across platforms. Every economic interaction on Nexora — hiring, paying, disputing, voting — is transparent, auditable, and user-controlled.

description.title: Future Society
description.body: Nexora is a direct answer to the coordination failures in the global freelance economy. We replace a centralised, opaque gatekeeper with a transparent protocol where funds are governed by smart contracts, disputes are resolved by the community, and reputation is owned by the individual. The platform empowers freelancers who have historically had no recourse against unfair rulings, and gives clients verifiable guarantees that no traditional platform can offer. Governance, fairness, and economic autonomy are not features we added — they are the architecture.

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body: Nexora is built to function as an agentic venture from day one. The AI evaluator operates as a fully autonomous on-chain agent — it has its own wallet, stakes DWK tokens on its assessments, pays for IPFS storage from its own treasury, and loses stake when the DAO overrides its judgment. It improves its model based on override feedback, creating a self-correcting loop with no human in the middle. The platform generates real revenue through a 1-3% fee on every escrow release, flowing directly to the DAO treasury governed by DWK token holders through Umia's decision markets. The DWK token has five concrete utilities — dispute staking, juror rewards, governance voting, reputation boosting, and fee discounts — making it a functional token, not a speculative one. Post-hackathon, Nexora will apply for a Tailored Auction on Umia, giving early community members (freelancers and clients who used the platform at launch) priority access via zkTLS proofs of their on-chain activity.

description.title: Best ENS Integration for AI Agents
description.body: The Nexora AI evaluator is not a backend service — it is an on-chain agent with its own wallet and ENS identity at evaluator.nexora.eth. Its capabilities, model version, accuracy rate, total evaluations, and specialisations are stored in ENS text records and publicly readable by anyone. When the escrow contract needs a completion assessment, it resolves evaluator.nexora.eth to find the agent's wallet, routes the evaluation request to it, and the agent signs its Completion Report with that wallet before submitting the IPFS hash on-chain. Removing ENS from this flow breaks it entirely — the contract has no other way to discover, authenticate, or trust the evaluator. Multiple specialised agents (code-eval.nexora.eth, design-eval.nexora.eth) can be registered as subnames with different capability records, enabling domain-specific evaluation routing.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body: Nexora uses ENS in three ways that go well beyond name-to-address resolution. First, juror access tokens — when a dispute jury is assembled, each selected juror receives a temporary ENS subname (juror-3.dispute-42.nexora.eth). Only wallets resolving to a valid juror subname can decrypt the encrypted dispute evidence on IPFS. When the dispute closes, subnames are revoked. ENS becomes a time-limited, role-based cryptographic access credential. Second, portable reputation — every freelancer's Elo rating, task history, and DAO reputation score live in their ENS text records at alice.nexora.eth. Any external platform can read this data by resolving the name — no API, no permission, no lock-in. Third, multichain payment routing — clients pay alice.nexora.eth regardless of which chain she prefers. ENSIP-9 coin types in her text records route the payment to the right address on the right chain automatically.

hallmark-3bb7.name: Hallmark
hallmark-3bb7.tagline: Ever wanted to have resume of your work onchain?

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Smart contracts are deployed anonymously — wallets, auditors, and agents have no standard way to judge if a contract is safe, verified, or trustworthy before interacting.

Hallmark solves this by giving every contract a structured **trust score** (0–100) built from five axes: source verification via Sourcify, pattern recognition, risk flags, ecosystem adoption, and static security checks. It also generates a **developer resume** — an aggregated view of all contracts a wallet has deployed across 10+ chains, with verification rates and risk summaries.

The **Agent tab** exposes an on-chain AI agent identity using ENS + ENSIP-26 text records, letting autonomous agents carry verifiable credentials on-chain rather than in a backend database.

Key integrations:
- **Sourcify**: full/partial match drives 0–20 of the verification score axis
- **ENS**: human-readable contract names + AI agent identity (ENSIP-26 subnames as agent credentials)
- **Blockscout**: multi-chain contract discovery across 10 EVM networks
- **OLI labels**: open labeling initiative data for contract classification

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Building a streaming analysis pipeline that fetches contract data from Blockscout, Sourcify, and ENS simultaneously without blocking the UI was the hardest part. We solved this with a server-sent events (SSE) stream from the API — each pipeline step fires a progress event so the UI updates in real time rather than waiting on a monolithic response.

Scoring normalization across five independent axes (each 0–20) required careful calibration so the total (0–100) feels meaningful: a contract with no Sourcify match but clean security still scores respectably, while a high-risk unverified contract bottoms out clearly.

The ENS agent identity layer (ENSIP-26) required writing a custom text record schema for agent metadata — there was no existing standard we could drop in, so we defined one compatible with EIP-7694 drafts and stored it on Sepolia ENS subnames.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body: Hallmark builds foundational trust infrastructure for Ethereum contracts. Every contract gets a deterministic ENS subname (`{addr6}.resume.{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth`) carrying a structured 0–100 trust score across five axes: source verification, pattern classification, static security analysis, risk flags, and ecosystem adoption. The result is written as ENS text records — permanently queryable by any wallet, agent, or tool with no backend dependency. Developer resumes aggregate all deployed contracts under a single namespace, making the contract layer of Ethereum navigable and auditable for the first time. This is core Ethereum usability work: making contracts safer to interact with, easier to evaluate, and harder to obfuscate.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: Hallmark tackles on-chain identity at two levels. For developers: a portable resume lives entirely in ENS — `resume.{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth` — no centralized store, no API key, no trust in Hallmark's infrastructure. For AI agents: the analysis agent carries a full ENSIP-26 identity (`agent-context`, `agent-endpoint[sse]` text records on its ENS subname), so any caller can verify who scored a contract and how to reach the agent's SSE endpoint. Every contract name includes an `issued-by` text record pointing back to the agent ENS name, forming a verifiable provenance chain. Identity and economic reputation are fully on-chain, user-controlled, and censorship-resistant.

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body: Sourcify verification is a first-class scoring axis in Hallmark — not a badge, but a scored signal. Full match contributes the full 20 points; partial match contributes 10; unverified contracts score 0 on this axis regardless of other signals. We call the Sourcify API live during every analysis pass and write the match type (`exact_match`, `partial_match`, `unverified`) as an ENS text record (`sourcify-verified`), making the result permanently on-chain and queryable without re-hitting Sourcify. This brings Sourcify's 27M+ contract dataset directly to end users and creates a strong incentive loop: verified contracts score higher, rank better in developer resumes, and are more trusted by agents — making verification economically rational.

description.title: Best ENS Integration for AI Agents
description.body: The Hallmark agent is an autonomous on-chain actor with a real ENSIP-26 identity — not a cosmetic ENS name. Its subname carries `agent-context` (JSON with model, version, capabilities, and URL to the security pattern.json living on our github), `agent-endpoint[sse]` (the live SSE analysis endpoint), `agent-endpoint[api]`, and `issued-by` records. Any client can discover the agent, verify its identity, and call it using only ENS — no hardcoded URLs, no centralized registry. The agent uses this identity functionally: it signs OLI attestations on Base under its ENS name, writes `issued-by` records on every contract it scores, and mints the entire developer resume namespace autonomously. ENS is the agent's credential system, service discovery layer, and trust anchor simultaneously.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body: Hallmark uses ENS in a way we haven't seen elsewhere: a four-level hierarchical subname tree as a portable identity and reputation system. The agent wallet owns `hallmarked.eth` and registers `{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth` → `resume.{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth` → `{addr6}.resume.{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth` for every contract a developer scores. The leaf name carries the full trust profile as text records. Reading back is done via direct `readContract` calls on the public resolver using `namehash` — same pattern as ENSIP-26 agent identity — bypassing the full ENS resolution chain entirely. The ENS namespace *is* the developer resume: enumerate all subnames under `resume.{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth` and you have their complete verified contract history, queryable by anyone, owned by the developer.

trololilo-611a.name: Manoli
trololilo-611a.tagline: get a quote from prediction market for your asset

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Traditional insurance is slow, opaque, and limited to standardized products. Anyone who wants to hedge a specific real-world risk — a missed flight, a bad harvest, a geopolitical event, a volatile crypto price — has no easy way to do it.

Insurance broker solves this by turning Polymarket's deep prediction-market liquidity into an instant, chat-driven hedging desk:

- **Describe your risk in plain language.** The LLM finds the right Polymarket market for your event.
- **Get a precise quote.** The broker computes the correct YES/NO position size against your dollar exposure, including expected ROI and cost.
- **Place the trade in one click.** After explicit confirmation, it submits the on-chain order through the Polymarket CLOB — no trading UI, no manual position sizing.

In short: it converts any insurable event into an executed, on-chain hedge in seconds.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**1. Mapping free-text risk descriptions to Polymarket markets**
Users describe risks in natural language (e.g. "I'm worried about a Bitcoin crash"). The hardest part was building a reliable routing layer that maps these descriptions to actual Polymarket market slugs across categories — weather, politics, crypto, sports, entertainment — and gracefully tells the user when no matching market exists.

**2. Correct hedge sizing math**
Computing the right YES/NO share quantity to fully offset a user's dollar exposure (not just buy an arbitrary amount) required careful `computeHedge` / `quoteFromMarket` logic accounting for current market prices and implied probabilities.

**3. Safe on-chain trading flow**
The trading flow spans wallet creation, USDC + MATIC funding, one-time CLOB approvals on Polygon, and finally order placement — all while never placing an order without explicit user confirmation in chat. Getting the state machine right and recovering gracefully from partial states (e.g. wallet funded but approvals not run) was tricky.

**4. Streaming tool calls with real-time UI state**
Integrating the AI SDK's streaming responses with live wallet/trade state updates in the Next.js UI — keeping the chat reactive while tool calls run asynchronously — required careful coordination between server actions and client components.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Lumen - Cryptographically Safe Whistleblowing

Workers who witness corporate misconduct face an impossible choice: speak up and lose your livelihood, or stay silent and watch it happen again.

Lumen makes whistleblowing cryptographically safe.

A worker proves they are a verified employee of a company without revealing who they are. The proof is a RISC Zero ZK-STARK anchored to a Poseidon Merkle tree of employee badges managed on-chain. The report goes to IPFS; the proof goes on Sepolia. No one - not the company, not the platform, not even Lumen - can link the submission back to an individual.

HOW IT WORKS

For Employees

Submit structured disclosures (misconduct, misclassification, misleading ESG claims, selective disclosure, hollow promises, in-name-only programs) with sanitized evidence - EXIF-stripped images, XMP-cleaned PDFs - so metadata cannot de-anonymize you.

You get a pseudonymous ENS subname like worker-7f3a.workers.acme.lumen-demo.eth that builds credibility across multiple reports without ever revealing your identity. Each report carries a nullifier (prevents double-filing per quarter) and a Merkle root freshness check (proves your badge was valid when the report was filed).

For Journalists and Researchers

Browse a public feed of on-chain-verified reports, filterable by company or category. Every report includes a cryptographically auditable paper trail, verifiable via standard eth_call.

Want deeper context? Purchase AI-enriched context packs via X402 micropayments (1 USDC on Base, powered by Apify) without touching a subscription or creating an account. Pay once, access immediately, no signup friction.

For Company Compliance Teams

See a live signal of internal sentiment you cannot suppress. Reports are immutable once the ZK proof is verified on-chain. The journal digest is verified by the RISC Zero router on Sepolia - mathematical proof, not trust.

For Investors and Regulators

Every report carries a nullifier (prevents double-filing per quarter), a Merkle root freshness check (badge was valid when filed), and a journal digest verified by the RISC Zero router on Sepolia. All readable via standard eth_call - no proprietary APIs.

ONBOARDING: NO WALLET, NO PROBLEM

A worker enters their work email, receives an OTP to verify domain ownership, and the backend derives a deterministic badge secret from a hash of the verified email domain.

A single claimBadge transaction (optionally gasless via ERC-2771 meta-transactions) places them in the Merkle tree. No wallet seed phrase is ever linked to an email address - the ZK proof is the only bridge between on-chain verification and off-chain identity.

Once claimed, the worker downloads their badge as a JSON file. That is their key. Losing it means losing the ability to file under that pseudonym, but it can never be traced back to their email.

INTEGRATIONS

Apify Context Packs (Live on Base)

When a journalist clicks "Enrich this report," Lumen triggers a 402 HTTP challenge. The frontend prompts the user to sign an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization typed-data payload for 1 USDC on Base mainnet. Apify verifies the transfer, runs a web scraping and LLM enrichment job cross-referencing the report against public filings, news articles, Glassdoor reviews, and SEC disclosures, and returns an IPFS CID of the enrichment pack within 60 seconds. No credit card, no subscription wall, no email signup.

Umia Trustless Compute (Future)

For automated verification of structured claims, Lumen is designed to integrate Umia's verifiable LLM inference. A ZK proof of the LLM inference is posted on-chain alongside the report's proof - cryptographic proof of both who filed the report and that an AI verified the claim's plausibility, without trusting the AI provider or Lumen.

THE STACK

Identity: ENS subnames for pseudonymous reputation (worker-7f3a.workers.acme.lumen-demo.eth)
ZK Proofs: RISC Zero zkVM (STARK), on-chain verification via Sepolia
Membership: Poseidon Merkle tree (depth 16, BN254 field) with 7-day root freshness
Storage: IPFS (Pinata) for reports and evidence, canonical JSON (RFC 8785)
Key Management: Space KMS (Orbitport) for secure badge credential storage
Payments: X402 (EIP-3009 USDC on Base) via Apify for context packs
Anti-replay: Nullifiers prevent double-filing per quarter (90 days)
Evidence sanitization: EXIF stripping (images), XMP removal (PDFs via qpdf)

WHY THIS MATTERS NOW

Greenwashing is a $2.4B/year problem. Workers see it first. But without protection, they cannot speak.

Lumen flips the incentive: filing a report is safer than staying silent. The proof is public. The identity is not. The truth is immutable.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges We Overcame
 1.⁠ ⁠Development vs. Production ZK Proof Verification
The production RISC Zero verifier on Sepolia rejected our development-mode proofs during initial testing. We implemented a mock verifier path that accepts dev proofs for rapid iteration while preserving the real verification flow for mainnet deployment.

 2.⁠ ⁠Cross-Language Cryptographic Serialization
Matching the ZK circuit's proof journal format with Solidity's ABI encoding required deep coordination between Rust and EVM serialization standards. We locked the encoding contract with cross-platform test vectors to prevent silent failures.

 3.⁠ ⁠Hash Function Constant Alignment Across ZK and EVM
Our Poseidon hash implementation needed identical round constants and domain separation tags in both the zero-knowledge circuit (Rust) and on-chain verification (Solidity). A single mismatch causes silent Merkle proof failures with no revert reason.

 4.⁠ ⁠ENS Permission Model vs. Worker Anonymity
ENS subname text records require admin signatures, but workers must remain pseudonymous. We redesigned the flow to decouple on-chain report verification from ENS metadata writes.

 5.⁠ ⁠HTTP Multipart Handling in Async Proof Pipeline
File upload middleware wasn't registered in the Fastify instance, causing runtime-only failures that TypeScript couldn't catch at compile time. We added startup smoke tests to catch configuration errors before deployment.

 6.⁠ ⁠IPFS Content Addressing for Evidence Integrity
Ensuring sanitized evidence files (EXIF-stripped images, XMP-cleaned PDFs) maintained cryptographic integrity while removing metadata required careful hash-then-pin workflows to prevent client-server hash mismatches.

 7.⁠ ⁠Merkle Tree Depth vs. Gas Cost Trade-offs
Balancing tree depth (depth 16 = 65K workers) against ZK proof size and on-chain verification cost. Deeper trees support more workers but increase proof generation time and circuit constraints.

 8.⁠ ⁠Nullifier Uniqueness Across Reporting Periods
Preventing double-filing within a quarter while allowing legitimate repeated reports across quarters required deterministic nullifier derivation tied to both the worker's badge and the time period.

 9.⁠ ⁠Root Rotation Without Invalidating Active Proofs
Companies need to add/remove workers by rotating the badge tree root, but workers mid-submission would have their proofs rejected. We implemented an 8-slot ring buffer with 7-day freshness windows.

10.⁠ ⁠X402 Payment Flow Without Custodial Wallets
Integrating EIP-3009 USDC transfers on Base with HTTP 402 challenges required careful signature validation and replay protection - all without Lumen ever holding user funds.

11.⁠ ⁠Browser-Side ZK Proof Input Generation
Building 16-level Merkle paths client-side in JavaScript using the same Poseidon constants as the Rust circuit, without leaking the worker's badge secret to the backend or leaving it in browser memory.

12.⁠ ⁠Async Proof Generation UX
Real ZK proof generation takes minutes on Boundless, not seconds. We built a polling-based status system with proper timeout handling and fallback to local proving for demos.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
Lumen gives workers a way to whistleblow without getting fired for it.

The problem is simple: the people who witness misconduct inside companies are also the most exposed if they say something. So they don't. Lumen changes that by making it cryptographically impossible to trace a disclosure back to the person who filed it, while keeping the disclosure itself fully verifiable on-chain.

Here is how it works. A worker proves they have a corporate email using ZK-Email, a zero-knowledge proof over DKIM signatures. Their actual email address never leaves the browser. They get an anonymous badge credential, stored in Space KMS, that proves they are a legitimate employee of a specific company without revealing who they are. They file a report. It gets anchored to Ethereum with a hash that ties the content, the company, and the category together. Permanent. Tamper-proof. Untraceable back to them.

This fits Future Society because it is literally a governance tool for the most local community most people belong to: their workplace. Every worker gets exactly one anonymous voice. The Merkle badge tree makes it Sybil-resistant so nobody can spam the system or claim memberships they do not have. And because everything lives on Ethereum, no employer can quietly bury a disclosure or threaten the infrastructure into silence.

Privacy, transparency, fairness. Not as design principles on a slide deck. Actually enforced by the math.

Lumen works today for traditional companies and is a natural fit for DAOs and gig platforms too. Wherever there is a power imbalance between an organisation and the individuals inside it, this is the missing layer.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
Lumen is a whistleblower platform. The entire product stands or falls on one guarantee: that a worker who files a report cannot be identified by their employer. Break that guarantee once, and nobody uses the platform.

That is exactly why Space KMS is not an add-on here. It is load-bearing.

When a worker onboards, Lumen generates a badge credential, a 32-byte secret that proves they are a legitimate employee of a specific company. That badge is the only thing linking their anonymous on-chain identity to a real person. If it ever leaks, the worker is exposed. So we do not store it in a database. We do not store it in a config file. We use Orbitport KMS to create a dedicated hardware-backed Ethereum key for that worker, and we bind the badge metadata to that key inside the KMS boundary. The private key material never leaves. Even if someone fully compromises the Lumen backend server, they cannot extract the badge credentials.

This fits directly into track 3 of the bounty: a secure signing and authorization service where trust and integrity are critical. The KMS key we create per worker is not decorative. It is the cryptographic anchor for that worker's pseudonymous identity. Down the line, that same key can sign on behalf of the worker's pseudonym without ever exposing who they are, enabling things like verifiable reputation without deanonymization.

The integration is intentional because the threat model demands it. A whistleblower platform with credentials stored in Postgres is not a whistleblower platform. It is a liability. Space KMS is what makes the security claim real rather than aspirational.

The depth is there too. We initialise the Orbitport SDK server-side only, credentials never touch the frontend, each badge claim creates a fresh KMS key with tagged metadata for recovery, and the entire flow is integrated into the onboarding transaction confirmation so the worker never has to think about key management at all. It just works, and it works safely.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Lumen uses ENS as its entire identity and credential layer. Not as a name resolver. As infrastructure.

Here is what that actually means.

Every company on Lumen is an ENS name. acme.shieldpass-demo.eth is not a label, it is the primary key. The ENS namehash of that name flows through every smart contract call, every report, every ZK proof. If you want to verify a report is about a specific company, you check the namehash. No hardcoded addresses, no lookup tables. ENS is the canonical source of company identity.

The badge tree root, the cryptographic commitment that proves which workers are legitimate employees, lives in an ENS text record under shieldpass.badge-tree-root. Companies update it on-chain. Anyone can read it. The ZK proof that a worker filed a report verifies against that record. ENS text records are functioning as a decentralized, tamper-proof credential registry.

Worker identities are ENS subnames. When someone onboards, they get a pseudonymous identity like worker-7f3a.workers.acme.shieldpass-demo.eth. They never chose that name. It was derived from their ZK proof. The namehash of that subname is their pseudonymNode, the on-chain handle that ties their anonymous reputation together across every report they file. A custom wildcard resolver (ShieldPassResolver) resolves the entire *.workers.acme.shieldpass-demo.eth namespace, meaning a company can have thousands of anonymous worker identities without registering each one individually.

So ENS is doing three distinct things here at once. It anchors company identity. It stores verifiable credentials as text records. And it generates a scalable namespace of pseudonymous human-readable identities via wildcard resolution, where the subname itself is a membership credential.

That is not a swap-in for a hardcoded string. Without ENS, none of this architecture works.

description.title: Apify Bounty
description.body:
Apify powers our pay-per-use context enrichment feature. When journalists or researchers want deeper analysis on a report, they pay 1 USDC on Base (no subscription, no account signup). Apify's X402 facilitator handles the payment settlement, runs an AI enrichment job that cross-references the report against public filings and news sources, and returns structured JSON that gets pinned to IPFS.

Why It's Novel:
The payment authorization itself becomes the API credential - no custody, no settlement layer on our side. The report's on-chain hash is the payment resource identifier, so the enrichment becomes permanently linked to that specific disclosure via IPFS, not a disposable API response.

Integration Status:
The payment challenge flow and signature handling are implemented. The Apify Actor integration is in various stages of completion depending on final testing outcomes - we've built the plumbing to support both live Actor calls and graceful fallbacks.

Future Vision:
Context packs could evolve into a marketplace of verification agents: multiple specialized Actors (ESG compliance checkers, financial disclosure validators, legal precedent scanners) competing on price and quality. Each enrichment becomes an auditable artifact pinned to the original report, creating a permanent knowledge graph of verified corporate disclosures and their corroborating evidence.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Prague Explorer is a privacy-first geocaching game for EthPrague attendees and Prague tourists. Players find physical QR codes hidden at six real Prague landmarks, scan them in person, answer a Czech history quiz, and claim an on-chain EAS attestation — without the contract ever learning who they are.

**The privacy model is the core innovation.** Presence is proved by combining a per-cache QR secret (only obtainable on-site) with a Semaphore v4 ZK proof generated entirely in the browser (~3 seconds). The contract sees only an opaque nullifier and a display name — never a wallet address, email, or any externally-linked identity. Nullifiers are scoped per-cache (`scope = cacheId`), so claiming two different caches produces cryptographically uncorrelated nullifiers that cannot be linked on-chain.

**Zero friction for users.** Privy embedded wallets let anyone sign in with email or Google — no MetaMask, no seed phrase. A Pimlico ERC-4337 paymaster on Scroll Sepolia covers gas entirely. A successful claim produces an EAS attestation the user owns permanently: a composable, portable credential, not a custodied badge.

**Cultural layer.** Each cache is tied to a real Prague landmark. Cache beneficiary addresses point to Czech cultural institutions that receive optional ETH micro-donations on claim. The app ships in Czech and English.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**In-browser ZK proving.** Integrating Semaphore v4 into a live Next.js frontend was non-trivial: the WASM circuit and proving key total ~6 MB. We preload the key on page mount and display a progress indicator so the ~3-second proving time feels intentional rather than broken.

**ERC-4337 on Scroll Sepolia.** Wiring Pimlico's paymaster with `permissionless` v0.3.5 required careful chain-ID configuration (534351) and handling the case where the paymaster rejects sponsorship. We built a fail-open fallback: if the paymaster declines, the user's EOA pays gas directly — the claim flow never breaks.

**Binding the display name to the proof.** To prevent front-running (changing the displayed name after proof generation), we embed the display name in the Semaphore message field: `message = uint256(keccak256(displayName)) >> 8`. The `>> 8` right-shift is required to fit within BN254's scalar field. Any post-generation name change produces an invalid proof, enforced at the circuit level.

**Semaphore anonymity-set trade-off.** The `joinCache()` call (group membership registration) is observable on-chain — an attacker can see that *someone* is joining cache X, but cannot determine who, because the identity commitment has no link to any external identifier. We mitigate this by funding user wallets from a separate deployer account so the gas-payer address is distinct from the Semaphore identity being registered.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body:
Built entirely on Ethereum's core stack:

- **Scroll Sepolia** — zkEVM L2, full EVM equivalence, EthPrague-native
- **Semaphore v4** — Groth16 ZK proofs for anonymous group membership
- **EAS (Ethereum Attestation Service)** — composable on-chain credentials, one attestation per cache claim
- **ERC-4337 (Pimlico + permissionless v0.3.5)** — Kernel smart accounts, gasless UX
- **Foundry** — 15 passing tests, Deploy.s.sol, contract verified on Scroll Sepolia

All contracts are open-source. The Semaphore verifier and EAS contracts are deployed and reused from their canonical Scroll Sepolia addresses.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Prague Explorer puts user control first at the protocol level. Identity is derived entirely client-side from a QR secret + Privy user ID; the contract never sees a wallet address on claim. Nullifiers are scoped per-cache, making cross-cache linkability cryptographically impossible — even the contract cannot correlate two claims by the same person.

An optional ETH micro-donation on claim routes value directly to a Prague cultural institution's beneficiary address — a lightweight economic layer built into the claim flow with no intermediary and no custodian.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
Prague Explorer embeds Czech cultural heritage directly into Ethereum. Each of the six caches is tied to a real Prague landmark; quiz questions cover Czech history and local significance. Cache beneficiary addresses point to cultural institutions — museums, archives — that receive optional ETH donations on claim.

The app is fully translated into Czech and English and designed so any tourist with a phone and an email address can participate — no crypto background, no wallet app, no gas required. Privacy is not a feature toggle: it is the default, enforced at the circuit level.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
# 🛡️ The Problem It Solves

Demo: https://share.descript.com/view/pnsbObRikUV

### The Challenge: Information Chaos & Adversarial Markets
Traders and participants in futarchic decision markets (such as **Umia**, **MetaDAO**, and **Polymarket**) operate in a high-stakes, high-noise environment. Currently, making an informed decision requires manually tracking scattered signals across Telegram, X (Twitter), Discord, GitHub activity, and on-chain movements. 

This fragmented landscape leads to critical failures:
* **High Cognitive Load:** Participants spend hours cross-referencing data, leading to slow and inefficient decision-making.
* **Vulnerability to Manipulation:** Markets are often swayed by coordinated misinformation and "pump-and-dump" schemes disguised as community consensus.
* **Inefficient Capital Allocation:** Poor information quality results in mispriced risks in high-stakes governance and prediction markets.

---

### The Solution: Umia Analyst Agent
The **Umia Analyst Agent** is an autonomous AI research analyst designed to turn chaotic data into actionable, auditable intelligence. It operates as a continuous intelligence layer that:

* **Smart Ingestion & Weighting:** Automatically classifies signals from multiple sources using a credibility-weighted model (**Verifiable** / **Partial** / **Manipulable**).
* **Adversarial Synthesis:** Generates structured Bull and Bear cases with direct citations, ensuring every claim is backed by evidence.
* **Anti-Manipulation Shield:** Actively flags coordinated manipulation attempts by cross-referencing social hype with on-chain reality.
* **Skin in the Game:** Beyond mere reporting, the agent publishes structured trading memos, takes its own positions, and maintains a public, transparent PnL track record.

---

### 🚀 Key Benefits
| **For Traders** | **For Protocols** | **For the Ecosystem** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Reduces research time from hours to seconds. | Improves the quality of governance decisions. | Enhances market efficiency and liquidity. |
| Minimizes exposure to social engineering. | Attracts informed capital via clear reporting. | Reduces the success rate of malicious actors. |
| Provides an auditable trail of logic for every trade. | Hardens the futarchy mechanism against "noise." | Sets a new standard for AI-driven financial transparency. |

**The Umia Analyst Agent doesn't just provide data—it provides the "Signal" necessary to navigate the "Noise" of decentralized governance.**

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
# Challenges WE Ran Into

Building the **Umia Analyst Agent** presented several unique technical and conceptual hurdles. Our goal was to move beyond simple "AI wrappers" and build a resilient, institutional-grade engineering system.

### 1. Adversarial Information Filtering
The biggest challenge was creating a system that doesn't just aggregate data but actively resists manipulation. In futarchic markets, we found that social signals (Telegram/X) are often heavily manipulated by proposal authors to create "fake consensus."
* **The Solution:** We implemented a **Source Classification Layer**. We assigned deterministic weights to data: verifiable sources (on-chain transactions, GitHub commits) are weighted at `1.0`, while manipulable social channels are strictly capped at `0.3`.

### 2. Ensuring Agentic Reliability
Standard LLM prompts often suffer from "hallucinations" or "groupthink." In a financial context, we couldn't risk the agent making biased or "hallucinated" trading recommendations.
* **The Solution:** We utilized a **LangGraph-based multi-node architecture**. By separating the pipeline into distinct stages—Source Classification, Synthesis, and Position-taking—and adding an autonomous **Self-Reviewer** node (the "Advocatus Diaboli"), we forced the agent to argue against its own conclusions before finalizing a memo.

### 3. Domain Shift & Architecture Repurposing
We started with a robust pipeline designed for corporate credit underwriting and had to transform it into a DeFi intelligence tool within 48 hours. Mapping "banking risk" to "governance risk" required a total overhaul of the business logic.
* **The Solution:** We maintained the underlying "plumbing" (deterministic logic gates, audit trails, and versioned skills) while completely swapping the domain layers. This allowed us to preserve institutional-grade reliability while moving at hackathon speed.

### 4. Data Ingestion Latency
Scraping decentralized forums and GitHub activity in real-time is computationally expensive and prone to rate limits.
* **The Solution:** We developed a dual-mode ingestion system. For the demo, we use a high-fidelity mock-market layer based on historical MetaDAO proposals, while the production environment is designed to utilize Apify actors for fresh signal ingestion.

### 5. Ecosystem Early-Stage Adaptation (The MetaDAO Bridge)
Since Umia’s native decision markets are currently in their earliest stages, we faced a "cold start" problem regarding live data for testing our agent's predictive accuracy.
* **The Solution:** We chose to stress-test our agent on **MetaDAO** (the pioneer of futarchy). This is a strategic advantage: by proving our agent can navigate the most adversarial and "noisy" established market in the space, we ensure it will be the most robust and battle-tested analyst the moment Umia’s mainnet markets go live. We aren't just building for a sandbox; we are building for the open ocean.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: We built Mochifi — an autonomous research analyst that makes futarchic decision markets function the way they were designed to. Today, governance markets suffer from thin liquidity and uninformed traders: social signals are manipulated, on-chain data is unread, and most token holders vote blind. Our agent ingests every signal — GitHub commits, on-chain wallet flows, Telegram, X — classifies each source by verifiability, and publishes an institutional-grade trading memo with a YES/NO/ABSTAIN position scaled by confidence. It then tracks its own realized PnL as markets resolve. We're not building another DAO dashboard. We're building the Bloomberg Terminal that makes decentralized governance economically rational.

description.title: Future Society

Our agent implements adversarial information filtering — verifiable on-chain data is weighted at 1.0, manipulable social signals are capped at 0.3 — and forces itself to argue against its own conclusions through an autonomous Self-Reviewer node before publishing any memo. The result is a system where governance decisions get priced on facts, not coordinated shilling. We believe this is what the next generation of community-driven organizations needs: not just a voting mechanism, but an intelligence layer that makes every vote worth casting.
