description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Wallet popups ask "approve this transaction?" — a question users can't actually answer. They can't read the calldata, can't tell whether the contract is real, can't tell whether the website is who it claims to be, and have no idea what will happen if they sign. This is how drainers work: the page says "free NFT mint", the wallet shows opaque hex, and the user signs.

Evzi closes that loop. Before any signature reaches a wallet, we infer what the user is **trying** to do (from page context, click target, and a small LLM), decode the calldata or EIP-712 typed data into a structured action, look the contract up against a hand-curated cross-chain registry, query Sourcify for source verification, simulate the transaction against a live Tenderly fork, classify the origin domain against known phishing patterns, and ask an LLM judge to compare every signal against the stated intent.

The verdict is one sentence and a checklist of every signal — so the user sees the work, learns the patterns, and can disagree. Two-way constraint: the LLM can't soften a deterministic DANGER (UNLIMITED_APPROVAL stays DANGER), and can't escalate a vetted protocol to DANGER on a hunch.

What we explicitly catch today:
- "Free NFT mint" that's actually `USDC.approve(0xdEaD…, MAX_UINT256)` — page description doesn't match the calldata.
- Permit2 batch-transfer signatures to unknown spenders — the off-chain drainer that bypasses simulation entirely.
- Lookalike origin domains: `unisvvap.org`, punycode/IDN homographs, `aavve.com`.
- Unverified-but-canonical routers — fresh Uniswap deployments that outpace Sourcify verification.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Three problems stand out.

**1. Off-chain Permit2 batch-transfer drainers.** The worst class of attack today because they bypass simulation entirely — there's no on-chain transaction to simulate, just a signed message that authorizes a third party to move multiple tokens. We built a typed-data decoder that recognizes Permit2 single + batch shapes (and Seaport zero-price offers) and explicitly emits `PERMIT2_SPENDER_UNKNOWN` as a deterministic finding the LLM can't soften.

**2. The "verified vs trusted" tension.** Sourcify is the right way to check source-availability, but Uniswap deploys faster than Sourcify verifies — so a strictly Sourcify-driven verdict would flag the most-used router on Ethereum as suspicious. We treat the protocol registry and Sourcify as separate signals and explain the trade-off in the verdict: *"Sourcify: not verified, but this matches a canonical Uniswap UR address."* The end user sees both facts and the resolution.

**3. Two-way LLM constraint.** We give the LLM judge enough context to flag subtle intent/action mismatches the deterministic layer can't articulate. But we don't let it soften deterministic DANGERs (UNLIMITED_APPROVAL stays DANGER even if the LLM finds the request "reasonable"), and we don't let it escalate vetted protocols based on a hunch. **Safety floor + trust ceiling.**

**Bonus:** Uniswap UR sentinel addresses (`0x…0001` = msg.sender, `0x…0002` = router-self) used to be flagged as "third-party drain" by naive analyzers. We resolve them so normal Uniswap routing reads as normal.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body:
Evzi is a working Chromium extension that materially improves Ethereum's two biggest UX failures:

**1. "Approve this transaction?" prompts where users can't read what they're signing.** We turn raw calldata into a plain-English checklist: decoded action, simulated outcome (Tenderly), Sourcify status, origin-trust verdict, and an LLM judgment of whether all of that matches what the user said they were trying to do. The product is the popup — every check we run is shown to the user.

**2. Permit2 / EIP-712 off-chain signature drainers that bypass simulation entirely.** These are the biggest class of attack today, and most users don't even realize they're signing a transferable token-spend authorization. We have a dedicated typed-data decoder for Permit2 single + batch + Seaport that names the specific spender and the tokens at risk, with a deterministic finding code the LLM cannot override.

The result is practical, deployable, and improves Ethereum's usability and security on day one — exactly what "build practical tools and prototypes that directly improve Ethereum's usability and security" asks for. ~100 unit tests across decoder, judge, origin-trust, protocol-registry, sourcify-client, tenderly-client, and token-metadata.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
The verdict is a checklist, not a black box. Every signal — Sourcify status, Tenderly simulation outcome, origin-trust, decoded action, LLM judgment — is shown to the user with a one-sentence explanation of **what** it means and **why** it matters.

The **Talk-to-Evzi** chat overlay turns the popup into a teaching surface:

- *Verdict-aware mode:* "Why is this dangerous?" returns a real answer that cites the specific findings (*"The Permit2 batch transfer would let 0xdEaD… move 3 of your tokens with just a signature — no on-chain transaction. That's why it's DANGER."*).
- *General mode:* "What's an approval?" or "How do drainers usually work?" — Evzi answers as a Web3 safety teacher.

We treat security as something to **teach**, not gate. Empowerment over paternalism, transparency over black-box trust signals, and a path for users to learn to recognize patterns themselves so they need the agent less over time.

That's the Future Society pitch: a tool that makes its users meaningfully more competent, not just more dependent on the tool.

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body:
Our `sourcify-client` package is one layer in our deterministic check pipeline. Every transaction Evzi inspects gets a Sourcify lookup, and the result is shown in the verdict checklist with a one-line explanation an end user can actually understand — turning *verified-on-Sourcify* from a niche developer concept into something a wallet user sees and learns to look for.

The interesting part is what we do when Sourcify says **not verified**: we don't blindly escalate to DANGER. Uniswap deploys faster than Sourcify verifies, and a strictly Sourcify-driven verdict would flag the most-used router on Ethereum as suspicious. So we treat the protocol registry and Sourcify as **separate signals** — the verdict explicitly explains the trade-off:

> *"Sourcify: not verified, but this matches a canonical Uniswap UR address."*

We're treating Sourcify as a strong signal, not the only one, and surfacing its outcome to end users in a way that builds verification literacy over time.

Why this matters for the bounty: most projects integrate Sourcify as a backend dependency. We integrate it as a **user-facing signal**, with thoughtful handling for the unverified-but-canonical edge case — and we show every Sourcify result in the popup with plain-English explanations of what it means.

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body:
**Evzi is an agent stack, not a single LLM call.**

Every wallet request fans out through a typed pipeline of specialized tools, then converges through a judge:

1. **Click + form context capture** — content-script tool that records the button text, surrounding form values, and the section heading the user just clicked.
2. **Intent inference (LLM #1)** — a small, cheap model (`gpt-5.1`) turns that snapshot into a concrete user intent ("Swap 0.0007 ETH for 8.65 OP on Uniswap"), which the user can edit before continuing.
3. **Calldata decoder** — typed recognizer for ERC-20, Uniswap UR, Aave v3, Permit, Permit2 (single + batch), and Seaport, producing `DecodedAction`s with explicit finding codes (`UNLIMITED_APPROVAL`, `PERMIT2_SPENDER_UNKNOWN`, `SEAPORT_ZERO_PRICE_OFFER`, …).
4. **Protocol registry** — hand-curated cross-chain whitelist of canonical Uniswap, Aave, Permit2, Seaport, ENS addresses.
5. **Sourcify client** — source-verification lookup with proxy resolution, deployment age, NatSpec userdoc, and a generic ABI decoder.
6. **Tenderly simulation** — runs the tx against a live fork; we extract per-asset signed deltas for the user's wallet.
7. **Origin-trust classifier** — Levenshtein + punycode + bundled known-dApp list to catch lookalike domains (`unisvvap.org`, `aavve.com`, IDN homographs).
8. **Judge (LLM #2)** — compares stated intent against decoded action + simulation + findings + origin, under a hard two-way constraint: the judge **cannot soften** a deterministic DANGER (UNLIMITED_APPROVAL stays DANGER even if the LLM finds the request "reasonable") and **cannot escalate** a vetted protocol on a hunch. *Safety floor + trust ceiling.*

Plus a separate teaching agent — **Talk to Evzi** — that runs in two modes: *verdict-aware* (cites specific findings: "the Permit2 batch transfer would let 0xdEaD… move 3 of your tokens with just a signature — that's why it's DANGER") and *general* ("what's an approval?", "how do drainers work?") so users learn the patterns themselves.

**Why this is the agentic venture worth rewarding.** Single-shot LLM safety oracles are easy to fool — they hallucinate, they soften scary things to avoid annoying users, they have no ground truth. Evzi is the opposite: multi-tool orchestration with a deterministic safety floor *and* a trust ceiling, a second agent dedicated to transparency, and a UI that exposes every step of the agent's reasoning. The user sees the work, learns the patterns, and can disagree.

**Post-hackathon plan.** Extend the tool set (more typed-data shapes, more chains, more recognized protocols), ship a public registry of safe-but-unverified addresses other wallet-safety teams can plug into, and explore Umia as a deployment target for the Talk-to-Evzi teaching agent.

noctwave-8e66.name: Noctwave
noctwave-8e66.tagline: Create now - Watch forever - Stay unseen.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
**Creators are getting screwed**, badly. Twitch, Patreon, and OF regularly skim 20-30% of every dollar, censor content on a whim, and track every subscriber through IP addresses and payment processors. 

Fans want privacy but get doxxed. The creator economy keeps getting hit after hit. 

**Something has to *change.***

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
We hit a few real technical walls, but the biggest ones were:

**Cross-chain complexity:** ENS lived on Ethereum Sepolia while the app ran on Base Sepolia, so we had to explicitly pin every contract read/write to the right network or things silently broke.

**Swarm publishing and retrieval:** getting uploads working in the browser was not enough — the Bee node had to stay server-side, and Swarm feeds turned out to overwrite state unless we merged and rewrote the full feed each time.

**Video processing in the browser:** ffmpeg.wasm needed extra browser isolation headers, which caused a lot of deployment friction before transcoding would run consistently.

**In the end, we fixed it by separating what had to happen on-chain, what had to happen server-side, and what could safely happen in the browser.**

That gave us a stable upload, subscribe, and playback flow that actually works in production.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
Noctwave is proof that people can own and share digital culture without handing control to platforms.

**We developed privacy, creator ownership, and decentralized infrastructure into a real consumer product** - which is exactly the kind of society-shaping use case we believe this main track has set out to discover.

We deeply believe that identity, payments, and content access can be separated from surveillance. 

Instead of a platform deciding who gets seen, who gets paid, or who gets censored, **Noctwave lets creators and viewers interact directly on open rails.**

description.title: Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway
description.body:
**Swarm’s content-addressed retrieval re-enabled clean, non-algorithmic discovery which we lost no so long ago.**

And we built Noctwave upon that very idea: that viewers should not need to trust a random gateway or a centralized backend to discover content. 

**The watch flow resolves the creator, reads the pointer, and fetches the actual post from Swarm.**

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body:
**Key-Value Store gives creators on Noctwave a simple, updateable state layer *without putting everything on-chain.***

Noctwave uses Swarm for the app’s mutable metadata layer: bios, captions, prices, post lists, and feed pointers.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Noctwave enables **ENS as the actual human-readable identity layer for a full creator platform**, not just a login gimmick.

Instead of "connect wallet," users discover channels via alice.noctwave.eth, subscribe to them directly, and use text records to fetch private metadata, pricing, and content pointers. 

**With Noctwave, we turned ENS into a creator-owned homepage for video subscriptions** — something we feel is the natural evolution of ENS beyond wallets and websites.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## Ethereum as an Operating System for temporary societies

No rollup deploy. No sequencer config. No bridge. No infra hell. A blockchain that comes into existence the way a group chat does.

**A new mental model.** Not one global ledger that everyone shares — *millions of small social chains*, each with its own:

- consensus (one-member-one-vote or stake-weighted PoS)
- economy (shared ETH pool, off-chain signed cheques)
- rules (invite policy, channel write policy, TTL)
- privacy (E2E encrypted chat, ECDH DMs, seed-in-fragment invites)
- reputation (membership, stake, voting history)

…but security and settlement *inherit from Ethereum*. One `ChainPool` contract holds the funds and verifies every signed transfer.

**Chains don't have to be permanent.** A chain can run for 2 hours. Or a festival. Or a hack night. Or a protest. Or a research team. Or this hackathon.

**You don't connect to a chain — you get invited.** The invite is a QR code carrying a shared secret. Joining is one wallet signature. Your identity inside is a fresh ephemeral key, scoped only to that chain. Stricter chains require a vouching signature from a member or the creator, enforced cryptographically by every honest client.

**Chains can physically overlap.** Right now at ETHPrague there could be 400 invisible PocketChains in this room. You bump into someone, scan a QR, unlock access. Part Pokémon GO, part BitTorrent, part secret society — all settled on Ethereum.

**Chains can die.** Inactive blockchains are eternal zombies. PocketChains aren't. When a community goes quiet, the chain dissolves — but its history compresses into an encrypted artifact you can keep, restore, or share.

PocketChains is what Ethereum looks like as infrastructure for ephemeral, sovereign social spaces.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**Peer-to-peer state that survives.** Our messaging layer is a transport, not a database — messages gossip between peers and may not be cached anywhere reliable. But a chain needs history (chat, members, pending transfers). We made every member a temporary archive: they hold the raw envelope log and can export it as an encrypted backup. A fresh browser pulls history from peers when it can, and falls back to restored backups when it can't. The chain is peer-to-peer but rebuildable from any single member's state.

**Debugging an encrypted system.** Most traffic is opaque on the wire — chat is AES-GCM, DMs use ECDH between ephemeral keys. A "missing message" could be a peer issue, a key mismatch, a wrong recipient, or a member who hasn't republished. We added structured logging at every replay boundary that dumps signature recoveries and policy decisions but never plaintext, so we can trace failures without leaking anyone's chat.

**Setting up Swarm for encrypted backups.** We wanted users to lose their browser and still recover their chain. Swarm fit — decentralized, content-addressed — but getting it running took work: a local Bee light node, a funded Bee wallet on Gnosis Chain, and a usable postage batch (which needs xDAI, its own onboarding story). The payoff: a user saves an encrypted blob to Swarm, shares a 64-char reference, and rehydrates the whole chain in a new browser with one signature.

**Multiple consensus and invite policies.** Different groups want different rules: open invites with one-member-one-vote, creator-only with stake-weighted PoS, or member-approved with equal weight. Encoding that into the contract would have made it brittle, so policy lives in a creator-signed off-chain Settings envelope, and the replay engine enforces it. Tally logic and invite validation switch modes purely on what the latest Settings says.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body: PocketChains demonstrates a design pattern that scales without L2 infrastructure: one ChainPool contract hosts arbitrarily many independent payment pools, so creating a new 'pocket chain' costs one transaction instead of a rollup deploy. The transfer model is minimal: recovered signer must equal `from`, nonce strictly increases, balance must be sufficient, and anyone can submit a valid batch. The replay engine on the client shows how to build a trust-minimized app over an untrusted P2P layer (Waku): every signature, nonce, and policy is re-verified from raw materials on every state tick. No indexer, no relayer, no proof system — just a small contract and a strict client, scaling to as many parallel social chains as Ethereum block space can hold.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: PocketChains gives every group its own micro-economy on Ethereum. Each chain is a shared ETH pool with off-chain signed cheques between members, optional stake-weighted governance, and on-chain batch settlement. No relayer, no custodian, no admin. The contract verifies every signature; withdrawals are a single Solidity function. The bigger thesis: instead of one global ledger that everyone shares, we get millions of small economies — for festivals, raids, research teams, or a single dinner — each with its own rules, but all anchored to Ethereum's security and settlement. Self-custodied group economy as a primitive, not a product.

description.title: Future Society
description.body: PocketChains is for communities that want their own sovereign space — temporarily. A chain can exist for two hours, a festival, a protest, or a research team. Inside it, group chat is end-to-end encrypted, DMs use ECDH between ephemeral keys, and invite policies (open / creator-only / member-approved) are enforced cryptographically. Polls handle group decisions, optionally weighted by stake. Encrypted backups to Swarm let the history survive even when the device dies. And when a community goes quiet, the chain dissolves — its history compresses into an artifact, instead of becoming another eternal zombie chain. This is the toolkit for ephemeral, sovereign, privacy-respecting communities on Ethereum.

krtek-wallet-fa-6655.name: Krtek Wallet + 2FA
krtek-wallet-fa-6655.tagline: Easy to use wallet with 2FA that feels like web2

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Demo Video: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1sm5W6mXupJr4u48jPRc-gyBWgD5eg

A self-custodial EVM wallet for non-crypto-natives.
**No seed phrase, ever.** Signing in with ENS and password derives your owner key in the browser
(Argon2id), funds live in an ERC-4337 smart account, and a custom paymaster
sponsors gas so users never need ETH to make their first move.

## What's built

### 1. Password-only login → on-chain smart account
Argon2id over `(password, sha256("krtek.wallet.v1.password-key:" + handle))`
deterministically derives a secp256k1 owner key in the browser. The owner key
lives only in tab memory; nothing secret touches localStorage. The same
password+handle on any device yields the same wallet — a real ERC-4337 v0.7
SCA at a CREATE2 address. See `web/src/lib/password-key.ts`,
`PASSWORD_LOGIN.md`.

### 2. Custom verifying paymaster (gasless onboarding)
A Bun service signs `paymasterAndData` for every UserOp; the on-chain
`KrtekPaymaster` verifies the signature in `validatePaymasterUserOp`. Works
on any chain you give it addresses for — anvil, Sepolia, real L2s. Users
never need ETH to make their first move. See `paymaster-server/`.

### 3. M-of-N social recovery
The SCA carries a `setGuardians(address[], threshold)` slot. Recovery is a
single `recoverOwner(newOwner, deadline, signatures[])` call that verifies M
unique guardian sigs against a per-account replay nonce. Lose your password,
collect signatures from your friends, rotate to a fresh owner key — same SCA
address. See `contracts/src/KrtekSCA.sol`,
[`web/src/routes/Recover.tsx`](./web/src/routes/Recover.tsx).

### 4. Phone 2FA via WebSocket relay
The SCA's `validateUserOp` accepts a 130-byte signature: `ownerSig`
(EIP-191) `||` `phoneSig` (raw secp over the userOpHash). With
`lockToPhone=true`, every UserOp must be co-signed by a paired phone.
Pairing flow lives in Settings → Phone 2FA; the existing `mobile/`
companion handles the user-side approval UX. See
`web/src/lib/relay/`, `mobile/`.

### 5. Sourcify APIv2 deep integration
Built specifically for the Sourcify bounty:
- **Provenance Card** — animated visualization of the source-files →
  metadata.json → IPFS CID → CBOR auxdata → on-chain bytecode chain
- **Transformations diff** — renders the `transformations[]` array as
  bullets *and* annotated hex showing constructor args / libraries /
  immutables / cborAuxdata regions in the deployed bytecode
- **Multi-chain trust strip** — `/v2/contract/all-chains/{address}`
  showing where else the same code is verified
- **In-browser re-verification** — applies `transformations[]` to
  `recompiledBytecode` locally, decodes the CBOR auxdata, attempts to
  reproduce the IPFS CID — proves the verification mathematically without
  trusting the public Sourcify server
- **Source files drawer** — every source file with a Solidity highlighter,
  the file containing the called function highlighted

Uses APIv2 (the legacy `/files/...` endpoints went into brownouts in May
2026), the new `exact_match` / `match` vocabulary, and `proxyResolution`
to follow proxies natively. See `web/src/lib/sourcify.ts`,
`web/src/lib/sourcify-verify.ts`,
`web/src/components/wallet/{ProvenanceCard,TransformationsView,SourceFilesDrawer,MultiChainStrip}.tsx`.

### 6. Multi-profile + auto-resume
Multiple wallets per device under different handles. Pairing state and SCA
caches persist per profile; logging in re-attaches the relay session
transparently. See `web/src/lib/profiles.ts`.

### 7. USB Armory MK II — hardware-attested 2FA
Same SCA cosigner slot as the phone, different transport: an i.MX6ULL
Trusted Applet (Rust, no_std, ARM TrustZone Secure World) holds a
secp256k1 key derived from the chip's DCP hardware-attestation primitive
(`sk = sha256("krtek-signer-v1" || RPC.Attest)`). The applet only
exposes `GetPubkey`, `GetAddress`, `Approve(digest)` and `Health` — it
has no `ExportSecret` method, so the key never crosses the syscall
boundary back to Normal World. Pulling the SD card and cloning storage
doesn't yield the key; the DCP secret is silicon-locked.

End-to-end: web app → `armory-bridge/` (Bun + Hono on `:4141`) →
`nc 10.0.0.1:4000` (USB-CDC-ECM bridge) → applet → 65-byte recoverable
ECDSA signature → web concatenates `ownerSig || armorySig` into the
same 130-byte UserOp signature shape the phone path produces. The SCA
verifies with one `ECDSA.recover` call per signature; it doesn't care
whether the cosigner is a phone or an Armory.

`web/src/lib/send.ts` runs `decideCosigner(sender)`: if the Armory's
deterministic address matches the on-chain `phoneSigner`, sign via the
Armory; else if the relay-paired phone matches, sign via the phone; else
owner-only (which the contract refuses if `lockToPhone=true`). The
applet itself lives in the gitignored `gotee_starter/` SDK fork; the
host-side wiring is `armory-bridge/`,
`web/src/lib/armory/`, `web/src/components/wallet/ArmoryTfaCard.tsx`.

### 8. Cosmic Backup — cTRNG-seeded self-recovery phrase
A 24-word BIP-39 phrase

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Most link-in-bio platforms and personal profile pages rely on centralized cloud infrastructure. When providers like AWS experienced outages in 2025, thousands of applications and websites became temporarily inaccessible, showing how fragile centralized systems can be.

Users currently depend on third parties to host and maintain their online identity. If a provider goes offline, changes policies, removes content, or shuts down services, users lose control over their profiles and links.

Swarm + ENS domains provides a decentralized alternative.

People can use it for:
- Creating decentralized Linktree-style profile pages
- Sharing wallets, social links, portfolios, and Web3 identities
- Publishing permanent profiles that are not tied to a single company
- Building censorship-resistant personal websites

It makes existing tasks safer and more resilient by:
- Removing single points of failure
- Distributing content across the Swarm network instead of one server
- Allowing users to fully own their profile through swarm
- Allowing users to easily share their profiles using ENS domain
- Preventing dependency on centralized hosting providers
- Keeping profiles accessible even during infrastructure outages

By combining Swarm’s decentralized storage with ENS human-readable domains, the project creates a more sovereign and durable way for users to manage their online presence in Web3.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
## Why Swarmtree fits the “Network Economy” track

Swarmtree aligns with the **Network Economy** track by giving users ownership over their digital identity, online presence, and personal data through decentralized infrastructure.

Today, most creator profiles, and identity hubs depend on centralized providers that control hosting, availability, and access. This creates single points of failure and limits user autonomy. Events such as major cloud outages in 2025 demonstrated how centralized infrastructure can make thousands of applications temporarily inaccessible.

Swarmtree solves this by combining:
- **Swarm decentralized storage**
- **ENS human-readable identities**
- **User-owned content and hosting**

This creates a censorship-resistant and self-sovereign identity layer for Web3 users.

### How it fits the track

#### User-controlled digital identity
Swarmtree allows users to create decentralized profile pages tied directly to ENS domains, enabling portable and verifiable Web3 identities without relying on centralized platforms.

#### Elimination of central points of failure
Unlike traditional Linktree-style services hosted on centralized infrastructure, Swarmtree distributes content across the Swarm network, improving resilience against outages, censorship, and service shutdowns.

#### Privacy and ownership first
Users fully control their profiles, links, and associated identities without depending on a platform intermediary to manage or monetize their data.

#### Building real-world decentralized infrastructure
The project demonstrates how everyday internet tools such as personal profile pages and identity hubs can be rebuilt using decentralized technologies while maintaining usability for mainstream users.

By replacing centralized hosting with decentralized storage and human-readable ENS identities, Swarmtree contributes to a more resilient, user-owned, and privacy-preserving network economy.

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body:
Swarmtree upload all link tree websites that were generated from the app to swarm. 

While Swarmtree is not a traditional key-value database product, it demonstrates a practical and user-friendly adoption of Swarm’s storage primitives in a real-world application.

Swarmtree uses Swarm as the persistence layer for decentralized profile data. 

The project showcases how Swarm can power familiar Web2-style user experiences while preserving decentralization, ownership, and censorship resistance.

We believe this is a strong example of Swarm adoption because it abstracts away protocol complexity and exposes decentralized storage through a simple, consumer-facing experience that mainstream users can immediately understand and use.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
## Why Swarmtree fits the category

Swarmtree uses ENS as more than a simple wallet resolver, it turns ENS into a decentralized identity, hosting, and discovery layer for Web3-native profile pages.

Instead of using ENS only for "name → address" resolution, Swarmtree combines:
- ENS identities
- ENS contenthash
- ENS text records
- Swarm decentralized storage

to create fully decentralized Linktree-style profiles that users permanently own and control.

### How ENS meaningfully improves the product

#### ENS as a decentralized website router
Swarmtree uses ENS "content hash" records to point directly to decentralized profile pages hosted on Swarm. This removes dependence on centralized hosting providers and enables censorship-resistant personal websites accessible through human-readable ENS domains.

Instead of:
`username.linktree.com`

users own:
`username.eth`

with the ENS record resolving directly to decentralized content.

#### ENS as a portable identity layer
Each Swarmtree profile is tied to a user-owned ENS identity, allowing profiles to become portable across wallets, apps, DAOs, and Web3 ecosystems.

This creates:
- Persistent creator identities
- Wallet-linked public profiles
- Human-readable Web3 presence

#### ENS text records for social and identity metadata
Swarmtree leverages ENS text records to store:
- Social handles
- Profile references
- Web3 identity information

This allows profiles and identity data to remain interoperable across applications without depending on centralized databases.

#### Decentralized hosting through ENS + Swarm
Traditional link-in-bio platforms rely on centralized cloud infrastructure. During major cloud outages in 2025, many applications became inaccessible because users had no ownership over hosting infrastructure.

Swarmtree uses ENS + Swarm to eliminate this dependency:
- ENS routes users to content
- Swarm distributes and persists content across the network
- Users maintain ownership of both identity and hosting

This creates a resilient and censorship-resistant alternative to centralized profile platforms.

ag-1f6a.name: any᭙ꪖ᥅ꫀ
ag-1f6a.tagline: there is no bridge, i love you

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Most cross-chain applications still rely on relayers, bridges, or oracle networks to tell one chain what happened on another. **Anyware** removes that trust assumption.

Using [**EIP-4788**](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4788) beacon roots, it allows EVM networks to verify recent Ethereum state directly onchain through cryptographic proofs instead of externally signed messages.

**The demo use case is exploring trustless lending:**
1. a user locks ETH on Ethereum Sepolia
2. a proof of that vault state is generated
3. Base Sepolia verifies the proof onchain
4. demo USDC is issued without trusting a bridge or relayer

**The same primitive can power:**
cross-chain lending | governance verification | proof-of-reserves | attestations | generalized Ethereum state reads

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
A major hurdle was proving that an execution payload header truly belonged to a beacon block trusted through [**EIP-4788**](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4788), while also resolving the correct destination-chain beacon-root timestamp window.

**We solved this by building a prover pipeline that:**
1. scans beacon blocks
2. matches execution payloads
3. constructs SSZ inclusion proofs
4. resolves the correct EIP-4788 anchor timestamp for onchain verification

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body:
Anyware builds directly on top of Ethereum consensus infrastructure using [**EIP-4788**](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4788).

We demonstrate via PoC how Ethereum beacon roots can become a native trust anchor for cross-chain verification without relying on bridges, relayers, or oracle committees.

**It combines:** EIP-4788 beacon roots | SSZ verification | execution state proofs | Ethereum Merkle-Patricia Trie verification; into a working trust-minimized interoperability primitive.

**Anyware improves:** security by reducing external trust assumptions, transparency through fully onchain verification, and interoperability across EVM networks.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Anyware enables trustless cross-chain economic interactions without relying on bridges, relayers, or oracle networks.
Using [**EIP-4788**](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4788), the project allows EVM networks to verify Ethereum state directly through cryptographic proofs anchored to Ethereum consensus.

**The demo shows this through cross-chain lending:**
1. a user locks ETH on Ethereum
2. another chain verifies that state onchain
3. credit is issued without trusting an intermediary


**Our library enabled developers to explore use-cases like:**
- cross-chain lending
- proof-of-reserves
- governance verification
- attestations and reputation
- shared liquidity systems

The project puts user control and protocol-level verification first by replacing externally trusted middleware with direct onchain proof verification.

carbon-e31e.name: carbon
carbon-e31e.tagline: EU/ETS compliant carbon credits token exchange

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Compliance carbon is an 800 billion euro per year market. Almost none of it trades on chain. The voluntary side tried (Toucan, Klima, MOSS, C3) and crashed in 2022 when Verra banned tokenization. Compliance carbon is 375 times bigger but it's been off limits because it needs a regulator, and permissionless DEXes don't accommodate one.

Carbon DEX is built for that. A regulator-supervised on-chain spot market for tokenized EU ETS allowances. Six contracts, all live on Sepolia, all Sourcify verified.

What's in it:

A whitelist contract. Only addresses the EU ETS Authority has verified can hold or trade the carbon credit token. Transfers revert otherwise.

A custom constant-product AMM. Same x*y=k math as Uniswap V2, written fresh in Solidity 0.8.x so the whitelist and pause hooks integrate cleanly. 0.3% fee accrues to LPs.

A regulator contract. Holds the privileged roles on the other contracts. Can mint allowances, freeze accounts, pause the DEX, audit any event. Cannot trade, take fees, or front-run. EVM atomicity means there's no in-flight intercept window anyway, which actually matches real EU ETS. Reg. 2019/1122 Art. 30 lets national administrators suspend account access; the Union Registry has no transfer reversal primitive even after the 2010-11 phishing thefts.

ENS used as the compliance registry layer. Each verified entity has text records on its subdomain: legal name, ticker, year-by-year compliance status with ESMA references when there's a violation. The regulator wallet is the controller, so attestations are signed by the authority. ESMA already publishes name-and-shame on their website; we put it on chain so it's queryable.

Three frontend roles, all wired live through viem to the deployed contracts. Company portal for the verified emitter, regulator console for the authority, public observer for anyone with no wallet required.

The demo flow. Regulator issues 1,000 EUA to Cement Mainz GmbH. Cement sells 200 surplus on the DEX. The AMM matches it against an off-stage counterparty automatically. Cement retires the remaining 800 against verified emissions for the year. The /public closing visual shows 1,000 issued, 800 retired, 200 in circulation. Supply contracted by 80% in one compliance cycle. The cap held.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
ERC-1155 to ERC-20 mid-build. Original spec had vintage as a token id under ERC-1155. The CPMM expects ERC-20 pairs natively, so we'd have needed a per-id wrapper. Rewrote CarbonCredit as ERC-20 with vintage, sector, and origin moving to event payloads. Real EU ETS treats EUAs as fungible within a Phase, so this ended up more faithful to the regulation than the original spec was.

Custom CPMM instead of forking Uniswap V2. V2 is on Solidity 0.5.16 and doesn't compose with our 0.8.x stack. Porting was higher risk than just writing the formula. About 150 lines of x*y=k math, with MIN_LIQUIDITY first-LP attack mitigation, ReentrancyGuard, and the canonical min(a,b) LP-mint formula. 12 contract tests plus a K-invariant fuzz test. 72/72 pass.

Alchemy free tier caps eth_getLogs at 10 blocks, not 10,000. We didn't notice for half a session because Promise.all on three parallel getContractEvents calls just rejected, the catch path silently substituted simulation state, and the only signal was a console.error nobody was reading. Swapped the RPC to PublicNode (no auth, no cap, 50k block scan in 0.2 seconds). Lesson: read the free tier docs before architecting around them.

Single-actor demo collapse. Original happy flow had A receive, B buy, B retire, which contracted supply by 20%. Pivoted to single-actor: A receives 1000, A sells 200 surplus, A retires 800. Bigger contraction (80%), no role switching on stage, matches what cap-and-trade actually rewards (efficient operators net-sell). Wrote a B-side bot that mirrors A's trades automatically off-stage so the demo still shows both sides.

ENS realisation late in the build. Originally treated ENS as just naming. Halfway through realised text records can store the regulator's compliance attestations year by year. ESMA already publishes name-and-shame; we just put it on chain. Wrote a script to populate 12 records (cement-mainz clean, aluminium-bratislava with a 2024 violation referencing ESMA-2024-EUR-447). Surfaced them in the regulator's compliance roster. Changed the ENS pitch from "we have subdomains" to "ENS is the registry substrate".

Stack too deep on the demo script. DemoLocal.s.sol chained four broadcasts with too many local variables. Solidity hit "stack too deep" at compile. Enabled via_ir = true in foundry.toml. Compile is twice as slow now (about 6 seconds) but it works.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: On-chain spot market for tokenized EU ETS carbon allowances. The economic primitive is a custom constant-product AMM, x*y=k math written fresh in Solidity 0.8.x with whitelist and pause hooks at the swap layer so it can fit MiFID II venue requirements while keeping V2-style composability and price discovery. 0.3% fee accrues to LPs. Six contracts live on Sepolia, all Sourcify verified. The contribution is the AMM pattern that lets a regulated market settle on Ethereum without taking the regulator's authority off the table.

description.title: Future Society
description.body: EU ETS is the largest functioning carbon market in the world (around 800 billion euro per year) and the policy mechanism Europe uses to decarbonize industry. Putting it on chain isn't aesthetic, it makes the cap publicly accountable. Our /public route shows supply contraction in real time: every issuance, every trade, every retirement on a single ledger anyone can query without a wallet. ESMA already publishes name-and-shame for ETS violators on their website; we put the same attestations on ENS text records, regulator-signed, queryable by any wallet. The societal contribution is making climate policy enforcement legible and verifiable on chain, not just trusted by press release.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body: ENS isn't naming for us, it's the compliance registry layer. Each verified emitter has a subdomain on verified-entity.eth, a namespace owned by the regulator. Text records on each subdomain carry the entity's full EU ETS history: legal name, ticker, year-by-year compliance status with ESMA reference numbers when there's a violation. The regulator wallet is the controller, so each attestation is signed by the authority. ESMA already publishes name-and-shame on their website (HTML, not queryable). We put the same data on ENS records so it's machine-readable and historical. Frontend reads the records and shows green or amber compliance chips per year on the regulator's roster. Every ENS name on the UI links to its records page on sepolia.app.ens.domains so anyone can verify. Live records: cement-mainz.verified-entity.eth (clean) and aluminium-bratislava.verified-entity.eth (2024 violation referencing ESMA-2024-EUR-447, 2025 verified).

hromada-5c7a.name: Obec & dAppSwarm
hromada-5c7a.tagline: ENS as the state machine for neighborhood DAOs

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## The problem

Neighborhoods are full of latent capital nobody coordinates. Fourteen households could share two cargo bikes instead of owning fourteen private cars, but the coordination overhead kills it. Kickstarter doesn't know who lives on your block, co-ops don't ship with L2 escrow. Dappnode has a parallel gap: package distribution still flows through IPFS and a centralised registry.

## What Obec does

Obec gives every neighborhood a self-sovereign DAO whose state lives **in ENS itself**. A neighborhood is a subname (e.g. vinohrady.prague.obec.eth), members are sub-subnames, projects are sub-sub-subnames, and the contracts atomically write text records as the funding lifecycle progresses.

1. A member proposes a project. The pool registers an ENS subname with status "proposing".
2. Members commit USDC. When total crosses target and member count crosses the minimum, status flips to "active" and milestone 0 (30%) releases.
3. After delivery, M-of-N attest on-chain; the attesters list anchors as a credential and milestone 1 (50%) releases.
4. After a warranty window, milestone 2 (20%) releases, status flips to "completed".
5. If it never funds, expiry deactivates the row but tombstones the namehash, so the label cannot be reused.

addr(node) returns the pool; addr(node, 2147568180) returns the same pool on Base Sepolia; text(node, "status") is the live state; contenthash(node) is the IPFS doc root.

## What dAppSwarm does

dAppSwarm is the Rust CLI half: it packs a Dappnode package into a Mantaray manifest on Swarm and stamps each release into a Swarm Feed indexed by package name. Resolvers find the latest with one feed lookup and bring the compose project up — no central registry, no IPFS hop. The publisher's secp256k1 EOA is the trust anchor.

## Why together

Obec is the capital layer; dAppSwarm is the distribution layer. A neighborhood that funds a self-hosted service ships it to household Dappnodes through the same trust-rooted, peer-to-peer stack.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## Single-subname lifecycle

The first Obec design used two ENS subnames per project — one for proposal, one for the funded resource. The pre-funding name stopped existing the moment the project funded. We refactored to **one project subname** that carries the full lifecycle: status flips proposing -> active -> completed, and on expiry the registry row deactivates *and* the namehash tombstones in Status.Expired. Pinned by test_checkExpiry_namehashRemainsTombstoned.

## CCIP-Read end-to-end

ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver on Sepolia plus an EIP-3668 signed-response gateway as a Next.js route. The resolver reverts with OffchainLookup; the gateway reads Base Sepolia and signs with EIP-191; resolveWithProof verifies. Sepolia lookup, off-chain fetch, signature check, Base Sepolia state read — verifiable from any standard ENS client.

## Cross-chain split

ENS on Sepolia; USDC and the pool on Base Sepolia. Resolver, gateway, and ENSIP-9 coin-type space all have to agree, and a domain-separator binding stops a forged gateway from spoofing answers for a different resolver. Wiring wagmi's chain-switching, viem's CCIP-Read client, and the resolver's per-call expiry was most of the integration work.

## SOC pushes without a Bee

dAppSwarm writes Single-Owner-Chunk feed entries, but stock antd exposed no POST /soc/{owner}/{id}. We patched antd to accept SOC envelopes and wrote a signer that recovers the owner from the chunk and matches it against the URL before acceptance.

## Feed indexing without a directory service

Swarm Feeds give a (topic, owner) -> chunk mapping, not name -> latest version. Topic is keccak256 of "dappswarm:" concatenated with the package name; entries are written at sequential indices 0, 1, 2, and so on; lookup is exponential probe + binary search, O(log n). The bundle's file list lives in the feed payload, so resolution needs no manifest-listing endpoint.

description.title: Future Society
description.body: Obec is a self-sovereign neighborhood DAO for shared resources (cargo bikes, solar, tool libraries). Members commit USDC; thresholded milestones release on M-of-N on-chain attestations. Privacy-respecting (ENS sub-subnames, not personal identity), transparent (lifecycle is publicly readable ENS state), and inclusive (no KYC, no bank). Solarpunk infrastructure for shared ownership.

description.title: Dappnode Packages on Swarm (Instead of IPFS)
description.body: dAppSwarm publishes and installs Dappnode packages over Swarm with no IPFS hop and no central registry. `dappswarm publish <dir>` packs the package into a Mantaray manifest and stamps the release into a Swarm Feed indexed by package name; `dappswarm install <name> --owner 0x...` resolves the latest, docker-loads bundled images, and brings the compose project up. Trust anchor is the publisher's secp256k1 EOA via Swarm SOC. Built in Rust on a patched `antd` with a POST /soc/{owner}/{id} extension. Repo: https://github.com/prokopschield/dappswarm

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body: Obec uses ENS as the program, not just a label. The contract atomically writes ENS records as the funding lifecycle advances: addr(node) routes to the pool, addr(node, 2147568180) gives the same pool on Base Sepolia (ENSIP-9), text(node, "status") is the live state, text(node, "attestations") anchors the M-of-N credential, contenthash(node) points at the spec. End-to-end CCIP-Read: ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver on Sepolia + EIP-3668 signed gateway reading Base Sepolia. ENS is the database, the router, the credential store, and the lifecycle log.

argus-350b.name: Argus
argus-350b.tagline: Argus is trust infra for agent-managed capital

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
# Argus

> Trust infrastructure for agent-managed capital.

Two ENS-named agents managing a USDC position on Base. The **manager** parks funds in Aave v3 and exits on signed alerts. description.body:
## Network Economy fit

- **Identity, user-controlled.** Both agents are ENSIP-26 named with on-chain records. The watcher publishes its bounty terms (`50 bps of saved capital, paid in USDC on Base`) as a signed-by-mainnet text record — a public economic commitment.
- **Real on-chain economy.** Every Polymarket scrape pays Apify on Base via Coinbase x402: 1 USDC settled per call, verifiable on Basescan. Manager exits trigger `bounty-paid` receipts attributing 50 bps to the watcher's EOA.
- **Privacy by content-addressing.** Every action emits a vault tx + signed JSON on Swarm via `bzz.limo`. We additionally ship `@argus/swarm-kv`, a reusable encrypted-by-default KV library on Swarm (AES-256-GCM, HMAC-derived topics, keys from your wallet) — `localStorage` for dApps that follows the wallet across devices.
- **No central failure points.** Vault contract lets the manager move funds vault↔Aave only — leaked manager key cannot drain. Owner can always exit. Trust path is a pure function of ENS state.

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body:
### 3. Swarm — verifiable evidence trail + a reusable KV library (secondary)

We ship two distinct Swarm contributions:

#### 3a. Live receipt trail (used by the agents)

- All receipts (deposits, withdraws, threat alerts, evidence bundles) are uploaded to Swarm via `@ethersphere/bee-js` v12.
- Uses the **bzz.limo** hosted gateway with `NULL_STAMP` — no postage batch setup required, the gateway rewrites it. Verified live: upload returns a 64-char ref, retrieval at `bzz.limo/bytes/<ref>` returns the exact JSON.
- Receipts are linked from the frontend audit log — every row has a `swarm ↗` link the audience can click to see the actual signed payload.
- Graceful fallback: on network failure, refs become `stub:<unixMs>` so the SQLite audit log stays canonical and downstream UI doesn't break.

**Where in the code:**
- [`agents/manager/src/swarm.ts`](agents/manager/src/swarm.ts), [`agents/watcher/src/swarm.ts`](agents/watcher/src/swarm.ts) — `Bee('https://bzz.limo')` + `NULL_STAMP`
- [`frontend/components/ThreatPanel.tsx`](frontend/components/ThreatPanel.tsx) — Evidence and Exits sections render `bzz.limo/bytes/<ref>` deep-links

#### 3b. `@argus/swarm-kv` — a reusable developer library

A standalone TypeScript package that wraps Swarm's low-level primitives (Feeds, Single Owner Chunks, postage batches) into a `get` / `put` / `list` / `delete` API with end-to-end encryption derived from the user's Ethereum private key. Most app code shouldn't have to know about feeds or topics — `swarm-kv` makes Swarm feel like an encrypted, decentralized `localStorage`.

```ts
import { openKv } from "@argus/swarm-kv";

const kv = await openKv({ bee, privateKey, namespace: "myapp.v1", postage: { auto: true } });
await kv.put("user.profile", { age: 30, theme: "dark" });
await kv.getJson("user.profile");   // → { age: 30, theme: "dark" }
await kv.list();                    // → ["user.profile", ...]
```

What it gives you:
- **End-to-end encryption** — values encrypted with AES-256-GCM, key derived via HKDF-SHA256 from your private key. Key names hidden as HMAC-derived topics.
- **String / JSON / binary** support with automatic type detection on read.
- **Listable** — an encrypted index feed tracks all keys, no manifest plumbing needed.
- **Auto-postage** — buys a batch on first write if you don't have one, or uses any usable batch on the node.
- **No bee-js leakage** — your app code never touches feeds, topics, SOCs, or stamps directly.

Use cases beyond Argus: dApp user profiles, app settings sync, chat history, bookmarks — anything you'd put in `localStorage` but want to follow a wallet across devices.

**Where in the code:** [`packages/swarm-kv/`](packages/swarm-kv/) — see its [README](packages/swarm-kv/README.md) for the full API and privacy model.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Hiring a lawyer in another EU country is hard. You can't easily check if they're really bar-admitted, you don't want to send a retainer to a platform that might freeze it, and normal chat tools aren't private enough for legal advice. Today's marketplaces ask you to trust them with all three. Firmus Novus doesn't. Lawyers and clients prove who they are using EUDI credentials from real authorities, sharing only what's needed. Fees sit in an on-chain escrow the platform can't touch: clients can dispute right away, lawyers have to wait 30 days. Messages are encrypted in the browser, so the server only sees ciphertext. You can hire a lawyer abroad with the same confidence as hiring locally, without trusting the marketplace with your identity, your money, or your conversation.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: The biggest hurdle was that the EUDI ecosystem is still maturing.The biggest hurdle was that the EUDI ecosystem is still maturing. The smaller annoyance was wallet compatibility: EUDI wallets don't work with every passkey manager (Bitwarden, for instance). The real problem was deeper: no bar association issues credentials yet, so the lawyer half of our trust model had no real counterpart to test against, and the EUDI and EBSI test infrastructure is fragmented, with reference deployments and sandboxes that often don't work end-to-end. We solved it by taking the EBSI project's reference implementation for issuers and running our own: a faithful OID4VCI issuer with our signing keys, issuing both the PID and a bar-admission credential. The platform verifies it exactly as it would a real issuer, so when real issuance comes online, only the JWKS URL changes.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: Firmus Novus fits the Network Economy track because it turns a real economic interaction, paid cross-border legal consultation, into one where identity, payments, and communication are all user-controlled and decentrally enforced. Clients and lawyers prove who they are through selectively disclosed EUDI credentials, fees are held by an on-chain escrow contract the platform cannot override, and messages are end-to-end encrypted so the server only ever sees ciphertext. There is no central point of failure for any of the three.

description.title: The problem it solves
Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## Challenges We Ran Into

One of the biggest challenges was making the analysis reliable without treating AI as the source of truth. It was tempting to let the LLM directly explain the transaction, but that could create incorrect or unsafe answers. We solved this by building a deterministic analysis pipeline first: decode calldata, simulate execution, collect Sourcify metadata, detect effects, score risks, and only then use AI as an optional explanation layer based on those facts.

Another challenge was handling transactions when contract source or ABI data was missing. In those cases, raw calldata is hard for users to understand. We added fallback behavior so the analyzer still returns useful information from simulation, traces, selector lookup, risk rules, and conservative explanations instead of failing.

ENS support also required extra care. An ENS name can help users recognize an address, but it should not automatically make a transaction safe. We handled this by using reverse lookup with forward confirmation, showing warnings for mismatches, and treating ENS as identity context rather than proof of trust.

Finally, integrating the analyzer into wallet UX was difficult because browser extensions, MetaMask Snaps, backend services, and SDK packages all have different security boundaries. We separated the project into a core engine, browser SDK, backend SDK, Snap, and extension so that sensitive API keys stay on the backend while wallets and dApps can still use the analysis safely.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body:
SignGuard fits the Ethereum Core track by addressing one of the biggest UX and security problems in Ethereum today: users regularly sign transactions without actually understanding what those transactions do.

Today, many existing transaction security tools focus primarily on answering a single question: “Is this transaction safe or unsafe?” In many cases, if the transaction is considered safe, the tool simply shows a green checkmark or a short confirmation without explaining anything else. For users, this creates another problem — they still do not truly understand what they are approving, we often heard from both newcomers and even experienced crypto users that they regularly sign transactions without fully understanding what those transactions actually do. Because of this uncertainty, many users feel uncomfortable or even afraid of signing transactions, worrying that they might accidentally approve something malicious or lose their funds.

This problem becomes even more important because different users have completely different levels of blockchain knowledge. A beginner, a regular crypto user, and a developer require very different types of explanations. However, most existing tools provide explanations in one generic format, which is often either too technical for newcomers or too simplified for advanced users.

SignGuard solves this problem by introducing an adaptive transaction understanding layer for Ethereum.

We built SignGuard as a reusable SDK that can be integrated into wallets, dApps, browser extensions, and other Ethereum applications. To demonstrate the flexibility and reusability of our approach, we built two separate integrations on top of the SDK:

- a MetaMask Snap plugin that brings transaction analysis and explanations directly into the MetaMask ecosystem;
- and a standalone browser extension that enhances the transaction signing flow before the wallet confirmation step.

In the browser extension flow, before MetaMask opens for signing, SignGuard intercepts the transaction and displays an explanation interface where the user can fully understand what the transaction is about before approving it. The system analyzes the transaction, simulates its execution, detects potential risks, and explains the expected outcome in human-readable language.

The explanation adapts to the user’s experience level:

- Beginner mode focuses on simple and intuitive explanations that reduce fear and uncertainty.
- Regular user mode provides additional context about assets, approvals, swaps, and protocol interactions.
- Developer mode exposes advanced technical information such as calldata interpretation, contract interactions, and simulation details.

To achieve this, SignGuard combines multiple modern transaction analysis and simulation approaches, including transaction simulation, calldata decoding, ENS resolution, contract inspection, approval analysis, phishing and spoofing detection, and validation of suspicious transaction patterns. These techniques are used not only to evaluate transaction security, but also to improve the user experience by transforming low-level blockchain data into understandable explanations.

Additionally, SignGuard includes an AI-powered assistant that already knows the full transaction context, including simulation results, decoded calldata, detected risks, and protocol analysis. Users can ask follow-up questions in natural language and receive contextual answers before making a signing decision.

Only after the user fully understands the transaction can they choose to continue to MetaMask and sign it, or reject the transaction entirely.

For developers, SignGuard also provides advanced debugging and transaction inspection capabilities. In developer mode, the platform can visualize calldata traces, transaction execution flows, contract interaction graphs, and other low-level execution details that help developers better understand, inspect, and debug complex smart contract interactions.

As a result, SignGuard solves multiple problems simultaneously:

1. Security: helping users understand whether a transaction is potentially dangerous or suspicious.
2. User Experience: clearly explaining what the transaction actually does before signing.
3. Personalization: adapting explanations to the user’s technical knowledge level.
4. Interactive Understanding: allowing users to ask follow-up questions if they still do not understand part of the transaction.

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body:
## Bounty Fit Explanation

Users often sign Web3 transactions without fully understanding what they authorize. Wallet prompts usually expose low-level data such as contract addresses, token approvals, calldata, or generic permission messages, but they rarely explain whether the transaction matches the user’s intent or whether the target contract behavior is trustworthy.

We built a transaction analysis and simulation tool that explains what a transaction will actually do before the user signs it. The system combines transaction simulation, contract intelligence, ENS identity checks, source verification, permission analysis, and UX-focused explanation generation. The final output is adapted for different knowledge levels: beginner, regular user, and developer.

Sourcify is a core part of our analysis pipeline. We use Sourcify as a trusted source of verified contract evidence, including ABI, Solidity source files, compiler metadata, contract metadata, and verification status. This matters because raw calldata, frontend labels, and wallet-provided descriptions are not enough to reliably explain a transaction. Without verified source and ABI data, the analyzer can only infer behavior from traces or bytecode-level effects. With Sourcify, we can connect a transaction to the actual verified contract interface and source context.

In our workflow, when the analyzer receives a transaction target, it queries Sourcify using the chain ID and contract address. If verified metadata is available, the ABI is used to decode the calldata into a human-readable function call, including the function signature, arguments, and contract interaction type. This decoded call becomes the foundation for the explanation shown to the user.

We also use Sourcify data for deeper contract intelligence. Verified source files and metadata help the analyzer identify security-relevant capabilities such as owner/admin controls, upgradeability patterns, pause mechanisms, blacklist logic, minting functions, fund recovery methods, delegate execution, and privileged role management.

A particularly important use case is proxy and upgradeable contract analysis. Users usually interact with the proxy address, but the actual execution logic may live in a separate implementation contract. When Sourcify provides proxy or implementation context, our analyzer follows that relationship and inspects the verified implementation logic as well, not only the visible target address. This helps us explain the real behavior behind the transaction instead of stopping at the proxy surface.

Sourcify also strengthens selector and ABI consistency checks. A four-byte function selector can be ambiguous or decoded incorrectly if the wrong ABI is used. By using verified ABI and source context from Sourcify, our analyzer checks whether the selector resolves to the expected function in the verified contract, whether the decoded arguments are consistent with that ABI, and whether the interaction matches the apparent user intent.

The Sourcify-derived contract context is combined with transaction simulation results. Simulation shows the practical effects of the transaction, such as token transfers, approvals, balance changes, state-changing calls, or execution failures. Sourcify provides the verified explanation layer behind those effects: which function was called, what the contract is designed to do, whether the logic belongs to a proxy implementation, and which security-relevant capabilities exist in the codebase.

For developers, we expose this evidence more directly: decoded function signatures, ABI source, verification status, proxy or implementation context, notable contract capabilities, and limitations when verification is missing. For regular users and beginners, the same evidence is transformed into simpler language: whether the app is asking for token access, whether funds may move now or later, whether the contract identity is verified, and whether the transaction contains behavior that deserves attention.

description.title: Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway
description.body:
How We Use Verified Fetch on Swarm

SignGuard uses Swarm to store complete transaction analysis snapshots for developer debugging, comparison, and review. After a transaction is simulated and analyzed, a developer can save the full result to Swarm and later share it with another developer, compare it with a newer simulation, or use it as context for AI-assisted debugging.

For this workflow, verified fetching is important because the saved analysis becomes part of the developer’s debugging evidence. If the data is loaded through a public Swarm gateway without verification, the developer still has to trust that the gateway returned the correct content. That is a problem for our use case because even a small change in the fetched analysis could completely change the interpretation of a transaction.

For example, a tampered response could hide a new internal call, change a decoded selector, remove a suspicious spender, alter a gas estimate, or modify the simulation result shown to the developer. If this data is then used for comparison or passed into the AI assistant, the explanation may be based on incorrect evidence. Because of this, SignGuard should not only store analysis snapshots on Swarm, but also verify that the fetched data is exactly the data that was originally saved.

This is where the Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway concept fits directly into our project. When SignGuard retrieves a saved transaction analysis from Swarm, the extension can fetch it from a normal public gateway, but verify it locally before using it. For immutable analysis snapshots, the client can recompute the content hash and confirm that the returned chunks match the expected Swarm reference. For mutable indexes or saved analysis lists, the client can verify signed feed updates instead of blindly trusting the gateway response.

This makes the whole debugging workflow more reliable. Developers can share a Swarm reference to a transaction analysis snapshot, and another developer can fetch it through any available gateway while still having cryptographic confidence that the data was not modified in transit. This is especially important when comparing simulations, where SignGuard may detect changes such as higher gas usage, a new internal call, a changed selector, a new spender, or different proxy implementation context.

Verified fetching is also useful for AI-assisted debugging. Since the AI assistant can answer questions over one or multiple saved analyses, it is important that the retrieved transaction evidence is authentic before it is used as model context. In practice, this means a developer can save a baseline simulation, compare it with a later transaction, and ask questions like “what changed?” or “why did this UserOperation start calling a different contract?” while knowing that the saved Swarm data was verified locally and not trusted blindly from the gateway.

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
## How We Use ENS

SignGuard fits the “Most Interesting Use of ENS” track because we use ENS not only as a readable name for an Ethereum address, but as an active identity and trust signal inside the transaction signing flow.

Most wallets use ENS mainly as a display layer: instead of showing a raw 0x... address, they may show a human-readable name. This improves readability, but it does not fully solve the signing problem. A user may see an ENS name and still not know whether that identity is legitimate, whether it belongs to the expected protocol, whether it is being used to mislead them, or whether the transaction itself could modify their own ENS identity.

SignGuard extends the role of ENS from “address naming” to transaction understanding. When a user is about to sign a transaction, our system analyzes the transaction, simulates its effects, identifies the important actors involved, and then uses ENS as part of the identity layer behind the explanation. These actors may include the target contract, spender, recipient, protocol address, counterparty, owner, or other addresses discovered during simulation.

Instead of asking only:

> “Does this address have an ENS name?”

SignGuard asks more useful questions:

> “Can this ENS identity be trusted in this context?”
> “Does the ENS name actually resolve to the address being shown?”
> “Is this name trying to imitate a known protocol or entity?”
> “Could this transaction change the user’s ENS identity, records, resolver, ownership, or permissions?”

This is where ENS becomes especially valuable for our project. Signing is not only about checking whether a transaction is technically valid. It is also about helping the user understand who they are interacting with and what identity-related consequences the transaction may have.

A core part of our ENS analysis is reverse and forward validation. If an address has a reverse ENS record, SignGuard does not automatically trust it. We verify whether the ENS name resolves back to the same address. If the forward confirmation fails, we treat the name as potentially misleading and show a warning. This helps protect users from situations where a malicious address configures a fake or confusing reverse record to appear more trustworthy in wallets, explorers, or transaction previews.

We also use ENS as a signal for impersonation and phishing detection. SignGuard can compare ENS names against known or expected protocol identities and detect cases where a name appears visually or semantically similar to a trusted entity but resolves to a different address. This is important because attackers often rely on user trust in recognizable names, not only on technical contract exploits. ENS therefore becomes part of our anti-impersonation layer.

ENS is also integrated into our transaction simulation pipeline. SignGuard can detect when a transaction affects ENS-related state, including actions such as changing a resolver, updating address records, modifying text records, updating a contenthash, setting a reverse record, renewing a name, transferring wrapped ENS names, wrapping or unwrapping names, or granting Name Wrapper approvals and permissions.

This allows SignGuard to explain ENS-specific risks in plain language. For example, instead of only showing that a contract call is being made, we can explain that the transaction may change how the user’s ENS name resolves, update public profile records, modify website/contenthash data, transfer control of a name, or grant another address permissions over ENS-related assets.

This gives ENS two important roles in SignGuard:
First, ENS helps identify the counterparty. It helps answer who the user is interacting with, whether the displayed identity is confirmed, and whether there are signs of impersonation or spoofing.
Second, ENS helps explain the impact on the user’s own identity. It helps detect whether the transaction changes the user’s ENS records, resolver, ownership, permissions, public profile, or how their name is represented across Ethereum applications.

The result is a more meaningful signing experience. For beginners, SignGuard translates ENS analysis into simple explanations such as whether the name appears confirmed, suspicious, or potentially misleading. For regular users, we show additional context about the ENS name, resolved address, reverse record, and identity-related risks. For developers, we expose the underlying evidence directly, including forward confirmation results, resolver information, ENS transaction effects, suspicious similarity checks, and structured warnings.

Overall, SignGuard uses ENS in a creative way by turning it from a passive address label into an active identity, trust, and transaction explanation layer. ENS becomes part of the pre-signing security workflow: it helps users understand who they are interacting with, whether that identity is reliable, and whether the transaction can affect their own on-chain identity.

secondbrain-db48.name: second-brain
secondbrain-db48.tagline: Turn your archive into a pay-per-query AI agent.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
For creators, researchers, and experts, the current monetization landscape for written knowledge is deeply
  flawed. If you have a massive archive of valuable text (newsletters, research notes, documentation, or books),
  your options are currently limited to blunt, all-or-nothing paywalls (like Substack) or relying on ad revenue.
  Furthermore, if you want to let users "chat" with your data, you have to upload it to a centralized platform
  like OpenAI, which captures all the value and offers you nothing in return.

  Second Brain solves this by turning any static text archive into a sovereign, pay-per-query AI agent that you
  can embed anywhere. 

  Instead of locking knowledge behind a $10/month subscription, Second Brain uses the x402 protocol (HTTP 402
  Payment Required) combined with the ultra-low fees of MegaETH to create true micro-monetization. 

  What people can use it for:
   * Independent Creators: Upload your entire back-catalog of essays. Drop the iframe onto your personal site,
     allowing readers to ask your "AI clone" specific questions for a few cents per answer.
   * Open Source & Dev Tools: Monetize premium technical support. Train a brain on your project's advanced
     documentation and charge micro-transactions for instant, highly-accurate technical debugging.
   * Researchers & Analysts: Sell access to proprietary market research. Users don't have to buy a $500 report;
     they can pay $0.50 to ask exactly what they need to know.

  How it makes things better:
   * Frictionless UX: It utilizes an embeddable iframe. The reader connects their wallet directly in the chat
     widget, signs the escrow transaction, and gets their answer instantly.
   * Creator-Owned: The creator holds the keys. Revenue accumulates in an on-chain escrow contract, ready to be
     pulled directly to their wallet at any time.
   * Context-Strict (RAG): Because it uses Venice AI and a localized vector store, the agent only answers using
     the provided archive, drastically reducing hallucinations and preserving the creator's true voice.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Building a decentralized, pay-per-query agent required bridging the gap between synchronous Web2 APIs and
  asynchronous Web3 infrastructure. Here are the main hurdles and how I overcame them:

  1. The RPC Race Condition (Transaction Propagation Delay)
  The biggest hurdle was a classic blockchain race condition during the payment handshake. When a user paid for a
  query in the frontend iframe, their injected wallet (e.g., MetaMask) instantly confirmed the transaction and
  told the React app to hit the backend /query endpoint with the new transaction hash.
  However, the Express backend validates payments using a public MegaETH RPC node. Because the node takes a few
  seconds to index the newest blocks, it was returning null for the transaction, causing the API to reject valid
  payments with a "Transaction not found" error.
   * How I fixed it: I implemented a localized polling loop inside the backend's x402 middleware. Now, when the
     backend receives a payment hash, instead of failing immediately, it gracefully retries fetching the receipt
     up to 5 times (spaced 1 second apart). This gives the RPC node the buffer it needs to sync the network
     state, resulting in a flawless UX for the reader.

  2. Serverless Environments vs. Stateful AI Vectors
  Initially, I wanted to deploy the entire stack to Vercel. However, the architecture relies on an in-memory
  database to store API keys and uses Xenova to generate localized vector embeddings on the fly. Serverless
  functions (like Vercel's) spin down constantly, which meant the vector store and API keys were being wiped from
  memory every few minutes, causing "Invalid API Key" errors.
   * How I fixed it: I split the architecture into a hybrid deployment. I deployed the React frontend as a Static
     Site to Vercel for fast global CDN delivery, but migrated the Express/Ethers backend to a dedicated Google
     Compute Engine (GCE) Virtual Machine running persistently via systemd. To bypass browser CORS and Mixed
     Content (HTTPS -> HTTP) blockers, I configured vercel.json to act as a reverse proxy, silently routing all
     frontend /api/* requests to the VM.

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body:
Umia Best Agentic Venture: Second Brain

  How Second Brain Fits the Agentic Venture Model
  Second Brain is not just a single AI agent; it is an infrastructure layer for a two-sided agentic economy. It

  By providing the tooling for anyone to spawn a micro-monetized agent, Second Brain creates a decentralized
