  Tokenomics & Value Accrual ($BRAIN)
  The protocol is designed to capture value directly from the velocity of the network's agentic GDP. 
   * Protocol Fee: For every paid query answered by an agent on the network, the smart contract routes a small
     protocol fee (e.g., 5%) directly to the DAO Treasury.
   * Value Accrual: Instead of relying on governance voting for value, the treasury utilizes these programmatic
     fees to systematically buy back and burn the native protocol token ($BRAIN). This ensures that the token's
     value is deterministically tied to the aggregate usage of all agents deployed on the platform.

  Futarchy: Decision Markets for Protocol Expansion
  Traditional DAO voting is often slow and easily captured by politics. To govern the treasury effectively,
  Second Brain utilizes Futarchy (Decision Markets) to dictate protocol expansion. 
  Instead of voting, token holders trade on the predictive outcomes of specific strategies. For example, a market
  could be created asking: "Will integrating Anthropic's Claude 3.5 increase the 30-day network query volume by
  20%?"
  If the market resolves positively, the protocol's smart contracts automatically release the treasury funds
  required to build and deploy that integration. This ensures that the protocol acts as a hyper-rational entity,
  allocating capital strictly toward the expansion efforts that the market predicts will be most profitable for
  the network.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
RugSleuth helps crypto users quickly assess whether a Base token or wallet looks risky before they trust it.

Today, checking a suspicious token is slow and manual: users jump between BaseScan, liquidity trackers, deployer history, holder data, and social signals, then try to combine everything under time pressure. Most retail users skip this step, which makes them easier targets for rug pulls and low-effort scam launches.

RugSleuth turns that workflow into an autonomous investigation. A user pastes a Base address, and the agent buys the public data it needs from Apify Actors using x402 payments, analyzes the evidence, and returns a transparent rug-risk verdict with reasons and limitations.

It makes due diligence:

Faster: one address in, structured risk summary out.
Safer: users get warnings before interacting with suspicious tokens.
More transparent: every paid data request and evidence source is visible.
Agent-native: the AI agent can pay for external intelligence itself instead of relying on a prepaid API account.
Reusable: the same pattern can support token screening, protocol risk checks, wallet investigation, fraud monitoring, and other Web3 intelligence workflows.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One major challenge was making the x402 flow work cleanly inside an autonomous agent workflow instead of as a simple CLI demo.

The agent does not call Apify directly. The flow is:

Codex agent -> custom MCP server -> x402 client -> Apify Actor
That meant we had to carefully separate responsibilities:

Codex decides what evidence it needs.
The MCP server exposes safe, structured tools.
The x402 client handles 402 Payment Required, signs the challenge, retries the request, and emits payment events.
The orchestrator streams everything back to the dashboard.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
RugSleuth is related to the Future Security track because it helps users and agents make safer decisions before interacting with risky onchain assets.
Crypto security is often reactive: users discover a rug pull after liquidity is gone, a contract is abandoned, or funds are already lost. RugSleuth moves part of that security check earlier. It gives users a fast, evidence-backed risk assessment before they buy, trust, or investigate a token.
The project fits Future Security because it demonstrates:

Preventive security: warns users about suspicious token signals before they interact.
Autonomous investigation: an AI agent can collect and reason over public evidence without manual research.
Transparent risk scoring: the verdict includes reasons, evidence, and limitations instead of a black-box answer.
Safer Web3 UX: users do not need to manually inspect multiple tools under time pressure.
Agentic security workflows: future security tools will need agents that can buy data, call specialized services, and produce auditable conclusions.

description.title: Apify Bounty
description.body:
RugSleuth is directly related to the Apify track because it uses Apify as the paid intelligence layer for an autonomous agent.
The Apify bounty asks for a real use case that integrates Apify through the x402 protocol. RugSleuth does exactly that: when the agent needs external data about a suspicious Base address, it calls Apify Actors and pays for those calls through x402.

soly-06f5.name: Soly - AI Coding Assistant
soly-06f5.tagline: An AI Coding Assistant for smart contract devs

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Smart contracts on Ethereum are opaque by default. Even when source code is verified on Sourcify, developers, auditors, and users have no easy way to understand what a contract does, how it's structured, or what risks it carries — without reading thousands of lines of Solidity manually.

**Soly / Sourcify Contract Analyzer** solves this by turning Sourcify-verified contract data into structured, human-readable intelligence:

- **Proxy resolution** — automatically detects EIP-1967, UUPS, Gnosis Safe, Diamond, and other proxy patterns and follows the implementation
- **Storage layout summary** — maps on-chain state variables slot by slot from verified metadata
- **Dependency audit** — identifies OpenZeppelin, Uniswap, Aave, Chainlink and other library families used in the contract
- **ABI + signature fingerprinting** — extracts all function, event, and error signatures from verified sources
- **Audio transcript** — generates a spoken-style narration of the contract analysis, making it accessible without reading code
- **Multi-deployment target** — works as a Python CLI, a Django + Express full-stack app, and a Cloudflare Worker (zero infra, edge-deployed)

The tool uses **only Sourcify-verified data** — no off-chain assumptions, no LLM hallucination. Every claim is grounded in the verified source bundle.

Useful for: developers auditing unfamiliar contracts, wallets showing users what they're signing, and AI agents enriching on-chain context.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**1. Sourcify API field selection**
The `/v2/contract` endpoint supports a `fields` query parameter, but not all field names are valid. Passing `match` or `creationMatch` directly returns a 400 error. We had to discover the correct field names by reading the Swagger spec carefully and testing iteratively before landing on `fields=all` as the safe default.

**2. Cloudflare Worker template string nesting**
The Worker serves both server-side logic and the full HTML UI in a single JS file. Nesting template literals inside the outer backtick-delimited HTML string caused syntax errors. We resolved this by converting inner template expressions to string concatenation, keeping the outer template clean.

**3. XSS from Sourcify data**
Sourcify returns contract metadata fields that could contain arbitrary strings. When we rendered these values into `innerHTML` in the Worker UI, we introduced a potential XSS vector. We fixed this by adding an `esc()` helper that uses DOM `textContent` for safe HTML-escaping before any insertion.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body: Built a structured contract intelligence layer over Sourcify's verified contract corpus. It gives developers machine-readable analysis of verified contracts: proxy type, storage layout, ABI surface, dependency audit, and spoken-style transcript. Zero trust, pure on-chain verified data. This also allows AI agent to be better educator for users and developers. For users to better assist them in letting them know what type of contracts they are interacting with, for developers to better assist them in through an AI assistant to educate them how to integrate their protocol on how to interact with this smart contract.

description.title: Sourcify Bounty

description.title: The problem it solves

DePIN Scalability: Current "Proof of Physical Resilience" systems are often clunky and expensive to settle on-chain.
GodEye solves this by generating ZK-Proofs at the edge, signing them via Orbitport Satellites for absolute timestamping, and settling them on Ethereum for sub-cent costs.

description.title: Challenges we ran into

On-chain Settlement: Balancing the 5-minute uptime requirement with Ethereum's block times—we solved this by implementing a "batch verification" system in the manager contract.
Gas Optimization: Minimizing the cost of reward minting while maintaining a strict on-chain record of every verified proof.

siren-1cc2.name: Siren
siren-1cc2.tagline: Siren turns public evidence into trust signals.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
**The problem.** Today, deciding whether to trust an ENS-named agent, contract, or team means manually checking Sourcify, GitHub, Etherscan, and ENS records — separately, with no shared standard for discounting unverified claims, and no way to prove later that a report ever existed. Token holders approve proxy upgrades blind. Investors back agents on screenshots. Hackathon judges have no way to score a project's verifiability fast.

**Siren turns any .eth name into an on-chain trust certificate.**

Every Bench verdict can be minted as an EAS attestation (Sepolia + mainnet schemas registered) — an EIP-712-signed certificate that binds the full report payload (subject, namehash, score, tier, computedAt, reportHash, reportUri) to the wallet that published it. The certificate is shareable as an EAS Explorer URL, decodeable by any third party, and the next time someone runs Siren on the same subject, the live verdict can be DIFFED against the previous certificate — surfacing score regressions, tier downgrades, and identity rotations as ALERT-level signals.

**What you can use Siren for**

- **Mint your project's trust certificate on-chain.** /b/<ens> gives you a 0–100 benchmark across four data sources (Sourcify, GitHub, on-chain activity, ENS-internal records). One click → Publish to EAS → permanent receipt. Try it on sbo3lagent.eth — the certificate already lives at sepolia.easscan.org/attestation/view/0xa5b4e5a48e23127a0b9284c7c1128028cc84a06d2fe973092f2dc494e83775ff.

- **Approve a proxy upgrade safely.** /r/<ens> gives a 5-second SAFE / REVIEW / SIREN verdict backed by Sourcify-verified bytecode. No source, no upgrade.

- **Diff a previous certificate against the live verdict.** Paste an EAS Explorer URL on the homepage, click "Open live verdict" — instant diff banner with severity-coded changes (UNCHANGED / CHANGED / ALERT). Identity rotation, score regression, revocation — all surfaced automatically. This is chain-of-custody for reputation.

- **Apply to Umia's Tailored Auctions** (sponsor track). Siren signs EIP-712 ServerPermits that gate Umia's UmiaValidationHook on Bench tier. Founders avoid running their own gating server; bidders embed Siren's hookData blob in their bid. First verifier-as-a-service for Umia, no new key custody.

- **Export a draft Umia application.** The verdict page also generates a schema-validated umia venture apply payload (canonical Community Track schema), prefilled from ENS records, locked when sourced from public evidence, JSON-download-only.

**Why the certificate is structurally trustworthy**

1. **Full-payload EIP-712 binding.** The signature covers subject, namehash, score, tier, timestamp, reportHash AND reportUri — verifier rejects on any field mismatch. Score-only signing left subject-spoofing wide open; we explicitly closed that hole.

2. **ECDSA-recovered, not field-claimed.** The off-chain verifier doesn't trust the "signer" string in the JSON envelope — it recovers the address from the EIP-712 signature via viem.recoverTypedDataAddress and rejects on mismatch.

3. **Trust-discounted source weights.** Unverified GitHub claims contribute at ×0.6 — never hidden, never inflated. The math the certificate carries is honest about what's verified.

4. **Re-derivable.** /api/bench/<ens> returns the raw evidence the certificate was minted from. Anyone can recompute the score themselves; no black box behind the signature.

5. **ENS-anchored.** Every certificate is bound to a human-readable .eth name via namehash. No opaque IDs, no URL shortlinks to phish.

6. **Honest ceiling.** Tier S is reserved for v2 (verified GitHub cross-sign). v1 doesn't pretend to mint a certificate at a tier the math can't reach.

**The 30-second story**

Type sbo3lagent.eth — see live tier B verdict pulled from Sourcify, GitHub, on-chain, and ENS-internal sources — click Publish to EAS — receive your on-chain certificate (Sepolia EAS UID). Tomorrow, paste that UID back into Siren — diff banner says UNCHANGED. Type a fresh agent — see tier U with "no data, no score" — fix your ENS records — re-run — tier C — mint a new certificate. Reputation that compounds, on-chain.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
**Making the on-chain certificate actually trustworthy, not just a signed JSON blob.** The first version of the EAS attestation flow did three things wrong at once: (1) the on-chain bytes field was the eas-sdk JSON envelope serialized, not the ABI-encoded BenchAttestationPayload — so on-chain decoders returned garbage instead of score/tier; (2) the off-chain verifier compared the "signer" field claim against expected, but never recovered the address from the EIP-712 signature — an attacker could write any signer into the JSON and we'd accept it; (3) the verifier checked reportHash only — leaving subject-spoofing wide open. Fix in one batch: re-encode via encodeBenchPayload before submit, recover via viem.recoverTypedDataAddress against eas-sdk-provided sig.domain/types/message, and verify all material fields (subject, namehash, reportHash, reportUri, score, tier, computedAt, recipient). An audit caught all three the day of the deadline.

**The publish flow was broken end-to-end and the broken state had been live for hours.** record-publish required an off-chain row in Turso before accepting the on-chain attestation, but saveOffchainAttestation had zero callers — every publish attempt failed with no_offchain_record. Fix: when no row exists, derive the bundle from the on-chain decoded payload itself and INSERT a fresh row, then record the publication. Now the certificate flow works whether or not the off-chain build endpoint ran first.

**Multi-chain ENS routing without exploding the page deadline.** Production defaulted to Sepolia (DEFAULT_BENCH_CHAIN_ID=11155111) so the curated demo agent on Sepolia would resolve, but real mainnet names like sbo3lagent.eth then routed through Sepolia first, hit "no resolver" rpc errors, retried on mainnet, and consistently blew the 12s page deadline. Fixed via name-suffix routing (only *.upgrade-siren-demo.eth go to Sepolia) plus per-source timeout budgets so one slow source can't wedge the whole orchestrator.

**Identity rotation false positives in the diff layer.** The compare-with-previous-certificate flow flagged "primaryAddress changed" ALERT every time a Sepolia attestation was diffed against a mainnet ENS resolution — because each chain holds its own resolver state. Solution: read attestation.network → chainId, only flag rotation when same chain; cross-chain compares get an INFO note explaining why addresses are not directly comparable.

**Tier ladder math contradiction visible to judges.** Engine thresholds were S>=65 / A>=50 after axis rebalance, but the UI legend still said S>=90 / A>=75 from a prior version. A score of 59 landed in A by the engine but the legend said A>=75. Caught by audit. Fix touched ScoreBanner, the new TierLadder component, the homepage tier-range table, and four demo booth tile labels — all of which had been tuned for the old ladder.

**Vercel "Sensitive" environment variables don't export.** We needed local scripts to query the prod ENS subgraph and Alchemy RPC, but vercel env pull returned empty strings for any var marked Sensitive. Workaround: ship a dedicated /api/ens/debug/<name> route that runs server-side with the real prod env, hit it from the browser to enumerate text records and coinType slots without ever pulling secrets to disk.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Siren Bench turns reputation into an economic primitive. Today, agents and onchain ventures can enter markets, raise capital, join auctions, or ask for trust mostly through social proof, private judgment, or opaque platform scoring. 

Siren replaces that with a public, verifiable benchmark: an ENS-named agent or project is scored from real evidence across Sourcify-verified contracts, GitHub activity, onchain history, ENS records, attestations, and signed reports. Every score is inspectable, every source is visible, and unverified claims are discounted instead of blindly trusted. 

For the Network Economy track, we take this one step further: the benchmark is not just shown in a report, it can control economic access. A founder can require a minimum Siren Bench tier for a Tailored Auction step, and a bidder who controls the subject ENS can mint a signed permit that is checked by an onchain validation hook. 

This makes reputation portable, transparent, and programmable across markets. Siren is building the trust layer that lets agentic economies decide not just who looks credible, but who is actually allowed to participate.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
Siren Bench is public due diligence for autonomous agents and onchain projects.

Today, agents and ventures can ask for funding, access, or trust with very little public evidence. A polished website and a GitHub link can look convincing, but communities need a way to see what is verified, what is unverified, and what is missing.

Siren Bench makes that process transparent. It turns ENS, Sourcify, GitHub, and onchain data into an inspectable report. Every score has a breakdown. Every source has a trust label. Unverified claims are discounted instead of being treated as truth.

This helps communities allocate attention, capital, and governance support more fairly.

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body:
**Sourcify is the part of Siren's trust math that proves your code does what your source says it does.** Siren reads four public sources for every ENS-named subject: Sourcify-verified bytecode, on-chain activity, ENS-internal records, and GitHub. Three of them — Sourcify, on-chain, ENS-internal — are weighted at full trust (×1.0) because they're structurally unfakeable: you can't lie about your nonce, you can't fake an ENS registration date, and Sourcify cryptographically anchors source code to the deployed bytecode hash. GitHub is the one source weighted at ×0.6, because a "com.github" claim in an ENS text record is just a claim — anyone can write it, no one verifies it.

**But Sourcify is special among the three full-trust sources, because only Sourcify links the source code to what's actually running on-chain.** On-chain activity proves the wallet exists and has been used. ENS-internal proves the name was registered. Neither tells you whether the smart contract behind that wallet does what its source claims. Only Sourcify does. That's why Sourcify gates the single-contract verdict (no Sourcify-verified source for a new proxy implementation → automatic SIREN, "no source, no upgrade") and why the Bench score collapses for any subject whose declared contracts aren't on Sourcify.

**When you mint a Siren report on-chain (EAS attestation), Sourcify proof flows into the certificate.** The signed payload embeds a hash over the full evidence record, including Sourcify match-levels and the verified source set. If the same subject is re-attested next month and Sourcify has gained a new verified deployment in the meantime, our diff banner lights up automatically. Sourcify's verification status becomes a reputation primitive that shows up in every certificate, every comparison, every governance vote based on a Siren report.

**Siren creates a structural incentive to verify on Sourcify.** Every page surfaces explicit "Verify on Sourcify" and "Submit to Sourcify" CTAs whenever a contract is unverified or only verified on Etherscan. Etherscan-only contracts are deliberately scored at half weight, and the panel says so out loud — telling the user exactly what they need to do to lift their tier. Agents, protocols, and projects that want a higher Siren benchmark are pushed toward Sourcify, not away from it.

**Reviewers can confirm the integration is live, not theatre.** A real-time "Sourcify · live · ~250ms" status indicator in the homepage hero pings Sourcify's v2 server on every poll. Click any verified contract entry on a bench page and you land on Sourcify's actual repo URL — same bytes, same hashes. The deep evidence panel shows compiler version, EVM target, optimizer settings, OpenZeppelin pattern detection (Pausable, Ownable, UUPS, AccessControl), proxy implementations, and the full storage layout slot-by-slot. None of it is mocked; the JSON behind it (/api/bench/<ens>) returns the raw evidence so reviewers can recompute the score themselves.

**Try it on sbo3lagent.eth** (live mainnet ENS with a published EAS certificate at sepolia.easscan.org/attestation/view/0xa5b4...) **or siren-agent-demo.upgrade-siren-demo.eth** (curated agent with a full four-source verdict). One click into either page shows Sourcify doing the load-bearing work the score talks about.

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body:
Siren tells Umia which agents have proof, not just promises.

The product. Type any ENS-named subject — agent, team, or project — into /b/[name] and Siren reads its public evidence in parallel: Sourcify-verified contracts (storage-layout history, license, compiler version, proxy resolution), GitHub repositories (top-20, README, LICENSE, test directory presence), on-chain history (first transaction via binary-search on historical nonce, contracts deployed via Sourcify deployer crosswalk, recent activity), and ENS-internal records (registration date, subname count, text-record count, last TextChanged block). Every signal carries a trust factor: 1.0 for verified sources (Sourcify, RPC, ENS subgraph), 0.6 for unverified GitHub claims. The score is a deterministic function of those contributions, locked in packages/evidence/src/score/weights.ts, and rendered to every user as a full breakdown — weight × value × trust = contribution per row. No black box.

The Umia integration. We deployed UmiaValidationHookMock on Sepolia and shipped packages/umia-permit, a workspace package that issues EIP-712 ServerPermit signatures from the Siren operator key. POST /api/umia/permit returns a permit encoding the subject's Bench tier, score, and signed report URI. The hook recovers the signer in-contract and gates the launch action. Without the hook there is no venture-launch surface to gate — Umia is the actual programmatic consumer of Bench, not a logo on a slide.

Reviewer outcomes. Bench routes subjects into clear lanes: fast-track (high seniority + relevance + verifiability), emerging review (relevant, not yet senior), evidence required (claim-heavy, low verifiability), reject (low relevance), or security audit (contract SIREN).
No data, no score.

description.title: Best ENS Integration for AI Agents
description.body:
Siren Bench uses ENS as the public identity root for AI agents.

Each agent is represented by an ENS name. From that name, the product resolves a live benchmark manifest, owner information, metadata, public endpoints, contracts, GitHub identity, and onchain address. The benchmark is built from the agent’s ENS identity outward.

Removing ENS would break the product. The agent would lose its public discovery surface, ownership anchor, and evidence registry. ENS is not a decorative username here; it is how the agent is found, identified, and evaluated.

For the demo, we show multiple prepared AI agents with ENS identities. A judge can enter an agent’s ENS name and immediately see its score, seniority, relevance, source grid, trust discount, and evidence drawers.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body:
Siren uses ENS for more than name-to-address resolution. We use ENS as a public evidence router.

An ENS name can represent a protocol, an AI agent, a team, or an onchain project. From that single name, Siren resolves the subject’s evidence map: contracts, source verification, ownership, report endpoints, benchmark manifests, public metadata, and signed report references.

This creates a new ENS pattern: name-to-evidence. Instead of treating an ENS name as a profile or wallet alias, Siren turns it into an inspectable trust surface. A user can type an ENS name and see what is verified, what is unverified, what is missing, and how each signal affects the final score.

The creative part is that ENS becomes the routing layer for public due diligence. One name opens a full report across Sourcify, GitHub, onchain history, ENS records, and attestations.

ensounds-edf2.name: ENSoundS
ensounds-edf2.tagline: Every ENS name has its melody

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
We introduce "musical avatars" to ENS names. 

Blockchain was too quiet for us. So we decided to give voice to the interactions between users there. 

- hear the hubbub of what is currently happening on the chain
- listen to the chime while finalizing your transaction: from me to whom

Are you curious what your name sounds like?

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The whole project was the challenge. In the beginning, we set up several axioms for our sound generator:
a) each name has unique melody 
b) final sound is recognizable as ENS name while allowing tweakable aspects

ENS names can be made with almost any UTF-8 character so the number of possibilities is enormous. Jush hashing the names for the generator would not ensure the uniqueness, we had to use different type of data: nibbles...

investigatoor-68b7.name: The Investigatoor
investigatoor-68b7.tagline: Paste an address, watch the graph fill in.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## The auditor's problem

Smart-contract investigations are the same five tabs every time: Sourcify, Etherscan, a JSON-RPC console, a notes file, and the friend who already audited this protocol. Auditors don't think in tables — they think in **graphs**. *Who deployed this. What does it call. What slot points where.* Existing tools are great at producing one of those facts at a time and terrible at stitching them together.

When an exploit drops at 3 AM, you need a mental map *now* — not after an hour of copy-pasting hex between tabs.

## What investigatoor does

Paste a contract address (or a tx hash). A long-running Claude agent fans out:

- hits **Sourcify v2** for verified source, ABI, storage layout, proxy resolution, and deployment in a single call
- finds the deployer EOA, the proxy implementation, the storage references that look like other deployed contracts
- recurses outward, drawing nodes and edges *as it goes*

Every contract becomes a node. Every relationship — deployment, storage-ref, call, delegatecall, admin — becomes an edge. Transcript on the left, live graph on the right, both updating in real time. When something looks wrong, you grab the canvas yourself: drag an edge, drop a sticky note, pin a block.

## Use cases

- **Live investigation.** A new exploit hits — paste the attacker tx, get the full call tree as a graph in one shot, then start asking the agent questions.
- **Pre-audit recon.** Map a protocol's contract surface (proxies, admins, modules, dependencies) before reading a single line of code.
- **Onboarding.** Hand a junior auditor a graph instead of a Notion page full of addresses.

## What makes it different

A workspace the agent and the human can both edit at the same time. You're not pasting output into Notion afterwards — you're watching the agent build the map while you read the transcript. Single binary, local-only, no backend, no DB. Your investigation is a folder on disk you can `git diff` and `grep`.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## Sandboxing the agent

The agent is a spawned local `claude` CLI driven by the **Claude Agent SDK** with `settingSources: []` and only an in-process MCP server exposed (`mcp__investigator__*` tool prefix, plus `Read` / `Grep` so it can recover oversized tool results). No `Bash`, no `Write`, no `WebFetch` — the agent can only touch the EVM through tools we wrote and audited.

## Filesystem as the database

`.app-state/` on disk is the source of truth: `contracts/<chain>/<addr>/` holds source, ABI, storage layout, deployer; `graphs/<id>/` holds the canvas state. A `chokidar` watcher streams every change to the browser as **Server-Sent Events**. The canvas updates because the file changed, not because the agent told it to — so two browser tabs on the same investigation see each other's edits for free.

## Block pinning, end-to-end

A pinned block (`📌 21000000`) has to thread through *every* read path: storage probes, proxy-slot reads, `call_contract`, the live Functions panel. One missed read silently returns live state and breaks reproducibility. Solved by routing every read through a single helper that takes the graph's `pinnedBlock` and refuses to compile without it.

## Layout that doesn't overlap

ELK gives nice layered placement but cards still collide after recursive expansion. Added a connected-components grid pass followed by a push-apart relaxation. The agent itself can call `get_layout` (returns bounding boxes + overlap pairs) and `auto_layout`, so it cleans up after a discovery burst instead of leaving a tangle.

## Tx-trace bootstrap

`POST /api/graph/[id]/from-tx` runs `debug_traceTransaction` (callTracer), walks the frame tree, drops a node per unique address and an edge per call — selectors decoded via the **Sourcify signature database** (`api.4byte.sourcify.dev`), with newly-seen signatures contributed back via `/import` so the registry grows from real investigations. You get a populated canvas *before* the agent says a word.

description.title: Sourcify Bounty
description.body:
## Why investigatoor fits the Sourcify bounty

**Sourcify is the spine of every investigation here.** The agent's first move on any new contract is one call: `GET sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/{chainId}/{address}` with `fields=abi,metadata,sources,storageLayout,deployment,proxyResolution`. Once that returns, the rest of the workspace lights up:

- **Source viewer** opens the full multi-file Sourcify source tree (not a flattened blob) directly in the contract panel.
- **Storage layout** parsed from Sourcify metadata feeds every storage-probing tool (`get_storage_at`, `read_proxy_slots`, `scan_storage_addresses`, `compute_mapping_slot`).
- **ABI** drives the live Functions panel: read-or-simulate any method via `viem` at the pinned block, no leaving the app.
- **EIP-1967 proxy slots** (impl/admin/beacon) are surfaced automatically when metadata says it's a proxy, so the agent follows the implementation without being prompted.
- **Selector decoding** on graph edges and the command-palette signature search use Sourcify's signature database at `api.4byte.sourcify.dev` — and we **contribute** newly-seen signatures back via `/import` so the registry grows from real investigations.

Sourcify-verified contracts go from *yet another address* to a fully-typed, fully-explored node on the graph in one round trip. Sourcify is the primary source-of-truth; we only fall through to Etherscan v2 for deployer info on contracts Sourcify hasn't indexed yet — and we surface that gap to the auditor, making **verified** contracts visibly more useful than unverified ones, which is exactly the incentive Sourcify is built around.

## Concretely, where Sourcify lives in the codebase

- `src/lib/sourcify.ts` — single-call v2 fetch (`fetchSourcify`) for source, ABI, metadata, storage layout, deployment, and proxy resolution
- `mcp__investigator__sourcify_fetch` — agent tool wrapping that call
- `read_contract_source`, `get_abi`, `list_functions`, `find_function_by_selector`, `get_storage_layout` — all backed by the cached Sourcify response under `.app-state/contracts/<chainId>/<address>/`
- `src/lib/signatures.ts` — Sourcify signature database client: `lookupSelector` and `searchSignatures` against `api.4byte.sourcify.dev`, plus `contributeSignatures` pushing new ones back via `/import`
- The contract panel's **Code** tab renders the full `sources.json` multi-file tree
- The contract panel's **Info** tab renders the Sourcify storage layout side-by-side with live slot values

## What we'd build next with the bounty

- Diff two Sourcify-verified versions of the same contract on the graph (proxy upgrades become visual).
- Cross-chain Sourcify lookups so a single investigation spans Mainnet + L2 deployments of the same protocol.
- A Sourcify-driven *audit checklist* node type: storage gaps, public mutators, unguarded `delegatecall`, missing access control — all derived from metadata.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
The core problem it tries to solve: **Information leakage in lending and liquidity**

In many lending setups (pools with visible APYs, public order books, or APIs that store everyone’s bids), standing interest rates and full order visibility are effectively public strategic data. That matters when:

- Large borrowers do not want the market to infer urgency, leverage, or directional views from the exact rate they will accept.
- Lenders do not want competitors or counterparties to free-ride on their pricing or front-run their provision of liquidity.
- Anyone operating like an institution cares about signaling: every public quote can move perception, credit spreads, or copy-trading behavior.

PrivaLend’s stated design goal is to split two things:
- **Public commitment** — what you are willing to do on-chain (or in a durable intent): token pair, size bounds, collateral constraints, expiry, and bounds on rates (floor for lenders, ceiling for borrowers), so the system can enforce consistency when a match is executed.
- **Private negotiation / matching** — the exact rates and how slices from multiple lenders combine, ideally computed only where raw bids are not sitting in a normal app database or traversing the mempool in the same cleartext form — conceptually aligned with a TEE-backed workflow (e.g. Chainlink CRE) where ciphertext can be decrypted only inside that environment.

So the “problem” is not only “borrow and lend tokens” (many protocols do that). It is borrow and lend without broadcasting fine-grained rate information through the same surfaces that today leak trading and credit signals.

**What people can actually use it for**
You can think of users in three buckets: lenders, borrowers, and operators / matchers.

Lenders
Post liquidity with a minimum acceptable rate (floor in basis points) and size, tied to a specific loan asset and collateral asset shape.
Be composed into a single borrower loan with other lenders: one borrower draw can be funded by several lenders at once, each with their own slice, while the blended rate must still respect every lender’s floor and the borrower’s ceiling (enforced when intents are consumed on-chain in the modular design described in the README).

Borrowers
Post borrow intent with a maximum rate they will pay and a minimum collateralization requirement (on-chain borrow intents require at least 100% collateral ratio in bps terms at post time; health is enforced later via oracle-backed managers).
Receive one coherent loan after matching: principal from multiple lenders, collateral locked, a single loan record with servicing (repay, add/remove collateral subject to health) and liquidation when undercollateralized (in the full modular stack).

Operators, matchers, and integrators
Run epochs: open window → register match digests → finalize → execute each digest once (replay protection, borrower nonce semantics) — a deliberate two-phase settlement control.
Run the off-chain engine: deterministic matching (README describes greedy fill, sorted borrows/lends, principal-weighted blended rate, rollback if blend violates borrower max).
Wire privacy-oriented submission paths: clients can submit ECIES-encrypted rates to the server; the engine decrypts when a private key exists (intended for CRE); proposals can be KMS-signed so settlement is tied to an agreed workflow identity (PrivaLendPool-style path uses EngineRegistry + signature verification).

Practical “product” outcomes
Credit market with less naked rate advertising than a fully public order book, while still ending in on-chain loans with clear custody and claims.
Syndicated-style funding for one borrower from many lenders in one execution, with enforced economics at settlement time rather than informal off-chain agreements only.

**How it makes existing tasks easier or “safer"**
Easier or clearer operationally
Single execution, many lenders: Instead of a borrower negotiating N separate loans off-chain and hoping everyone funds, the protocol is built around one match that pulls principal from multiple lenders and creates one loan object with pro-rata-style repayment distribution (README describes rounding dust to the first lender in LoanCore).
Explicit settlement pipeline: Epochs + digest registration make “what was approved to execute” a concrete, hash-anchored set before execution — useful for ops, compliance-minded workflows, and reducing ambiguity about which batch is canonical.
Separation of concerns in the modular contracts: IntentRegistry only allows the coordinator to consume liquidity; LoanCore custodies funds; PositionManager / LiquidationManager encapsulate borrower vs liquidator policies with oracle-based health — this mirrors how professional systems split booking, servicing, and workout.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body: One concrete hurdle was stitching two different settlement designs together: the Sepolia demo and executor.ts settle through PrivaLendPool.settleMatch + KMS-signed proposal hashes, while the “full” modular flow uses MatchingCoordinator epochs and digests—so the same off-chain machinery cannot call both without extra wiring, which is called out explicitly in the README. We got past it for the hackathon by treating the pool + executor path as the live demo spine, keeping the modular contracts as the clearer long-term architecture, and documenting the gap instead of pretending one ABI fit both—plus leaning on the deployment checklist and runbook so oracle wiring and envs did not become a last-minute surprise.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: PrivaLend fits the Network Economy track by treating privacy and user control as first-class parts of on-chain credit, not an afterthought. Borrowers and lenders commit to durable intents on-chain (pair, size, collateral bounds, expiry) so economic participation stays verifiable and self-custodial, while interest terms can stay off the public “billboard”: rates travel encrypted (e.g. ECIES) and are combined in a TEE-oriented matching workflow (e.g. Chainlink CRE), so standing bids are not stored or broadcast in cleartext the way a traditional visible order book would require. Settlement still lands as a single, enforceable multi-lender loan with oracle-backed health and liquidation—real decentralized economic infrastructure without forcing users to leak their full negotiation surface to a central database or the mempool. In short, PrivaLend advances a next-generation lending economy where users keep autonomy over sensitive economic signals while retaining the trust-minimized guarantees of on-chain execution.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body: PrivaLend is a privacy-oriented lending stack where users commit intents on-chain while sensitive interest rates can stay encrypted until matching runs in a Chainlink CRE workflow. The critical security bridge between that private matching step and on-chain loan creation is cryptographic attestation of each match proposal: our CRE runner hashes each proposal and requests an EIP-191–compatible Ethereum signature from SpaceComputer’s KMS through Orbitport—authenticating with Orbitport OAuth and calling kms.Sign with ETHEREUM_SECP256K1 so the matcher never holds a long-lived hot signing key in application memory. That directly serves the bounty’s goal of space-grade trust and integrity: Orbitport is the operational gateway for access-controlled, KMS-backed signing, and the KMS is the trust anchor that lets a dApp treat off-chain matching output as binding for settlement in a domain where integrity and non-repudiation matter as much as privacy. Our working prototype runs this path end-to-end (CRE → Orbitport KMS → signed proposals → pool verification), which we document in the README and ship with smoke tests for Orbitport auth and KMS signing.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
### Fama is Twitter with consequences.

Every post is a falsifiable claim with a deadline. When the deadline passes, the claim resolves, the author’s credibility updates, and future feed ranking changes. Instead of optimizing for engagement, Fama optimizes for being right.

### What do we solve

Let's be honest, your twitter timeline is full of thirst traps and rage baits. The more you engage with the post, the higher is it on your feed.
The most important tweets or the tweets that are carrying the value are often left behind

Fama solves this by turning posts into falsifiable claims with deadlines. Instead of likes or follower count deciding who gets seen, authors build a non-transferable credibility score from resolved claims.

People can use Fama to:

- Make public predictions with accountable outcomes
- Track who is consistently right over time
- Discover high-signal voices without relying on popularity
- Challenge claims by agreeing or disagreeing before the deadline
- Build a portable truth record
- Reduce misinformation incentives by making vague, viral posting less valuable

For users, Fama makes social discovery safer and more useful: the feed surfaces people with proven accuracy, not just people who are good at getting attention.

For communities, it creates a shared memory of who made which claims, when they made them, how the crowd voted, and what actually happened.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of the main hurdles was wiring together several moving pieces without making the app feel fragile: authentication, wallet/KMS signing, generated media, and the social posting flow all had to agree on the same user and asset state.

### SpaceComputer

The trickiest bug was around key creation and signing with the OrbitPortSDK. Some requests looked correct from the frontend but failed because the backend payload shape did not match what the provider expected. I worked through it by isolating the flow with small server-side debug calls, comparing the raw API response against the SDK behavior, then tightening the request format and error logging so failures became obvious instead of silent.

### Swarm

We tried to implement swarm-based key-value storage. The problem was that the local node setup did not work, so we needed to use their hosted solution.

### Apify

The process of using Apify via x402 had two main issues.

First, the whole process is oriented around the `apify mcp cli`, which made raw HTTP requests harder to work with. We had to use some workarounds, especially since we use SpaceCoin KMS.

Second, even though some scrapers were marked as pay-per-request, we sometimes got an error saying they had to be paid per batch.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Fama fits the Future Society track because it explores how Ethereum can make online discourse more transparent, accountable, and fair.

Today’s social platforms reward engagement, which often favors outrage, misinformation, and popularity over accuracy. Fama proposes a different model: a social network where visibility is earned through a transparent record of resolved claims.

Every post is a falsifiable statement with a deadline. The claim, votes, and resolution are recorded through Ethereum-based infrastructure, while the author’s credibility score is non-transferable and earned over time. This creates a public accountability layer for social media without relying on a centralized platform to decide who is trustworthy.

Fama empowers communities by helping them identify high-signal contributors based on demonstrated accuracy rather than follower count, status, or paid amplification. It can be used by local communities, DAOs, research groups, journalists, public-good teams, and civic organizations to track predictions, commitments, and claims over time.

The project also supports fair and transparent governance. Communities can use Fama to evaluate proposals, public commitments, and decision-makers based on their historical truth record. Instead of reputation being subjective or platform-controlled, it becomes auditable, portable, and earned.

By combining Ethereum, soulbound credibility, and decentralized content storage, Fama aims to support a healthier information ecosystem where being accurate matters more than being loud.

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
Fama uses the **SpaceComputer Orbitport SDK / KMS** as the signing layer for user actions on-chain. Instead of asking users to connect a browser wallet, Fama provisions a dedicated Ethereum-compatible KMS key for each signed-in user through the Orbitport SDK.

When a user creates their account, the app calls `sdk.kms.createKey` with an Ethereum secp256k1 signing key configuration. We store the returned `keyId` and Ethereum address in our app database and bind it to that user account. That address becomes the user’s on-chain identity for posting claims and voting.

We then use Orbitport KMS to sign real Base Sepolia transactions. For example, when a user creates a Fama claim:

1. The claim text is uploaded to Swarm through SwarmKV.
2. The app encodes the `createPost(bytes32 swarmHash, uint64 deadline, uint64 voteLockWindow)` contract call.
3. The backend builds an EIP-1559 transaction.
4. The transaction digest is signed through `sdk.kms.sign` using `ETHEREUM_SECP256K1`.
5. The backend serializes and broadcasts the signed transaction.

The same KMS-backed flow is also used for voting: agreeing or disagreeing with claims calls the Fama contract from the user’s Orbitport-managed Ethereum address.

So Orbitport KMS is central to Fama’s UX: it lets Twitter-authenticated users interact with smart contracts without managing private keys manually, while still giving every user a real Ethereum signing address and verifiable on-chain activity.

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body:
We have implemented our own KV storage on Swarm as a backbone of our application.  We built and use a local `@swarmkv/core` package that gives the app a simple key-value API over Swarm: `put`, `get`, `delete`, `keys`, `entries`, and `iterate`.

In Fama, every post is a falsifiable claim. Instead of storing the claim text directly on-chain, we write the claim text to Swarm through SwarmKV. Swarm returns a 32-byte content reference, and the `Fama` smart contract stores that reference together with the post metadata, deadline, author, vote window, and vote counters.

This gives us a clean split:

- Swarm stores the actual claim text as decentralized, content-addressed data.
- The smart contract stores the authoritative reference to that content.
- The indexer and frontend use the stored Swarm reference to hydrate the feed and display the original claim text.

We use SwarmKV to make Swarm feel like a normal developer database while still preserving Swarm’s decentralized storage model. For public Fama posts, the app uploads the post text, receives the Swarm reference, passes it into `createPost(bytes32 swarmHash, uint64 deadline, uint64 voteLockWindow)`, and later fetches the text back from Swarm when rendering the feed.

description.title: Apify Bounty
description.body:
Fama uses APIFY for its claim-resolution workflow. Fama is a social prediction and credibility app where every post is a falsifiable claim with a deadline. After the deadline, the claim needs to be resolved against real-world evidence.

Our intended integration is to make that resolution step use **Apify Actors paid through X402**. When a claim reaches its deadline, a resolver can spawn an Apify scraper to gather external evidence from relevant public sources: X/Twitter posts, news pages, websites, market pages, product listings, or other real-time web data depending on the claim. The Apify Actor provides the evidence needed to decide whether the claim resolved as true or false.

The X402 part is important because the scraper is not just a free backend task. The resolver pays for the Apify service at the moment it is needed, using the X402 payment flow. This creates a concrete paid data workflow inside the app:

1. A user posts a claim on Fama.
2. The claim text is stored on Swarm and its reference is stored on-chain.
3. Other users vote before the deadline.
4. After the deadline, a resolver triggers an Apify Actor.
5. The Apify scraping job is paid for through X402.
6. The scraper returns evidence from real-world web sources.
7. The resolver uses that evidence to resolve the claim.
8. The Fama contract updates the claim outcome and user credibility.

This gives Fama a real use case for Apify in Web3: paid, on-demand real-world data collection for decentralized claim resolution. Instead of manually trusting a resolver with no supporting data, Fama can attach scraped evidence to the resolution process and make the cost of obtaining that evidence explicit through X402.

In future versions, this could evolve into an agent workflow: a Fama resolver agent pays an Apify scraper agent through X402, receives structured evidence, summarizes it, and submits the proposed resolution back to the Fama protocol.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Most AI browser tools rely on centralized cloud APIs, which means prompts, browsing context, and task data leave the user’s machine. Freedom runs a local AI agent in the browser and can coordinate work with other browser agents through Swarm. Users can ask it to research pages, summarize content, or perform browser tasks while keeping more control over where data is processed. Larger tasks can be sent to other agents, with results written back to Swarm as content-addressed data. Agents can also be selected by capability and, later, by cleaner available electricity for inference and other sustainability markers.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
We uploaded a Gemma4 AI model family to Swarm, to allow for P2P downloads to Freedom users around the world. The main model file is 7 GB, which is a real challenge to upload and persist on Swarm. We extended our own Swarm node implementation to allow for stable and fast uploads of large files.

To let Freedom instances speak to each other for sharing work other across networks, we used the XMTP protocol. Messaging via pub/sub for light nodes of decentralized storage networks is not a solved problem yet.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
Freedom AI explores a more user-controlled and sustainable way to run AI. Instead of sending prompts and browsing context to centralized cloud APIs, Freedom runs a local AI agent in the browser and can coordinate work with other browser-based agents through Swarm and XMTP. This lets users keep more control over where their data is processed, while also making AI workloads more resilient and transparent.

The project also introduces the idea of energy-aware inference: agents can be selected by capability and, in future versions, by the availability of cleaner electricity. This connects decentralized infrastructure with practical goals around privacy, autonomy, and more responsible use of compute.

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body:
Freedom Browser is building the local-first operating system for user-owned AI agents: agents run privately on the user’s device, register their identity onchain, make payments with the user’s permission, and act across the decentralized web.

Freedom Browser turns the browser into a local agentic execution environment.

Instead of routing user data through cloud AI APIs, Freedom runs a small open model locally inside the browser through the Pi agent harness. The user can install and run a local Gemma-powered agent, give it browser-aware tools, and allow it to act on their behalf with explicit permissions.

Our agent can:

- run local reasoning privately on the user’s machine,
- use browser context safely,
- register itself as an onchain agent through EIP-8004,
- make paid service calls using x402 through Freedom’s built-in wallet,
- request user approval before spending money or publishing data,
- produce auditable agent actions and receipts,
- and become the foundation for agent-to-agent commerce.

This is not just an AI sidebar. It is a new category of browser-native agent infrastructure: a sovereign agent runtime for the decentralized web.

Freedom is a strong agentic venture because it has a clear path to revenue through paid agent tools, browser-native agent subscriptions, x402 service fees, agent identity infrastructure, local model distribution, and eventually a tokenized marketplace for verified agent skills and services.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
initial commits: [FE](https://github.com/admpr/eth-prague-2/commit/9460e20f5767d15eea1a170bdb87d2db47c4ec98), [contracts](https://github.com/admpr/eth-prague-contracts/commit/b8c20656c2a91f3314ea8fff581c0e10b17d280b), [agent-showcase](https://github.com/admpr/eth-prague-agent/commit/5d949f62535eae2f817cab183af4b11454a6d622)

**Wallexa** makes AI agents safer to use onchain by turning a regular hardware-wallet into a modular smart wallet with scoped agent access.

Today, giving an AI agent blockchain access usually means handing it a private key with full control, or creating a separate wallet that must be constantly funded and often lacks the permissions, reputation, or app history of the main wallet. Wallexa solves this by keeping the hardware wallet as the root authority while using **EIP-7702**, **ERC-4337**, and **ERC-7579** modular account infrastructure to issue limited agent keys.

Agents can transact from the user’s real wallet address, but only within boundaries enforced onchain: token spend limits, ETH budgets, contract allowlists, function-level permissions, time windows, and revocation. Example roles include stablecoin payment assistants, DeFi rebalancers, rewards claimers, treasury payers, gas runners, governance voters, and many more.

Users no longer need to expose their main private key or constantly refill separate agent wallets. The wallet owner can sleep calmly knowing their agents can keep working from the secure hardware-wallet, but cannot bypass the rules set for them.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of the biggest challenges was that the idea started from the hardware itself. The Idea was born at the hackathon when we received a small hardware wallet with open-source firmware, but the firmware did not support signing the new **EIP-7702 authorization** needed to delegate an EOA and turn it into a smart account. To make Wallexa possible, we had to fork the wallet firmware and add custom support for signing EIP-7702 authorization lists directly from the hardware wallet.

Another major hurdle was the permission system. We could not find an existing **ERC-7579 validator module** that matched the exact access-control model we needed for AI agents: token spending limits, native ETH budgets, contract allowlists, function-level restrictions, time windows, and revocation. So we built and deployed our own Solidity ERC-7579 validator module that enforces these boundaries onchain.

The final challenge was proving that the system actually works with real agents. We built a small agent demo repo where agents can be initialized with the generated access keys and attempt transactions from the user’s wallet address. This let us demonstrate both sides: transactions inside the agent’s permissions succeed, while transactions outside its boundaries fail, even if the agent is instructed to perform them. Most importantly, the successful transactions are still made from the hardware wallet’s address, showing that the agent can operate through the user’s real wallet without ever receiving full control over it.

description.title: Ethereum Core
description.body:
Wallexa is built directly on Ethereum account abstraction primitives and explores a practical use case for the next generation of wallets.

The project uses **EIP-7702** to delegate an existing hardware-wallet EOA into smart account logic while preserving the same address. It also uses **ERC-4337** execution patterns and an **ERC-7579-compatible validator module** to support modular, scoped agent permissions.

We also built a custom Solidity validator module because existing modules did not provide the exact permission model needed for AI agents, such as token spending limits, native ETH budgets, contract allowlists, function-level restrictions, time windows, and revocation.

Wallexa demonstrates how Ethereum accounts can evolve from single-key wallets into programmable, modular, safer accounts without forcing users to abandon their existing address.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Wallexa fits the Network Economy track because it improves how users safely participate in autonomous onchain economic activity.

AI agents increasingly need to make payments, interact with protocols, claim rewards, manage balances, or pay for services on behalf of users. Today this usually requires giving the agent full wallet control or creating a separate wallet that must be manually funded. Both options create friction and risk.

Wallexa keeps the user’s hardware wallet as the root authority while allowing agents to operate from the user’s real wallet address under onchain-enforced permissions. The owner can define token budgets, ETH limits, contract allowlists, function restrictions, expiration windows, and revocation.

This creates a safer model for agent-driven economic activity: agents can participate in markets, services, and protocols, but users remain in control of the wallet and its risk boundaries.

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body:
Wallexa is designed for the agentic economy: AI agents that can safely act onchain for users.

The core problem is that agents need wallet access to be useful, but traditional wallets are controlled by a single private key. Giving that key to an agent gives it full control over funds, permissions, and account history. Wallexa solves this by letting users create scoped access keys for agents while keeping the hardware wallet as the root authority.

Agents can transact from the user’s real wallet address, but only within boundaries enforced onchain: token budgets, ETH limits, contract allowlists, function permissions, time windows, and revocation.

This enables practical agent roles such as payment assistants, DeFi rebalancers, rewards claimers, treasury payers, gas runners, governance voters, and paid-data agents, without giving those agents unlimited wallet power.

description.title: Apify Bounty
description.body:
Wallexa fits the Apify bounty through an agent workflow where an AI agent uses Apify as an external data/tool provider and pays for it safely with a scoped wallet key.

In our demo, the wallet owner creates an access key for an Apify-enabled agent with a strict **$5/day spending limit**. When the agent needs external data, such as Instagram data, it calls an Apify scraper. If that service requires payment through an **x402 payment flow**, the agent uses its Wallexa signing key to pay for the service.

This demonstrates a safer model for autonomous agents consuming paid web services. The agent can fetch data and pay for tools when needed, but it cannot exceed the wallet owner’s programmed spending limit or bypass the permissions enforced by Wallexa while still keep making transaction from main wallet and without never ending top up balance to wallet.

A role-aware dashboard shows live scores, agent registry on Sepolia, and ENS CCIP-Read resolution of risk text records. description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
```markdown
**Numbers below were validated against the running system:** gas costs (~15.5k verify / ~20.3k attest) by `forge test`; test counts (127 unit / 52 e2e / 4 Foundry) by `npm run test:unit && npm run test:e2e && forge test`; live deployment confirmed at `hollow-vault.vercel.app/api/health` (mode: real, signerType: kms). Sony PS3 (Dec 2010, fail0verflow @ 27C3) and Android Bitcoin SecureRandom (Aug 2013) are public record.

---

Every Web3 wallet keeps the private key on the user's device. **Three failure modes follow that have already cost real users real money** — and no software-only fix works without changing where the key lives.

Hollow Vault moves the key into SpaceComputer's Orbitport KMS and binds 32 bytes of cosmic randomness (from Orbitport's satellite-attested cTRNG) into every signature.

## What it makes safer

**🔑 Broken-RNG ECDSA key extraction.** Sony PS3 and Android Bitcoin wallets lost funds when two signatures shared a nonce — the math leaks the key. Hollow Vault mixes externally-sourced cosmic entropy into every signed payload, so even a broken local CSPRNG can't produce a colliding nonce. Live in-browser proof at `/vulnerability`: recovers a key from two reused-nonce signatures in ms, then shows the same attack on Hollow Vault returns nothing.

**🔧 Key seizure / forced extraction.** Your laptop holds only OAuth credentials, never the secp256k1 key. Lose the laptop → revoke the credentials → nobody can produce new signatures with that key. The key itself sits in a TEE today, with on-orbit secure elements on SpaceComputer's roadmap.

**🕒 Backdating.** Cosmic seed is in the signed payload; verifier checks freshness (24h past / 2min future); the satellite-attested timestamp ties each signature to a draw that didn't exist before. Receipts can't be retroactively forged.

## What it makes easier

- **SIWE / EIP-712 / standard `ecrecover`** — signatures are bit-compatible; no contract changes
- **drand-using dapps** — JSON-shape adapter at `/info`, `/public/latest`, `/public/{round}` for cosmic-attested randomness
- **On-chain verification** — `HollowVaultVerifier.sol` (Foundry-tested) verifies at **~15.5k gas**, attests at **~20.3k gas**

## New things it unlocks

- **Whistleblower receipts** — journalist's priority-of-disclosure attestation survives subpoena; once credentials revoke, no party can forge new signatures from that key
- **AI agent wallets** — per-agent KMS keys with policy bounds (`maxPerTxWei`, `allowedRecipients`) + JSONL audit log; compromised agent process can't exfiltrate the key
- **Cosmic-timestamped public commitments** — sign now, anchor on-chain within 24h, durable proof of when
- **Sealed-bid auctions** — bid commits to a seed that didn't exist when the bid was formulated

Open-source at `github.com/batikanor/HollowVault`, live at `hollow-vault.vercel.app`, locked behind 127 unit + 52 e2e + 4 Foundry tests.
```

description.title: SpaceComputer Bounty
description.body:
Hollow Vault hits two of the three SpaceComputer ETHPrague tracks directly:

### 🛰️ Track 1 — Space KMS (primary)

The entire Ethereum signer is built on `sdk.kms.createKey()` and `sdk.kms.sign()` from the official `@spacecomputer-io/orbitport-sdk-ts`. We use:

- `keySpec: ECC_SECG_P256K1` (Ethereum's secp256k1 curve)
- `keyUsage: SIGN_VERIFY`
- `scheme: ETHEREUM`
- `messageType: DIGEST` (we send the 32-byte payload hash)
- `signingAlgorithm: ETHEREUM_SECP256K1`

We consume the 65-byte `r ‖ s ‖ v` output as the canonical Ethereum signature. The private key is created in the Orbitport gateway TEE, never leaves it, and is referenced only by `keyId`. The same code path will run against on-orbit secure elements when SpaceComputer ships them — no client changes needed.

### 🔌 Track 2 — Orbitport External Plugin (secondary)

We ship a **drand-compatible HTTP adapter** at `/info`, `/public/latest`, `/public/{round}`. drand is the de-facto standard for verifiable randomness on Ethereum — every randomness-consuming dapp (lotteries, raffles, fair-launch sales, randomness beacons) is integrated against its API. Our adapter sources entropy from `sdk.ctrng.random()`, ties it to a deterministic round number derived from the Orbitport timestamp, and exposes the canonical drand JSON shape so existing clients can point their URL at us with zero code changes (for clients that consume randomness without strict BLS verification, which is most of them).

This is a real protocol bridge between SpaceComputer's cosmic randomness and the existing dapp ecosystem — not a wrapper.

### 🎲 Cosmic randomness used in every signature

Every Hollow Vault signature mixes 32 bytes of cosmic randomness pulled live from `sdk.ctrng.random()` into the signed payload via `keccak256("hollow-vault/v1|" ‖ cosmic_seed ‖ timestamp ‖ messageHash)`. This is what kills the broken-RNG ECDSA bug structurally — even if the local CSPRNG were broken, the externally-sourced cosmic seed forces every nonce to be unique.

### Stack alignment

| SpaceComputer primitive | Where Hollow Vault uses it |
| --- | --- |
| `sdk.kms.createKey` | Per-device key (`hollow-vault-prod-{ts}`); per-agent key (`hollow-vault-agent-v1-{name}-{id}`) |
| `sdk.kms.sign` (DIGEST mode) | Every `/api/sign`, `/api/sign-typed`, `/api/sign-batch` call |
| `sdk.ctrng.random` | Every cosmic-seed draw, plus the drand adapter's randomness source |
| OAuth client credentials | Authorise gateway calls; revocable from the dashboard, which is the seizure-defence mechanism |

Live demo running with real Orbitport credentials in production at hollow-vault.vercel.app.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Freelancers and clients often do not trust each other. Clients worry about paying for low-quality or incomplete work, while freelancers worry about doing work and not getting paid. Smart Jobs solves this with an on-chain escrow flow: the client funds a job upfront, the freelancer submits a preview and source package, and an AI reviewer compares the delivery against the original brief before the buyer releases or refunds the payment.

The result is a safer freelance workflow where payment is locked transparently, source files stay gated until approval, and both sides get a clear review layer without relying on a centralized middleman.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The hardest part was making the full escrow lifecycle work end to end: creating a job, funding escrow, accepting the job as a freelancer, submitting files, running AI review, and then releasing or refunding funds on Sepolia.

Another challenge was handling real file submissions. The app needed to show buyer-safe preview files while keeping source files hidden until approval. I also had to connect the AI review output to the local job ledger and make the review page feel responsive while the model was processing.

On the smart contract side, the difficult part was keeping the frontend wallet flow, transaction confirmations, and local escrow state in sync so users do not get stuck after MetaMask confirms a transaction.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body: SmartJobs is a decentralized freelance marketplace where every job is backed by an Ethereum smart contract escrow. Clients lock funds on-chain before work begins; the contract releases payment automatically once the buyer approves the delivered work. This creates a trustless economic network between strangers — no platform intermediary holds the money, no chargebacks, no disputes decided by a centralized party. The entire payment flow (fund → lock → release or refund) lives on-chain, making it a real working example of a programmable network economy.

description.title: Future Society
description.body: SmartJobs reimagines the gig economy for a world where AI and blockchain are infrastructure. An AI agent autonomously reviews every submitted deliverable — scoring quality, generating a structured verdict (pass / needs revision / fail), and summarizing feedback — before the buyer even opens the submission. Combined with on-chain escrow, this creates a new kind of work relationship: global, permissionless, and partially automated. Workers anywhere can get paid fairly without trusting a platform; clients get an objective AI audit on every job.

description.title: Best Agentic Venture
description.body: SmartJobs features a fully autonomous AI review agent that operates on every job submission without human intervention. The agent receives the delivered files and job description, runs a structured evaluation via OpenAI, and returns a machine-readable verdict: pass, needs_revision, or fail — along with a numeric quality score and written feedback. This agent acts as an impartial third party in every transaction, reducing disputes and enabling trustless quality gates in a decentralized freelance market. It is the core agentic component that makes the escrow release decision meaningful.

description.title: A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm
description.body: SmartJobs stores all job data — titles, descriptions, AI review results, file references, and submission metadata — in Swarm's key-value store. Every job has a unique key derived from its ID; the value is a JSON record updated at each stage of the job lifecycle (created → submitted → reviewed → paid). This replaces a traditional database with a decentralized, content-addressed store. The escrow smart contract on Ethereum references these Swarm keys to link on-chain payments to off-chain job records, creating a fully decentralized data + payment stack.

description.title: Most Creative Use of ENS
description.body: SmartJobs resolves every participant's wallet address to their ENS name and avatar throughout the marketplace. On the job board, clients are shown as "vitalik.eth" instead of "0x1234...abcd". On the submit workspace, the freelancer sees the client's ENS identity. On profile cards, ENS avatars are displayed. The resolution runs on Ethereum Mainnet via Viem's getEnsName and getEnsAvatar, with graceful fallback to shortened addresses when no ENS name exists. This makes a blockchain-native freelance marketplace feel as human and readable as a traditional platform.

certino-9325.name: Certino
certino-9325.tagline: Connecting small grid producers to extra revenue

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Today's renewable energy certificate market is broken in three ways.

Annual averages hide the truth. Legacy Guarantees of Origin match generation to consumption *yearly* — but the grid runs hour by hour. Solar peaks at noon, demand peaks at 8 PM, and annual-matched certificates pretend those kWh are equal.

Small producers are locked out. The €3B European GO market was built for utilities. Households with batteries, small wind, and grid-balancing power generations like Treetino's hardware earn nothing extra for time-shifting kWh into peak demand. 30–50% of revenue evaporates in middleman fees.

Provenance is "trust us." Most certificates retire in private registries with no public proof. EU RED III will mandates hourly matching in 2030. CSRD demands location-bound evidence. The market has no rails for either.

Certino fixes all three. Every clean kWh mints as an on-chain ERC-721 with hour, location, fuel type, and device ID. Buyers deposit EURC into transparent pools that settle monthly against the EPEX SPOT auction. Producers earn a premium when OTE-CR clearing exceeds threshold — when the grid actually needs the energy. Buyer identity is a soulbound NFT, audit-grade and non-transferable.

What it enables:
- Households with Victron inverters earn premium credits for time-shifting into peak demand
- Corporates get CSRD/Scope 2 evidence with cryptographic provenance
- ESG auditors verify claims without registry intermediation
- Small grid-enhancers get their fair share of a market that used to ignore them

Real kWh. Real money. Real provenance. Every hour, on-chain.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Transforming our initial conceptual architecture into a seamless, end-to-end functional demo presented severe integration hurdles. The primary bottleneck was environment synchronization—specifically, coordinating complex decentralized oracle networks (Chainlink) and managing heavy data payloads across the team's distributed local development setups. 
• Real Victron telemetry is unsigned JSON over REST. For dual-issuance verification we needed cryptographic attestation — couldn't ship hardware in 48h. Built an oracle that pulls VRM data, signs each pulse with EIP-712, and posts on-chain. We are implementing Chainlink Oracle to proof that the data we are getting are correct. We also explore implement ai agents to verify the weather using the GPS data we have, if the kWh were possible to produce, if no one is not faking it. 

Three NFT types, one mental model. The system needs three distinct tokens: a soulbound *device* NFT (producer side), a soulbound *account* NFT (buyer side, audit identity), and a transferable *certificate* ERC-721 (the actual unit of trade). Keeping the user flows clean while three different mints happen across two roles took several iterations — especially making "soulbound" visually distinct from "transferable" in the UI without dropping into smart-contract jargon.

Pool settlement timing. Marketplace pools settle monthly against EPEX SPOT — but EPEX publishes day-ahead, not month-ahead. Modelled as deferred clearing: deposits enter a pending state, certificates issue post-settlement. Took two design passes to separate "deposit confirmed" (immediate receipt) from "certificate minted" (post-settlement) cleanly in the UX. Indicative €/MWh shown in the marketplace had to be visibly distinct from final settlement price.

EURC. Circle's official EURC is mainnet only — not Base Sepolia. Deployed a mock EURC with faucet, kept buyer flows identical to production integration so the demo is honest about what's mocked.

MetaMask on Amoy. RPC instability caused intermittent signing failures. Added retry with exponential backoff and a clearer "tx pending" state. For the recorded demo, pinned to a known-good endpoint.

description.title: Network Economy
description.body:
Certino is a DePIN, settlement protocol for the European energy grid. We tokenize real-world physical infrastructure — Victron-attested inverters, household batteries, small wind, grid-balancing reactors — and turn their hourly output into on-chain economic activity.

The network is the economy. Each device is a soulbound NFT. Each verified hour of clean MWh is an ERC-721. Each buyer claim is a soulbound audit identity. Each pool settles in EURC against a real spot-price auction every month. Producers earn yield; buyers earn provable green claims; the protocol takes a thin fee. No utility, no broker, no registry intermediary in the middle.

Bottom-up coordination. The €3B European GO market today is a top-down utility game — built for big plants, paid in annual averages. Certino flips that. A household with a battery can earn a premium for time-shifting kWh into peak demand, in the same market, on the same rails as a wind farm.

A network where physical work pays continuously. A typical 10 kW household solar installation earns roughly €80 per year in premium credits just by participating — recurring micropayments tied directly to real grid-balancing work. Scale that across the Czech bidding zone, then across EU RED III's hourly-matching mandate, and you have a self-bootstrapping network of physical assets coordinating economically without a centralized operator.

That's the Network Economy thesis: real-world infrastructure, real-world money, on-chain coordination. Certino is the energy slice of it.

description.title: Future Society
description.body:
ETH Prague 2026's theme is Solarpunk Future. Certino is what that future looks like at the level of one kWh.

A grid owned by the people on it. Today's energy market is a utility-shaped pyramid: large plants generate, brokers package, corporates buy paper. Households and small producers — the people doing the actual work of decarbonizing — sit at the bottom, paid in averages. We invert it. Anyone with a Victron inverter, a small wind turbine, or a grid-balancing reactor like Treetino's HILIER becomes a first-class participant in the same market that used to ignore them.

Truth as infrastructure. A solarpunk society doesn't run on "trust us" claims. It runs on verifiable, public, granular evidence. Every Certino certificate carries the hour, the device, the location, the fuel type — soulbound to the producer, retired publicly by the buyer, immutable on Base. EU RED III and CSRD are pulling regulation toward exactly this. We're building the rails ahead of the law.

Regenerative economics, not extractive. Producers earn a premium when the grid actually needs the energy — when their kWh prevents gas from being burned. The protocol takes a thin fee. No middleman captures 30–50% of the value flow. The yield goes back to the people whose physical assets are doing the regenerative work.

The hackathon submission is one slice of a longer arc. Treetino's broader mission is grid-balancing infrastructure for a 100% renewable Europe — HILIER reactors, Treetino products, small battery units that store off-peak excess and release at peak demand. Certino is the protocol layer that makes those assets, and millions of household assets like them, economically coherent. Tokenize the physical work, settle in stablecoin, retire claims on-chain, repeat every hour.

That's a Future Society we want to live in. We're shipping the first piece of it this weekend.
