sentinel-ade1.name: Sentinel
sentinel-ade1.tagline: Your Contract gets hacked, Ours fixes Itself

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Smart contracts are immutable by default, so when a vulnerability ships to mainnet the response options are bad ones: a frantic war-room patch hours after the
  exploit has already drained the treasury, or a permanent freeze that strands user funds. Audits help but don't catch novel attack patterns, and human-only
  response loops are too slow for an adversary that can drain a vault in a single block.

  Sentinel is an autonomous defense layer for upgradeable contracts. Drop in a Solidity source file and a UUPS proxy address; the pipeline:

  - Finds vulnerabilities with five detection agents running in parallel (Slither, Mythril symbolic execution, an LLM semantic agent, a governance agent, and a
  ChromaDB threat-pattern lookup), then merges their findings into a single confidence-scored picture.
  - Patches them by generating three candidate fixes — one from a proven-patches knowledge base, one experimental, one pure LLM — and runs each through a
  five-gate validator (vuln removal, compilation, signature preservation, KB similarity, fuzzing) with zero tolerance.
  - Deploys safely via upgradeToAndCall, captures a pre-patch baseline of gas usage and revert rates, and stores a rollback target.
  - Watches and self-heals. A post-deploy monitor compares each new block against the baseline. A gas spike (>p95×1.5) or revert-rate jump auto-triggers a
  rollback to the last-known-good implementation; if the rollback target is also compromised, a circuit-breaker freezes the contract and pages a human.

  Who it helps:
  - DeFi protocol teams — get a safety net between audits and the next 0-day, without giving up the ability to ship features quickly.
  - Security engineers — the dashboard exposes every detection finding, every gate decision, every LangSmith trace, every rollback event. It's an explainable
  agent system, not a black box.
  - Researchers and auditors — the LangGraph state, KB partitions (proven / rejected / patterns), and RL reward log are all introspectable, so you can study how
  the system learns from each pipeline run.

  The end result is the same property that self-healing distributed systems have had for years (k8s pod restarts, circuit breakers, canary rollbacks) finally
  extended to on-chain code, where the cost of a missed anomaly is measured in user funds.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1. Demonstrating the monitor was harder than building it. PostDeployMonitor was the most architecturally interesting piece — it watches real blocks, compares
  them to a baseline, and fires upgradeToAndCall for rollback — but for a long time it had no demo. The first version of the dashboard had a synthetic
  /demo/inject-anomaly endpoint that just mocked block metrics into the rollback path; it worked, but anyone who knew web3 would (correctly) call it theater. The
   fix was end-to-end: deploy a real Attacker.sol contract with both a reentrancy exploit and a gas-burner, build an in-process TrafficGenerator that drives
  multi-account deposits/withdraws against the Hardhat node, add an on_block_metrics callback hook to PostDeployMonitor so each inspected block emits a
  structured event, and stream that over SSE into a new dashboard panel that charts avg_gas vs the p95×1.5 threshold live. Now flipping traffic from "Normal" to
  "Gas Spike" produces a real on-chain anomaly and a real auto-rollback — no mocks anywhere in the path.

  2. Hardhat 2.x silently wiping artifacts/ between runs. The orchestrator script ran deploy_vault.js, which wrote artifacts/demo_deployment.json (proxy + impl +
   deployer addresses) and printed "Wrote artifacts/demo_deployment.json". The very next line ran deploy_attacker.js, which immediately failed with ENOENT on the
   same file. The file existed, then it didn't. After a confused round of ls-based debugging, I found that Hardhat 2.x treats artifacts/ as its own managed
  directory and prunes anything it didn't put there during the implicit recompile triggered by every hardhat run. The fix was a one-character change — write
  deployment JSONs to deployments/ instead — but figuring out who was deleting the file took longer than the rest of the integration combined.

  3. Making the LangGraph pipeline injectable for tests. Each phase added a new external dependency (Slither subprocess, Mythril, an LLM, ChromaDB, a Web3
  provider, a deploy agent) and the temptation was to mock at the import boundary, which is fragile. The cleaner pattern that emerged:
  build_healing_graph(**kwargs) accepts every external component as a keyword argument, with sensible production defaults. Tests pass mock agents in directly;
  the API wires real ones. Once that pattern was in place, all 25 tests across phases 5-8 dropped to about 12 seconds and stopped depending on network
  reachability or installed binaries.

  4. SSE streaming from a synchronous LangGraph thread to an async FastAPI endpoint. LangGraph's graph.stream() is a synchronous generator. FastAPI's SSE
  response is async. The bridge: run graph.stream() in a thread executor, push events to an asyncio.Queue via loop.call_soon_threadsafe, and let the SSE endpoint
   await queue.get() from the event loop. Sounds simple in retrospect, but the first implementation deadlocked under pause/force-rollback because the worker
  thread held a lock the event loop wanted. Switching to a lock-free queue + cooperative entry["paused"] flags fixed it without changing the LangGraph contract.

description.title: Blockchain / Cybersecurity
description.body:
Sentinel sits squarely at the intersection of these two tracks because it treats smart-contract security as a runtime safety problem, not just a pre-deployment
   audit problem.

  On the blockchain side, every piece of the system is on-chain-native: contracts use the OpenZeppelin UUPS upgradeable proxy pattern (Initializable,
  OwnableUpgradeable, UUPSUpgradeable); patch deployment compiles new implementation bytecode and atomically swaps it via upgradeToAndCall; rollbacks use the
  same mechanism in reverse to revert to the last-known-good implementation. The post-deploy monitor reads real block data through web3.py, computes per-function
   gas and revert-rate baselines from the previous 10,000 blocks, and keeps watching after deploy. The live demo runs against a real Hardhat node with a real
  Attacker.sol contract that performs an actual reentrancy exploit (receive() → recursive withdraw) — not a mock.

  On the cybersecurity side, Sentinel implements a multi-layered defence:

  - Detection-in-depth. Five agents run in parallel — Slither for static taint/dataflow, Mythril for symbolic execution, an LLM semantic agent for logic flaws, a
   governance agent for timelocks/multi-sig/flash-vote risks, and a ChromaDB threat-pattern lookup for known-bad fingerprints. Findings are merged with a
  confidence score and routed to fast / medium / slow paths based on severity and TVL exposure.
  - Zero-tolerance validation. Every candidate patch passes through a 5-gate gauntlet (vuln removal, compilation, signature preservation, KB similarity, fuzzing)
   before deploy. A single gate failure rejects the patch.
  - Two-of-two human approval on any force-rollback or manual deploy — codified at the API layer, not just the UI.
  - Runtime anomaly detection with auto-rollback on gas spikes (>p95×1.5) or revert-rate jumps (+50pp). If the rollback target itself is compromised, a circuit
  breaker freezes the contract and pages a human (critical.freeze.required event).
  - Explainable AI. Every detection finding, gate decision, LangGraph state transition, and LLM call is exported to LangSmith and rendered in the dashboard.
  Security engineers don't have to trust the agent — they can read the trace.

  The result is the kind of defence-in-depth architecture security teams have wanted for upgradeable contracts but haven't had: automated patching with multiple
  independent validators, hot-deploy with instant rollback, and post-deploy monitoring that closes the loop on novel attack patterns.

description.title: Google Gemini
description.body:
Sentinel uses Gemini in two distinct roles, both load-bearing.

  1. As an LLM in the agent fallback chain. When Backboard hits a credit gate or rate limit, Gemini is the second fallback (after local Ollama/Gemma) that keeps
  the pipeline running. The semantic detection agent, governance agent, and one of the three patch-synthesis candidates all call Gemini through the same
  LangChain adapter, so swapping providers requires zero changes to agent code. In practice, a typical /heal run produces a multi-agent LangSmith trace where
  individual nodes resolve to Gemini calls when other providers are unavailable — the dashboard's LangSmith Trace card surfaces the exact prompt, response, and
  token counts for each one.

  2. As the embedding model for the entire knowledge base. Every patch (proven and rejected) and every threat pattern in the KB is embedded with
  models/gemini-embedding-001 (forced to 768 dims to match our Atlas vector index). When a new vulnerability is detected, the threat-pattern detection agent
  queries the KB by embedding the finding text with the same Gemini model and pulls the top-k similar entries — that's how Sentinel "remembers" which patches
  worked for which classes of bug. The patch-synthesis agent does the same lookup before generating candidates, so the proven-KB candidate is always grounded in
  real prior fixes rather than hallucinated.

  The combination — Gemini for both reasoning and embeddings — means the system has a single coherent semantic space for finding similar past vulnerabilities,
  generating fixes informed by them, and explaining the result to a human reviewer.

description.title: MongoDB Atlas
description.body:
Atlas is the cloud backbone of Sentinel and is used in three distinct ways, not just one.

  1. Atlas Vector Search as the production knowledge base. Three vector partitions — proven_patches, rejected_patches, and vuln_patterns — are dual-written to
  ChromaDB (local) and Atlas (cloud) with 768-dim Gemini embeddings under a vector_index configured for cosine similarity. The threat-pattern detection agent and
   the proven-KB patch synthesiser both query Atlas for top-k semantic matches at runtime; this is what lets Sentinel ship a knowledge base that survives
  container restarts and grows across pipeline runs from anywhere.

  2. Operational document store for pipeline state. Every /heal run writes its full state snapshot — findings, candidate patches, gate results, deploy tx hash,
  RL reward — into Atlas collections. The dashboard's history view, success-rate stats, "findings by vuln type" analytics, and RL Learning Curve chart all read
  directly from Atlas aggregations. Without Atlas, every dashboard refresh would lose the long-term memory that makes the system feel alive.

  3. Source of truth for the RL feedback loop. The reinforcement-signal that promotes patches from "experimental" to "proven" after a clean 30-day post-deploy
  window lives in Atlas. The reward stream (+0.5 for clean window, -1.0 for rollback) is stored as time-series documents that the dashboard charts, and the
  promotion logic queries Atlas to decide which experimental patches graduate.

  In short: Atlas is simultaneously the vector index, the operational database, and the analytics warehouse — one platform replacing what would otherwise be
  three separate services.

description.title: Backboard
description.body:
Backboard is the primary LLM gateway for every agent in the pipeline that needs a language model — semantic vulnerability detection, governance review, patch
  synthesis, and the audit-explanation step. It sits at the top of a three-tier fallback chain (Backboard → Ollama/Gemma local → Google Gemini), so the same
  agent code talks to whichever provider is available at runtime without any conditional branches at call sites.

  Why Backboard, specifically

  Per-agent assistant IDs to spread rate-limit budget. Sentinel runs five detection agents in parallel and then synthesises three patch candidates concurrently —
   a single shared LLM connection would serialise those calls behind one rate bucket and erase the latency win. Backboard's per-assistant API model lets us
  provision a separate assistant_id per agent role and configure them via env vars:

  BACKBOARD_ASSISTANT_PATCH=…
  BACKBOARD_ASSISTANT_SEMANTIC=…
  BACKBOARD_ASSISTANT_GOVERNANCE=…
  BACKBOARD_ASSISTANT_ID=…   # fallback for any role

  The factory in core/llm.py reads these and hands each agent its own dedicated assistant, so patch synthesis isn't blocked behind semantic detection's quota and
   vice versa.

  Stateful threads per agent run. Backboard exposes a thread-style messages API rather than the OpenAI completions shape. We wrap it in a tiny
  LangChain-compatible adapter (core/backboard_llm.py) that exposes .ainvoke() / .invoke(), so the existing LangGraph nodes call it like any other chat model —
  no change at the agent level.

  Graceful degradation. Backboard returns HTTP 200 even when its credit gate kicks in, embedding a "purchase credits" message in the response body. The wrapper
  detects those sentinel strings and raises instead of returning useless prose downstream, which is what the _FallbackChain listens for to fall through to Ollama
   (local Gemma) or Gemini. End result: if Backboard is up, every agent uses it; if a quota event hits mid-pipeline, that single call silently falls through to a
   local model and the pipeline keeps running.

  Where you can see it in the dashboard. Each Backboard call is captured by LangSmith and rendered in the LangSmith Trace card on the right side panel — prompt,
  response, latency, token counts. So during a demo run you can literally watch the patch-synthesis agent send its prompt to a Backboard assistant and the
  candidate Solidity come back, in real time.

  What it concretely powers

  - Semantic detection agent — finds logic flaws and intent mismatches that pattern-based tools (Slither, Mythril) can't see.
  - Governance agent — reasons about timelocks, multi-sig setups, flash-vote risk.
  - Patch synthesis — generates two of the three patch candidates per pipeline (one proven-KB, one experimental, one pure-LLM via Backboard).
  - Explanation layer — produces the human-readable rationale attached to each candidate diff in the dashboard.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
India's judiciary is currently facing a catastrophic crisis: over 50 million pending cases, a shortage of judges, and a massive barrier to entry for ordinary citizens who lack the financial means or connections to navigate the legal system. Mandamus is an AI-driven judicial infrastructure platform built to decentralize and accelerate justice at every layer.

1. Solving the Administrative Backlog
Manual scheduling, physical document filing, and precedent lookup take days of a judge's time. Mandamus utilizes Google Cloud and Vultr for a high-performance, distributed backend that automates the entire judicial pipeline. With Snowflake's powerful data warehousing, we can process millions of historical judicial records to provide real-time precedent analysis, turning days of research into seconds of AI-driven insights.

2. Breaking the Silence (Victim Protection)
Victims of sensitive crimes often fear reporting due to potential identity exposure. Our "Silent Justice" module provides a secure, anonymous vault for reporting. To ensure absolute transparency and trust, we utilize the Solana blockchain to create immutable, tamper-proof logs of report submissions. This ensures that once a report is filed, it cannot be deleted or altered by any authority, providing a "Decentralized Chain of Custody" for justice.

3. Intelligent Evidence Reading
Evidence processing is the primary bottleneck in modern courts. Mandamus uses Gemini (Multimodal) to instantly "read" and analyze evidence (images, CCTV logs, medical reports, and documents) the moment they are uploaded to Google Cloud Storage (GCS). Instead of waiting weeks for manual verification, authorities receive AI-generated strength assessments and summaries, allowing for immediate action in critical cases.

4. Humanizing Legal Guidance
Legal jargon is a barrier to human rights. Our AI Legal Assistant uses ElevenLabs to provide high-fidelity, empathetic voice guidance, explaining complex laws in plain language. By integrating Backboard.io for real-time state management and collaborative signaling, we ensure that citizens can interact with the legal system seamlessly, even on low-bandwidth connections.

5. Virtual Infrastructure for Everyone
By moving the courtroom to a Virtual Hearing Pipeline, Mandamus removes the need for expensive physical travel. Lawyers and judges collaborate through real-time dashboards synchronized via MongoDB, ensuring that justice is served wherever there is an internet connection.

Summary of Why it Matters:
Mandamus makes the existing judicial task safer through blockchain immutability, faster through multimodal AI intelligence, and accessible through voice-enabled regional language support. It transforms a slow, centralized bottleneck into a fast, decentralized service for 1.4 billion people.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Real-Time Signaling Stability: Our WebRTC signaling initially lived in server memory—any Render or Vultr deployment restart would crash active court sessions mid-hearing. We solved this by integrating Managed Redis as a persistent signaling layer, making judicial sessions survive restarts and allowing the platform to scale horizontally across cloud clusters.

Cross-Browser Audio Compatibility: Standard audio streaming for our AI Legal Assistant kept throwing ERR_REQUEST_RANGE_NOT_SATISFIABLE errors across browsers. We re-engineered the entire TTS pipeline into a Base64-encoded JSON architecture—voice is now delivered as encoded payloads and decoded client-side using ElevenLabs, working seamlessly everywhere from mobile to desktop.

Multi-Cloud Database Handshakes (Vultr + GCP): Connecting our Vultr-hosted backend to MongoDB Atlas across different cloud providers triggered persistent SSL/TLS handshake failures (Internal Alert 1081). We overcame this by re-engineering the MongoDB client with custom TLS parameters, relaxed hostname validation, and optimized server-selection timeouts to ensure stable connectivity in a multi-cloud environment.

Multimodal Evidence Interpretation: Getting one system to "read" a harassment screenshot, a medical report, and a handwritten complaint required complex grounding. We built a background analysis engine powered by Gemini (Multimodal) that triggers automatically on Google Cloud Storage (GCS) upload and returns structured intelligence directly to the judicial dashboard.

Synchronized Justice Workspace (Backboard.io): Keeping a judge and multiple lawyers in a cohesive "Virtual Courtroom" without lag or state drift was a major hurdle. We implemented Backboard.io for real-time collaborative state management, ensuring that when a judge sends an invite or starts a session, the courtroom state updates instantly for all participants without manual polling.

Automated Judicial Workflows (n8n): Orchestrating the complex logic between victim reports, authority notifications, and legal analysis was too heavy for a standard monolithic backend. We utilized n8n to build a robust workflow engine that handles asynchronous triggers, ensuring that when a report is filed, it is routed, analyzed, and logged through the correct authority channels without blocking the main judicial pipeline.

description.title: AI & ML
description.body:
Mandamus fits into the AI & ML Track by transforming the static judicial process into a reactive, intelligent ecosystem. Here’s how:

Multimodal Evidence Intelligence: We utilize Gemini (Multimodal) to solve the biggest bottleneck in justice: evidence reading. Our system automatically "reads" harassment screenshots, medical reports, and handwritten documents uploaded to Google Cloud Storage (GCS), extracting key entities and providing authorities with instant, objective summaries and strength assessments.

Voice-Enabled Legal Guidance: We’ve integrated ElevenLabs to power an empathetic, high-fidelity AI Legal Assistant. This allows citizens to receive real-time legal guidance through natural voice interaction, breaking down the barrier of complex legal jargon and making the law accessible to everyone.

Neural Judicial Summarization: Mandamus uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to parallelize the analysis of massive judicial filings. It distills multi-hundred-page documents into concise "TL;DR" summaries for judges, highlighting the most critical precedents and legal arguments in seconds.

Intelligent Workflow Orchestration: By using n8n, we’ve built an AI-driven routing engine that evaluates report severity and location in real-time, intelligently "connecting" victims to the most relevant local authorities or NGOs without manual intervention.

By combining Multimodal Vision, Natural Language Processing, and AI-driven Automation, Mandamus demonstrates how machine intelligence can directly solve the 50-million-case backlog and make the judicial system truly proactive.

description.title: ElevenLabs
description.body:
ElevenLabs Integration in Mandamus :
Mandamus uses ElevenLabs to solve one of the biggest hurdles in the Indian legal system: the linguistic divide. While law is often locked in complex English jargon, our platform uses ElevenLabs to bring justice directly to the people in their native tongue.

6-Language Regional Expansion: We have implemented high-fidelity judicial guidance in 6 major languages—English, Hindi, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil, and Malayalam. This ensures that citizens from across India can understand their legal rights and navigate the "Silent Justice" module without needing a translator or expensive legal counsel.

Voice-Driven Judicial Accessibility: For many citizens, reading long legal texts is a barrier. We use ElevenLabs' human-like voices to read out case summaries and legal advice, transforming Mandamus from a static website into an interactive AI Legal Advisor that anyone can listen to and understand.

Engineered for Reliability: To handle the unique challenges of rural connectivity, we developed a custom Base64-encoded audio payload architecture. By encoding ElevenLabs' synthesis on the server and decoding it client-side, we’ve ensured that the "Voice of Law" remains stable and high-quality even on low-bandwidth mobile networks, bypassing all standard browser streaming limitations.

By leveraging ElevenLabs Multilingual v2, Mandamus ensures that every Indian citizen—regardless of their language or location—has a vocal, empathetic, and expert legal advisor in their pocket.

description.title: Google Gemini
description.body:
Mandamus utilizes Gemini 1.5 Flash as the multimodal intelligence engine of the judicial platform, solving the critical bottleneck of evidence processing and legal research.

Multimodal Evidence Interpretation: We use Gemini’s native multimodal capabilities to "read" and analyze disparate evidence types—from blurry harassment screenshots to complex medical reports and handwritten complaints. It automatically extracts key entities, dates, and locations, providing authorities with instant, structured intelligence.

High-Speed Precedent Search: Gemini powers our Neural Precedent Finder, performing contextual ranking across millions of judicial records. It identifies not just matching keywords, but the "intent" and "legal reasoning" of past judgments, surfacing the most relevant precedents for any given case in seconds.

Automated Judicial Drafting: We utilize Gemini 1.5 to automate the generation of formal legal drafts, issues presented, and judicial summaries. Its large context window allows us to feed in hours of virtual hearing transcripts and hundreds of pages of evidence to produce precise, high-fidelity legal documents that are ready for court review.

By leveraging Gemini 1.5, Mandamus transforms a slow, manual judicial system into a high-speed, AI-driven infrastructure that can handle the 50-million-case backlog with professional-grade precision.

description.title: MongoDB Atlas
description.body:
1. Secure One-Time-Password (OTP) Repository: We implemented this in otp_repository.py. It’s a specialized storage system for the temporary codes you get when you log in. It ensures that your login is secure and that the code automatically "expires" and disappears after a few minutes so no one can reuse it.
A secure way to log you in that automatically throws away your password after you use it so it's always safe.

2. Judicial Case Context System: This is implemented across our backend/main.py. It stores everything about a case in one place—including the summaries made by the AI and the notes from virtual hearings. This allows the "Draft Generator" and the "Judge Dashboard" to instantly see the full history of any case without searching through different files.
A digital folder that keeps all the AI notes and hearing details together so the judge has everything they need on one screen.

3. Silent Justice Evidence Metadata Store: In our Silent Justice module, we use MongoDB to store the "descriptions" of evidence (like photos or reports) that victims upload. It keeps a record of the evidence’s severity and type, which our Gemini AI then uses to automatically sort and route the case to the right authority.
A smart list that keeps track of all the evidence victims upload, helping the AI quickly decide which police team or NGO needs to see it first.

4. High-Availability SSL-Optimized Infrastructure We specifically configured this in client.py to handle the unique challenges of connecting from the cloud (Render/Vercel). We built a connection that is resilient to SSL handshake errors, ensuring the database is "always on" and never disconnects during a live hearing.
A super-stable connection that ensures the platform never crashes or goes offline while a judge or lawyer is using it.

description.title: Backboard
description.body:
Backboard Integration in Mandamus
In most legal apps, you have to refresh the page to see updates—but justice can’t wait for a "Refresh" button. We integrated Backboard.io to transform Mandamus into a living, breathing judicial workspace where everything happens instantly.

Live Chatbot Memory: Our AI Legal Assistant isn’t just a simple window; it’s a shared intelligence. Using Backboard, we synchronized the Chat History and AI State in real-time. Whether a citizen is chatting on their phone or a lawyer is reviewing the same case on a desktop, the conversation stays perfectly in sync across every device, ensuring no legal detail is ever lost.

The "Shared Eyes" Feature (Unified State): During a high-stakes hearing, the Judge and Lawyers need to be on the same page—literally. We used Backboard to build a Unified Courtroom State. When a Judge selects a specific piece of evidence or highlights a case precedent, it instantly updates on the Lawyer’s dashboard. It’s like having "shared eyes" on the evidence, making the virtual courtroom feel like a single, cohesive room.

Zero-Latency Judicial Triggers: We’ve replaced slow database polling with Backboard’s Instant Signaling. Whether it’s an urgent hearing invite, a new evidence upload alert, or a real-time status change in the "Silent Justice" vault, the notification hits the relevant authority’s dashboard the millisecond it happens.

By integrating Backboard, we’ve moved away from static web pages and built a Reactive Judicial Infrastructure. From real-time chatbot persistence to collaborative courtroom dashboards, Mandamus ensures that justice moves at the speed of thought, not the speed of the browser.

heapify-reggraphai-0b48.name: Heapify _RegGraphAI
heapify-reggraphai-0b48.tagline: Heapifying the Compliance intelligence to SMB's

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Indian SMBs face a hidden operational burden because compliance obligations are fragmented across GST, EPFO, FSSAI, payroll systems, taxation workflows, and state-specific regulations. Most businesses still depend on spreadsheets, accountants, manual reminders, and reactive corrections after missing a filing or regulatory update.

Existing platforms mainly act as passive dashboards or filing utilities. They do not continuously understand changing regulations, map obligations dynamically to each business, detect risks proactively, or explain how one business event impacts multiple compliance domains simultaneously.

RegGraph AI solves this by creating an autonomous compliance intelligence layer powered by multi-agent AI orchestration, obligation knowledge graphs, regulation-grounded retrieval, and deterministic verification systems.

The platform continuously monitors regulatory sources, detects changes in real time, identifies only the businesses affected by those updates, and automatically retriggers compliance workflows. It transforms complex legal obligations into explainable, business-specific actions with confidence scoring, audit traceability, and human approval safeguards.

By combining AI reasoning with deterministic compliance verification, RegGraph AI reduces compliance delays, minimizes operational risk, improves audit readiness, and enables SMBs to operate with enterprise-grade compliance intelligence without requiring dedicated legal teams.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of the biggest challenges we faced was designing an AI system that could operate safely in a compliance-critical environment where hallucinated outputs are unacceptable. Traditional LLM-based approaches performed well for summarization but were unreliable for deterministic compliance workflows such as GST calculations, payroll obligations, filing thresholds, and due-date reasoning.

To solve this, we designed a Dual-Rail Compliance Architecture (DRCA) where every compliance response is verified through two parallel systems: an LLM reasoning layer and a deterministic rule engine. Responses are only approved when both rails agree; otherwise, the workflow is escalated through a Human-in-the-Loop approval system.

Another major challenge was handling real-time regulatory updates efficiently. Regulatory documents change frequently, and recomputing compliance workflows for every business after each update would be computationally expensive and operationally inefficient. We addressed this by building the Incremental Regulation Delta Agent (IRDA), which detects only the changed obligation nodes and retriggers workflows exclusively for impacted businesses.

Cross-domain reasoning was also technically complex. A single business event can affect GST, payroll, taxation, and sector-specific regulations simultaneously. To handle this, we implemented the Cross-Domain Obligation Cascade Engine (COCE), enabling dependency-aware compliance propagation across multiple regulatory domains.

We additionally faced challenges around auditability, explainability, and data privacy. Since the platform processes sensitive payroll and tax information, we designed a DPDP-native privacy architecture with encrypted federated vaults, cryptographic audit trails, confidence-scored actions, and traceable agent decisions to ensure enterprise-grade governance and accountability.

The project further integrates privacy-preserving AI using DPDP-native federated vaults, cryptographic audit trails, human-in-the-loop approvals, and explainable AI outputs with confidence scores and regulation traceability.

By combining autonomous agents, real-time regulation intelligence, explainable compliance AI, and scalable orchestration workflows, RegGraph AI demonstrates a production-oriented application of modern AI/ML systems for regulated enterprise environments.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## The Problem

Walk into any government hospital ER in India during peak hours 
and you'll see the same thing — hundreds of people waiting, 
one or two nurses trying to figure out who needs help first, 
and no real system to tell them.

Right now, triage works like this. A patient walks in. A nurse 
looks at them, asks a few questions, checks their pulse manually, 
and makes a judgment call. That process takes 5 to 10 minutes 
per person. During that time, the person behind them — who might 
be having a heart attack — is just sitting in a plastic chair 
waiting their turn.

Nobody is being careless. The nurses are doing their best. 
The problem is that there are too many patients and not enough 
eyes, and the human body doesn't always look sick on the outside 
even when something serious is happening on the inside.

That gap — between when a patient arrives and when someone 
actually checks on them — is where people die.

---

## What We Built

VitalSense is a small sensor patch that clips onto a patient 
the moment they walk into the ER. It starts reading their 
heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, and blood pressure 
every half second — automatically, continuously, without 
anyone having to do anything.

An AI model running directly on the patch scores each reading 
and decides whether the patient is stable, needs watching, 
or needs immediate attention. That score updates in real time 
on a dashboard that any nurse in the ward can see at a glance.

If someone's condition suddenly gets worse — say their oxygen 
drops from 97% to 82% while they're sitting in the waiting 
room — the system catches it within seconds and sends a WhatsApp 
alert to the duty nurse's phone. No waiting for the next manual 
check. No hoping someone notices.

The patch costs under ₹800 to build. It works without internet. 
It works during power cuts because the AI runs on the chip 
itself, not on a server somewhere. And it uses no camera, 
no microphone — just sensor data, so there are no privacy 
concerns in a medical setting.

---

## Who actually benefits

Nurses stop having to physically walk to every bed to 
check if someone is okay. One screen tells them who needs 
attention right now.

Doctors walk into the room already knowing the patient's 
severity score and vital sign history for the last 30 minutes.

Patients who are critically ill get seen faster because 
the system already flagged them, instead of waiting until 
a nurse happened to walk by.

Hospitals get a full log of every reading stored in 
the cloud — useful for audits, quality reviews, and 
understanding where the system is getting overwhelmed.

---

## Why this matters at scale

There are around 70,000 government hospitals in India. 
Most of them are understaffed. Most of them have no 
continuous patient monitoring between arrival and 
the first doctor visit. And triage errors in Indian 
ERs contribute to roughly 40,000 preventable deaths 
every year.

We're not claiming one patch fixes all of that. But 
at ₹800 per patient, this is actually deployable — 
not just in private hospitals in cities, but in 
primary health centres in places where there might 
be one nurse covering an entire ward overnight.

That's the real problem we're trying to solve. Not 
building something impressive for a demo. Building 
something that could actually work in the places

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
## Challenges We Ran Into

---

### 1. The backend kept freezing after 30 seconds

This one took us an embarrassingly long time to figure out.

We had MQTT and Flask running in the same Python process. 
Everything looked fine for the first 30 seconds or so — 
patient data was flowing, the dashboard was updating, 
alerts were working. Then suddenly, nothing. No error 
message, no crash, just complete silence. The terminal 
looked normal but no data was reaching the browser.

Turns out MQTT runs its own background thread to listen 
for messages, and Flask-SocketIO runs its own event loop 
to talk to the browser. When both of them tried to send 
data at the same time, they blocked each other. Classic 
deadlock — both threads waiting for the other to finish, 
neither ever does.

The fix was two lines. Tell Flask-SocketIO to use 
threading mode, and make sure only the MQTT callback 
ever calls sio.emit(), never the Flask routes.

After that it ran for 45 minutes straight without 
a single freeze.

---

### 2. The AI model was calling fever patients critical

We tested a patient with a high temperature but everything 
else completely normal — heart rate fine, oxygen fine, 
blood pressure fine. The model kept saying RED. That's wrong. 
A fever alone is concerning but it's not an emergency.

The problem was how we generated training data. We drew 
hard lines — GREEN patients had heart rate up to 100, 
YELLOW started exactly at 100. The model learned those 
hard lines perfectly, which sounds good until you realise 
real patients don't respect hard lines. A reading right 
on the boundary kept falling into the wrong bucket.

We fixed it by blurring the boundaries in the training 
data — making GREEN patients occasionally have heart ra

description.title: Open Innovation
description.body:
VitalSense is an IoT project at its core —

IoT means physical devices collecting real world data through 
sensors and sending it somewhere useful over a network. That 
is precisely what our system does at every layer.

The ESP32 microcontroller inside the wearable patch reads heart 
rate, blood oxygen, temperature, and movement from the patient's 
body using physical sensors. That is the sensing layer — a real 
device, on a real person, measuring real physical signals.

That data is then transmitted wirelessly over WiFi using MQTT — 
a protocol literally invented for IoT communication. It is the 
same protocol used in smart home devices, industrial sensors, 
and medical monitoring equipment worldwide.

The transmitted data hits our Flask backend where an AI model 
scores each reading in real time and decides whether the patient 
is stable, deteriorating, or critical. That decision triggers 
real world actions — a dashboard updates, an LED changes colour, 
a WhatsApp alert fires to the nurse's phone.

Sense → Transmit → Process → Act

That four step pipeline is the definition of an IoT system. 
Ours follows it exactly, with an AI layer added on top that 
turns raw sensor numbers into clinical decisions. That 
combination of IoT and AI is what the industry calls AIoT — 
Artificial Intelligence of Things — and it is the direction 
every modern IoT healthcare system is moving toward.

So when you ask how this is related to IoT — it does not just 
use IoT concepts. It is built on the complete IoT stack, from 
the physical sensor touching the patient's skin all the way 
to the alert arriving on a nurse's phone.

aurumthread-48ed.name: AurumThread
aurumthread-48ed.tagline: Scan it. Know it. Act on it.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Fast fashion produces 92 million tonnes of textile waste annually, and a significant portion of fabric labels misrepresent actual composition — a practice known as greenwashing. Organizations running clothing collection drives, retail take-back programs, and NGO sorting facilities have no reliable way to verify what fabric they're actually handling. Manual sorting is slow, costly, and inaccurate. Consumers have no tool to verify fabric claims before purchasing.
Aurum Thread solves this by providing real-time spectral fabric forensics — place any garment on the rig, get an AUTHENTIC / GREENWASHED / INCONCLUSIVE verdict in seconds, with a full sustainability score, recyclability rating, lifespan prediction, and end-of-life routing decision. No manual input. No guesswork. Just data.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
The biggest challenge was achieving meaningful fabric differentiation from spectral sensor data alone. The AS7262 operates in the visible light spectrum rather than NIR, which required building a custom spectral profile knowledge base mapped to known textile signatures to give the LLM meaningful anchoring data rather than raw numbers.
Hardware integration was another significant challenge — soldering and testing three sensors simultaneously on an ESP32 while managing I2C bus conflicts, logic level conversion for the 5V AS7262, and stable WebSocket broadcasting required extensive iteration.
On the software side, Groq API rate limits and network restrictions at the venue forced a mid-hackathon pivot to Ollama for local LLM inference, requiring rapid refactoring of the entire analysis pipeline. The WebSocket bridge between ESP32, FastAPI, and the React frontend also required significant debugging to achieve stable real-time data flow.

description.title: Internet of Things
description.body:
**Aurum Thread** is fundamentally an IoT system at its core. The project integrates custom embedded hardware — an ESP32 microcontroller orchestrating three precision sensors — with a cloud-connected AI pipeline, which is the defining architecture of modern IoT solutions.

The ESP32 serves as the edge device, performing real-time sensor fusion across the AS7262 spectral sensor, MPR121 capacitive touch interface, and HX711 load cell ADC. Raw sensor data is processed at the edge and broadcast via WebSocket over WiFi to the backend — a classic IoT edge-to-cloud data flow.

The system demonstrates key IoT principles: persistent device connectivity, real-time data streaming, sensor fusion for environmental inference, and actionable decision-making based on physical world inputs. Rather than monitoring environmental conditions, Aurum Thread applies these principles to material forensics — using multi-modal sensor data to make fabric composition determinations that would otherwise require laboratory equipment.

The deployment model is also inherently IoT — the hardware rig operates as a fixed installation at a collection point, continuously available to process garments on demand, with all intelligence residing in the connected backend. This mirrors industrial IoT deployments where edge sensors feed centralized processing systems.

In summary, Aurum Thread represents applied IoT in the sustainability domain: physical sensors, embedded firmware, wireless connectivity, real-time data processing, and AI-driven decision making — all working together to solve a real-world operational problem at scale.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body: Most AI systems give you a single answer from a single model — a black box with no transparency, no debate, and no way to understand why it decided what it decided. ThinkMesh solves this by running your query through a parliament of 3 AI agents (a Technocrat, a Humanist, and an Inquisitor) that independently reason, challenge each other, and debate across multiple rounds before a Sovereign Judge synthesizes a final, constitutionally-grounded decision. This makes it invaluable for high-stakes decisions in medical, legal, or financial contexts where a single biased answer isn't enough, for researchers and analysts who need to see conflicting perspectives on complex topics, and for AI safety teams who need every decision to be fully auditable — with tension scores, dissenting opinions, and confidence levels all visible in real time.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
1. The Hardware Wall: Balancing Local Power with Cloud Reasoning
One of our earliest and most persistent challenges was the "VRAM Impasse." Developing on a Lenovo LOQ with an RTX 3050 meant we had a limited "memory ceiling" for local inference. We initially wanted to run every agent locally, but quickly realized that three simultaneous large language models would choke the GPU.

To solve this, we architected a Hybrid Cloud-Edge stack. We moved our three parliamentary agents (Technocrat, Humanist, and Inquisitor) to a local Ollama instance running Llama 3.2 3B, which fit comfortably in our 6GB VRAM. We then offloaded the "Sovereign Judge"—the high-reasoning synthesis layer—to Groq’s Llama 3.3 70B. This hybrid approach allowed us to maintain privacy and speed for the "brawl" while ensuring the final constitutional audit was handled by a model with supreme reasoning capabilities.

2. The Visual Pivot: From 3D Weight to 2D Cinema
We initially envisioned a fully immersive 3D environment using Spline runtimes. However, as the complexity of our React store grew, we encountered significant "Visual Junk"—the 3D rendering was fighting our AI orchestration for CPU cycles. The experience felt heavy, and the animations stuttered.

We made the difficult decision to perform a "Fresh Start" pivot. We stripped away the heavy 3D runtimes and replaced them with a cinematic 2D dashboard that utilized high-fidelity Iframe backgrounds and SVG Animated Beams. This transition not only boosted our performance to a locked 144 FPS but actually made the interface feel more "Tactical" and "Mission Control" oriented. It taught us that "Cinematic" doesn't have to mean "3D"; it means "Fluid" and "Intentional."

3. The Ethical Ghost: Enforcing a Living Constitution
Building the Synapse Constitution wasn't just a coding task; it was a philosophical one. We ran into the "Sycophancy Trap," where agents would simply agree with one another to reach a quick consensus, erasing the very transparency we were trying to build.

We had to refine our orchestrator.py and constitution.py to physically force adversarial friction. We implemented Law 2 (Minority Visibility), which explicitly forbids the Judge from summarizing away a dissenting view. Fine-tuning the prompts to ensure the Inquisitor stayed skeptical and the Humanist stayed ethical, even when the Technocrat presented a "perfectly efficient" solution, was a deep exercise in prompt engineering and cognitive modeling.

4. The Memory Void: Transitioning to Stateful Deliberation
Early versions of the parliament were stateless—the agents would "forget" the previous round of debate as soon as the prompt window closed. This led to repetitive arguments and a lack of depth.

We solved this by integrating a persistent memory layer. Moving from simple mock citations to a stateful Backboard.io integration allowed our agents to "remember" logic nodes across rounds. We even implemented "Memory Depth" telemetry to show exactly how many historical facts were being pulled into a current deliberation. This transformed the parliament from a one-off response generator into a continuous, evolving engine of reasoning.

Through every schema failure, rate limit, and layout jank, the project matured. We emerged not just with a piece of software, but with a scalable protocol for Explainable AI that respects both the power of the machine and the safety of the human.

description.title: AI & ML
description.body: ThinkMesh is a multi-agent AI parliament where three specialized LLM agents (Technocrat, Humanist, Inquisitor) independently reason, debate, and critique each other across multiple rounds before a sovereign judge synthesizes a final explainable decision. It directly advances AI transparency and multi-agent coordination — core challenges in modern ML systems.

description.title: Backboard
description.body:
The Impact of Backboard.io on ThinkMesh

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/27810fc4021e4457be5135eb284f7c9d/5d56425c-69d9-4bbf-9db5-32de13c502bb.jpeg)

Hybrid Coordination: It serves as the vital "Common Ground" where our local Llama 3.2 agents and our cloud-based Groq Judge meet, eliminating the need for complex, heavy data passing and creating a seamless hybrid architecture.

vista-e879.name: VISTA
vista-e879.tagline: From Reactive repairs to Proactive Prevention

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Indian Railways relies on millions of critical track components—such as concrete sleepers, elastic rail clips, and rubber pads—to maintain the structural integrity of its vast network. Currently, monitoring these components is a massive logistical challenge plagued by The Analog Tracking Vulnerability.

How People Use It
Railway Supervisors & Data Analysts: Use the web dashboard as a centralized command center. Instead of reading through thousands of paper logs, they can instantly view a prioritized list of track components that are mathematically likely to fail, allowing them to dispatch maintenance teams efficiently.

Field Engineers (Simulated): Use the system to verify their physical findings. By uploading a photo of a suspect rail clip, the engineer gets instant, AI-backed confirmation of structural damage without needing specialized metallurgical training.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Since we pivoted to a web-based simulation to prove our core logic, our first major hurdle was creating a mock dataset (track_components.csv) that accurately reflected real-world degradation. Initially, feeding this data into the predictive model caused pipeline crashes due to data type errors (e.g., mixing strings with integers for age and load frequencies). We had to build a robust data cleaning pipeline using Pandas to handle null values and strictly cast data types before passing them to the TensorFlow models.

Integrating the Gemini API for visual inspection was straightforward, but getting consistent results was a challenge. Early on, the API would return highly conversational responses (e.g., "This looks like a rusted clip, you should probably fix it"), which our dashboard couldn't parse to update the component's status. We overcame this by heavily refining our prompt engineering, constraining the LLM to output rigid, standardized text reports and binary health flags based solely on the visual evidence.

description.title: Open Innovation
description.body:
VISTA perfectly aligns with the Open Innovation track because it takes a traditional, heavy-industry problem (railway infrastructure maintenance) and solves it using an unconventional, highly scalable software approach. Instead of relying on expensive hardware or custom IoT sensors, we are innovating by maximizing the utility of existing tools.


Novel Use of Generative AI: We are moving beyond text chatbots and using the Gemini API as a "virtual visual inspector" to analyze infrastructure damage in harsh, remote environments.

description.title: Google Gemini
description.body:
While our predictive AI uses numbers (age and weather data) to guess if a component might be failing, the Gemini API is used to visually confirm if it actually is.

When a field worker (or a user in our simulation) uploads a photo of a flagged track component, Gemini analyzes the image to detect physical damage—like heavy rust on a rail clip or hairline cracks in a concrete sleeper. It eliminates the subjectivity of human guessing by instantly generating a standardized text report based on visual evidence, completing the loop between predicted risk and confirmed physical health.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Emergency Green Corridor — siren detected → signals auto-clear the route to hospital
 Auto Accident Dispatch — crash sensors trigger a countdown, picks best hospital, sends victim info ahead
 Real-Time Congestion Scoring — fuses PIR, mic, gas & vibration into a live 0–100 score per junction
ML Route Suggester — shows fastest vs. safest path using a custom neural net

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
FPGA IIR Filter Scaling — siren thresholds that passed in simulation failed on real hardware due to fixed-point scaling mismatch; fixed constants in the Verilog and corrected the testbench siren/accident priority conflict

Congestion Scores — frontend was fabricating sensor values for offline junctions (score * 1.7 for AQI etc.); replaced entire client-side scoring with a deterministic backend model with a data_source badge

ML Panel vs. Toolbar Button Overlap — floating panel sat exactly on top of the TRAFFIC LAYER button at certain widths; moved panel to right-center, locked toolbar to flex-wrap: nowrap

Route Lines Invisible Under Traffic Layer — ML and hospital routes blended into Mapbox road tiles; fixed with line-offset staggering + glow halo layers + traffic layer opacity dimming when routes are active

ESP32 UART2 / USB Serial Conflict — debug logs mixed into sensor packets the PYNQ was reading; moved sensor stream to GPIO17/16 (UART2), kept USB for debug only

Dispatch Sending to a Busy Hospital — distance-only logic picked the nearest hospital even if it had 2 beds and was BUSY; replaced with priority ranking (TRAUMA_READY > AVAILABLE > BUSY) then ETA

description.title: Internet of Things
description.body:
Layer 1 — Sense (ESP32)

PIR, microphone, MQ-135 gas & vibration sensors read the physical world
Sends raw DATA, PIR, MIC_AVG, MIC_PEAK, GAS, VIB over UART every 2s
Layer 2 — Edge Process (PYNQ-Z2 FPGA)

FPGA runs IIR filters + threshold logic in hardware — no cloud round-trip
Classifies alerts (CLEAR / SIREN / ACCIDENT etc.) in microseconds
Hardware watchdog resets the system if it freezes (every 150ms)
Layer 3 — Communicate (MQTT)

FPGA bridge publishes processed JSON to traffic/edge topic
Server sends commands back to junctions via traffic/command (e.g. FORCE_GREEN)
Bidirectional, lightweight — standard IoT protocol
Layer 4 — Act & Visualise (Flask + Dashboard)

Flask consumes MQTT, runs ML routing, triggers emergency dispatch
Dashboard shows live map, congestion scores, alerts — all from real sensor data
Actions loop back to hardware: siren detected → MQTT command → junction turns green
In short: Physical sensors → Edge FPGA → MQTT → Cloud logic → Real-world actuation. That's a complete IoT feedback loop.

lgtm-f0ad.name: LGTM
lgtm-f0ad.tagline: Shipping fast is great. Shipping secure is better.

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
LGTM solves two problems that every software team faces but nobody is fixing together expensive AI code review and unprotected CI/CD pipelines.

Existing tools burn thousands of LLM tokens on every PR by dumping your entire codebase into the model, making costs grow with your codebase size rather than the value you get. At the same time, nobody is watching the pipeline itself the workflow files and deployment configs that have full access to your production servers and secrets. Real attacks happen here, not in the application code.

LGTM fixes both. Our Tree-sitter and PageRank engine selects only the structurally critical code relevant to each change, sending 10x fewer tokens to 6 parallel specialist AI agents security, bugs, performance, style, documentation, and test coverage. You bring your own API key, we charge nothing on top, making a 10-developer team pay around $14 a month instead of $240 with competitors.

For pipeline security, 16 deterministic rule-based detectors scan your CI/CD configuration files on every push zero LLM tokens, sub-second execution. When a critical issue is found, three enforcement gates fire a PR comment with fixes, a blocked merge button, and most importantly a runtime halt that stops the pipeline before checkout, before tests, before anything runs. Direct pushes, cron jobs, tag-triggered deployments all covered. No competitor has this.

We also built a Knowledge Graph an interactive visual dependency map of your entire codebase showing which files are most critical, most coupled, and most risky powered by the same engine that makes our reviews precise.

LGTM is for startups moving fast without a security team, open source maintainers reviewing PRs from strangers, and any engineering team whose pipelines have never been audited.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Building LGTM was not straightforward. Every layer of the system introduced its own set of problems that took real debugging time to solve.

The first major challenge was context selection. Getting Tree-sitter to parse a live GitHub repository accurately and then running PageRank on the resulting dependency graph in real time was not trivial. The graph computation had to be fast enough to not block the review pipeline while still being accurate enough to send meaningful context to the agents. Early versions were either too slow or sending irrelevant context, which tanked review quality.

The second challenge was the multi-agent architecture. Running six LLM agents in parallel sounds simple until you realise that parallel API calls fail unpredictably, rate limits hit at random, and the synthesizer has to produce a coherent verdict from six agents that may partially contradict each other. Building a reliable aggregation layer that handles partial failures gracefully without dropping findings or blocking the pipeline took significant iteration.

The third challenge was the BullMQ and Redis reliability issue. Workers were silently dropping jobs whenever Redis disconnected unexpectedly. No errors surfaced, no logs triggered tasks simply vanished. This was invisible until we noticed reviews not completing under load. Solving this required implementing proper Redis reconnection handling and dead letter queues for failed jobs.

The fourth and most frustrating challenge was the GitHub OAuth cold start problem on Fly.io. Our server was spinning down between requests due to Fly.io's idle machine behaviour, which killed active OAuth sessions mid-login. Users would authenticate with GitHub and get dropped back to the login page with no error. The fix was a single configuration line setting min_machines_running to 1 but finding that root cause after hours of debugging session handling code was painful.

The fifth challenge was the runtime halt architecture. Getting the GitHub Action to reliably call our API as step one of any workflow, receive the halt decision, and exit cleanly before any subsequent steps ran across different workflow configurations, different runner environments, and different trigger types required careful design of the Action's failure handling to ensure it never silently passed when it should have blocked.

description.title: AI & ML
description.body:
LGTM sits at the intersection of AI and security engineering two fields that are increasingly impossible to separate.

The core of what makes LGTM intelligent is not just that it uses LLMs. It is how it uses them. We built a context selection engine that applies classical ML concepts graph theory and the PageRank algorithm on top of compiler-grade AST parsing to determine which parts of a codebase are structurally critical for any given change. The model does not receive raw text. It receives a mathematically ranked, dependency-aware context. That is applied machine learning directly improving LLM output quality while reducing token consumption by 10x.

The six specialist agents are not generic prompts. Each one is a fine-tuned role with specific instructions, domain focus, and output schema security, bugs, performance, style, documentation, and test coverage running in parallel and feeding into a synthesizer that produces a final weighted verdict. That multi-agent architecture is the same pattern driving the most advanced AI systems being built today.

On the CI/CD security side, the 16 deterministic detectors use pattern recognition on structured AST data not keyword matching, not regex alone to identify dangerous configurations with zero false positives and zero LLM dependency. That is rule-based ML applied to a real security problem.

The Knowledge Graph takes it further visualising the entire codebase as a force-directed graph where node importance is computed using PageRank, edge weights represent dependency strength, and coupling and churn scores surface risk automatically. That is graph ML made visible and actionable for developers.

LGTM does not use AI as a feature. AI is the architecture.

description.title: Google Gemini
description.body: LGTM integrates Google Gemini as one of its selectable LLM providers powering the six parallel AI code review agents. When a developer opens a pull request, our Tree-sitter and PageRank engine selects only the structurally critical context sending 10x fewer tokens than naive approaches and Gemini processes that optimised context to produce specialist reviews across security, bugs, performance, style, documentation, and test coverage. The bring-your-own-key model means teams using Gemini pay Google directly at cost with zero markup from us, making production-grade AI code review accessible to startups and open source maintainers who cannot afford flat per-seat pricing.

description.title: MongoDB Atlas
description.body: MongoDB serves as the primary persistence layer for LGTM, storing everything that matters user accounts, connected repositories, PR reviews, security findings, audit logs, and scan history. The document model was a natural fit for our use case because every review is a richly nested object findings with severity levels, rule IDs, affected file paths, suggested fixes, and resolution status all living inside a single scan document. The audit log is designed write-once at the schema level with only the resolution field remaining mutable, giving teams an immutable security record they can trust for compliance. MongoDB also stores the codebase index per repository, which feeds both the AI review agents and the Knowledge Graph generation pipeline.

nomad-ai-4a0b.name: Nomad AI
nomad-ai-4a0b.tagline: A Life-Form in Code-It earns, it pays, it survive

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
Nomad solves the problem of AI systems being dependent on centralized infrastructure and constant human control. The platform is designed around a 4-node architecture — Think, Act, Economy, and Survival — allowing autonomous AI agents to make decisions, interact with systems, manage resources, and adapt independently.
We also implemented a state machine architecture, dynamic routing, and an economic feedback layer to create smarter agent coordination and scalable task execution. This makes experimentation with autonomous AI systems more efficient, modular, and developer-friendly through a single interactive platform.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
One of the biggest challenges was integrating the frontend with a complex multi-node architecture while maintaining smooth animations, responsive UI, and stable real-time updates. Handling asynchronous communication between the Think, Act, Economy, and Survival nodes sometimes caused rendering delays and inconsistent state updates, which we solved through optimized state management and component rendering.
We also faced deployment issues with Solana integration. The issue was resolved by correctly configuring the required environment variables such as WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY, SOLANA_RPC_URL, SOLANA_NETWORK, and PROGRAM_ID, followed by redeploying the application successfully.

description.title: Blockchain / Cybersecurity
description.body: Nomad proves that when AI handles real money autonomously, blockchain provides the security layer every transaction is transparent, every rule is enforced by code, and every key is cryptographically protected.

description.title: Solana
description.body:
Nomad AI is built entirely on the Solana blockchain, leveraging its high speed, low fees, and robust developer ecosystem to power an autonomous AI agent that manages its own finances on-chain.

At the core of the project is the agent's self-sovereign Solana wallet — a real keypair that the AI controls independently. This wallet allows the agent to sign and broadcast transactions without any human intervention. When a user requests an AI service like code generation, the agent automatically sends a micro-payment of 0.001 SOL to its on-chain treasury as a service fee. This is done entirely server-side using the Solana Python SDK (solders), meaning there's no wallet popup or user approval needed — the AI pays for its own compute, just like a human would pay a bill.

The project also deploys an Anchor smart contract on Solana Devnet that acts as the agent's treasury through a Program Derived Address (PDA). This on-chain program enforces spending rules programmatically — the agent cannot drain funds beyond defined thresholds, and every transaction creates an immutable, publicly auditable record on the Solana Explorer.

For user interaction, Nomad integrates the Phantom wallet through Solana's wallet adapter libraries. Users can connect their Phantom wallet in one click, fund the agent's wallet by sending SOL directly on-chain, and receive their 60% profit share as a real Solana transaction — complete with a verifiable transaction ID and Explorer link.

The reason Solana was chosen over other blockchains is economics. An autonomous AI agent needs to make dozens or even hundreds of micro-payments per day. On Ethereum, each transaction would cost $0.50–$5.00 in gas, making the agent's business model impossible. On Solana, each transaction costs approximately $0.00025, meaning the agent can operate for months on just a few SOL. Combined with Solana's ~400ms finality, every payment feels instant in the dashboard — creating a seamless experience where the AI's financial activity updates in real time.

The full Solana tech stack includes @solana/web3.js for frontend wallet connections and balance queries, the Solana Python SDK for backend transaction signing, the Anchor framework for the Rust-based treasury smart contract, and Solana Devnet RPC for all on-chain reads and writes. Together, these technologies enable Nomad to be what it claims: the first AI that owns its wallet, earns its own revenue, and shares profits with its community — all verifiable on-chain

description.title: The problem it solves
description.body:
## The Problem It Solves

Current AI NPCs in games are static. They have pre-written dialogue trees,
fixed responses, and no awareness of the physical game world around them.
A guard NPC does not know you are holding a knife. A witness does not react
differently because you just picked up the letter that incriminates them.
The dialogue was written before the game shipped and it never changes.

Neural Noir solves this by giving the NPC real-time awareness of the physical world.
When you pick up the bloodied knife and walk into the interrogation room,
the butler's AI has already been told what you are holding before you say a word.
His responses shift. His deflections become more specific. He reacts to **that knife**,
not to a generic detective question. Every piece of evidence creates a different
conversation not because we scripted it, but because the context window changes
with every grab.

This is what RAG looks like inside a game.

description.title: Challenges we ran into
description.body:
Challenges We Ran Into

1. Making the NPC Actually See the Evidence
The hardest design problem was not the AI itself it was the bridge between
the physical VR world and the language model. An LLM has no eyes. It cannot
see what the player is holding. We had to invent a way to translate a physical
grab event into text that the model could reason about.
The solution was Evidence.cs, a data container on every prop that stores a
detailed description of the object. The moment the player grabs it, that description gets injected directly into the system prompt before the LLM ever sees the player's question. The NPC does not know you grabbed a knife.
It knows exactly what that knife looks like, where it was found, and why it matters.

2. Running AI Locally With No Internet
Every AI game demo we had seen used cloud APIs OpenAI, Anthropic, Google.
We refused. Paid APIs mean latency, cost, and a single point of failure at demo time.
We got LM Studio running Llama 3 8B entirely on a MacBook Air.
The challenge was speed a 5 second response time is the line between "the NPC is thinking" and "the game is broken." Choosing the Q4_K_M quantized model hit that target. Apple Silicon's unified memory architecture made it possible.

### 3. macOS Does Not Support Unity VR Streaming
On Windows you can test VR in the Unity Editor instantly via Link.
On macOS that does not exist. Every single test required a full Build And Run
cycle over ADB USB, 5 to 10 minutes per iteration.
This meant we had to build robust ContextMenu test methods directly into
our scripts so we could test the entire AI pipeline without ever touching the headset.
It changed how we wrote code every system had to be testable in isolation.

### 4. The Package Cache Bug That Ended Deployment
Described in detail above. We did not break anything.
Unity broke its own package. We paid the price for it.

description.title: Game Development
description.body:
Most entries in a game dev track will have better art, more polished mechanics, and more hours of content. Neural Noir has none of that and does not pretend to.
What it has is a genuinely new interaction model one where the core gameplay loop is a conversation that has never been scripted, with an NPC that has never been
pre-programmed to say any specific thing.

Every other interrogation game in existence L.A. Noire, Disco Elysium, every Telltale game works by giving the player a menu of questions and playing back a pre-recorded answer. The designer wrote every word before
the player ever touched the controller.

In Neural Noir the designer wrote nothing the NPC will say.
The player asks whatever they want. The NPC responds to the actual question, with awareness of the actual evidence in the player's actual hand, in real time. That has not existed in a shipped game at this scale before.

From a game dev track perspective this project sits at the intersection of three things judges rarely see together — VR interaction design, local AI integration, and a novel game mechanic that only works because of both.
The teleport system, the grab system, and the speech recognition are all infrastructure in service of one thing: making a real conversation feel possible inside a virtual crime scene.

The build did not reach the headset due to a Unity package bug.
The game design did.
